News.title: Tragedy as body of boy, 12, is pulled from river after police divers scour water for hours
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

'DEEPLY TRAGIC' Tragedy as body of boy, 12, is pulled from river after police divers scour water for hours

THE body of a 12-year-old boy was pulled from a river following a desperate search by divers.

Emergency crews were called to reports of a person in the water near Hackney Marshes shortly after 6pm on Saturday.

The London Fire Brigade joined Metropolitan Police officers in a desperate search of the River Lea.

But after hours of searching, cop divers recovered the boy’s body at around 12.15am on Sunday.





He was pronounced dead at the scene.

The tragedy has left the local community in shock, with Hackney’s mayor describing the death as a “devastating loss”.

“This is a devastating loss for our community, and I know many will be feeling a deep sense of shock and sadness,” she said.

“The boy’s family will need time to grieve this unimaginable loss, so please respect their privacy.”

The force said the boy’s death was being treated as unexpected.

His next of kin have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers.

Detective Inspector Azmeen Pinnu, who is leading the investigation, said: “This is a deeply tragic incident and our thoughts are with the boy’s family, friends and the wider community.

“This incident is now being investigated on behalf of the coroner, and enquiries remain ongoing to establish the full circumstances of what happened.”

News.title: Pregnant woman & child among three killed in horror shooting after masked men open fire at Spanish holiday resort
News.content:
GUNNED DOWN Pregnant woman & child among three killed in horror shooting after masked men open fire at Spanish holiday resort

A PREGNANT woman and a child are among three people who have been killed in a shooting at a Spanish holiday resort.

Two masked men on a motorbike opened fire at a family on the Costa de la Luz near the southern border with Portugal.



The youngster, whose age has not yet been revealed, his mum and his maternal grandmother all died at the scene.

Police confirmed that two others were injured in the shooting, with one rushed to hospital “in a serious condition”.



The horror unfolded around 10pm last night in the city of Isla Cristina, which is roughly 5 miles from the Spanish-Portuguese border.

The victims’ bodies have been transferred to the Institute of Forensic Medicine in the provincial capital Huelva so autopsies can take place.

Grisly photos, which The Sun has chosen not to show, were taken by horrified locals and tourists and appeared on social media but were removed.

No arrests have yet taken place, but the incident has already been linked to a previous shooting that took place in Huelva in September 2024, which left one person dead and two injured.

Well-placed sources told local press the three people killed last night are the sister, mum, and nephew of the man arrested over the earlier shooting.

He was held in Gijon in northern Spain after going on the run and remanded in custody pending a trial.



Several relatives of the suspect, thought to include those killed last night, are said to have moved to Isla Cristina from the provincial capital following the earlier crime.

The Civil Guard is leading the probe into the fatal shootings.

It said in a statement: “The initial lines of investigation indicate that it could be a settling of scores between members of different clans, although no hypothesis has been ruled out.



“The Guardia Civil has activated a large-scale security and search operation to locate the alleged perpetrators.

“Any information can be provided confidentially.”

The police spokesman confirmed a secrecy order had been placed over the case by a judge.

A secrecy order is a tool commonly used in Spain to protect judicial probes, especially in their infancy, and limits the amount of information civil servants can give out.

Isla Cristina, one of southern Spain’s most important fishing ports, is known for its fine sand beaches.



The nearest airports are Faro on the Portuguese Algarve which is just 40 miles away and Seville which is 80 miles away.

The shooting comes after six people were gunned down at another popular Spanish holiday resort in May.

Two were killed and four others, including two children, were rushed to a hospital.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The victims include a seven-month-old baby who was taken to the intensive care unit.

After fleeing the scene last night, a 25-year-old man surrendered to police and was arrested.

News.title: Urgent search for missing man, 22, last seen near bridge in early hours as cops release CCTV
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FIND HIM Urgent search for missing man, 22, last seen near bridge in early hours as cops release CCTV

COPS and emergency services have launched an urgent search for a missing 22-year-old man who was last spotted near a bridge.

Liam, was last seen heading towards Wylam from Wylam Bridge in Northumberland, in the early hours of Saturday morning.



But Liam has not been seen since and his disappearance has sparked a massive search in the area with a large number of police vehicles and mountain rescue teams deployed yesterday.

He is described by cops as a white man, 6ft 3ins tall, of medium build with dark hair.



Police added that he also has tattoos down his right arm.

Liam was last seen wearing black joggers, black Nike trainers and a black T-shirt with white text and a diamond logo on the back,.

Northumbria Police have released a CCTV image of what he was wearing when last spotted.

Liam is also believed to be wearing a gold chain, the force added.

His family are growing increasingly concerned for his welfare, said Northumbria Police.

A large number of police vehicles and mountain rescue teams were spotted entering the water near Wylam Bridge on Sunday as a search began.



Emergency services have been scouring the River Tyne and are understood to be searching for Liam.

Anyone who has seen Liam or knows where he might be is asked to contact Northumbria Police by sending a direct message on social media or using the live chat and report forms on the force’s website.

Anyone contacting Northumbria Police can use reference number: NP-20260815-0424.

It comes after emergency services were called to Wylam Bridge in the early hours of Saturday morning following a collision involving a pedestrian.

The crash happened shortly after midnight and an ambulance crew treated one person at the scene before taking them to hospital.



The extent of the person’s injuries are currently unknown.

News.title: M6 closed after ‘serious’ crash involving three lorries and car with 30-minute delays and 3 miles of congestion
News.content:
A MAJOR UK motorway has closed after a “serious” crash involving three lorries and a car.

The smash on the M6 in North Staffordshire this morning saw the motorway closed off in both directions between junctions 15 and 16.

National Highways has confirmed the smash occurred at around 4.10am this morning on the northbound stretch.

Motorists are also being warned the northbound stretch could stay closed for hours.





Three-mile tailbacks have been reported on the M6 as commuters heading to work during rush hour face travel misery.

Delays of up to 30 minutes are also to be expected, said National Highways.

According to National Highways the “northbound closure is likely to remain into this afternoon”.

Meanwhile, the southbound carriageway has been shut to help emergency services access the scene of the smash.



It has left drivers bumper-to-bumper as they head on diversion routes.

Pictures show huge delays around junction 15 as rush-hour chaos commences.

A full investigation, recovery and clean-up are required in the area before reopening, National Highways added.

Drivers have been warned to plan ahead with their journeys today.



Motorists have also been urged to find alternative routes if possible.

News.title: Body of missing man, 50, found in ancient woodland as cops probe ‘unexplained’ death
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

TRAGIC END Body of missing man, 50, found in ancient woodland as cops probe ‘unexplained’ death

THE body of a 50-year-old man has been found in an ancient woodland spot with police probing the “unexplained” death.

Thames Valley Police officers said they made the tragic discovery in Shenley Wood, Buckinghamshire, on Saturday evening.



The force said though formal identification has not yet taken place, the body is believed to be that of a missing man named Joseph, also known as Joe.

His surname has not been released.



The death is currently being treated as “unexplained but not suspicious”, said the force.

Cops added that a file will be prepared for the Buckinghamshire Coroner.

Joe, 50, was last seen near Well Street in Buckingham, at about 8am on Saturday morning.

Cops launched a public appeal in an attempt to find him.

A spokesperson for the police added: “His family has been informed, and our thoughts are with them at this very difficult time.”

News.title: Inside Majorca’s ‘drive-thru’ drug supermarket where toddlers dish out cocaine – just minutes from Brit tourist hotspot
News.content:
SAT on his wooden throne like a sun-scorched sentry guarding the wasteland beyond, a guard catches my eye and lazily points to a tiny hut.

I swing the car towards it and pull to a halt. The man, his face shaded by a battered straw hat beneath the blistering Spanish sun, strides towards my window. I have barely cracked it open an inch before he leans in and asks: “Cocaine or heroin?” without a flicker of hesitation.





Welcome to Son Banya – Majorca’s notorious drug supermarket, lurking just minutes from Palma’s airport, where thousands of sun-starved British holidaymakers touch down each year.

What may look like a sprawling shanty town is in fact a narcotics kingdom where the island’s illegal drug trade has flourished for decades.

Now carved up between several criminal clans, the territory was once presided over by Spanish drug matriarch Francisca Cortés Picazo – better known as La Paca.

Davide, a 25-year-old local, told me: “The old woman who lived there controlled the entire drug world in Majorca.

“Her grandchild used to go to school with me and everyone knew he was a relative – we were scared of him because of her.”

The feared matriarch of the Son Banya clan was sensationally arrested in 2008 after a sweeping police operation smashed her criminal empire and sent members of her family to jail.





She was also accused of running an elaborate money-laundering web spanning nightclubs, restaurants, industrial warehouses and a string of properties scattered across Majorca.

But even from behind prison walls, La Paca’s fortune remained buried beneath the dusty streets of her old fiefdom.

While the now 71-year-old was serving a five-year sentence, cops raided her home in the slums and discovered a concealed hole.

At the bottom of the pit lay five boxes stuffed with €4.3million in cash, alongside seven kilograms of jewellery – a treasure trove hidden beneath the dilapidated settlement.

Dubbed a “drive-thru” drug supermarket, Son Banya is today home to between 600 and 700 residents, including around 200 children.

But Davide warned: “People should not be entering that area”.

He added: “Some children, including toddlers, are often seen handing out drugs to buyers from the huts.”

Along the busy road that divides Majorca’s glossy holiday playground and this triangle of hell, stolen and torched cars sit abandoned like blackened carcasses.



The vehicles are brought in by criminal clans to be stripped for parts, set ablaze and positioned as makeshift barricades around the settlement.

Officers entering the area must be prepared for the possibility of armed resistance, leaving the shanty town with a sparse police presence compared with other parts of Palma.

That has made the maze of huts and narrow paths into an attractive hiding place for criminals who know the terrain.

And even British offenders have become familiar with the settlement’s lawless reputation.

A middle-aged British couple allegedly lured a man deep into Son Banya under the pretence of collecting or settling a financial debt.

Once they had guided him away from the main road and into the maze of shacks, one of the attackers allegedly pressed a saw against the victim’s neck.

The helpless victim was then battered across his head and torso before being robbed of his belongings.

Eventually residents intervened and broke up the attack, giving the man a chance to escape as the Brit couple fled the scene.



His injuries were so severe that emergency crews took him to hospital, where doctors used staples to close deep wounds to his head and back.

National Police eventually tracked the British couple to their home and arrested them on suspicion of robbery with violence and grievous bodily harm.

As the dealer stood planted beside my window, I scanned the scene around me and began to see the bizarre architecture of the “supermarket” – hundreds of low-rise modular units arranged almost like shelves in a grotesque open-air store.

To my right, children wander along the cobbled path weaving through the very heart of Son Banya’s drug epicentre as though taking an ordinary stroll home.

Wood, drywall, brick and battered panels have been fashioned into sales booths, purpose-built for drug deals rather than domestic life.

Crude as they are, the makeshift huts mark a new chapter in Son Banya’s narcotics trade, replacing the older system of dealers operating from family homes or passing drugs through barred windows.

Amid the grimy shacks, Spanish flags flutter in the breeze, clamped into the ground outside the huts like jaunty little shop signs advertising the wares within.

In June this year, cops descended on Son Banya once again, tearing into a cluster of newly erected structures that had sprouted across the settlement – including two lookout towers built to watch over the narcotics trade.



Yet instead of having to hunt for evidence of criminal activity, officers were shocked to stumble across advertising for a “Black Friday” drug sale.

Cocaine was being hawked for €45, while heroin and crack were priced at €50 – grim cut price deals taking place a world away from the Black Friday of the British high-street.

Alongside the haul of narcotics, cops seized accounting ledgers believed to document the mechanics of the underground trade.

Even as they ripped through the settlement, a car rolled in carrying a group of tourists who had apparently only just arrived in Majorca.

The visitors had been brought to Son Banya by a German resident of Palma, who officers established had an arrangement to chauffeur the group around the island.

But instead of collecting drugs, the group saw their car impounded and an investigation opened into to the driver for allegedly breaching passenger transport regulations.

Their trip may have been thwarted, but countless others are not.

And Davide tells me business at Son Banya boomed this summer as Spain began their victorious journey to the World Cup.



He continued: “Before the World Cup, the clan built a Spain-themed shack for the tourists to find more easily during the tournament.”

“They wanted to make it more luxury for the guests,” he added while laughing.

During the tournament, the walls of a drug shack was transformed into an shrine to Spanish football, its battered exterior splashed with hand-drawn silhouettes and murals celebrating the country’s sporting royalty.

Among the painted figures were Real Madrid and Spanish national team legends Iker Casillas and Raúl González.

Powerful floodlights swarmed the sales point in artificial daylight, while red-and-yellow LED strips flickered around the structure and enormous Spanish flags flapped proudly nearby.

Yet behind the patriotic bunting and bright lights, cocaine, heroin and crack were being sold.

After the World Cup decorations attracted widespread media attention, the National Police and Palma Town Hall moved in with heavy machinery.

Municipal bulldozers and police squads have torn the shack down time and again, only for clan members to resurrect it seemingly overnight, replacing the rubble with a fresh decorative makeover.

And this is not the first time criminal clans have tried to makeover the settlement to make it more attractive to customers.

In 2025, criminal bosses – including one known as El Vito, a nickname lifted from The Godfather – embarked on a bizarre attempt to give Son Banya a glitzy new identity.



Their chosen inspiration was Sin City.

The main commercial stretch was christened “Las Vegas”, transforming the heart of the drug market into a surreal imitation of a neon-lit entertainment district.

At the entrance to the sales strip, dealers installed a huge illuminated “Las Vegas” sign, while LED strips and floodlights bathed the surrounding huts in a lurid glow.

The intention was to make the narcotics hub bright, welcoming and easy to navigate after dark.

To give their Las Vegas fantasy some physical substance, the clans allegedly paid a local contractor in cash to construct a 90-metre concrete access road leading towards the sales hub.

They even added a decorative roundabout, complete with an anchored boat.

Residential areas were separated from the sales strip, while burnt-out cars and piles of debris were cleared away – stripping the area of some of its ramshackle clutter and leaving behind a cleaner drug zone.

But soon after municipal bulldozers, escorted by police squads, rolled into Son Banya and began dismantling the fantasy.

The “Las Vegas” sign was ripped down, five associated drug-selling booths were flattened and the illegally constructed concrete road was torn up.

Son Banya has long been blighted by deadly gangland violence, with fatal shootings erupting from bitter turf wars between rival family clans battling for control over the heroin and cocaine trade.



The shanty town’s bitter rivalries boiled over in 2009 when a brutal shooting left the settlement gripped by fear.

Seven people were arrested and a ring of steel was thrown around the area in a bid to prevent further bloodshed between the warring factions.

On the evening of September 7, members of the rival Ortega family – known as Clan del Peludo – confronted Moreno Cortés outside her home on Street 4 in the heart of the shanty town.

In the middle of the confrontation, a gun was drawn and Cortés was shot point-blank in the head, leaving the settlement once again stained by the violence of its feuding clans.

At the heart of the bloody dispute was an unpaid drug debt worth between €12,000 and €18,000.

This year, a drug trafficker linked to a fatal hit-and-run was arrested again after allegedly firing a gun into the air in Son Banya – before leading cops on a high-speed chase through the maze of shacks.

During the pursuit, he allegedly hurled a plastic box from the window.

Tucked into the Tupperware was a pistol, two magazines and a barrel, all wrapped in plastic as though hastily concealed for disposal.

The vehicle itself yielded another haul: more than €2,100 in cash and several spent shell casings.

Police then turned their attention to the shack from which the suspect had emerged.



Inside, they allegedly discovered an arsenal that included a katana – a traditional Japanese sword – quantities of marijuana and cocaine and more than €240 in cash.

And as the notorious crime den continues to cast a long shadow over Majorca, the battle to finally wipe out its deadly drug trade goes on.

News.title: Groom-to-be, 24, found dead in rubble after 7.4-magnitude earthquake rocks Colombia just 2 days before his wedding
News.content:
QUAKE TRAGEDY Groom-to-be, 24, found dead in rubble after 7.4-magnitude earthquake rocks Colombia just 2 days before his wedding

THE body of a groom-to-be who was just two days away from his wedding has been found in the rubble of a collapsed hotel in Colombia.

Juan Felipe Giraldo, 24, was due to marry the mother of his child, Natalia Patiño, on August 16 when he went missing in the city of Pereira.



After news of his disappearance emerged, Juan’s father, Hernán Giraldo, travelled to Pereira and joined rescue teams searching day and night for his son.

Juan had reportedly sent his fiancée a video shortly before the disaster, which helped rescuers pinpoint his location after the earthquake caused the hotel to collapse.



Before his son’s body was discovered, Hernán said in a heartbreaking video: “There is life, there are small signs of life, and if there is life there is hope.

“Son, I love you. On Sunday you are going to be getting married, and if not on Sunday, it will be in eight, 15 days, but you will be there, son.”



But the family’s worst fears were realised when Juan was eventually found dead.

“Forever and always my heart, you were the most complete love I ever had. I love you forever,” his grieving fiancée wrote on Instagram.



The couple had a two-year-old son and lived together in Colombia‘s capital, Bogotá.

Juan had travelled to Pereira on a work trip just hours before the deadly quake struck, and ended up staying at the doomed Hotel Dibeni in the city centre.

This comes after a triplet had her life ripped apart after losing both of her sisters and her parents in Colombia’s devastating 7.4-magnitude earthquake.

Ana María Saavedra, 23, was pulled alive from the rubble of her destroyed four-storey home in Cali, the worst-hit city.

She survived after taking shelter beneath a sturdy wooden table as the building came crashing down around her.



But her parents, Jairo Hernán Saavedra, 63, and Victoria Caicedo, 61, were tragically found dead in each other’s arms.

Her sister Sofía was also killed after becoming trapped beneath a collapsed staircase.

And the body of Ana María’s third triplet, Isabella, was recovered late on Thursday night.

The earthquake struck at a depth of around 64 miles in Chocó province and was felt across a vast area of western Colombia.

Tremors were felt hundreds of miles away in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, as well as across parts of Ecuador and Panama.



Officials said 294 people had been confirmed dead and 3,935 injured, according to a Saturday report from Colombia’s National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD).

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has deployed 1,000 members of the security forces to Cali following reports of looting.

The disaster is an early test for the president, who was inaugurated just days ago on August 7.

On Tuesday, he flew to Pereira with his wife, First Lady Ana Lucía Pineda, to inspect one of the worst-hit areas.

“My commitment is to each and every one of the affected families,” he wrote on X.



“We remain on the ground, working for our people.”

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said America “stands ready to support” Colombia.

The US Department of State described the disaster as “devastating” and pledged £11.5million to provide emergency shelter and supplies.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The EU is also providing funding and supporting rescue operations, foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.

The Colombian government has meanwhile announced an immediate emergency rent subsidy for people who have lost their homes.

News.title: M56 shut near Manchester Airport after major crash as car on fire and emergency crews swarm scene
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

CRASH CHAOS M56 shut near Manchester Airport after major crash as car on fire and emergency crews swarm scene

THE M56 has been shut near a major airport following a multi-vehicle crash causing one car to catch fire.

Emergency services have rushed to the M56 in Cheshire near Manchester Airport and closed the road eastbound between J7 Bowden Interchange and J6 Hale Four Seasons Interchange.

The road was shut early this morning as the crash caused one car to overturn and another to become engulfed in flames.

Greater Manchester Police, Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue, and paramedics from North West Ambulance Service have raced to the scene.





Due to the severity of the crash, the road surface and barriers need to be inspected before other vehicles can use the motorway.

There is currently two miles of congestion with those heading to Manchester Airport advised to allow extra time for their journey.

A national highways spokesperson said: “The M56 eastbound between J7 and J6 near Manchester Airport is being closed following a two-car collision.

“One of the cars has overturned. The other car has caught fire.



“The collision has resulted in infrastructure damage.

“National Highways contractors are being despatched to scene to inspect the nearside barrier and road surface as well as support in implementing the closure of the motorway.

“Current delays of 20 mins on approach and two miles of congestion.”

News.title: HMRC tax rule means 'immediate exemption' for UK families
News.content:
HMRC tax rule means 'immediate exemption' for UK families

Families could save thousands of pounds in tax

View 2 Images The payments must also form part of a regular pattern of giving (Image: shurkin_son via Getty Images)

Millions of families could be missing a little-known tax loophole that allows them to hand money to children and grandchildren without it being swallowed up by the HMRC.

‌



Seven in ten adults have never heard of the exemption, research has found. The warning comes from Which? Money, which has highlighted how regular gifts made from surplus income can potentially be immediately exempt from inheritance tax.

‌



Known as 'normal expenditure out of income', the exemption means some regular gifts do not have to wait seven years before becoming free of inheritance tax. But there are strict rules – and families need to make sure they can prove they qualify.

‌



How the loophole works

Many people know about the £3,000 annual gifting allowance. Others are familiar with the seven-year rule, under which larger gifts can generally become exempt if the person giving the money survives for seven years.

But the surplus-income exemption is much less well known. Research by insurer Canada Life found seven in ten UK adults were unaware that regular gifts made from surplus income could qualify.

The gifts must come from income rather than savings or other capital. This can include salary, pensions, rental income, dividends and savings interest.

‌



View 2 Images Seven in ten adults have never heard of the exemption (Image: alvaro gonzalez via Getty Images)

You must not give away too much

The person making the gifts must still have enough income left to maintain their normal standard of living. That includes household bills, everyday spending and lifestyle costs such as holidays and travel.

If making the gifts means they have to dip into savings to pay normal expenses, HMRC could decide the exemption does not apply. For example, someone with £3,000 of monthly income and £2,500 of living costs could potentially give away £400 a month.

‌



But if they gave away £800 and had to use savings to cover their bills, the exemption could be challenged. The calculation is based on the individual's own income and spending – not the combined finances of a couple.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Gifts must be regular

The payments must also form part of a regular pattern of giving. This could be monthly help with household bills, an annual contribution towards school fees or regular birthday payments.

‌



Which? Money says a pattern lasting three to four years would normally be considered reasonable, although a shorter period could qualify if there is clear evidence of an intention to continue.

Keep records

The exemption will normally need to be claimed after the donor's death, so good records are vital. Which? Money recommends keeping details of income, spending and gifts, using standing orders where possible and considering a written statement explaining the intended payments.

Bank statements covering the seven years before death can also help prove the pattern and affordability of the gifts. The consumer champion suggests using HMRC's IHT403 form as a template for recording gifts.

Article continues below

The 40% tax threat

Inheritance tax is normally charged at 40% on the taxable part of an estate above the relevant thresholds. More families could potentially be caught as thresholds remain frozen, while unused pension pots are due to come within the scope of inheritance tax from April 2027. More information here.

News.title: Laptops top list of university essentials as technology takes over
News.content:
Laptops top list of university essentials as technology takes over

Following A Level results day, parents prepare to send their teenagers to university equipped with the latest tech.

View 4 Images More than half of parents said a laptop is the most important purchase for a child going to university (Image: Getty)

A poll of 1,200 students past and present found alarm clocks and contact books full of handwritten phone numbers aren’t as vital as they were back in the mid-90s. Books and kettles were considered must-haves for getting through the term - but now laptops, chargers and reusable water bottles have taken their place. Mobile phones, headphones and portable speakers are now seen as essentials for student life.

‌



The average pupil 30 years ago would take as many as 10 books with them for revision and notetaking, but today's carry just three with them as everything is used and kept on a laptop or tablet.

‌



View 4 Images Six in 10 Gen Z consider a laptop to be the most essential university possession (Image: Getty)

‌



Most of those polled (58%) believe university life has become more opulent than it once was, with nine in 10 Brits believing today's university students rely more heavily on technology than those who studied three decades ago.

When asked about how they have prepared their teens for university, two-thirds of parents (66%) said they believe technology can have a direct impact on their child’s academic success.

Nearly the same amount (65%) agreed it is one of the most important investments ahead of university.

‌



More than half (55%) of parents said a laptop is the single most important purchase for a child going to university.

Annika Bizon, a spokesperson for Samsung, which commissioned the research, alongside the Galaxy Book6 Pro, said: "Thirty years ago, university survival meant a kettle and an alarm clock and something to take notes on.

View 4 Images Only a quarter of students who consider books most essential (Image: Getty/Franziska & Tom Werner)

‌



“Today it involves keeping on top of lectures, deadlines, part-time work, family life and the admin like food shopping and bills.

"Parents understand this and are helping their teenagers be more equipped with the right technology that supports their academic needs and everyday life as they navigate their first years away from home

Nearly nine in 10 (85%) agreed the average university student's belongings are not the same as they were three decades ago.

‌



Only a quarter (26%) of Gen Z students still handwrite their lecture notes in a notebook, while 19% take notes with a mix of digital and handwritten methods and 43% of Gen Z students exclusively use their laptop for notetaking throughout university.

According to research by OnePoll.com, more than two-thirds (67%) of Gen Z admitted they couldn't complete their studies without one.

View 4 Images More than eight in 10 say the university students' belongings now (Image: Getty)

‌



However, 35% of those who attended university more than 30 years ago wished they could have taken a laptop with them.

The top purchases for recent university students was a laptop (53%), with bedding (38%), kitchen essentials (37%) and clothing (33%) not far behind.

Beyond lectures, students today use their laptops to research assignments (76%), keep on top of life admin like budgeting, timetables and emails (47%), stay connected with family and friends (41%), and stream entertainment (46%).

Article continues below

Six in 10 Gen Z students consider a laptop to be the most essential university possession, compared to only 24% who consider books most essential.

When choosing a laptop for university, more than a quarter (26%) of current and recent students prioritised reliability, long battery life and fast performance.

News.title: I got rid of fish when I was told they were to blame for rash but it was my bra
News.content:
I got rid of fish when I was told they were to blame for rash but it was my bra

Morgan Lee now avoids wearing a bra or leggings

I got rid of fish when I was told they were to blame for rash but it was my bra

A teaching assistant rehomed her goldfish after doctors said they were responsible for her rash - only to discover her bra was the trigger for a condition that affects millions. Morgan Lee Godden unexpectedly broke out in hives across her back in January, but put the rash down to an allergic reaction to her new bedding.

‌



However within a few days the 22-year-old's eyes and lips had swollen to double the size - and the rash had spread across her entire body. After visiting her doctor, Morgan Lee said she was told her symptoms were 'likely an allergic reaction' and advised to remove anything new from her bedroom.

‌



This included Morgan Lee's new goldfish Flow and Rick that she had recently welcomed into her home, with doctors concerned that the water or fish food was triggering her allergies. But after rehoming her pets and other bedroom items, Morgan Lee was still breaking out in painful rashes, noticing that her flare-ups were particularly bad after wearing her bra and leggings.

‌



It's not what you eat but when you eat, keep an eye on your belly not BMI, using the internet makes you grumpy, and cutting your run short is dangerous = all this and more in our science newsletter

View 6 Images The rash was unexplained (Kennedy News and Media)

‌



It was only when Morgan Lee went to hospital after suffering a high temperature and diarrhoea for two weeks that doctors confirmed her symptoms were not an allergic reaction. A specialist confirmed that Morgan Lee had chronic urticaria - a long-term skin condition defined by itchy red welts, swelling, and a rash, caused by the release of histamine - and angioedema, a sudden swelling beneath the skin caused by a build-up of fluid.

The condition is thought to affect between 0.5 and 1% of the population in the UK at any one time and women are more than twice as likely than men to be diagnosed. Luckily, Morgan Lee is able to manage her symptoms with medication, but has been told a sudden release or overproduction of histamine in the body could cause her to go into anaphylactic shock.

View 6 Images She was told the fish could be to blame (Kennedy News and Media)

‌



Morgan Lee, who lives in Sheerness, Kent, said: "The first symptom I had was that I came up in hives on my lower back. It was really itchy and I could feel raised lumps on my back. I thought it was an allergic reaction to my new bedding I'd got as a present.

"Within that week, my eyes and lips had swelled and then over my entire body. I went to the doctors and they said it was very likely an allergic reaction. I was told to remove my fish tank that I had recently got in case it was the bacteria in the water or the fish food.

‌



View 6 Images Morgan Lee had other symptoms and had to go to hospital (Kennedy News and Media)

"Apparently it's quite common. I had to rehome my two goldfish Flow and Rick I'd had for about four months. I'd also bought a blue rug from Shein so they thought the chemicals from the blue dye could be causing some sort of reaction. I was told to remove basically everything new from my bedroom."

‌



Despite rehoming her pet fish and removing her rug, Morgan Lee was still breaking out in hives - and soon realised that her symptoms arose after wearing tight clothing and doing exercise. Morgan Lee said: "I had to stop wearing makeup, stop wearing perfume. I also realised tight clothing was a trigger, especially underwear.

"The rash would be in the shape and outline of my bra. I used to wear leggings for work. The material of them, I could just feel them irritating my skin. I was later told sweat, overheating, stress, hormones can all be triggers.

View 6 Images She says the rash made her look like a pizza (Kennedy News and Media)

‌



"Every time I come on my period, I get a rash. Once me and my partner went swimming and I came out of the pool and I came out and my entire body was covered in a rash. I started noticing what my triggers were. I was going on bike rides and swimming and noticed if I'm exercising it's worse.

"When I do get a flare-up, it's really itchy and painful. And it burns - it feels like I'm on fire. I look like a Pepperoni pizza. And I get a temperature and diarrhoea as well. The rash was actually the easiest thing to deal with, it's everything else that came with it."

‌



View 6 Images The fish were rehomed (Kennedy News and Media)

In June, Morgan Lee was eventually diagnosed with two long-term skin conditions - urticaria and angioedema - after being referred to a specialist. Luckily, Morgan Lee's symptoms are managed with medication and through avoiding triggers such as: tight clothing, sweating, excessive exercise, stress, hormonal changes.

‌



Morgan Lee said: "I felt relieved because I thought at least now I can get better. I've always wanted children, but now I'm worried if that's an option for me because of how much pain I could be in because of the hormone change.

View 6 Images Morgan Lee Godden (Kennedy News and Media)

Article continues below

"They told me my body could go into anaphylactic shock but it wouldn't be from an allergic reaction, it would be because my body was overproducing histamine. That does scare me. My anxiety is higher. I never wear leggings anymore, I don't wear bras as much and, if I do, I just have to deal with the flare-ups.

"The medication has massively made a difference. The rashes are controlled. I just feel more like myself."

News.title: Jet2 bans family from flight home from Greece after girl was sick at airport
News.content:
Jet2 bans family from flight home from Greece after girl was sick at airport

Hayley Waters says her daughter was only ill because it was 30C in the airport and their flight had been delayed

View 3 Images Addyson Waters, six, upset at Rhodes Airport after Jet2 refused to let her family board their flight home

A family was left stranded on a Greek island after Jet2 refused to let them fly home because their six-year-old daughter was sick in the departure lounge. Hayley Waters, 37, was waiting at Rhodes Airport with husband Jason, 40, and kids Addyson, six, and Xander, three, when the youngster vomited at the gate.

‌



She said staff immediately barred the family from boarding their delayed flight to Leeds Bradford Airport shortly after midnight. They were told they could not travel with Jet2 for at least 24 hours and would have to arrange their own accommodation, transport and alternative flights - which cost them around £1,000.

‌



Hayley, a performance analyst from Leeds, West Yorks., said: "While waiting at the gate, my six-year-old daughter was sick once. I cleaned it up immediately. She'd had no illness all holiday - she was simply exhausted after the delay, it was around midnight, and over 30C in the airport."

‌



Lab-grown mini-brains could replace AI, being a braggart works, ghosts are good for you, and it's not what you eat but when you eat - all this and more in our weird science newsletter

View 3 Images Hayley and Jason Waters with children Addyson and Xander, who were left stranded in Rhodes

‌



The family had been due to catch the 11.15pm flight on July 31, which eventually departed at around 12.05am. They were travelling as part of a larger group of nine when a member of Jet2 staff spotted Addyson being sick.

But Hayley said nobody assessed her daughter or asked whether she had been ill during the holiday before the family was stopped from boarding. She said: "The only explanation given was 'policy' because my daughter had been sick.

"Nobody asked whether she had any underlying medical conditions, whether she'd been unwell during the holiday, or how she was feeling. No medical assessment was carried out - the decision was based solely on a member of staff seeing her vomit once."

‌



The family were forced to book an easyJet flight to Newcastle for the following day to get home. Hayley said: "We have no written explanation for why we were denied boarding, no paperwork, no medical assessment, no duty of care, and we were left stranded abroad with two young children."

View 3 Images Six-year-old Addyson was sick once at the gate before her family were barred from flying to Leed

‌



Jet2 said its team in Rhodes had followed procedures and helped the family find somewhere to stay. The airline said staff also advised them to retain their receipts so they could make a claim through their travel insurance.

A Jet2 spokesperson said: "The safety and wellbeing of our customers is our absolute priority, and our teams have processes in place to help prevent the spread of illness onboard our aircraft. We are sorry to hear that Mrs Waters was unhappy with her experience and we are in contact with her to discuss the matter further."

However, Hayley has disputed the airline's claim that it had been in contact with her. The airline said it had promised a response within 14 days, by August 20, and remained on track to provide one.

Article continues below

Hayley said the family have not had acknowledgement that their written complaint has been received - and that they have not been told about the timescales Jet2 are working to.

News.title: Andy Burnham 'communicated with someone impersonating Donald Trump's closest adviser'
News.content:
Andy Burnham 'communicated with someone impersonating Donald Trump's closest adviser'

New Prime Minister Andy Burnham is said to have engaged with messages sent by someone impersonating Susie Wiles, the White House's chief of staff

View 2 Images Andy Burnham reportedly communicated with someone pretending to be one of Donald Trump's closest advisers (Image: Finnbarr Webster/PA Wire)

Andy Burnham communicated with someone pretending to be one of Donald Trump's closest advisers, it is understood.

‌



The new Prime Minister - who will be trying to get on the front foot with the erratic US President - is said to have engaged with messages sent by someone impersonating Susie Wiles, the White House's chief of staff. Mr Burnham communicated with them before becoming suspicious, reports said.

‌



One person who had been informed of the incident told Politico a “few messages” were exchanged after the PM entered Downing Street but insisted they were “of no significance". It is unclear what the pair talked about.

‌



Downing Street refused to comment on the specifics. “We do not comment on national security matters,” a No10 spokeswoman said. The British embassy in Washington DC reportedly raised the incident with the White House over concerns. UK officials feared Ms Wiles had been hacked.

The FBI and White House started probing reports of someone pretending to be Ms Wiles last year, according to reports by US media.

Ed Miliband to tell Donald Trump's White House ending Iran war will bring down prices READ MORE :

View 2 Images Donald Trump with Susie Wiles, the White House's chief of staff (Image: AP)

‌



Last May, the Wall Street Journal reported that senators, governors, top American business bosses and other well-known figures had received calls and text from someone saying they were her. “The White House takes the cybersecurity of all staff very seriously, and this matter continues to be investigated,” a White House spokeswoman said at the time.

Mr Burnham held a phone call with Mr Trump shortly after he became Prime Minister. No10 said he set out his "vision" for the UK and that he hoped to show the US President "what Manchester had to offer during a visit in the future".

The pair also spoke about the World Cup, which was co-hosted by the US, security of the UK and the situation in the Middle East, including the need to secure the movement of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

‌



In his first major interview as PM, Mr Burnham last month said he would be prepared to call out Mr Trump to defend Britain's "national interest before anything else".

He told the BBC: "I can't at any point say that I won't take a different opinion from him [Trump], that I will need to voice a different idea that is right for Britain."

Asked if he would call out Mr Trump if it was the right thing to do, he said: "Of course." He continued: "You have to defend your own national interest before anything else. That's what you're required to do if you're to do this job properly."

Article continues below

Mr Burnham will be hoping for a smooth transition with the White House after Keir Starmer faced an up-and-down journey with the US President. The relationship between the pair came under strain after Mr Starmer voiced disagreement with US-Israel strikes on Iran at the end of February.

In a series of deranged rants earlier this year, the US President repeatedly mocked the former British PM, accusing Mr Starmer of being "no Winston Churchill" over his reluctance to let the US launch attacks on Iran from British soil. Mr Trump has also previously ridiculed UK aircraft carriers, calling them "toys", and lashed out at NATO for doing "absolutely nothing" to help the US in his conflict.

News.title: Pensioner facing legal action after installing drive in front of his house
News.content:
Pensioner facing legal action after installing drive in front of his house

He had the lawn turned into a paved driveway to make it easier to get in and out of his home

View 5 Images David Siggins outside his home in Essex

A pensioner said he has been threatened with legal action after turning a grass verge outside his home into a driveway. David Siggins, 85, paved over the area to make it easier to access his property due to his struggles with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

‌



Mr Siggins, from Rochford, Essex, said he had been given the go-ahead by Rochford Council two years ago for his £2,200 driveway which is 3m wide by 5m long. But earlier this month, he was told the land belongs to the authority and must be restored.

‌



Mr Siggins, who relies on two crutches to get around, insisted he tried to follow the correct process before carrying out the work and is seeking legal advice. The former tiler, who has lived in the property for 42 years, said: “This has made me quite ill. I'm quite close to a breakdown.

‌



View 5 Images The controversial drive

“I cannot walk, that’s the problem. I use two crutches. It just seems so unfair. It looks nice - it certainly looks better than the grass. Two years ago I was told they didn't own the land so I could do what I wanted with it. I did try."

‌



Mr Siggins said the debacle goes back twenty years, when he was given permission by Essex Highways for a drop curb. He claimed that three months after work had completed, he was told by Rochford Council they wanted the curb reinstated and he was paid for the inconvenience.

And in 2024, he contacted Essex County Council in 2024 about the verge with his plans for a driveway - but said was told the land was not under its control. Mr Siggins said: "I spoke to a very nice planning officer at Rochford Council who advised me to speak to Essex Highways. They told me it wasn't anything to do with them.

"I went back to Rochford Council and I was told they definitely didn't own it so I should go ahead. I have it in writing it was confirmed we could do it."

‌



View 5 Images The area is said to be shared land

However, a subsequent planning application was refused and an appeal was later dismissed - both of which Mr Siggins said he had no knowledge of. Now, with a deadline looming at the end of August, Mr Siggins, who received notice the driveway had to be removed a few weeks ago, said the situation has become increasingly stressful.

‌



Mr Siggins, who lives with his partner and stepson, said: “It is very stressful. It's getting me down. I've not had any complaints. The close we live in has 13 houses and there are 31 vehicles. They're all really relieved I've got [the driveway] as I can get my cars off the road as there's more space. I've got a solicitor involved."

View 5 Images David Siggins says he needs the drive due to ill health

‌



Mr Siggins added that the grass verge had largely been maintained by him and his stepson over the years and noted that council workers have only recently begun regularly cutting it since the dispute arose. Rochford Council said the issue centres on ownership of the land and its status as public open space.

A council spokesman said: “The resident removed a grass verge owned by Rochford District Council to install a block-paved driveway. The council has received a number of complaints. The grass verge forms part of a larger title that is subject to restrictions due to its designation as public open space.

View 5 Images There has been confusion over the land for years

Article continues below

“A planning application for the work that was previously submitted by the resident had been refused and an appeal dismissed.”

The authority said Mr Siggins has been given until the end of August to consider how he wishes to proceed.

News.title: Seven dead and dozens injured after deadly stampede at Hindu temple
News.content:
Seven dead and dozens injured after deadly stampede at Hindu temple

A deadly stampede broke out at a Hindu temple in eastern India’s Bihar state on Monday after a snapped electric wire reportedly triggered panic among worshippers, officials said – killing seven people and injuring more than a dozen.

View 2 Images An ambulance at the scene of the stampede (Image: CNN-News18)

At least seven people have been killed and many more injured following a stampede at a Hindu temple.

‌



A snapped electric wire reportedly triggered panic among worshippers near Ashok Dham Temple in Lakhisarai district, in eastern India’s Bihar state on Monday causing the tragic incident.

‌



Thousands of devotees had gathered to offer prayers on the third Monday of Shravan, one of the holiest months in the Hindu calendar when the stampede happened.

‌



The period, which usually falls between July and August, is dedicated to the worship of Hindu god Lord Shiva and is marked by fasting, prayers and colourful monsoon festivals across India.

View 2 Images The stampede happened by the Ashok Dham Temple

Met Office maps show 60 UK areas drenched by heavy rain on Tuesday - full list READ MORE :

More than a dozen people were taken to a government hospital for treatment, said Shailendra Kumar, a civil official. Mr Kumar said the cause of the stampede was still being probed.

‌



According to preliminary reports, an electric wire snapped outside the temple premises at around 6.30am, sparking panic as devotees rushed to escape what they feared was a risk of electrocution.

A section of the barricades collapsed under the weight of the surging crowd, leading to a crush in which people fell over one another, said Mr Kumar, according to the Press Trust of India news agency.

Mr Kumar stated: "It is being said that an electric pole fell there and people were electrocuted which led to a stampede-like situation. We can tell you the exact reason only after verifying everything."

‌



Lakhisarai district magistrate Shailendra Kumar said, "The crowd swelled in an unprecedented manner. At around 6.30-6.45am two trains came here and that two added to the crowd. Arrangements were made as we had anticipated the crowd."

Crowd crushes are relatively common in India during religious festivals, as large crowds, sometimes in the millions, gather in confined areas with few safety or crowd control measures.

Last year in January, at least 30 people were killed as tens of thousands of Hindus rushed to bathe in a sacred river during the Maha Kumbh festival, the world’s largest religious gathering.

Article continues below

In 2013, pilgrims attending a Hindu festival at a temple in the central state of Madhya Pradesh panicked amid fears that a bridge would collapse. At least 115 people were crushed to death or drowned in the river below.

News.title: Parents pushed to breaking point by Child Maintenance Service, BBC told
News.content:
In March last year, the CMS said it would apply for a liability order for Katy's ex, but warned it would take 26 weeks to go to court. Katy was relieved and put a note on the calendar.

But as the date approached, the CMS told her it had still not obtained the order. In September, the CMS again told her it would apply for a liability order - worth about Â£6,000.

Katy said the service told her last month it was no longer confident of her ex-partner's address it needed to send him the paperwork.

She is now in debt herself and her case is, in effect, on hold.

"I was really upset because it just came as such a shock. I thought that I was going to get somewhere and just haven't," she told us.

"I'm not sure I'm ever going to see the money."

Katy's ex-partner did not respond to our questions.

The CMS said it had apologised for delays in progressing the liability order and made a consolatory payment. It said the case has been affected by ongoing difficulty confirming and maintaining a reliable address for the paying parent.

Mother Susan told Panorama the CMS's efforts to chase her ex partner for money owed had been "a waste of everybody's time... a waste of everyone's money".

Her ex stopped paying child maintenance regularly five years ago, and is more than Â£10,000 in arrears. He was abusive, so we have changed her name to protect her identity.

The lack of financial support, she said, meant she had been forced to skip meals.

"No matter how many hours I was working, it wasn't making up for the payments that should have been coming from the paying parent," she said.

In Susan's case, financial investigators at the CMS found her ex had the money to pay. The CMS took him to court but he failed to appear.

The CMS told Susan the court had issued a warrant but it could not take further action.

"They... told me they had no warrant officers," she said, calling it an "embarrassment".

The CMS said it had apologised for failings in this case. It said enforcement action could be complex and it must follow statutory processes.

The DWP told Panorama "continued modernisation" of the service meant it was "progressing cases more quickly and effectively".

Director of the CMS, Simon Hunter, said a lot of the service's 800,000 cases were "highly satisfied" with the service and compliance had improved in the past three years.

"We are working hard behind the scenes to try and make sure that we can facilitate regular child maintenance payments," he said. "Where the case might be in an enforcement which is a very, very small percentage of our customer base, that journey can be quite an extensive period for customers to be in, and I can totally accept and appreciate that it can feel like it has taken a long time."

News.title: Rain on way for UK with temperatures to drop to overnight lows of 3C in some places
News.content:
High pressure has been dominant this summer leading to hot and dry weather, particularly across England and Wales.

There's been no significant rain in southern England for around two months which has led water levels in our rivers and reservoirs to drop significantly. All of Wales and most of England are in drought.

However, through this week high pressure will be replaced by the influence of low pressure and more unsettled conditions.

Some light rain is likely on Monday, mostly across northern areas of the UK.

Into Tuesday and Wednesday this will turn heavier and start to move into southern England.

While rain is therefore finally going to fall across the south, it may become more showery. This means the exact location and distribution of rainfall is still uncertain.

And while of course any rain will be welcome, it won't bring much improvement to conditions.

It will take weeks of above average rainfall into the autumn to make any significant changes to the drought.

However, it is likely to make a big difference to the emergency services who have been battling against the extreme weather and wildfires over the last few weeks.

The fire severity index - how severe a fire could be, should one start - will come down to low or moderate, according to forecasts from Natural England and the Met Office.

News.title: Burnham exchanged messages with White House imposter
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham exchanged messages with a person posing as the chief of staff to US President Donald Trump.

Downing Street has declined to comment on the security breach, first reported by Politico.

Politico reported that officials said Burnham communicated with the person claiming to be Susie Wiles "before becoming suspicious that the contact was illegitimate" and claimed only a "few messages" were exchanged.

A government spokesperson said: "We do not comment on national security matters."

It is understood the communication between Burnham and the person posing as Wiles was in the form of messages and there was no conversation between the two.

"No messages of significance" were exchanged and the texts were "quickly reported to the appropriate authorities" once they were believed to be suspicious, sources said.

The BBC has previously reported an FBI probe into Wiles' phone being hacked in May last year.

At that time, Wiles said her phone had been hacked after an impersonator, or impersonators, used her contacts file to message other top US officials.

The impersonation was targeted at her personal phone, not government phone, but recipients included US senators, governors and top business executives.

Wiles, a key Trump ally, was also among those targeted by a cyber espionage unit associated with Iran's Revolutionary Guards - a powerful branch of Iran's armed forces - in 2024.

News.title: Post-mortems due on five boys killed in crash on wrong side of motorway that injured four in Ireland
News.content:
Post-mortem examinations are to be carried out later on the bodies of five teenage boys killed when their car being driven the wrong way down a motorway in County Kildare collided head-on with another car.

Three women, two aged in their 30s and one in her 20s, and a child who were in the second car were taken to hospital with serious injuries.

The crash happened between junction 3 and junction 4 of the M9 motorway, at Moone, at about 03:00 local time on Sunday.

The vehicle the teenage boys were in was travelling southbound on the northbound carriageway when it hit the second car.

GardaÃ­ (Irish police) have said no pursuit was taking place before the collision occurred.

The Republic of Ireland's police ombudsman, FiosrÃº is carrying out its own investigation into the crash.

Police have appealed for witnesses to the crash or anyone driving on that stretch of the motorway at the time to contact them.

Forensic investigators have completed their examination of the scene.

Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly described those injured in the crash as "family members" who were "travelling innocently" when they were struck by the car driving on the wrong side of the motorway.

News.title: History for Hunt and Asher-Smith in golden finish for GB
News.content:
Amy Hunt and Dina Asher-Smith made history and Georgia Hunter Bell claimed a commanding 1500m gold in a spectacular finish for Great Britain at the European Championships.

Sprint sensation Hunt held up four fingers to the camera after holding off Germany's challenge on the home straight of the mixed 4x100m relay as another sell-out crowd roared the 24-year-old on to an unprecedented fourth gold in Birmingham.

The world silver medallist completed victory for the quartet in a European record 39.97 seconds to add to her triumphs in the 100m, 200m and women's 4x100m in the past seven days.

"Oh my gosh, I am over the moon. I think to finish it off with some of my best friends in the sport is incredible," Hunt told BBC Sport.

With her eighth gold and 11th medal overall, Asher-Smith is unparalleled as the most successful athlete in the competition's 92-year history, with a team also featuring Jeremiah Azu and Zharnel Hughes extending the hosts' domination of the sprint events.

Hunter Bell expertly controlled the women's 1500m final before bursting clear to continue her golden year by adding to world indoor and Commonwealth glory.

That represented the 32-year-old's seventh international medal in two years as she continues to build momentum on her fairytale return to the sport which she quit for five years following a promising junior career.

News.title: Hundreds attend emotional Cambridge vigil for Jason Arday
News.content:
The vigil was organised by Arday's postdoctoral students and was held on Sunday afternoon.

Kahn added: "Hold your friends close and know that we stand strong because we stand together.

"Now, there is a time for anger, of justifiable anger, and that time will come - but today is not that day.

"Today is about celebrating the life of a brilliant man, Professor Jason Arday.

"Today we share the ways Jason made a difference in our lives and in the lives of those around us."

She said there would be a "promise to seek justice" for him.

Another student told the crowd: "Racism did this."

She said: "For so many of us Cambridge was once imagined as an arrival. We worked towards places like this; we believed in the university... there was a hope that, having arrived, we might belong.

"Jason's death and the cruelty and smear that surrounded him reminds us that, for many, we do not belong. An institution can give you a room and still withhold a home.

"It can give you a title and still question your right to speak."

News.title: 'I want my brother back' - Tupac’s brother tells BBC murder trial won’t bring justice
News.content:
The BBC's Shaimaa Khalil sat down with Mopreme Shakur, Tupac Shakur's stepbrother, ahead of opening statements on Monday in trial of the man accused of killing the rapper.

During the interview, Mopreme reflected on Tupac's legacy 30 years after his death, recalled the night of the shooting, and shared what it was like to grow up alongside one of the most influential figures in hip-hop.

Read more about the case here.

News.title: Reform UK benefits ban for foreign nationals would include EU citizens
News.content:
It is the latest announcement ahead of a speech on Monday by Reform's shadow chancellor Robert Jenrick to formally unveil the party's welfare plans.

"Forcing British workers to pay for the benefits of foreigners is not just economically illiterate but plain immoral," Jenrick said in a statement.

"People are more than happy to support their neighbours in hard times, but the British taxpayer cannot afford to subsidise everyone on the planet, especially those who have not paid in."

This year the government expects, external to spend a total of Â£322bn on welfare in Great Britain, or 10.6% of GDP, just over half of which goes to pensioners.

Reform says it has spent six months drawing up a 50-page plan that it claims will save a total of Â£50bn a year.

On Saturday, the party said it would replace the disability payments system, Pip, if it entered Number 10 at the next election.

The latest proposals would ban foreign nationals from almost all welfare payments including housing benefit, pension credit, jobseeker's allowance, child benefit, free childcare and disability benefits.

Only a small number of exemptions would apply, including the war widows pension and Armed Forces compensation.

The party had previously pledged to ban foreign nationals from claiming Universal Credit.

News.title: Changing pubs into homes to be made harder under new rules
News.content:
The Campaign for Real Ale has previously said that pubs are being "lost forever to conversion or demolition as developers look to cash in on the desirable locations and unique architecture of pubs and social clubs".

The British Beer and Pub Association and UKHospitality have also campaigned against pub closures, with both largely blaming tax rises and other costs.

Allen Simpson, chief executive of UKHospitality, said: "The biggest issue facing hospitality businesses is costs like VAT and business rates pushing pubs out of business in the first place."

Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, he said: "The reality is it's quite difficult to make money out of a pub or a restaurant or a hotel with the current tax system so people do end up having to find other routes.

"You can legislate to stop a pub being sold as a flat but what you can't do is legislate to force them to stay open if they're not viable," Simpson added.

He said unless government policies are changed to cut running costs, "what we'll be left with is not pubs which are open but actually just empty premises because they can't be used as a pub or a house".

In July, the Labour government said pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England will be given a 20% cut to business rates on top of rates relief announced in January.

The NPPF update being published Monday also includes default approval for homes being built around railway stations in England in an attempt to increase housebuilding numbers.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner said: "By unlocking thousands of homes around well-connected transport hubs, we're helping people live closer to work, school and the services they rely on, while backing local businesses and driving growth in our communities."

The update also means that some groups will no longer need to be consulted on housing development plans as part of the process of getting permission.

The Gardens Trust, a parks and gardens heritage and conversion charity, called the decision to remove its role as a statutory consultee "devastating".

It said it devalued parks and gardens and "makes them vulnerable to poorly informed development".

Under the changes, the Gardens Trust and Theatres Trust will still be notified of relevant applications and Sport England will continue to advise on significant cases.

Labour has set a target to build 1.5 million homes by 2029. According to official data, external, it has so far built 392,000 homes in England since coming into power in July 2024.

Shadow housing secretary Sir James Cleverly said Labour is "failing abysmally" to meet their target because of taxes and red tape.

"To try to fix their own mess, Labour are planning a power grab, seizing control from local communities and forcing them to accept development in the wrong areas because Labour won't build in the right areas," he added.

News.title: Emergency phone alert put domestic abuse victims at risk, campaigners say
News.content:
Most people received the blaring alert at 19:00 BST on Friday - and it came as a surprise given the government had not told people it was coming, as it has done for tests of the system.

The notification, which cautioned against the use of disposable barbecues, naked flames or fireworks, was the biggest use yet of the emergency alert system and Prime Minister Andy Burnham urged the public to take it "seriously".

A Cabinet Office press release, posted to their website at about 18:45 on Friday, was missed by many in the media, which meant there was little warning to the public.

This potentially jeopardised domestic abuse victims trying to hide secret phones they use to seek support and try to escape abusers, some campaigners have said.

Women's Aid, the national charity aiming to end domestic abuse, is calling for more forewarning of alerts wherever possible.

Veronica Oakeshott, the charity's head of external affairs, told BBC News: "Survivors of domestic abuse frequently turn to second phones to help them access lifesaving support or flee from abuse."

It is vital the devices stay hidden, she said, before adding: "We would urge the government to forewarn the public that alerts might be issued, when possible."

It has been reported that senior government figures were discussing whether or not to send the alert hours before, on Friday morning.

The alert came after a spate of wildfires including one that destroyed 19 homes in Stourbridge, West Midlands, on Thursday.

News.title: Thousands of Bonnie Tyler fans set to gather in singer's hometown for funeral
News.content:
Thousands of Bonnie Tyler fans are set to gather in Swansea on Monday ahead of a church service held as part of the legendary singer's celebration of life.

It comes after huge crowds of emotional fans lined the streets in the coastal suburb of Mumbles on Saturday as her coffin - draped in a Welsh flag - was driven through the place she called home.

As the procession began, Total Eclipse of the Heart could be heard playing on the busy street, as crying fans broke into applause.

The singer died "unexpectedly" on 8 July, aged 75, at a hospital in Portugal.

Despite Tyler's career taking her all over the world, she has been described by those living in Mumbles as a "Swansea girl through and through", and someone who "never forgot where she came from".

Monday's service for family and invited guests will be held at St Mary's church, Swansea, and will be live-streamed on the star's official website, with fans also able to watch it on screens outside.

The cortege will then travel to Skewen, Neath Port Talbot, where Tyler was born and grew up, arriving in the village for a private family service.

There will be a heavy emphasis on Tyler's Welsh identity, with an organist playing music from Welsh legends before the service starts - with songs from Tom Jones, Shirley Bassey and Tyler herself.

Choir Only Men Aloud will sing her huge hit Total Eclipse of the Heart and Simon and Garfunkel's Bridge Over Troubled Water, while the congregation will sing hymn Calon Lan.

The exit music will be a song that was close to Tyler's heart - Mary Hopkin's 1969 hit Those Were The Days.

She performed it at a local talent contest in Skewen when she was young.

As the two singers were from the same area, Tyler, whose real name was Gaynor Hopkins, would later change her name to avoid confusion with Hopkin.

News.title: Sainsbury's pauses AI cameras after shopper ousted
News.content:
Sainsbury's has suspended its use of live facial recognition technology at one of its London branches after a customer was wrongly challenged as a shoplifter and asked to leave.

Matt Arnold, 46, was buying items at the East Dulwich store when he was stopped by management at a self-service till.

Describing the experience as a "terrifying glimpse of the future," he has warned that retail surveillance tech risks humiliating customers and creating a system where staff feel compelled to follow automated alerts without applying human logic.

The supermarket said it had apologised to Arnold and claimed the mistake was "caused by human error", but critics have called for the technology to be scrapped.

The incident happened on 6 August as Arnold - a comedy promoter getting supplies for a stand-up event hosted at the next door Dulwich Hamlet Football Club - was waiting for a staff member to approve an alcohol purchase.

Having already scanned his items alongside his Nectar loyalty card, he said he had waved an attendant over.

Instead, he said he was approached by two of the management staff and told he could not be served due to an incident "earlier in the week".

News.title: Boy, 12, drowns in River Lea at Hackney Marshes
News.content:
A 12-year-old boy has drowned in north-east London.

The London Fire Brigade (LFB) said it was called to reports of a person in the water in the River Lea, near the Hackney Marshes, just after 18:00 BST on Saturday.

Crews searched the river alongside the Metropolitan Police, and the boy's body was recovered by police divers hours later, at about 00:15 BST on Sunday. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

Mayor of Hackney, ZoÃ« Garbett, said she was heartbroken to learn of the boy's death, adding: "All of our thoughts are with the child's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time."

Garbett thanked the emergency services for their "rapid response" and "extensive efforts".

"This is a devastating loss for our community, and I know many will be feeling a deep sense of shock and sadness," she said. "The boy's family will need time to grieve this unimaginable loss, so please respect their privacy."

The Met said the boy's death was being treated as unexpected, and his next of kin had been informed and were being supported by specialist officers.

Det Insp Azmeen Pinnu, who is leading the investigation, said: "This is a deeply tragic incident and our thoughts are with the boy's family, friends and the wider community.

"This incident is now being investigated on behalf of the coroner, and enquiries remain ongoing to establish the full circumstances of what happened."

The LFB said it sent fire engines from Homerton, Leyton and Leytonstone fire stations to the scene along with specialist fire rescue units from Edmonton and Bethnal Green fire stations, and the brigade's drone team.

Firefighters left the scene just after 21:30 on Saturday, the LFB added.

News.title: Cat missing for 10 years returns home on owner's 30th birthday
News.content:
A 13-year-old tabby cat that went missing 10 years ago has found her way back home.

Her owners Lucy and Hannah Robertson were "heartbroken" in April 2016 when Charlie, then three-years-old, disappeared.

As an outdoor cat, Charlie would spend her days roaming the streets but one day, after recently moving to a new area, she never returned home.

The family spent months looking, never finding any leads.

But last month, the "impossible" happened on Lucy's 30th birthday, they received a call from the vet saying Charlie had been found.

Hannah, 37, moved from Newbridge to Abercarn, in Caerphilly county, a few miles away, 10 years ago.

Within three days, Charlie, whom she described as a "bit fiery", had vanished.

"We did have one or two tip-offs... we tried to find her, but we kept missing her," Hannah said.

"We never lost hope. But sadly, we just couldn't find her," she told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast.

Lucy said that, despite having asked around, as well as posting on Facebook, there was no sign of Charlie.

"It was heartbreaking. We were scared that she had been knocked over or that she wasn't around any more," she said.

But on 29 July, Hannah was left "gobsmacked" after receiving a call from a veterinary practice in Abercarn saying Charlie had been found.

News.title: Somali man charged with attempted murder at Surrey asylum hotel
News.content:
Police have charged a man with attempted murder at a hotel used to house asylum seekers in Stanwell.

Armed officers were dispatched to the Stanwell Hotel, near Heathrow Airport, on Saturday evening over reports a man had been stabbed, Surrey Police said in a statement.

Paramedics took the victim, a hotel staff member in his 30s, to hospital with life-threatening injuries. He is now in a stable condition, police wrote in the latest update.

Police said that 22-year-old Somali national Abdifatah Yusuf Adani remains in custody and is due to face one charge of attempted murder when he appears at Staines Magistrates Court on Monday morning.

"There remains a heightened police presence in the area," the police said in a statement shared on Sunday night.

Earlier on Saturday, Detective Superintendent Kate Hyder of Surrey Police said "we understand this incident has caused concern within the local community, and I encourage you to speak to local officers."

Police said they are not pursuing anyone else connected to the incident.

News.title: Murder inquiry after man bitten by dog dies
News.content:
A murder inquiry has begun after the death of a man who was bitten by a dog on a footpath in West Yorkshire.

The 55-year-old was injured in an altercation on a disused railway line off Blacker Lane in Calder Grove, Wakefield, at about 13:30 BST on Saturday. He was taken to hospital in a critical condition but died just after 19:00.

West Yorkshire Police has appealed for two people, one of whom is called Sophie, who stopped to help the injured man to come forward.

A force spokesperson said a 55-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of murder and of being the owner of a dog dangerously out of control in a public place, causing injury. He remains in custody.

Police said a German Shepherd dog believed to have been involved in the incident has been seized by officers.

Det Ch Insp Michael Cox said: "Sadly, a man has died and it is really important that we understand the circumstances of what has taken place.

"We know that two people, one named Sophie, stopped to assist the injured man and direct officers."

He added: "We would urge these two people to come forward to help us with our ongoing inquiries into this tragic incident.

"The initial altercation happened in an area used by walkers and we are urging anyone who has seen or heard any part of the exchange between these two men to please make contact."

News.title: Transfer news LIVE: Liverpool and Arsenal get Barcola boost, Man City identify Rodri replacement
News.content:
Bradley Barcola was left out of Paris Saint-Germain’s squad for the French Super Cup in a boost to Liverpool and Arsenal’s chances of signing the France international winger. Barcola was also an unused substitute in PSG’s Super Cup win over Aston Villa on Wednesday. The European champions were set to demand £145m for the 23-year-old but Liverpool are prepared to play the long-game as they bid to negotiate a price as Andoni Iraola targets a new winger.

Elsewhere, Manchester City will sell Rodri to Barcelona in a deal worth up to £65m after finally accepting the advances of the Spanish champions. It means City will now accelerate their pursuit of Ayyoub Bouaddi, the 18-year-old Moroccan wonderkid, as they enter talks to finalise a fee with Lille for the midfielder. And City could yet go back for Enzo Fernandez, despite missing Chelsea’s deadline for offers.

Arsenal are bidding to finalise their squad before the Premier League season, with Gabriel Martinelli and Ethan Nwaneri both left out of Sunday’s Community Shield. Both players have been linked with a move away and Martinelli turned down a move to Galatasaray on Friday. Arsenal have been keen to sign a defender following the injury to William Saliba and England defender Jarell Quansah, formerly of Liverpool, would be able to cover both centre-back and right back positions.
