World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Disaster diplomacy and a persistent peso
World.content:
President Claudia Sheinbaum spent the weekend before this week began in Puebla, kicking off the 2026 National Reforestation Day from the mountain pass between the Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl volcanoes. There, marking the International Day of the World’s Indigenous Peoples, she declared that the Paso de Cortés — named for the conquistador who marched through it in 1519 — would be a great candidate for a new name.

On Monday morning, the president’s attention had shifted south: a powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia, killing hundreds. Sheinbaum immediately pledged Mexico would send Colombia everything it needed, but the country’s military rescue brigade quickly ran into a diplomatic hurdle, part of a tangle of certification disputes and friction that unfolded even as quietly extraordinary Mexican solidarity continued — not just with Colombia, but with wildfire-stricken Canada as well. Colombia’s quake also revived an old question for Mexico, one we explore in more depth here: with Venezuela and now Colombia both rattled by major temblors this year, does Mexico’s own position on the Pacific Ring of Fire mean its odds just went up?

Otherwise, the week of Aug. 10-14 in Mexico brought big economic headlines, athletic glory and advances in the Ayotzinapa criminal case.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Mexico extends a hand abroad

Mexico’s instinct to help its neighbors was on full display this week. More than 300 Mexican firefighters traveled to British Columbia to help battle over 100 active wildfires that have forced tens of thousands to evacuate, drawing an outpouring of gratitude on Canadian social media. Farther south, a 45-member team of Mexico’s famed “Topos” rescue brigade reached Cali, Colombia, on Wednesday to dig through earthquake rubble — but only after Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella initially rejected their help, citing sovereignty concerns.

On Thursday, Sheinbaum confirmed that an official Mexican Army rescue brigade had not been authorized to enter Colombia and therefore remained at home. According to the president, Colombia’s new government demanded a type of certification the Mexican team does not have. Mexico kept sending humanitarian aid regardless — more than 58 tonnes of food, water and medicine by week’s end.

Ex-governor bound over in Ayotzinapa case

In one of the week’s most significant justice developments, former Guerrero Governor Ángel Aguirre was ordered to stand trial over his alleged role in the 2014 disappearance of 43 Ayotzinapa students. Prosecutors allege Aguirre ordered the destruction of security footage from Iguala’s Palace of Justice on the night the students vanished, partly to protect a nephew with ties to a local criminal gang. Aguirre, who resigned as governor weeks after the disappearances, remains jailed at the Altiplano maximum-security prison as the case — one of Mexico’s most notorious unsolved human rights tragedies — grinds toward trial nearly 12 years later.

The super peso returns

Mexico’s currency briefly broke back below 17 to the US dollar on Friday morning for the first time since 2024, in what analysts are calling the return of the “super peso.”

The peso has now strengthened for four consecutive days and appreciated more than 5% this year, a move Citibanamex attributes largely to global dollar weakness rather than Mexican fundamentals. Still, by the MND Peso Index™, which compares a basket of goods in Mexico and Dallas, the currency looks overvalued by 2.4% — a smaller gap than June’s 2.9%, suggesting the exchange rate isn’t too far removed from what prices on the ground would imply.

Homicides fall, but Sinaloa gets reinforcements

Security officials reported on Wednesday that the daily homicide average has fallen 51% since Sheinbaum took office, with July recording the lowest monthly tally of her administration so far. Even so, nearly half of the country’s murders remain concentrated in just seven states, Sinaloa among them. That reality was underscored by the Navy’s deployment of over 1,700 personnel to Mazatlán after the port city logged its bloodiest month of the year in July, as fighting between rival Sinaloa Cartel factions Los Chapitos and Los Mayos continues to spill beyond Culiacán into the tourist-heavy coastal city.

Visa fights spill into the mañanera

Washington’s campaign against Mexican political figures widened this week.

Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, the son of former President López Obrador and a former Morena party organization secretary, said the United States had revoked his visa, accusing Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his deputy of a politically motivated move. At Friday’s mañanera, Sheinbaum called the decision “essentially political in nature,” urging Washington to produce evidence against anyone it targets while insisting the dispute won’t spiral into a broader conflict with the United States.

Business indicators to know

Peso: Trading just above 17 to the dollar, its strongest level since February, even as the MND Peso Index™ pegs it as 2.4% overvalued.

Trading just above 17 to the dollar, its strongest level since February, even as the MND Peso Index™ pegs it as 2.4% overvalued. Inflation: July’s headline rate came in at 3.12%, its lowest since May 2020, though Banxico Governor Victoria Rodríguez says it’s too early to “claim victory.”

July’s headline rate came in at 3.12%, its lowest since May 2020, though Banxico Governor Victoria Rodríguez says it’s too early to “claim victory.” Jobs: Formal employment shed 19,550 positions in July, a seasonal dip IMSS attributes to the school year’s end, even as average wages hit a record daily high.

Formal employment shed 19,550 positions in July, a seasonal dip IMSS attributes to the school year’s end, even as average wages hit a record daily high. Industry: Industrial activity grew 0.2% month-on-month in June, lifted by mining and construction, while manufacturing logged its 12th straight month of annual decline.

Cyclospora cleared in the Riviera Maya

After British health authorities flagged a spike in cyclosporiasis cases among travelers returning from Mexico, Cofepris tested food and water samples from 16 Riviera Maya hotels — and found no trace of the parasite. All 43 samples, drawn from Playa del Carmen, Puerto Morelos, Tulum and Isla Mujeres, tested negative, and no contamination indicators turned up elsewhere. Mexico’s Health Ministry has confirmed 33 cyclosporiasis cases nationwide this year, a tiny fraction of the population, though the source of the UK cases remains unidentified.

Tourism notes

June brought 4.11 million international tourists to Mexico, up just 1.1% year-on-year — a muted bump given that Mexico hosted 12 of its 13 World Cup matches that month.

Tulum’s airport will regain five international routes this winter to cities in Canada and the United States, part of a state push to reverse a steep decline in international traffic.

Sargassum accumulation, though still tracking toward the second-heaviest year on record, has begun easing across most monitored stretches of the Quintana Roo coast as collection efforts and shifting currents bring relative relief to hard-hit beaches like Tulum and Playa del Carmen.

Mexican athletes seize the moment

It was a banner week for Mexican sport. The under-20 men’s soccer team defended its Concacaf title, beating the United States 2-0 at Mexico City’s Estadio Banorte for a record 15th championship, with defender Cristóbal Alfaro scoring twice.

Meanwhile, Mexico delivered its best-ever medal haul at the Central American and Caribbean Games, where the delegation topped the table with a record 407 medals in Santo Domingo. The government announced every medal — not just an athlete’s best result — will now earn a cash prize, a change Conade chief Rommel Pacheco said was Sheinbaum’s own idea.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: How fragile is Chacahua’s lagoon ecosystem? A conversation with locals on the Oaxaca coast
World.content:
A bus from Puerto Escondido. A minibus, aka colectivo, from Rio Grande. Then a lancha, or small boat, across the water to Zapotalito. One more open-air truck and you’ve made it.

Laguna de Chacahua sits along the western coast of Oaxaca, part of the state’s more than 300 milePacific coastline – a lagoon ecosystem padded with jungle flora, where the network of mangroves roots the island in its gurgling brackish tides.

It is part of the municipality of Villa de Tututepec de Melchor Ocampo and around 100 miles down the coast from the popular beach city of Puerto Escondido. In the daytime, the high sun smelts the soft sand and rocks while hammocks loll idly in the low breeze. After sunset, bioluminescent plankton set the water aglow in a neon blue glacé.

Technically, Chacahua is a barrier island, meaning it is not entirely separate from the mainland but is only accessible by boat. The community is predominantly Black and Afro-Indigenous, partially linking back to the Spanish enslavement of Africans and their forced labor in Mexico in the 16th and 17th centuries. But many residents make their way over from the mainland to surf, fish and enjoy the more relaxed pulse of daily life.

“Here, you can be whatever you want to be,” Augusto, an architect living in Chacahua, tells me. “And nobody is going to look down on you; you’re living in a free place.”

‘The sea is starting to reclaim the land’

But it isn’t all peace in paradise. Coastal environments and their communities are facing increased exposure to natural hazards.

The rainy season from June to September brings storms and natural climate variations, but Oaxaca state’s geography, situated along Mexico’s southwest Pacific coast, leaves it particularly vulnerable to climate change. Pacific hurricanes and Atlantic basin tropical systems pose a dual threat, alongside the increasing reality of heavy rains, droughts, and rising temperatures and sea levels.

While it is difficult to find more localised data for the island, average yearly temperature in Oaxaca City rose by 1.1 degrees Celsius (2 degrees Fahrenheit) between 1994 and 2024. While this figure may seem small, it represents a rapid change over three decades, even at the local level.

Global sea level rise has been affecting the coast of Oaxaca, and Chacahua is no exception. Drawing from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC) 6th Assessment Report, NASA’s Sea Level Projection projects extreme sea level rise along Oaxaca’s Pacific coast, and the lagoon’s low relief offers little defense.

Sitting in a cabana just 100 meters inland, Augusto points towards Playa Chacahua. “The sea is starting to reclaim (the) land. That’s why the houses over there are collapsing.”

It was Hurricane Pauline in 1997 that dramatically shifted the landscape of Chacahua, the lagoon rising to such a level that a new inlet was created and swathes of the beach were eaten away. Today, the beach faces an ever-greater risk due to the damaging erosion.

‘Everyone fishes sooner or later’

Fishing is integral to life in Chacahua, and the catch is diverse – shrimp, puffer fish, oysters, blue crabs, and red snapper by the Bajo Este. “There are all kinds of fish,” Antonio says. “There’s a bit of everything here.”

Antonio started fishing at the age of 8 with his grandfather. At 17, he began fishing for sharks; tiburoneros (shark fishermen) use a simbra, a 14-kilometre-long (9-mile) fishing line with around 300 hooks every 18 meters.

“We’d head out along the Guerrero coast, going out toward the horizon where the sun sets … to where you can’t see a thing anymore,” Antonio tells me. “Transatlantic ships pass through there. We’d stay one night and head back the next day.”

The population is no more than 800 and, according to Antonio, more than half of its residents are fishermen.

“Everyone fishes sooner or later,” he says. But security isn’t promised. “Later, some move onto other jobs because fishing is just a matter of luck.”

Santiago was born on the island and has been a fisherman for 20 years.

“Because of the rains and the storms that come, it’s more dangerous now. It’s more dangerous than compared to before. It used to be a good life.”

The ecocide of the Chacahua-Pastoría Lagoons is a key culprit, with toxic chemical influx from local oil-crop industries, as well as chemical waste from a lime-oil factory beyond Zapatalito. Shrimp and fish populations are declining. Locals have faced the consequences of diminishing catch and have even demanded government action.

In 2013, local fishermen’s collective, supported by the Human Rights Ombudsman of the People of Oaxaca (DDHPO), produced a report regarding violations against the inhabitants of Zapotalito, Chacahua, La Pastoría and El Corral details the public health risks, loss of livelihood and environmental degradation that communities have faced due to federal infrastructure projects, such as Irrigation District 110 and breakwaters in the Boca de Chacahua.

The resilience of mangroves

Part of a roughly 51-square-mile national park designated in 1937, Chacahua Lagoon is surrounded by a network of mangrove corridors, anchoring the island in verdant, woody tresses. Mangroves are trees or bushes that thrive in brackish tidal waters, often where a river meets the sea, offering nesting grounds for a diversity of wildlife.

The red mangrove (Rhizophora mangle), black mangrove (Avicennia germinans), white mangrove (Laguncularia racemosa), and buttonwood (Conocarpus erectus) are also essential to maintaining the health of the local ecosystem.

Their long, complex root systems are adapted to survive in low-lying waters, optimising oxygen absorption and filtering out saline contamination. They endure conditions that are virtually impossible for other plants, and their resilience is recognized by the locals.

Angél runs a grocery shop in the central square. His family has been living on the island for generations. The salinity of the sea is getting worse, he concedes, but “the mangroves are strong. We don’t have to cut them that much.”

“The mangroves are doing well,” Antonio agrees. “They’re tough. When they fall, they land upright,” due to their roots.

The resilience of locals

Perhaps Antonio and Angél aren’t giving themselves enough credit. In reality, mangroves are vulnerable to climate change, specifically increasing salinity, hurricane events, and worsening El Niño patterns. But it’s the locals who demonstrate climate resilience every day, in working as a community to restore the things that Angél says the government is neglecting financially and administratively.

“The effort is made every day; it’s part of life here on the island,” Augusto says. “People engage in what’s called tequio, voluntary community work to help the environment.”

In the same way, the fishermen are taking it upon themselves to try and mitigate the marine pollution, but there is a limit to what can be done without wider support.

Tequio “takes place because people love their land,” Augusto explains, but as Angél marks, the climate is getting hotter, the sea saltier, and the water warmer.

On top of this, the briny waves of gentrification are lapping at the island’s shores. Lavish cabanas with their polished wood walls and hiked-up rent are beginning to rear their haute heads.

Tourism has also been shown to worsen pollution. In Mexico’s Caribbean coast, the tourism sector accounts for one-third of the region’s total waste, and light pollution has been proven to pose threats to turtle populations, of which species such as the Leatherback are populous in Chacahua.

What’s in store for Chacahua?

Oaxaca has been strongly affected by hurricanes Otis, John, Erick, and Boris in the last four years.

While federal budgeting continues to be an issue for Natural Protected Areas across Mexico, local cooperatives, in tandem with the National Commission of Protected Natural Areas (CONANP), are taking measures to respond to growing tourism in the state of Oaxaca and have made major steps in wildlife protection and sustainable infrastructure, but the direct effects on Chacahua are yet to be comprehensively reported.

Looking into its climate future, Chacahua is standing at a delta. It goes without saying that the community has demonstrated its climate resilience through supporting mangroves, keeping the waters around the island clean, and reconstructing and relocating seafront buildings.

However, without sufficient government support, the effects of environmental jeopardy and injustice may ultimately uproot the mangrove system and local way of life to an irremediable degree.

Millie Deere is a freelance journalist.

World.title: Venezuela Economic Emergency Decree: What It Does
World.content:
Venezuela · Economy

Key Facts Decree 5.414: Signed 8 August 2026, published the same day in official gazette No. 7.066 Extraordinario.

Signed 8 August 2026, published the same day in official gazette No. 7.066 Extraordinario. Sixty days: Exceptional powers over tax, financial, budgetary and procurement matters, extendable once.

Exceptional powers over tax, financial, budgetary and procurement matters, extendable once. Court approval: The Supreme Court’s Constitutional Chamber ruled it constitutional on 11 August.

The Supreme Court’s Constitutional Chamber ruled it constitutional on 11 August. Fifth in a row: Acceso a la Justicia counts five such decrees since April 2025 — roughly five times the constitutional limit.

Acceso a la Justicia counts five such decrees since April 2025 — roughly five times the constitutional limit. Government claim: Delcy Rodriguez says 21 straight quarters of growth and food consumption up 9.6%.

Delcy Rodriguez says 21 straight quarters of growth and food consumption up 9.6%. Independent view: Forecasters see 2%-6.6% growth alongside inflation of 200%-387% in 2026.

Forecasters see 2%-6.6% growth alongside inflation of 200%-387% in 2026. Oil flows: Venezuela shipped 1.16 million barrels a day in July, with US cargoes the highest since early 2019.

Decree 5.414 gives the executive exceptional powers over tax, budgets and public contracts for 60 days — and extends a state of exception now in its second year.

A new Venezuela economic emergency decree took effect on 8 August 2026, placing the country under exceptional economic powers for 60 days. It is the fifth such decree since April 2025 — and it lands as the government claims a growth streak no published data can confirm.

Venezuela is again under an economic emergency decree, its fifth since April 2025. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the decree actually does

Decree No. 5.414 was signed by acting president Delcy Rodriguez and published the same day in official gazette No. 7.066 Extraordinario. It declares a state of economic emergency nationwide for 60 days.

It rests on Article 338 of the constitution, which permits a single extension of equal length. It hands the executive exceptional powers over tax, financial, budgetary and public procurement matters, according to Venezuela Red Informativa.

Finanzas Digital reported that the published text spells out neither the economic reasons for the declaration nor the concrete measures it will produce.

The Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court declared it constitutional on 11 August in ruling No. 824, according to Contrapunto and Finanzas Digital. The watchdog Acceso a la Justicia noted the same day that neither the ruling nor the gazette text was publicly available.

The Rio Times found no record of a National Assembly vote on the decree. Venezuela’s emergency decrees have historically moved without the legislature.

Not new — a state of exception that keeps rolling

Acceso a la Justicia describes the measure as a fresh extension of an existing state of exception, not a new departure. It counts Decree 5.414 as the fifth since April 2025, with the previous four all prolonged.

On that arithmetic Venezuela has spent roughly a year and a half under emergency rule — about five times the 120-day maximum the constitution allows.

Transparencia Venezuela made the comparison explicit in a 15 August report headlined “Delcy copies Maduro’s emergency decrees”. Nicolas Maduro governed under an economic emergency for five straight years, from 2016 to 2021.

The watchdog argues the decrees centralise budget and law-making powers while sidelining the National Assembly, and have served political control and corruption rather than fixing any emergency.

Why now

Rodriguez has been acting president — “presidenta encargada” in the official wording — since around late January 2026. State news agency AVN referred on 27 July to “200 days” of her administration, which points back to that date.

Venezuelan outlets including La Patilla have reported that Maduro left power after a US military operation that ended in his capture and transfer to the United States. The Rio Times could not verify a published legal act recording the succession.

The decree follows a punishing few months. Earthquakes struck on 24 June, power shortages forced public sector hours to be cut, and the presidency said on 8 August that Rodriguez had reviewed the spending of post-earthquake emergency funds.

The growth claim, and what independent forecasters say

On 16 August, at the opening of a Mercal state supermarket in Caracas, Rodriguez said Venezuela had strung together 21 consecutive quarters of growth. “We have now travelled this road for 21 consecutive quarters,” she said, as quoted by Banca y Negocios.

She also said food consumption rose 9.6% in the first seven months of 2026, El Universal reported. Outlets published different figures for the sub-components, and no national accounts tables were released to support any of it.

That is the core difficulty. The central bank has for years published little macroeconomic data, and published it late, so the growth streak cannot be independently checked.

Independent forecasters do see growth — but paired with brutal inflation. The UN Development Programme projects about 6.5% growth and roughly 385% inflation for 2026, according to EFE.

The IMF’s April 2026 outlook puts Venezuela’s average inflation at 387.4%, the highest in the world. Caracas consultancy Ecoanalitica models 5.8% growth with 251.5% inflation under disciplined policy, or 6.6% growth with 361.4% inflation if spending runs hot.

Economists at the University of Zulia are far more downbeat. They told El Impulso in July they expect about 2% growth and inflation near 200%, and note the economy shrank roughly 73% between 2012 and 2025.

The currency points the same way. Ecoanalitica sees the official rate ending 2026 near 1,062 bolivares to the US dollar, with the parallel rate around 1,521 bolivares per US dollar.

The military and the oil economy

Claims are circulating that the armed forces are militarising the oil industry. The Rio Times could not confirm any August 2026 news report documenting troop deployments at oil facilities or fresh military appointments at PDVSA.

What is documented is a broader pattern. A study summarised by Voz.us on 13 August counts 44 entities tied to the Defence Ministry across oil, mining, banking, insurance and agriculture — a footprint it compares to Cuba’s GAESA conglomerate.

It singles out CAMIMPEG, the armed forces’ own oil, gas and mining company, active in the Orinoco Mining Arc. Transparencia Venezuela, in work reported by La Patilla on 10 August, said PDVSA still runs an “irregular” tanker fleet.

El Nacional, an opposition-leaning paper, addressed the emergency on 16 August — but in an opinion column, not a news report.

Oil, sanctions and why this matters outside Venezuela

Venezuela shipped 1.16 million barrels a day in July, down slightly from 1.2 million in June, Reuters reported on 3 August. Cargoes to the United States rose to about 786,000 bpd — the highest since early 2019.

Chevron’s exports held near 293,000 bpd, and its PDVSA joint ventures produced about 280,000 bpd in the first half.

US sanctions have not been lifted; they are being managed through selective licences, including one covering refinery-grade diluents from the United States. Two-way US-Venezuela trade rose 113% to about US$9.5 billion in the first half of 2026.

That is why a Caracas decree travels. Powers over budgets, procurement and contracts change the risk calculus for anyone signing with the Venezuelan state — and Gulf Coast refiners now lean on those barrels for fuel margins across the Americas.

There is a human ledger too. Roughly 7.7 million Venezuelans have left over the past decade, according to UN agencies, reshaping labour markets in Colombia, Peru, Chile and Brazil.

Whether that flow reverses depends on whether growth reaches ordinary households — and Colombia’s Norte de Santander and Brazil’s Roraima absorb the spillover first.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Venezuela economic emergency decree? Decree No. 5.414, signed on 8 August 2026 by acting president Delcy Rodriguez, declares a 60-day state of economic emergency nationwide. It grants exceptional powers over tax, financial, budgetary and public procurement matters, and the Supreme Court’s Constitutional Chamber ruled it constitutional on 11 August. Is this a new emergency or a renewal? It is effectively a renewal. The legal watchdog Acceso a la Justicia counts it as the fifth economic emergency decree since April 2025, with the previous four all extended, leaving Venezuela under a state of exception for roughly a year and a half — about five times the 120-day constitutional maximum. Are Venezuela’s 21 quarters of growth verified? No. The figure is a government claim made by Delcy Rodriguez on 16 August, and no national accounts tables were released to support it. Independent forecasters see growth of anywhere from about 2% to 6.6% in 2026, alongside inflation estimates ranging from roughly 200% to 387%. How does the decree affect foreign investors and oil trade? The decree gives the executive exceptional powers over budgets, procurement and contracts, which can alter the legal footing of joint ventures and state deals. Venezuela’s oil shipments to the United States are at their highest since early 2019, so policy instability in Caracas feeds into refinery margins and fuel prices across the Americas.

World.title: French Press Files Google AI Complaint in Paris
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.





France · TECHNOLOGY

Key Facts —Formal complaint: The Alliance de la Presse d’Information Générale filed a complaint with France’s competition authority on 11 August 2026. —Publisher coalition: Nearly 300 French newspapers and magazines joined the challenge against Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode. —Traffic impact: APIG cites an Arcom estimate that AI summaries could cost publishers 33 to 38 percent of traffic. It is based on European markets where the features are already live. —Roll-out date: Google deployed AI Overviews and AI Mode in France on 22 July 2026 without prior consultation, APIG says. —2022 commitments: APIG argues the unilateral AI roll-out violates Google’s earlier settlement obligations on paying for press content. —Publisher options: Google offered only an updated licence or a technical opt-out that would remove publishers from search visibility.

Nearly 300 French newspapers have asked the competition authority to act against Google AI summaries. They say the features strip publishers of traffic and breach a 2022 settlement on paying for press content.

French press body demands action against Google AI summaries (Photo: Internet reproduction)

What the French press body is demanding

The Alliance de la Presse d’Information Générale, known as APIG. Filed a formal complaint with the Autorité de la concurrence on 11 August 2026.

The federation represents nearly 300 general-interest newspapers and magazines across France.

APIG says Google deployed AI Overviews and AI Mode in France on 22 July 2026. It says there was no prior consultation or negotiation over payment.

The publishers argue this unilateral move violates commitments Google made in 2022 to negotiate and pay for use of press content.

The complaint asks the competition authority to intervene against what APIG describes as new uses of press content without dedicated payment. Reuters reported that the association wants the watchdog to act because the AI summaries “deprive newspapers and magazines of readers.”

The traffic and revenue damage behind the Google AI summaries fight

APIG cites an Arcom estimate that AI summaries could cost publishers 33 to 38 percent of traffic. Based on European markets where the features are already live.

France has had the features for only three weeks.

The core problem is what researchers call zero-click behaviour. Users get their answers directly on Google’s interface and never click through to the original articles that supplied the information.

DMG Media told the UK Competition and Markets Authority that click-through rates fell by up to 89 percent where AI Overviews appear. That figure is the publisher’s own submission.

This is a publisher’s claim, not an independent finding.

APIG frames this as an existential threat to advertising-funded news models that depend on search traffic. The concern echoes across Europe and carries direct implications for smaller newsrooms in Global South regions.

Google’s response to the complaint

Google says it told French publishers how they would be compensated when their content is used in AI Overviews. It said it was surprised they had filed an antitrust complaint.

Its public line is that AI Overviews “help people ask more complex questions, discover new content. Give publishers tools to manage how their content appears”.

Google disputes the traffic framing, arguing AI summaries absorb shallow clicks while passing higher-intent traffic through.

Publishers have an opt-out control in Search Console, Google added. The company has not yet responded publicly to the specific allegations in APIG’s complaint.

Google’s offer: updated licence or search invisibility

APIG says Google presented French publishers with only two choices. They could accept an update to existing licensing agreements covering AI Overviews and AI Mode.

Or they could technically withdraw their content from being used.

The catch is that opting out means losing visibility in search results altogether. This is not a meaningful choice, since disappearing from Google’s main search page would be commercially devastating.

APIG argues Google is using its dominant position in search to impose AI summaries. It says the company captures value from publisher content.

The complaint rests on Google’s commitments in decision 22-D-13 of 21 June 2022.

The legal hook and past penalties

Google’s 2022 commitments bind it to good-faith negotiation, transparency and non-discrimination on neighbouring rights until 2027. Under Article L.464-2 of the Code de commerce, the Autorité de la concurrence can modify or end the commitments.

Impose interim measures, or fine up to 10 percent of global turnover.

Google was already fined 500 million euros in 2021 for breaching the negotiation obligation. That is about US$581 million at 1.161 dollars to the euro on 17 August 2026.

APIG argues the AI roll-out repeats that pattern.

A European regulatory wave against AI search summaries

The French complaint is part of a broader European push. On 30 April 2026, Italy’s communications authority AGCOM referred the matter to the European Commission.

The Italian federation of newspaper publishers, FIEG. Complains that AI summaries divert users away from original news content and threaten smaller independent outlets.

FIEG also warns about AI hallucinations and the lack of clear source verification.

A coalition of independent publishers filed a complaint with the European Commission in 2025 alleging Google abuses its dominance in general search. The European Publishers Council has separately described AI Overviews as a mechanism for structural disintermediation of publishers.

The European Commission opened a formal antitrust investigation on 9 December 2025 into Google’s use of online content for AI purposes. It remains open with no decision.

What to watch next in the AI search battle

The Autorité de la concurrence must now decide whether to open a formal investigation into Google’s AI summaries. The regulator has a track record of extracting commitments from the company, including the 2022 settlement on neighbouring rights.

The European Commission’s investigation is live and separate from the French case. Any ruling could force Google to re-architect search, introduce stronger opt-outs, or pay licensing fees across Europe.

For publishers in France, Italy and beyond, the outcome will shape whether AI-driven reuse of journalism must be paid for. For Global South newsrooms, it will help determine who sets the rules for AI-mediated knowledge and whose voices remain visible.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are Google AI summaries? Google AI summaries are the AI Overviews and AI Mode features. They generate short answers at the top of search results, drawing on outside sites including news publishers. Who filed the complaint against Google in France? The Alliance de la Presse d’Information Générale represents nearly 300 French newspapers and magazines. It filed the complaint with the Autorité de la concurrence on 11 August 2026. How much traffic could publishers lose to Google AI summaries? APIG cites an Arcom estimate that AI summaries could cost publishers 33 to 38 percent of traffic. It is based on European markets where the features are already live.

World.title: Uganda to Stay in Somalia, but Maybe Not Under the AU
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Uganda · DEFENSE

Key Facts —First deployment: Uganda sent troops to Somalia in March 2007 under the African Union Mission in Somalia, known as AMISOM. —AUSSOM allocation: Uganda is allocated 4,500 troops under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia. The mission began on 1 January 2025. Other allocations include Ethiopia with 2,500, Djibouti with 1,520, Kenya with 1,410 and Egypt with 1,091. —Bilateral presence: Uganda has about 2,000 more troops under a bilateral agreement signed with Mogadishu at the end of 2024. —New minister: Kiryowa Kiwanuka became Minister of Defence on 11 June 2026. He replaced Jacob Oboth-Oboth, who became Speaker of Parliament on 25 May 2026. —Cost of service: An al-Shabaab attack on 26 May 2023 killed 54 Ugandan peacekeepers at Bulo Marer. President Museveni announced the toll on 4 June 2023. —Exit plan: The AUSSOM communique of 31 July 2026 calls for a phased exit of the mission within 18 to 24 months.

Uganda is staying in Somalia, but the African Union mission is leaving. Minister of Defence Kiryowa Kiwanuka spoke on 15 August 2026.

He said the arrangement for Uganda’s presence “is going to evolve” as AUSSOM winds down.

Uganda announces it will maintain troops in Somalia (Photo: Internet reproduction)

Uganda stays as AU mission exits

“Uganda is going to remain in Somalia,” Kiwanuka said on 15 August 2026. He added that the structure of that presence will change, with troops increasingly under bilateral arrangements.

The trigger is Washington ending payments to UNSOS, the United Nations Support Office that provides AUSSOM’s logistics, by the end of 2026. AUSSOM launched on 1 January 2025 under UN Security Council Resolution 2767 of 27 December 2024.

Uganda has about 4,500 troops in AUSSOM, whose authorised strength is 11,900. It also keeps about 2,000 more under a bilateral agreement with Mogadishu signed in late 2024.

Kiwanuka is new in post, having taken office on 11 June 2026. He replaced Jacob Oboth-Oboth, who became Speaker of the 12th Parliament on 25 May 2026.

The phased exit of AUSSOM

On 26 January 2026, Uganda’s Chief of Defence Forces, General Muhoozi Kainerugaba. Posted that Uganda planned to withdraw “very soon” after 19 years.

Uganda then had 5,000 to 6,000 troops there.

Uganda hosted the AUSSOM Troop-Contributing Countries Extraordinary Summit from 29 to 31 July 2026 at Speke Resort Munyonyo in Kampala. The adopted communique on 31 July called for “an orderly, coordinated and phased exit of AUSSOM”.

Foreign ministers were directed to form a joint task force on predictable financing plus a donors’ conference. The communique also called for a unified integrated mission support capability for 18 to 24 months.

President Museveni said on 31 July that “Somalia is not going to be abandoned because of some other people outside”. On Western funding, he said: “The group of Western countries pulling out is not a problem.”

Historical context and costs

Uganda first deployed to Somalia in March 2007 under AMISOM. It has remained a major contributor ever since.

In April 2024, Deputy Head of Mission Nathan Mugisha said Uganda would remain “in whatever form” under UN Security Council Resolution 2719. That statement concerned the earlier ATMIS mission, not AUSSOM.

An al-Shabaab attack on 26 May 2023 at Bulo Marer killed 54 Ugandan peacekeepers. Museveni announced the death toll on 4 June 2023.

Burundi withdrew from AUSSOM over its allocation. Other contributors include Ethiopia, Djibouti, Kenya and Egypt.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many Ugandan troops are in Somalia? Uganda is allocated 4,500 troops under AUSSOM, with about 2,000 more under a bilateral agreement separate from the AU mission. When did Uganda first deploy troops to Somalia? Uganda first deployed troops to Somalia in March 2007 under the African Union Mission in Somalia, known as AMISOM. Is Uganda planning to withdraw from Somalia? No. Uganda is staying, but the AU mission is on a phased exit. The bilateral arrangement with Somalia will carry the presence forward.

World.title: Kenya Gold Bill Stalls at Committee Stage Since 2025
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Kenya · MINING

Key Facts —The bill: The Gold Processing Bill, 2023 is National Assembly Bill No. 46 of 2023. It is item 84 in the Assembly’s bills tracker as of 28 May 2026. —Central institution: The bill would create a gold processing corporation. It would license and regulate processing, smelting, fabrication, sampling, monitoring and transport. —Penalties: Working gold without a permit carries a maximum fine of Sh10 million. About US$77,400, or up to 10 years in jail, or both. A processing licence lasts 25 years initially, with renewals capped at 15 years. —Royalty split: Kenya’s existing mining framework splits royalties three ways. The national government takes 70 percent, counties 20 percent and local communities 10 percent. —Status: The bill completed its Second Reading on 27 February 2025. It has been stalled at the Committee of the Whole House stage for 18 months. —Obstruction offence: Clause 47 covers obstructing the Board or Corporation. The maximum is a fine of 500,000 shillings, about US$3,870, or five years in jail.

Kenya’s Gold Processing Bill, 2023 has stalled at the committee stage of the National Assembly for 18 months. The bill would create a dedicated legal regime for gold processing, licensing, smelting and transport.

It has not moved since completing its Second Reading in February 2025.

Gold Processing Bill stalled at committee stage in Kenya (Photo: Internet reproduction)

What the Gold Processing Bill actually does

The Gold Processing Bill, 2023 is formally National Assembly Bill No. 46 of 2023. It was published in Kenya Gazette Supplement No. 132 on 11 August 2023.

The bill seeks to establish a gold processing corporation to license and regulate the sector. Clause 4 covers collection, smelting, fabrication, sampling, registration, monitoring and transport of gold.

Clause 5(4) sets a maximum fine of ten million shillings, about US$77,400. Or up to ten years in jail, for exploring or exploiting gold without a permit.

Clause 35 allows an initial processing licence of 25 years, while Clause 43 caps any renewal at 15 years.

Why Kenya wants more control over gold

The bill’s logic aligns with the Mining Act, 2016, which regulates prospecting, mining, processing and transport of minerals. Royalties are shared 70 percent national government, 20 percent county government, and 10 percent local community.

Kenya has also updated mining governance with new regulations on health, safety and explosives licensing in 2026. The Gold Processing Bill fits into a broader effort to formalise the sector and make royalties and taxes easier to enforce.

What MPs said during debate

Sponsor Bernard Shinali, MP for Ikolomani, argued gold processing has boosted exports and revenue in other countries including Sudan. He spoke during the Second Reading on 20 February 2025.

Migori MP Fatuma Mohamed said licensing is prohibitive. With fees raised from 20,000 to 500,000 shillings, and applications taking up to four years.

No vote count is on the public record.

Parliamentary progress and current status

The bill had its First Reading on 18 October 2023. The Second Reading took place on 19, 26 and 27 February 2025.

The Committee of the Whole House stage is pending, and the Third Reading has not been put. The bill has not lapsed, but the Assembly returned from recess in late July 2026 with no movement recorded.

What to watch next on the Gold Processing Bill

The next milestone is the Committee of the Whole House stage, not presidential assent. After that come the Third Reading, possible transmission to the Senate, and then assent.

Clause 47 also proposes a fine not exceeding 500,000 shillings, about US$3,870. Or up to five years in jail, for obstructing the Board or Corporation.

The bill’s fate will determine whether Kenya captures more domestic value from gold.

What is the Gold Processing Bill in Kenya? The Gold Processing Bill, 2023 is National Assembly Bill No. 46 of 2023. It would create a legal framework for processing, licensing, smelting, transport and monitoring. What penalties does the Gold Processing Bill propose? Working gold without a permit carries a maximum fine of Sh10 million. About US$77,400, or up to 10 years in jail, or both. Obstructing the Board or Corporation carries a maximum fine of 500,000 shillings, about US$3,870, or up to five years. How are mining royalties shared in Kenya? Kenya’s existing mining framework splits royalties three ways. The national government takes 70 percent, counties 20 percent and local communities 10 percent.

World.title: Tunisia’s Grain Harvest Rebounds as Dams Refill
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Tunisia · AGRICULTURE

Key Facts —Recovery status: Tunisia is in its second year of recovery, with 2025 cereal production estimated at 1.7 million tonnes. That is nearly 18 percent above the five-year average. Per the Food and Agriculture Organization’s Global Information and Early Warning System on 18 February 2026. —2026 harvest: The Ministry of Agriculture targeted 22 million quintals from 991,000 hectares. By end-July 2026, over 10.752 million quintals were collected, hitting 98 percent of the campaign. —Soft wheat jump: Soft-wheat collection nearly doubled from 600,000 quintals in 2025 to 1.1 million in 2026. Durum stocks cover national needs to January 2027. —Import reliance: The Food and Agriculture Organization forecasts 2025/26 wheat imports at 2 million tonnes. That is 3 percent below average, covering about 55 percent of wheat demand. —Dam levels: Fill rates reached 57 percent on 24 March and 67 percent on 2 May. They stood at about 60 percent on 23 June 2026. This compares with 41 percent on 30 May 2025. —Infrastructure strain: Evaporation exceeds 1 million cubic metres daily in heat, against a 500,000 to 600,000 normal. A 59,000 km pipe network, mostly over 40 years old, adds pressure.

Tunisia’s cereal production is rebounding, but the real challenge is distribution, not drought. The 2026 story is about water loss and aging infrastructure, even as dams fill and harvests beat averages.

Tunisian farmers manage harvests amid infrastructure strain (Photo: Internet reproduction)

A Mediterranean recovery under pressure

The Food and Agriculture Organization reported on 18 February 2026 that Tunisia’s 2025 cereal production hit 1.7 million tonnes. The figure comes from its Global Information and Early Warning System.

This is nearly 18 percent above the five-year average.

January 2026 brought abundant rainfall that offset earlier deficits. The Ministry of Agriculture then targeted over 22 million quintals from about 991,000 hectares for 2026.

Harvest results beat expectations

By end-July 2026, more than 10.752 million quintals had been collected, hitting 98 percent of the campaign. The total harvest is estimated above 20 million quintals.

Soft-wheat collection nearly doubled, from 600,000 quintals in 2025 to 1.1 million in 2026. Durum stocks now cover national needs to January 2027.

The 2025 campaign collected 12 million quintals, so 2026 is down year-on-year. Still, production held above 20 million quintals in both years.

Distribution is the real 2026 challenge

Evaporation exceeded 1 million cubic metres a day in the late-June heat. The normal rate is 500,000 to 600,000 cubic metres daily.

The 59,000 km pipe network is largely more than 40 years old. Electricity cuts have hit 1,500 pumping stations and 1,200 deep wells.

Central dams such as Nebhana remain weak, while the north and Cap Bon did well. The Ministry’s Director General of Dams called the overall position “very reassuring”.

Import needs ease with recovery

The Food and Agriculture Organization forecasts 2025/26 wheat imports at about 2 million tonnes. That is roughly 3 percent below average, covering about 55 percent of wheat demand.

Total cereal imports were 4.1 million tonnes in 2024. This recovery contrasts with the 2023 trough, when drought forced heavier buying.

Water outlook brightens in 2026

Dam fill rates reached 57 percent on 24 March and 67 percent on 2 May. By 23 June, they stood at about 60 percent.

This contrasts with 41 percent on 30 May 2025. The improved position supports continued agricultural recovery.

What to watch next

Policy focus is on fixing the aging pipe network and securing power for pumping stations. Evaporation losses remain a key risk in summer heat.

Authorities are centralising water decisions, but local capacity is limited. Recovery is real, yet distribution bottlenecks could cap the gains.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Tunisia’s current harvest status? The 2026 harvest is estimated above 20 million quintals, with collection at 98 percent by end-July. Soft-wheat output nearly doubled to 1.1 million quintals. How much grain is Tunisia importing now? Wheat imports for 2025/26 are forecast at 2 million tonnes, about 3 percent below average. This covers roughly 55 percent of wheat demand. Are dams recovering in 2026? Dam fill rates reached 67 percent in early May and about 60 percent in late June 2026. This is a clear improvement from 41 percent in May 2025.

World.title: Ekurhuleni Toilet Tenders Paid US$99m to Limpopo Firms
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

South Africa · POLITICS

Key Facts —Contract value: The City of Ekurhuleni awarded a mobile chemical toilet tender worth about R1.8 billion, or US$111 million. It runs until 30 June 2028. —Beneficiaries: Two Limpopo firms, linked to Selby Manthata, are among the largest beneficiaries. Tebadi Collins Foromo’s company also benefited. —Decade of payments: The two Limpopo companies have collected more than R1.6 billion (about US$99 million) from Ekurhuleni since 2016. —Auditor killed: Mpho Mafole was Ekurhuleni’s Divisional Head for Forensic Audit. He was shot dead on 30 June 2025, days after submitting a probity report. —Murder charge: Thabani Ntshalintshali, 40, was charged with Mafole’s murder in July 2025. —Earlier case: Manthata was charged alongside Malema in 2012 but acquitted in 2014. No one has been charged over the Ekurhuleni tenders.

The Ekurhuleni toilet tenders have turned Selby Manthata into one of the largest beneficiaries of a R1.8 billion municipal sanitation contract. Neither Manthata nor another key figure, Tebadi Collins Foromo, has been charged with any offence arising from the tenders.

Selby Manthata is a former Malema business associate who was charged alongside him and acquitted (Photo: Internet reproduction)

From political associate to major contractor

Selby Manthata is a former Malema business associate who was charged alongside him in the On Point Engineering case and acquitted.

News24 describes Manthata as once close to Julius Malema. Malema leads the Economic Freedom Fighters, and Manthata was also close to former Limpopo premier Cassel Mathale.

News24 reported that two Limpopo companies have collected more than R1.6 billion from Ekurhuleni since 2016. That is about US$99 million.

The current contract cycle is worth about R1.8 billion and runs until 30 June 2028.

The On Point Engineering case

Manthata’s history with Malema stems from the Limpopo road tender scandals of the early 2010s, centred on On Point Engineering.

Both men were charged with corruption and money laundering in 2012.

The court record shows Oceanside Trading 777 CC paid R1 million to a conveyancer. That was about US$122,000 at the 2012 rate of 8.2 rand to the dollar.

It was part-payment for Farm Schuilkraal 632, for the benefit of the Ratanang Trust. Manthata was a signatory on the Oceanside account.

The court found the State proved nothing against Manthata.

He was acquitted in the Mokopane Regional Court on 26 March 2014, discharged at the close of the State’s case.

His wife Helen Moreroa and his brother were also acquitted.

The State appealed and lost. The Gauteng High Court in Pretoria dismissed the appeal on 22 January 2016, in S v Moreroa and Others, case A523/2015.

That court found irregularities tainted the tender process but that the State failed to prove its case.

Malema’s own case was struck off the roll in Polokwane on 4 August 2015.

The prosecuting authority declined to prosecute in November 2019.

A deadly audit and a murder charge

Mpho Mafole was Ekurhuleni’s Divisional Head for Forensic Audit, three months into the job.

He submitted a probity audit report on 26 June 2025 and was shot dead on 30 June 2025.

Eyewitness News reported the audit “could be” the reason for his killing.

A News24 journalist said: “We are not yet in a position to pronounce why he was killed.”

Thabani Ntshalintshali, 40, appeared in the Kempton Park Magistrate’s Court in July 2025 charged with Mafole’s murder.

He was on bail for another murder at the time.

A second suspect was reported at large.

The trial has been repeatedly delayed.

A cash cow with little oversight

A 2019 Daily Maverick and amaBhungane investigation characterised an earlier Ekurhuleni chemical toilet project as a black hole and cash cow.

It alleged that some companies had links to municipal officials and politicians, including then executive mayor Mzwandile Masina.

The investigation found serious lack of oversight, with companies making between R10 million and R42 million per year.

Ekurhuleni spent R1.9 billion on chemical toilets over three financial years from 2017 to 2019.

Theuwedi Trading Enterprise, with sole director Nakampe Aubrey Moliwa, took more than R100 million despite a registered address 400km away.

TTE and Moliwa tried to gag News24 and lost.

Judge Elmien du Plessis, Gauteng High Court Johannesburg, dismissed the application with costs on 2 May 2026.

On 29 June 2026 South Africa’s Press Council partly upheld a complaint by Phillip Rakgwale, Ekurhuleni’s Group Chief Audit Executive.

News24 was found to have breached press-code clauses for not disclosing it relied on a draft report.

News24 was ordered to apologise for singling Rakgwale out.

What to watch next

Opposition councillors in Ekurhuleni have called for the chemical toilet tender to be withdrawn or re-tendered.

The Democratic Alliance has demanded full publication of Mpho Mafole’s probity audit.

The contract runs until 30 June 2028, keeping the R1.8 billion framework in the spotlight.

Any criminal investigation into Mafole’s assassination could draw fresh attention to the tender process.

Frequently Asked Questions

He is one of the largest beneficiaries of Ekurhuleni’s chemical toilet contracts. How much money has Ekurhuleni paid to Manthata’s companies? Two Limpopo companies linked to Manthata have collected more than R1.6 billion from Ekurhuleni since 2016. The current contract cycle is worth about R1.8 billion. What happened to the auditor who investigated the toilet tender? Mpho Mafole was shot dead on 30 June 2025, days after submitting a probity audit report. Thabani Ntshalintshali was charged with his murder in July 2025.

Note Neither Selby Manthata nor Tebadi Collins Foromo has been charged with any offence arising from the Ekurhuleni tenders. No arrests and no prosecuting-authority action are on the public record.

World.title: Argentina LNG Export Deal With Germany Is Now Binding
World.content:
Argentina · Energy

Key Facts Binding contract: SESA and SEFE signed a Sales and Purchase Agreement on 4 March 2026.

SESA and SEFE signed a Sales and Purchase Agreement on 4 March 2026. First deal: It is Argentina’s first long-term LNG export contract — a framework deal came first, on 1 December 2025.

It is Argentina’s first long-term LNG export contract — a framework deal came first, on 1 December 2025. Volume agreed: 2 million tonnes of LNG a year, for eight years, from late 2027.

2 million tonnes of LNG a year, for eight years, from late 2027. Seven billion: The US$7 billion figure is an estimated revenue total over eight years — not a guaranteed price.

The US$7 billion figure is an estimated revenue total over eight years — not a guaranteed price. Floating plants: Two ships will chill the gas at sea in the Golfo San Matias, off Rio Negro.

Two ships will chill the gas at sea in the Golfo San Matias, off Rio Negro. Ship moving: The Hilli Episeyo left Cameroon on 4 August 2026 for a refit in Singapore.

The Hilli Episeyo left Cameroon on 4 August 2026 for a refit in Singapore. Dollar case: Argentina’s energy trade surplus hit US$5.076 billion in the first half of 2026.

Germany lost Russian pipeline gas and went shopping. It found a seller in Patagonia that has not loaded a single export cargo yet.

Argentina has signed its first long-term contract to export LNG, and it is binding rather than a statement of intent. The buyer is SEFE, the gas company owned by the German state.

Argentina has signed its first long-term LNG export contract, with deliveries due from late 2027. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What Was Actually Signed, and When

The seller is Southern Energy S.A., known as SESA. It is an Argentine consortium put together in 2024.

Its shareholders, as reported by industry press, are Pan American Energy with 30% and YPF with 25%. Pampa Energia holds 20%, Harbour Energy 15% and Golar LNG 10%.

The buyer is SEFE Securing Energy for Europe, a company owned by the German state. It is the former Gazprom Germania, which Berlin took over in 2022.

Step one was a Heads of Agreement, signed on 1 December 2025. That is a framework deal — it sets the terms but still needs a final contract.

Step two was the binding Sales and Purchase Agreement. Trade press dated the signature to 4 March 2026.

So this is not a memorandum of understanding, and it is not a letter of intent. It is a signed, enforceable sales contract for LNG — natural gas chilled to liquid so it can travel by ship.

The US$7 Billion Figure, Handled With Care

You will see this reported as a US$7 billion deal. That number needs a caveat, and it needs it up front.

It is an estimate of total export revenue across the whole eight-year term. It is not annual revenue, and it is not the money being invested in the project.

The original Spanish wording said the contract “could generate revenue above US$7 billion over its life”. Then it added the crucial condition — depending on how international prices move.

The pricing formula has not been made public. Nobody outside the deal knows whether the price tracks Brent oil, Asian spot gas or European hub gas.

So treat US$7 billion as a working estimate, not a guaranteed sum.

How the Gas Gets to the Sea

The volume is 2 million tonnes of LNG a year, sold on FOB terms. That means the buyer takes the cargo at the loading point and arranges its own shipping.

The gas comes from Vaca Muerta, the shale formation in Neuquen province. It will travel about 500 km east on a new dedicated pipeline, the San Matias Pipeline.

That pipeline’s approved regulatory plan showed construction starting on 30 June 2026. Operations were estimated to begin on 1 May 2028.

The liquefaction happens at sea rather than on land. Two floating plants will sit in the Golfo San Matias, off Punta Colorada in Rio Negro province.

Ship one is the Hilli Episeyo — 2.45 million tonnes a year, on a 20-year charter, producing from late 2027. Ship two is the MKII unit, named Esperanza by owner Golar LNG, at 3.5 million tonnes a year from late 2028.

Together that is roughly 6 million tonnes a year. It is a large step for a country that exports no LNG today.

The only earlier exports were a handful of one-off cargoes from a small floating unit called Tango, at Bahia Blanca. Those shipped in 2019 and 2020, and that unit no longer operates in Argentina.

Where Things Stand in August 2026

Golar LNG, the owner of both floating plants, published interim results on 13 August 2026. The Hilli Episeyo delivered its final Cameroon cargo on 26 July 2026, after eight years and 156 cargoes.

It left Cameroonian waters on 4 August 2026, helped by two tugs. It is bound for Seatrium’s shipyard in Singapore for upgrades and life-extension work.

Golar has budgeted US$350 million for that refit, the repositioning, fuel, crew and insurance. The budget runs from August 2026 to the start of commercial operations in Argentina, in the second half of 2027.

Of that sum, US$71 million had been spent by 30 June 2026. Golar expects the Argentina contract to earn about US$285 million a year in operating profit, before any gain from higher commodity prices.

The second ship, Esperanza, was 74% complete at the end of the second quarter of 2026. Golar says it is on schedule and on budget, with a conversion budget of about US$2.2 billion.

Sail-away for Esperanza is targeted by the end of 2027. Production follows in the second half of 2028.

Why This Matters for Investors

Argentina is chronically short of hard currency. Energy exports have become one of its most dependable sources of dollars.

INDEC, the national statistics agency, reported a fuels and energy trade surplus of US$5.076 billion in the first half of 2026. That was up from US$3.139 billion a year earlier — a rise of 61.7%.

Energy exports in that half-year reached US$6.594 billion, up 42.5%. The main driver was a 47.7% jump in crude oil shipments, and energy imports came to US$1.518 billion.

Argentina’s total goods trade surplus for the same six months was US$13.923 billion. LNG matters because it turns Vaca Muerta gas into a year-round dollar export.

Today that gas is boxed in — the domestic market is small and demand swings with the seasons. Shipping it abroad breaks that ceiling.

That conversion is the heart of the Vaca Muerta investment case. It is also why outside money keeps arriving, as Peter Thiel’s stake in Vista Energy showed.

Be honest about the timing, though. None of this LNG revenue arrives before late 2027, and the eight-year estimate rests on prices nobody can fix today.

Do Not Confuse This With the Bigger Project

A separate and far larger plan is also moving. YPF, Italy’s Eni and XRG filed a project called Argentina LNG under RIGI, the country’s big-investment incentive regime, around 13 August 2026.

That one carries a US$51 billion investment figure and targets 12 million tonnes a year by 2031. YPF chairman Horacio Marin said on 14 August 2026 that Argentina “will export US$10 billion per year from 2031”.

It is a different project on a much later timetable. Eni is not a party to the German contract.

SESA is reported to hold a 30-year LNG export licence and Strategic Investment status under RIGI. SEFE, meanwhile, has been seeking up to US$2.35 billion in fresh capital.

That raise could open the door to partly privatising Argentina’s first European LNG buyer.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Argentina-Germany LNG deal signed or just an intention? It is signed and binding. SESA and SEFE agreed a Heads of Agreement on 1 December 2025, then signed the binding Sales and Purchase Agreement in early March 2026. It is Argentina’s first long-term LNG export contract. What does the US$7 billion figure actually refer to? It is an estimate of total export revenue over the full eight-year term, based on price assumptions at the time. It is not annual revenue, not a fixed contract price, and not the investment in the project. The pricing formula has not been disclosed. When do the first LNG cargoes leave Argentina? Deliveries are due to begin in late 2027, from the Hilli Episeyo floating plant in the Golfo San Matias. No exact first-cargo date has been made public. Who owns Southern Energy S.A.? Industry press reports the shareholders as Pan American Energy with 30%, YPF with 25%, Pampa Energia with 20%, Harbour Energy with 15% and Golar LNG with 10%. Those percentages come from industry reporting rather than a corporate filing.

World.title: Argentina Public Works Funds: US$3 Billion Held Back
World.content:
Argentina · Fiscal Policy

Key Facts Headline number: About US$3 billion left unspent in national trust funds during 2024 and 2025.

About US$3 billion left unspent in national trust funds during 2024 and 2025. Road fund: SISVIAL took in ARS 1.503 trillion (about US$1.01 billion) and spent 26.2% of it on roads.

SISVIAL took in ARS 1.503 trillion (about US$1.01 billion) and spent 26.2% of it on roads. Parked cash: ARS 1.001 trillion (about US$673 million) of road money sat in bonds and deposits on May 31, 2026.

ARS 1.001 trillion (about US$673 million) of road money sat in bonds and deposits on May 31, 2026. Government line: Luis Caputo calls the reports a political smear and says roughly 40% of the money is already spent.

Luis Caputo calls the reports a political smear and says roughly 40% of the money is already spent. Court status: A criminal complaint was filed on August 10, 2026 — no judge, no charges, no findings.

A criminal complaint was filed on August 10, 2026 — no judge, no charges, no findings. Fiscal record: Argentina booked a ARS 3.81 trillion (about US$2.56 billion) bottom-line surplus from January to July 2026.

Argentina’s surplus is real. The fight is over how much of it was earned by saving — and how much by simply not building.

Argentina’s government has piled up about US$3 billion inside funds meant to pay for roads and water works. The cash came from earmarked taxes — then went into Treasury paper rather than concrete.

Argentina’s trust funds collected earmarked taxes faster than they spent them. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the US$3 Billion Actually Measures

Argentina runs dozens of trust funds, known locally as fondos fiduciarios. Each is a pot of money fed by a specific tax and reserved by law for one job.

One pays to patch highways. Another subsidises household gas bills.

The US$3 billion is what those funds had left over across 2024 and 2025. It is what they collected minus what they actually spent on their legal purpose.

The 2024 leftover was ARS 1.86 trillion (about US$1.98 billion at that year’s average rate). The 2025 leftover was ARS 1.23 trillion (about US$973 million).

Add them and you get roughly US$2.95 billion, rounded by the press to about US$3 billion. Each year was converted at its own official rate, not today’s.

This is not the whole public-works budget, and it is not a court finding. It is also not all of Argentina’s capital spending.

Capital spending is the money a state puts into new roads, dams and buildings. The trust funds are only one channel for it.

Who Counted It

The trail starts with La Nacion reporter Hugo Alconada Mon. He obtained the road fund’s accounts in early August and found most of the cash unspent.

LMDiario put the US$3 billion headline on it on August 16, citing official spreadsheets. Clarin ran the same figure that day, sourced to the Instituto Consenso Federal.

That institute is run by former congressman Alejandro “Topo” Rodriguez, a Peronist opponent of the government. So the headline number is an opposition reading of official data.

No Treasury table breaks the sum down fund by fund. Across all the trusts, 55.8% of the money collected was spent in 2024, and 69.5% in 2025.

The Road Fund at the Centre

The clearest case is SISVIAL, the national road fund created by decree in 2001. It lives off a slice of the tax on liquid fuels.

Between December 2023 and May 2026 it collected ARS 1.503 trillion (about US$1.01 billion). It spent ARS 394,406 million (about US$265 million) on actual road works.

That is 26.2% of the intake. Spending ran at 11.3% in 2024, 39% in 2025 and 18.5% in the first five months of 2026.

On May 31 the fund held ARS 1.001 trillion (about US$673 million) in financial investments. More than 85% of that sat in government bonds such as Boncap and Lecap.

Another ARS 37,761 million (about US$25 million) lay idle in a current account. Because the holdings are mostly Treasury paper, the road fund is in effect lending to the Treasury.

The water works fund tells the same story. On April 6 it held ARS 258,000 million (about US$173 million) in short-term Treasury notes — 88% of its assets.

Caputo’s Answer, and the Fiscal Record

Economy Minister Luis Caputo calls the whole thing “una operacion” — a political smear. He spoke in Cordoba on August 12.

He said: “That was already voted in Congress, it is in the budget, and we are on the way to delivering it.”

About 40% of the infrastructure money has been spent, Caputo added. He expects that to reach roughly 70% within two months.

No governor has complained to him, the minister says. A working group with governors and transport officials picks which projects get built.

Presidential spokesman Adrian Ravier was blunter. He could not say how much fuel-tax money reaches road maintenance.

Part of it, Ravier said, is directed by the Economy Ministry to help achieve fiscal balance. “Of course the law is being complied with,” he added.

That is the zero-deficit rule in practice — the promise that the state will not spend more than it takes in. Roads, Ravier argued, should increasingly be paid for by private investors.

The surplus itself is real. In July alone Argentina posted a primary surplus of ARS 4.79 trillion (about US$3.22 billion).

A primary surplus is what is left over before paying interest on the debt. After interest, July still ended ARS 4.47 trillion (about US$3.00 billion) ahead.

For January to July the primary surplus reached ARS 13.46 trillion (about US$9.04 billion), up 4.1% on the year. After interest it was ARS 3.81 trillion (about US$2.56 billion), down 26.8%.

Here is the awkward comparison. The US$3 billion built up in the trusts over two years is roughly the size of that whole seven-month bottom line.

The periods do not match, so it is not a like-for-like swap. It does show how much of the cushion comes from money that was not spent.

What the Complaint Does and Does Not Prove

On August 10 opposition congresswoman Victoria Tolosa Paz filed a criminal complaint in Buenos Aires federal court. It names Caputo, ministry and roads-agency officials, and Banco de la Nacion as trustee.

She alleges misuse of public funds. Tax money with “a specific and irrevocable destination” was “placed massively in financial instruments”, her filing says.

The complaint is days old. There is no case number, no named judge, no charges and no court finding.

Filing a complaint in Argentina is easy and settles nothing. Keep the two claims apart.

That the money was collected and not spent on roads is documented, and the government does not deny it. That it was illegally diverted is an untested allegation.

Opposition senators want to summon Caputo and Chief of Staff Diego Santilli. Decree 215/2024 handed the Economy Ministry control of every trust fund holding state money.

Why This Matters for Investors and Provinces

Argentina’s bond story rests on whether the surplus lasts. A surplus built partly on not building is easier to reverse than one built on permanent savings.

Deferred maintenance is a bill, not a saving. Potholed highways raise freight costs for grain, mining and energy — the exports foreign money is buying.

Provinces feel it first, and governors control votes in Congress. Milei needs those votes to keep his programme alive.

There is one more wrinkle for bondholders. When earmarked funds buy Treasury paper, the state is partly financing itself with its own reserved cash.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is an Argentine trust fund, or fideicomiso? It is a pot of public money fed by a specific tax and reserved by law for one job. Examples include repairing national highways or subsidising household gas bills. What exactly does the US$3 billion figure measure? It is the leftover in Argentina’s national trust funds across 2024 and 2025 — money collected under earmarked taxes but not spent on its legal purpose. It is not the whole public-works budget. Has anyone been charged with a crime? No. A criminal complaint was filed on August 10, 2026, but there is no case number, no charges and no court finding. The government says it is following the budget Congress voted. Why should an investor outside Argentina care? Because the durability of the surplus underpins the bond story. Roads and water systems that go unmaintained also raise costs later for farm, mining and energy exports.

Sources: Clarin – Trust funds under scrutiny: opposition says Economy piled up over US$3 billion; La Nacion – Government collected ARS 1.5 trillion for roads and spent barely a quarter; Telefe Cordoba – Caputo defended the works funds and denied delays in execution; Clarin – Tolosa Paz files complaint against Luis Caputo over ARS 1 trillion earmarked for road works; Infobae – Ravier backs Sturzenegger and addresses the fuel tax controversy; La Gaceta – Milei government collected ARS 1.5 trillion for road works but put over ARS 1 trillion into financial investments; LMDiario – Government retained some US$3 billion of works funds to feed the zero deficit; Agenda Salta – July closed with a bottom-line surplus after a sharp spending cut; Reporte del Valle – National government withheld funds destined for roads and water infrastructure

World.title: Family Demands Answers on Missing Political Prisoners in Nicaragua
World.content:
Relatives of a retired military officer and his wife, who were detained a year ago in Nicaragua, demanded Saturday that the government of Daniel Ortega and Rosario Murillo provide information about their whereabouts and health amid fears they could die in prison. Retired Colonel Carlos Brenes, 71, and his wife, Salvadora Martínez, 68, were detained last August, during police raids in the cities of Carazo and Masaya, in which several other people were also arrested, Thelma Brenes, the retired officer’s daughter, said.

“They have a duty to tell us where they are, how they are doing and to return them to us alive,” Brenes said from exile. Human rights organizations and relatives of detainees who maintain a search mechanism say that as of the end of July, there were 60 political prisoners in Nicaragua, 23 of whom were considered victims of enforced disappearance.

They warn that 15 are older adults, including Brenes and Martínez. Brenes’ daughter said the family fears a repeat of the case of leader Brooklyn Rivera, who died in May while in state custody after nearly three years without any information about his whereabouts.

She said her father, who was imprisoned between 2018 and 2019 and released under an amnesty, suffers from diabetes, high blood pressure and mobility problems. She also said Nicaragua’s prison system does not provide political prisoners with the medical care they need.

She also denounced what she described as a pattern of “detention by association” in Nicaragua, in which relatives of government opponents are also arrested, as she said happened with Martínez, her stepmother. Ortega and his wife Murillo, who holds the title of co-president, tightened their control over Nicaraguan society following the 2018 protests, whose repression left more than 300 people dead, according to the United Nations.

Opposition figures say Murillo is carrying out an internal purge across state institutions in preparation for the possible death of Ortega, who suffers from lupus and kidney failure. The government’s offensive against its opponents has also included a constitutional reform aimed at excluding opposition parties from elections. It is scheduled to be put to a vote in early September.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Route 32 Reopens After a Morning Landslide Shuts the Highway
World.content:
If you are driving to the Caribbean today, Route 32 is open. It was not open this morning, and the conditions that closed it have not gone anywhere. The Ministry of Public Works and Transportation shut the highway shortly after 9 a.m. this morning, when material came down onto the road. Crews cleared it and the ministry restored traffic at 1:39 p.m., about four hours later.

No reopening time was given while the road was shut. That is standard, and it is not the authorities being cagey with you. Nobody can estimate a reopening until crews reach the site, see how much material came down and confirm the slope above it has stopped moving.

If the next closure catches you, you have three ways around. Route 10, between Siquirres and Turrialba, takes any vehicle. So does the Bajos de Chilamate-Vuelta de Kooper corridor. Vara Blanca is open to light vehicles only, so leave the loaded pickup and the heavy SUV off it.

All three add real time to the trip, and all three get crowded fast when Route 32 goes down. Build in the extra hours before you leave rather than discovering them at the Zurquí backup. The reason this keeps happening sits in the terrain. Route 32 climbs through Braulio Carrillo National Park on a stretch cut between steep, forested slopes, and the ground there has been saturated for weeks.

Once soil is that wet, it stops absorbing rain and starts sliding. It does not take a downpour to bring rock, mud and whole trees onto the lanes. A moderate shower on already-soaked ground will do it.

That is exactly the pattern today. Tropical Wave No. 32 crossed the country this morning with the Intertropical Convergence Zone sitting overhead, and the Caribbean slope and Northern Zone are under a yellow alert because of it. Six-hour rainfall totals of 20 to 50 millimeters (0.8 to 2 inches) were forecast for the region, with localized peaks near 75 millimeters (3 inches) in the mountains.

So check the road right before you leave, not the night before. A highway that reopens at lunchtime can be shut again by dinner, and the status you saw yesterday tells you almost nothing about the status now.

Road updates go out on the ministry’s social media as they happen rather than on a fixed schedule, which is worth knowing if you are used to checking a website and assuming silence means the road is fine. Today’s closure also landed on a holiday. Saturday is Mother’s Day, a mandatory-pay national holiday, which puts far more cars on the road than an ordinary weekend and makes every alternate route slower than the map suggests.

This is at least the second time this month the highway has been cut. It closed on the evening of August 5 and stayed shut into the following morning, and it went down repeatedly in July during the flooding that followed Tropical Wave No. 24.

Route 32 is the only fast link between the Central Valley and Limón, and it carries commuters, tour buses and the freight moving to and from the ports at Moín. When it shuts, the cost lands on everyone at once, which is why a four-hour closure counts as a good outcome here.

Green season runs to November, and the slopes above this road will keep giving way until the ground dries out. The realistic answer is not to avoid the Caribbean but to treat the drive as something to time rather than assume.

World.title: The Panama Canal Opened 112 Years Ago Today
World.content:
Twelve years of digging, an estimated 27,500 deaths and roughly $375 million ended quietly on the morning of August 15, 1914, when a single steamship slipped into a lock chamber on Panama’s Caribbean coast and began climbing a staircase of water.

The SS Ancon, a cargo and passenger vessel of the Panama Railroad Company, left Cristóbal at Colón and reached the Pacific port of Balboa about nine hours later. It was the first official transit of the Panama Canal, and it joined the Atlantic and Pacific for the first time in human history.

The ship covered roughly 80 kilometers (50 miles). Electric towing locomotives, still known as mules, guided it through the three chambers of the Gatún Locks, lifting it about 26 meters (85 feet) above sea level and into Gatún Lake.

From there the Ancon crossed the lake and entered the Culebra Cut, the narrow slot carved through the continental divide and the deadliest, most unstable stretch of the entire project. Landslides had swallowed months of work there. On that morning the ship passed through without incident, dropped down through the Pedro Miguel and Miraflores locks, and reached the Pacific.

Chief engineer George W. Goethals, the U.S. Army officer who had driven the project to completion, watched much of it from a railcar running alongside the ship. Senior canal pilot John A. Constantine had the helm.

What was missing was the celebration. Panama had planned an international fleet review, with warships gathering off Virginia and steaming through the new canal to San Francisco for the Panama-Pacific International Exposition. The First World War had begun in Europe two weeks earlier, and the fleet never sailed. The opening of one of the largest engineering projects ever attempted went almost unnoticed outside the isthmus.

The Ancon was not, strictly speaking, the first vessel through. A French-built crane boat, the Alexandre La Valley, had worked its way across in stages during construction and reached the Pacific on January 7, 1914. The Ancon’s sister ship, the Cristóbal, carried a load of cement through on August 3. But the Ancon’s run was the ceremonial one, the transit that opened the waterway to commercial traffic.

The change it produced was immediate and permanent. Ships moving between the east and west coasts of the Americas had until then rounded Cape Horn or threaded the Strait of Magellan, adding thousands of kilometers and weeks of sailing to every voyage, along with some of the worst weather on the planet. The canal erased that detour overnight and cut freight costs across two oceans.
