World.title: Exclusive: Brussels keen to monitor UFOs under the radar
World.content:
The European Commission seems to have been monitoring unidentified aerial phenomena (UAP) under the radar since at least 2023, according to a document from the Commission's defence department seen by Euronews, which pertains to sky and space observations in Malaysia.

 

"We are getting better at seeing it (UAPs) and better identifying it as our technological capacities improve, but we need to get even better," the letter read, signalling the EU executive is actively monitoring the phenomenon more than officially stated and seems keen to investigate it.

Formerly known as unidentified flying objects (UFOs), the term UAP was introduced by the United States defence department, the Pentagon, in August 2020, when Washington established the ⁠UAP Task Force to investigate inexplicable occurrences in restricted airspace.

The topic took on a more serious tone after a New York Times report revealed in 2017 that the US defence department files contained UAP footage from military flights that the US Navy had released.

Euronews also identified a Malaysian father and son — amateur astronomers internationally recognised by space agencies for their discoveries of the surfaces and activities on the moon in 2020 — who reached out to the Commission with a letter titled "UAP captures in the airspace and deep space using our UV infrared telescope" in October 2022.

The family duo sent 37 sky and space footage images to the Commission, including alleged UAPs, and asked President Ursula von der Leyen about their origins.

They noted that "all governments simply have no opinions" of these UAPs when confronted about them, and said they appear to be flying "very near to aircraft and important targets, such as military and nuclear facilities".

"We have also detected various signals from up above through the local networks Wi-Fi frequency," the Malaysian duo wrote.

Since these UAPs were spotted over Malaysia, the Commission would have no authority to investigate the matter, the EU executive responded.

However, the Commission said it would propose to its 27 member states to "increase its ability to detect objects in the space environment around the Earth".

"This is partly to help us better identify the UAPs that you have seen and the many pieces of space debris that endanger the many uses of space," the Commission said.

"We do not claim that in the future this will solve all cases like those you have reported, but maybe some of them."

The Malaysian amateur astronomers also reached out to NASA, the director general of the Malaysian Nuclear Agency, Abdul Rahim Harun, the Malaysian Ministry of Science, Technology & Innovation and the Canadian Defense Ministry. All entities politely shunned the appeal.

Former Canadian MP Larry Maguire, who was also approached individually by the Malaysians, encouraged the pair.

"I suspect that more and more people around the world will be turning their attention to the skies and will be collecting even more data and recordings in the coming year," Maguire wrote in an email in June 2022, seen by Euronews.

"At the end of the day, the skies aren't classified, and as more information is collected, it will lead to more public awareness of the issue."

US landmark Congress hearing

A landmark US Congress UAP hearing, hosted by the House Oversight Committee's National Security Subcommittee, took place on 26 July 2023. The hearing focused on national security implications and explosive allegations of classified government programmes that retrieve and reverse-engineer UAPs, according to the US government.

The change in designation, from UFO to UAP, was meant to kill the stigma associated with UFOs and more exotic theories that have circulated for decades, and to widen the scope of the phenomena.

In the EU, discussions about the topic remain limited and subject to stigma. This starkly contrasts with countries such as the US, which has released several confidential files in recent years. Most recently, it established a UAP Science Council chaired by Avi Loeb, a theoretical physicist who specialises in astrophysics and cosmology at Harvard University.

Harvard physicist Avi Loeb, left, listens as former NASA astronaut Dr. Mae C. Jemison speaks during a press conference, April 12, 2016, in New York. AP Photo / Bebeto Matthews

France is the only EU country with a dedicated, state-funded UAP monitoring and investigation centre: the Study Group and Information on Non-Identified Aerospace Phenomena, more commonly known as GEIPAN.

Since its inception in 1977, GEIPAN has analysed over 3,300 UAP cases. Exactly 106 investigations have been classified as unexplained after thorough analysis. Another 1,014 cases are unresolved due to insufficient data to conduct a proper investigation.

On 29 June, the French Parliament held a major discussion on UAPs. The debate centred on UAP research, work on UAPs by GEIPAN and the French Air and Space Force, and potentially liaising with the US to garner “responses from public authorities”.

“We want to move beyond sensationalism and fantasies and instead address, in a serious and rational way, an issue that is generating significant interest,” French MP Arnaud Saint-Martin, who has a background in aerospace and astronautics, told Le Parisien.

Flight safety concerns

Over the past decades, several EU lawmakers have questioned the Commission about the phenomena, more recently raising flight safety concerns as reports of pilot sightings increase.

These safety concerns gained momentum after several US congressional hearings featured testimony from military pilots describing "unexplainable" flying behaviour that defied the laws of physics.

In 2025 and 2026, MEP Fabio De Masi (Germany/Non-attached) asked the Commission several times to review and update EU aviation reporting systems to introduce a dedicated and standardised reporting category for UAP incidents. This would ensure consistency, data integrity and higher standards of flight safety across EU countries.

The plea has also been raised by pilots who argue that the lack of standardised reporting protocols for UAP encounters hampers data collection and risk mitigation.

Brazilian commercial airline pilot Gerson Macial de Britto sketches the object he said accompanied his VASP Airlines jet for 1 hour 20 minutes, at a news conference, in 1982. AP

They argue that sudden appearances of UAPs may lead to a loss of situational awareness or to emergency manoeuvres, fearing that the phenomena could temporarily cause malfunctions in aircraft sensors and communication systems.

Rob Akkermans, a commercial pilot working for a Dutch airline, spoke to Euronews about his experiences over the past 35 years. The first was in the early 1990s and the last two in 2023 and 2024.

"We, two pilots and four cabin crew members, were on a flight in 2023 from the Middle East to the Netherlands. For over two hours, starting around 19:30 UTC, we witnessed this strange phenomenon, which we found truly remarkable," Akkermans told Euronews, noting that all six crew members viewed the scene from the cockpit.

"It began while we were south of Cyprus. Precisely on a heading of 300 degrees (Magnetic North) — at an elevation of roughly 25 to 30 degrees and at a very high altitude — we saw a light flare up intensely and then slowly fade out. Subsequently, this occurred more frequently, often accompanied by one or two other lights that would also flare up and fade," the Dutchman explained.

"The most bizarre aspect was that one of the three lights would sometimes manoeuvre around the others. It resembled a chase — what air forces call 'dogfighting' — after which two or all three of them would fade out again," he said.

"Initially, we thought it might be a mission over the Balkans, but upon reaching the Balkans, we witnessed the same spectacle — still on the same heading, at the same angle, and at a very high altitude. After approximately 21:30 UTC, the lights suddenly vanished with incredible speed, and we did not see it again," he added.

Akkermans said that the following day, one of his colleagues witnessed the same from his back garden in the Netherlands.

The Dutch pilot said that after his experiences, he felt "a mix of wonder and surprise because what I saw was completely unexplainable," saying that such an experience "never truly leaves you".

But that excitement quickly turned into a distraction during the flight.

"Emotionally, the worrying part to deal with was frustration and concern over the stigma. You are forced to carry this experience in silence, worrying far more about the professional consequences of the taboo than the actual safety risk you just witnessed," he said.

Related Fighter jet tracks UFO in newly released Pentagon footage

Christiaan van Heijst, 43, a Boeing 747 captain with over 20 years of commercial flying experience, shared with Euronews four experiences he had between 2005 and 2010. Two of them were particularly noteworthy.

His second sighting, in Greece in 2005, probably on the island of Mykonos, was late in the evening.

"After landing at night, we made a 180° turn on the runway, and during the turn we saw a bright light appearing in the sky at extremely high altitude. It moved instantly, disappeared, appeared again, moved roughly the same distance, disappeared again — about three times," the Dutch pilot told Euronews.

"Before it appeared roughly two times that distance and instantly shot off at instant and unbelievable speed, without acceleration: just instant speed and it was gone from sight."

Van Heijst noted that the US Carrier Strike Group 2 with the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier was passing by in the Mediterranean on its way to the Persian Gulf that night for the Second Gulf War.

"This was mentioned in airspace closure (NOTAMS) as well (...) Unknown if these events are connected," van Heijst said.

His fourth sighting took place during a flight with a 737 from Amsterdam to Málaga in the late afternoon of 23 January 2010.

UAP Coalition Netherlands / Christiaan van Heijst UAP Coalition Netherlands / Christiaan van Heijst

"We noticed a certain object far ahead of us showing a rounded rectangular shape as if we were looking in the rear side of a contrail. But we were flying at 41,000 feet and there is hardly any commercial and/or military traffic above us at these altitudes," van Heijst said.

"While still flying in the north of Spain, we asked Madrid Air Traffic Control if there was any known traffic ahead and above us. They told us there was no traffic at all, and wondered why we asked. So, we told them we saw an object far ahead of us and rather large," he added.

"We were just casually wondering what it was. He immediately asked us to contact the military air traffic control frequency and tell them what we saw. Military air traffic control was prompt, interested and took serious note of all we saw," the Dutch pilot continued.

"Military air traffic control confirmed there was no other traffic at all, all the way down to Morocco — no military activity, no commercial traffic, no weather balloons, nothing. We saw the stationary object all the time for an hour at least, until we descended into the clouds over Málaga, far to the south of the Iberian peninsula," he added.

While van Heijst said he felt "no emotional response to any of those sightings", he emphasised that if something is present in the airspace and authorities are unable to identify it, then "first and foremost it is a safety issue and not science fiction".

Related Declassified Pentagon UFO footage shows unexplained aerial phenomena

Joachim Dekkers is the founder and chairperson of the UAP Coalition Netherlands, a foundation that supports professionals who have encountered UAP. He said the greatest threat to European flight safety is the silence caused by stigma. This means that 90% of pilot sightings go unreported.

"Without a dedicated UAP category in aviation safety systems, flight crews are forced to misclassify critical data. The EU cannot maintain global leadership in aviation safety while ignoring a reality other major powers measure," Dekkers told Euronews.

"We must normalise UAP reporting across member states to guarantee total sovereignty and airspace transparency."

Although no conclusive evidence links UAPs to foreign adversaries, the possibility that some UAPs represent advanced espionage technology, such as drones, cannot be dismissed.

But MEP De Masi countered this argument. He said that neither the EU Commission nor the Council claims to possess specific evidence on the origin of these airspace incursions.

"This is quite astonishing given surveillance of airspace and critical infrastructure. Either our airspace is vulnerable, and we have a major flight safety and security risk, or the EU is misleading public opinion," De Masi told Euronews.

"Either way, it is imperative to create more transparency and remove stigma around the UAP issue and follow international efforts to create better reporting systems. This is not about green little men but the safety of our airspace and the vested interests of the military-industrial complex and national intelligence services," he added.

Reporting gap?

Despite several calls to include a standardised category for UAP reporting, the European Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) said it already provides a framework for reporting "any occurrence that may have an impact on aviation safety", including UAPs.

"Pilots and other aviation personnel are encouraged to report anything they consider to represent a potential safety risk, regardless of its nature," EASA told Euronews. The agency dismissed pilots' requests to designate a UAP-specific category, instead of a miscellaneous incidents category.

EASA assesses incidents based on available evidence and the potential impact on aviation safety, the agency said.

"At present, EASA has not identified evidence indicating that reports of UAP represent a systemic aviation safety issue requiring additional measures," it added.

However, some safety advocates suggest EASA's lack of evidence may stem from a reporting gap rather than an absence of events.

In the Netherlands, the Dutch Safety Board has stepped in to accept UAP reports from flight crews under a general category. Germany's Federal Aviation Office has also engaged in scientific research on the topic.

Without a standardised central database, advocates say, these localised insights remain fragmented, leaving the European agency with an incomplete picture of airspace anomalies.

Nuclear power plants

The plot thickens when UAPs are widely reported near nuclear facilities.

A 2015 French economic study confirmed that sightings of unexplained phenomena in France correlate with proximity to atomic sites. One such site is the ⁠La Hague reprocessing plant, where large quantities of highly radioactive materials are stored before and after reprocessing.

Similarly, incidents in the UK, such as the 1993 sightings over the ⁠Hartlepool nuclear power station and the infamous 1980 Rendlesham Forest incident near the RAF Bentwaters nuclear storage bunkers, have long fuelled public speculation.

UAP sightings have been associated with US nuclear facilities since the 1940s. Military personnel have reported unexplained objects near nuclear missile silos, weapons storage sites and nuclear power plants.

One of the most well-known cases occurred in 1967 at Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana, where former US Air Force officers claimed that a UAP was observed near missile silos just before several nuclear missiles became temporarily inoperable.

Similar incidents have been reported at other military installations, including Minot Air Force Base and sites in the southwestern United States.

While many witnesses consider these events significant, no conclusive evidence has been found to establish the origin or nature of the objects involved. The US government is currently investigating UAP reports, but the causes of these incidents remain unresolved.

The paradox of boosting defence capabilities

The EU is currently asking EU countries to increase defence spending, cooperate more closely and invest jointly in European defence capabilities under the bloc's binding industrial and military targets to ensure Europe is defence-ready by the end of the decade.

But when it comes to UAPs, Brussels argues this must be monitored at the national level.

Euronews asked the Commission whether it was considering any information-sharing mechanism between the US and the EU regarding UAPs, or whether it intended to act on its own to monitor and assess them, taking into account possible impacts on flight safety.

Related EU says drones are a threat but scrambles for common response

"UAP are the responsibility of EU member states, which handle them according to national security and defence priorities," a Commission spokesperson responded.

Akkermans urged the EU to treat UAPs as an aviation safety reality rather than a taboo.

"We need the EASA, the European Commission and the Parliament to formally update our aviation safety frameworks with a standardised UAP reporting category, ending the policy of ignoring or misclassifying data. Right now, the system is forcing us to stay silent," the Dutch pilot said.

For van Heijst, it is crucial to "get rid of the stigma" around the UAP topic since "there is a genuine concern for flight safety".

"This is highlighted by the swarms of (potentially Russian military) drones that invaded European airspace en masse last year. Ignoring these things is in complete contradiction to the high standards of aviation safety in the EU," van Heijst said.

World.title: Europe wildfires: German border town partially evacuated but France blaze stabilised
World.content:
Europe is tackling a spate of wildfires spurred by high temperatures and tinder-dry conditions due to a historically hot summer that has already contributed to the deaths of thousands of people.

 

Scientists blame ever hotter and more frequent heatwaves on human-caused climate change.

Here are the latest developments this Monday morning.

Rain boosts Belgium's fight

Rain started falling in Belgium on Monday to help its fight against the country's biggest modern-day wildfire that has devastated some 3,000 hectares (30 square kilometres) of the High Fens park on the border with Germany.

Some 500 firefighters and troops are battling the blaze that has sent a huge cloud of black smoke across the region into neighbouring Germany and France.

Germany's defence ministry said on Monday that two military water-bombing helicopters would be sent to Belgium.

The German town of Monschau, close to the border, ordered nearly 30 people living in two streets near the frontier to evacuate.

Like much of Europe, Belgium has experienced a new spell of intense heat and drought in recent days.

Temperatures reached as high as 37C in some parts of the country on Friday, creating conditions conducive to wildfire outbreaks.

Smoke rises from burned-out parts of the Hautes Fagnes near Waimes, 16 August, 2026 AP Photo

Greece deaths

Two people died and hundreds were evacuated from popular beaches when two fires broke out on the Greek island of Salamis near Athens, the fire department said.

"Over 570 people were evacuated on coast guard patrol boats and other vessels," a coastguard spokesperson told the AFP news agency.

After largely escaping the heatwave temperatures that blanketed much of Europe, Greece has been hit with several major wildfires since late July, fuelled by strong winds.

Thirty-six blazes have broken out over the past 24 hours around the country, according to the fire department.

A firefighter walks through a burned area as flames engulf a house during a wildfire on the island of Salamina, 16 August, 2026 AP Photo

Portugal fires

Hundreds of firefighters in Portugal were battling a series of blazes there.

At one near the border with Spain, near the village of Dine, five firefighters sustained minor injuries when their vehicle caught fire, local media reported.

Firefighters were battling several other fires near the Spanish border, including at Boticas and Chavez, said the civil protection agency ANEPC.

Death in Spain

A Spanish soldier died on Sunday while helping efforts to extinguish a major wildfire in Aragon, the northeastern region's leader said, as the authorities deployed the largest firefighting arsenal in the region's history.

French reinforcements were due to help contain the wildfire, which broke out on Monday and has threatened a 1,000-year-old monastery.

Smoke rises from burned-out parts of the Hautes Fagnes near Waimes, 16 August, 2026 AP Photo

Croatia arrests

Croatian police said they had arrested four people suspected of starting some of the wildfires that have swept parts of the Adriatic coast in recent days.

The four are suspected of setting fires that scorched pine forests and olive groves as Croatia battles a wave of blazes fuelled by drought and heat.

A view of a beach bar in the aftermath of a wildfire on the Adriatic coast near Omiš, 14 August, 2026 AP Photo

France fire stabilised

A fire that burnt 1,700 hectares in the Landes department of southwestern France has been stabilised after three days of ground and air operations.

Local official Gilles Clavreul said the situation was evolving "favourably" as temperatures had dropped, 28C expected in the afternoon compared with 40C when the fire broke out on Thursday, and humidity had risen.

The local prefect said a first group of the 650 people who had evacuated due to the fire would be allowed to return to their homes Sunday evening

World.title: Kushner to meet Israeli PM Netanyahu after talks with Hamas on Gaza peace plan
World.content:
US envoy Jared Kushner is due to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday after holding talks with Hamas leaders in Egypt aimed at reviving a US-backed Gaza peace plan that Israel has so far rejected.

 

The meeting comes two weeks after Hamas endorsed the latest stage of Trump's Gaza plan, which Netanyahu has refused to support, insisting any settlement must ensure the group is "genuinely disarmed."

Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, met Hamas' new leader Khalil al-Hayya in the Egyptian Meditarranean city of El-Alamein on Sunday, sources with knowledge of the talks told the AFP news agency.

Kushner pushed for Hamas to take "concrete, verifiable steps" and relayed a message that "Gaza can never again be a source of terror for Israel," said one source who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the discussions.

Hamas again voiced its commitment to the plan, another source said.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks at the Mount Herzl Military Cemetery in Jerusalem, 14 July, 2026 AP Photo

The group said afterwards that it had called on mediators and Trump's so-called Board of Peace to "compel" Israel to "approve the roadmap...and begin establishing a timetable for its implementation."

A picture released by host Egypt did not include al-Hayya, but showed Kushner at a table alongside members of the Board of Peace, including British former prime minister Tony Blair. Qatar and Turkey, key mediators alongside Egypt, also joined.

The United States refused contact for years with Hamas, which it classifies as a terrorist organisation and which led the 7 October 2023 attack on Israel that sparked the latest Gaza war.

But the Trump administration has increasingly been comfortable with direct contact in hopes of ending the devastating conflict, negotiating the October ceasefire agreement that led to the release of remaining Israeli hostages.

Muslim states press Israel

The three regional mediator countries and five fellow Muslim nations, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Pakistan and Indonesia, condemned Israel's rejection of the plan on Sunday.

In a joint statement, they said "Israel bears direct and full responsibility" for obstructing peace, adding its refusal "directly threatens to derail extensive efforts" by Trump.

In response, Netanyahu's Likud Party charged that "the Arab countries want to bring down the prime minister" in the election.

The inclusion of the UAE is significant as it normalised relations with Israel five years ago, kickstarting an economic and strategic relationship that Netanyahu considers a key achievement.

Palestinians remove iron from the rubble of buildings destroyed by Israeli air strikes in Gaza City, 16 August, 2026 AP Photo

Netanyahu expressed opposition to the US plan even after he was assured by Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace's high representative for Gaza, that Israel would not need to pull troops out of the war-battered territory until complete disarmament by Hamas.

The board had initially said Israel would start a phased withdrawal in tandem with Hamas's disarmament.

Israel keeps up strikes

Israel has resumed airstrikes in Gaza after a lull following Trump's promotion of the peace plan, though the October ceasefire had never fully halted the violence in the Strip.

Several people were injured on Sunday after Israeli aircraft targeted a house west of Nuseirat, said Mahmoud Bassal, spokesman for Gaza's civil defence agency, which serves as a rescue service under Hamas.

The Israeli military said it was responding to a threat by Islamic Jihad militants and that it had tried to mitigate civilian casualties.

"The terrorists advanced terror attacks and were struck in precise aerial strikes to remove the threat," it said.

Several others were wounded after Israeli forces opened fire on tents housing displaced people west of Khan Yunis, where separately the body of a child was recovered after he was killed by Israeli fire on Saturday, the civil defence agency said.

Israeli operations have killed at least 1,262 Palestinians since the ceasefire came into effect on 10 October, according to figures by Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry. Its figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

The Israeli army has reported five deaths in its ranks during the same period.

World.title: Is the EU cracking down on Tobacco? Ask the Euronews Chatbot.
World.content:
According to the European Commission, existing tobacco rules have helped reduce cigarette smoking but failed to keep pace with the fast growth of newer nicotine products and online marketing.

 

Although the European Parliament did not adopt a formal opinion on the proposal in June 2026, the legislation remains under negotiation in the Council of the European Union, where all 27 member states must agree unanimously before it can become law.

Around 24 percent of Europeans still smoke, with about 300 billion cigarettes sold each year across the bloc. Tobacco-related illnesses contribute to around 700,000 deaths annually and cost an estimated €25 billion each year in healthcare spending.

A big part of the issue is related to younger smokers, who are turning to alternative nicotine products such as vapes, heated tobacco devices, and nicotine pouches. The World Health Organization estimates that 11.6 percent of teenagers aged 13 to 15 in the European region use these products. While generally considered less harmful than cigarettes, health experts say they still carry risks because they contain addictive nicotine and other harmful substances.

The proposed directive would apply minimum excise taxes to newer nicotine products and expand the EU's tobacco tracking system to include raw tobacco. The Commission says the measures would reduce tax gaps between products, make nicotine products more expensive, and help tackle illegal trade as part of its goal of creating a "Tobacco-Free Generation" by 2040. If approved, the directive would raise prices for cigarettes and many alternative nicotine products while increasing costs for tobacco companies.

World.title: Can the EU stop smoking by taxing cigarettes? Take our poll
World.content:
This decision stems from the European Commission's Tobacco Control Framework Evaluation, which found that existing legislation is increasingly outdated. While smoking rates have fallen from 28 percent to 24 percent of adults across the EU, around one in four Europeans still smoke and roughly 700.000 people die from tobacco-related diseases each year.

 

The proposed revision of the Tobacco Taxation Directive would increase minimum excise duties on cigarettes by 139 percent, introduce EU-wide taxes on new nicotine products for the first time, and extend the bloc's tracking system to raw tobacco to combat illicit trade.

Consumption is shifting away from traditional cigarettes towards products such as e-cigarettes, heated tobacco devices like IQOS and nicotine pouches. The World Health Organisation reports that 11.6 percent of 13- to 15-year-olds in the European region now use these products. Health experts warn that, while they may expose users to fewer harmful chemicals than cigarettes, they are not risk-free, remain addictive and are increasingly marketed through flavours, social media and youth-oriented branding.

The tax proposal remains controversial. In June 2026, the European Parliament failed to adopt a non-binding opinion after MEPs rejected a watered-down report, divided over the scale of the reforms. The legislative process continues, as tax legislation is decided by the Council of the European Union, where all 27 member states must agree unanimously.

Should the proposal go through? Will implementing it curb smoking in the EU? Our poll is anonymous and takes only a few seconds to complete. The results will be featured across EU-wide XL coverage, in videos, articles and newsletters, and will help shape our reporting as we examine how Europe can secure its position in the age of artificial intelligence.

World.title: What Nvidia's $500 billion Wall Street deal signals about the AI boom
World.content:
Nvidia has recruited Wall Street to bankroll its own customers.

 

The US chipmaker said last week it had signed memorandums of understanding with Wall Street's largest asset managers, including Apollo Global Management, Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs and KKR to raise upwards of half a trillion dollars for AI companies to borrow against, money that will buy its chips and build the servers that run them.

The six firms will set up what Nvidia calls "compute financing platforms," drawing on institutional money, insurance funds and private credit. Borrowers can use the proceeds for the chips as well as servers, networking equipment, buildings and power supply.

Nvidia has the option to guarantee up to a quarter of any given deal, which lowers the interest rate its customers pay while leaving most of the credit risk with the lenders.

CEO Jensen Huang said he approached only these six companies and none refused.

Keeping that spending off their own books is precisely the point, and the fact that such a structure is needed at all tells investors a great deal about where the constraints in the AI boom now lie.

The financial engineering rests on a single reclassification. Graphics processing units (GPUs) have always been treated as equipment that loses value quickly, superseded whenever a faster generation arrives.

Nvidia is effectively asking lenders to treat them instead as long-lived infrastructure, closer to a toll road or a power plant, that can be borrowed against for years.

"These are revenue-generating assets now," Huang said, describing them as productive, long-lived and transferable between customers.

Why the money had to come from somewhere else

The timing reflects a squeeze that has been building all year.

Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and other hyperscalers whose cloud platforms host most of the world's AI workloads have together guided roughly $720 billion (€624bn) to $745 billion (€646bn) of capital spending in 2026, an increase of about 77% on last year.

What analysts expect the hyperscalers to spend in 2027 alone has more than doubled in the space of a year, from a consensus of $480 billion (€416bn) in August 2025 to $1.08 trillion (€943bn) this month, a rise of about 127%, according to Bank of America.

The pattern has repeated at every stage.

Analysts who already considered last year's investment unsustainable then watched the hyperscalers guide higher at the start of 2026, revise those figures upward again through the year, and pencil in larger sums still for next year and 2028.

Moody's has warned that spending on this scale is eating into free cash flow and pushing tech groups into heavier borrowing. Alphabet recorded negative free cash flow of $5.9 billion (€5.1bn) in a quarter when it spent $44.9 billion (€38.9bn) on projects.

That is the pressure the structure of Nvidia's Wall Street deal relieves.

Debt raised through these "compute financing platforms" sits with the financing vehicles rather than on a hyperscaler's own accounts and also has Nvidia's backing, which protects credit ratings and leaves room for conventional borrowing elsewhere.

For smaller operators the effect is larger still as companies such as CoreWeave and Nebius, which lack investment-grade ratings and pay dearly for credit, gain access to capital on terms previously reserved for the giants.

What the market actually read into it

The reaction was more ambivalent than the headline number suggests, and came weeks after a July selloff driven by doubts over whether AI spending will pay for itself.

Essentially, equity investors saw a bottleneck being cleared while credit investors saw something else: the cost of insuring Nvidia's own debt against default rose after the news and has roughly doubled since late May.

Their doubt concentrates on the reclassification previously mentioned.

"Chips depreciate fast and lose value the moment a newer generation arrives," warned Nigel Green of financial advisory firm deVere Group, noting that lending against them only works if the collateral holds its value.

Critics also point out that Nvidia is helping finance purchases of its own products, deepening the circularity that already worries the sector.

Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon called it "a pivotal moment of a historic AI investment cycle."

Whether it proves pivotal in the direction Solomon means depends on a question nobody can yet answer: what will the value of a current GPU be in five years?

World.title: In Turkey, one of the world's longest conflicts reaches a turning point
World.content:
Turkey stands on the threshold of closing a conflict spanning almost 50 years, after the Turkish parliament this week passed a law allowing exiled Kurdish militants to return home and rejoin society. The legislation aims to end the war with the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), which has battled the Turkish state for independence since 1984.

Advertising

On Monday, legislators voted 468-88 in favour of a law detailing how the PKK will lay down arms, disband and guide most members back into civilian life.

Many see this legislation as a turning point after decades of bloodshed.

“This law in question is going to make a giant contribution,” predicts sociologist Mesut Yegen of the Diyarbakir-based Kurdish Studies Center.

“If the PKK militants are convinced that they can be safe in Turkey, it's estimated that some 15,000 people in Europe, in Syria, in Iraq and in the prisons in Turkey are going to be either released or are going to be able to come back home.”

The PKK leadership, based primarily in Iraq, is not covered by the legislation. Nor is the group's founder and leader Abdullah Ocalan, imprisoned since 1999 in a Turkish jail.

He initiated the peace process and last year called for the disarmament and dissolution of the PKK.

People hold a photograph of Abdullah Ocalan, the jailed leader of the militant Kurdish group PKK, in Diyarbakir, Turkey, on 27 February 2025. © AP - Metin Yoksu

Hope, caution

Istanbul, now the city's with the world’s largest Kurdish population, became a sanctuary in the 1990s as hundreds of thousands fled the violence raging in Turkey's southeast. At the conflict’s peak, the Turkish army destroyed villages in relentless scorched-earth campaigns.

In Istanbul's Bagcilar district, home to a vibrant Kurdish community, conversations reveal a fragile mix of hope and caution.

“This law seems good for the honour of the Kurds and to stop bloodshed,” said 31-year-old Ahmet, who only wanted to be identified by his first name. “Mothers should not shed tears anymore.”

But others were more wary. “The state has been delaying our rights for decades; I do not believe this process will be different,” said Kava, who also preferred not to give his full name. “I do not trust an arrangement in which Kurds do not have legal status.”

Kurds make up around a fifth of Turkey’s population, but are not legally recognised as a minority.

Emotions appear equally divided among Turks. “If they’re agreeing to live under the Turkish flag and love our country, that’s fine – let them,” said 51-year-old Mehmet Tas.

But 40-year-old Ertugral Zengin is unconvinced. “They committed a crime – and now they are to be pardoned? Do I want something like that? No, I won’t accept it.”

PKK ends 40-year fight but doubts remain about the next steps

Political momentum

The decades-long conflict has claimed 40,000 lives and forced more than 3 million people from their homes.

While major political parties support the peace process, hardline nationalist groups remain staunchly opposed, insisting it rewards a PKK they see as already defeated.

The process hinges on the laborious task of disarming the PKK and verifying its weapons are gone.

Maintaining the current political momentum is vital, warns Asli Aydintasbas, a Turkey expert at the Brookings Institution, a think tank in Washington DC.

“If this drags on, political support for the legislation and for the return of former PKK members, seen by many Turks as terrorists, would become politically problematic for the government. Timing and moving fast is very important to achieve reconciliation,” she says.

The government is expected to face growing pressure to address Kurdish rights, including Kurdish-language education in schools and local autonomy, along with broader democratic reforms.

Social media buzzes with questions: how can PKK members walk free while critics of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan remain behind bars?

Kurdish demonstrators in Diyarbakir, Turkey, on 27 February 2025. © AP - Metin Yoksu

Peace or politics? Turkey’s fragile path to ending a decades-long conflict

Yegen warns that since the new legislation fails to address Kurdish rights and democratisation reforms, the government needs to move swiftly.

“The fact that these two issues are not touched upon by the law has created many doubts on both Kurdish and Turkish sides about whether disarmament will be the government's only agenda,” he says.

For Erdogan, steering the peace process to success could secure the vital Kurdish vote in the 2028 elections. Yet extending Kurdish cultural rights risks alienating Turkish nationalists, and relaxing pressure on the opposition brings its own perils as their electoral strength grows.

For now, the negotiations present a rare window for reconciliation and lasting peace.

World.content:
Skip next section India's opposition calls for NTA to be 'held accountable'

Published 08/17/2026 Published August 17, 2026 India's opposition calls for NTA to be 'held accountable'

Rahul Gandhi (center) is Prime Minister Narendra Modi's biggest political contendor and a vocal Modi critic Image: @INCIndia X/ANI

In the hours after the NTA announced retests for the University Grants Commission - National Eligibility Test (UGC-NET), India's opposition leaders began once again pointing out alleged educational failures under Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

"Modi ji, look at what your NTA has just done," Rahul Gandhi, Modi's biggest political rival and leader of the opposition in the lower house of the parliament, said on X.

"This is no longer an education system. It is an extraction machine. It takes your money, your years, your mental health, and your confidence and returns nothing. Not even a job," Gandhi said.

"Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation was the first step, not the last. NTA's leadership must be held accountable too," he added.

Several other allied leaders echoed Gandhi on social media.

Some called for the resignation of NTA Chairperson Pradeep Kumar Joshi, while others called for the agency to be dissolved completely.

Prime Minister Modi installed party veteran Pralhad Joshi as India's new Education Minister on July 25, after Pradhan resigned under pressure of protests. The rare resignation was viewed as a dent in the government's invincibility aura, over 12 years into Modi's dominance in Indian politics.

Modi has since sought to reassure students by announcing new student-friendly schemes and introducing legislation to increase punishment over paper leaks.

World.title: Fatty food raises risk of colorectal cancer
World.content:
Did you know fatty foods can increase production of an acid in your gut that promotes tumor growth? That's on top of all the other health risks linked to fatty foods, like fries and burgers.

The list of health risks associated with foods high in fat and low in fiber is long:

low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL) or "bad" cholesterol

clogged arteries

weight gain

heart disease

liver stress

blood sugar spikes

bad digestion

And the list goes on.

Now a team of German researchers has shown how so-called Western diets that are often full of fatty foods can lead to the development of one of the most common — and deadliest — cancers in adults under 50 years of age.

The researchers from the Technical University of Munich, RWTH Aachen and the German Institute of Human Nutrition Potsdam-Rehbrücke (DIfE) found that these unhealthy diets sustain certain gut bacteria that produce a secondary bile acid — which in turn promotes tumor growth.

Their results were published in the August 2026 issue of the journal Gut .

"What's special about our study is that it shows the causality," Annika Osswald, the first author of the study and a PhD student at the German Institute of Human Nutrition, told DW. "Until now, we only knew there was some sort of connection between [a certain] secondary bile acid and colorectal cancer."

How diet fuels silent inflammation — and how to reverse It To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How bile acid is linked to colorectal cancer

The fat in the food you eat triggers the production of primary bile acids in your liver. These acids are important ― your body needs them to break down and absorb fats. Most of the primary bile acids are reabsorbed and returned to the liver.

But a small fraction reaches the colon, where certain bacteria convert them into secondary bile acids, including one called deoxycholic acid (DCA). The more fatty foods you eat, the higher the concentration of DCA in your colon. And that's where the problems start.

Osswald and her colleagues tested this in mice in a lab. "At the core of our work to prove causality were the mouse models," Osswald explained.

The research team implanted DCA-producing bacteria into mice whose intestinal microbiome they controlled completely. Then the scientists induced colorectal cancer in these mice, and also in mice without the bacteria. The mice that had DCA-producing bacteria in their gut saw more tumor growth than the mice that didn't have it.

Cell division in the mice with DCA was increased as well. Increased cell division makes it more likely for cancer to develop, because it multiplies the chances of DNA replication errors. These DNA mutations during cell division can stack up and lead to cancer.

To see whether the process they had observed in mice also takes place in humans, the researchers analyzed stool samples from more than a thousand people, both with and without colorectal cancer. Genes of DCA-producing bacteria were found more frequently in people with colorectal cancer.

"Our results show how much a Western high-fat diet and the associated changes in the gut microbiome can affect human gut health," said microbiologist Sören Ocvirk, another author of the study.

Osswald emphasizes that the team's work is foundational, and that more research needs to be done. Still, having proven the causality between more DCA-producing gut bacteria and increased tumor growth points to possible treatments of colorectal cancer as well.

Why it's vital to better understand colorectal cancer

Colorectal cancer is the only cancer for which the mortality rate in people under 50 years has increased in the past few decades. That's according to findings published in the Journal of the American Medical Association in January 2026.

The number of deaths from brain cancer, breast cancer, leukemia and lung cancer all went down in the US from 1990 to 2023. But the number of deaths from colorectal cancer increased by 1.1% annually, starting in 2005. While the US is only one region in the world, it is often considered a sufficient indicator of such trends, especially when it comes to the Western diet.

When detected early, cancer starting in the colon or the rectum is treatable.

But symptoms frequently don't present in the early stages of the disease. And when they do, they may be misinterpreted as indications of less harmful conditions like hemorrhoids or irritable bowel syndrome.

Symptoms for colorectal cancer include:

blood in or on your stool

intermittent or constant diarrhea or constipation

persistent abdominal pain

gas or cramps

feeling bloated

Another obstacle to early detection is that some people may feel embarrassed discussing colorectal health symptoms with their doctor.

So, try not to be embarrassed, talk to your doctor.

Is your gut your second brain? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How can study results help with treating colorectal cancer?

One option to be considered in the future could be microbiome transplants.

"You could transplant the microbiome of people who have fewer DCA-producing bacteria in their gut into patients with colorectal cancer," Osswald said. "That could potentially slow down tumor growth."

But the best option is to prevent colorectal cancer in the first place. While some people may have a genetic disposition to developing colorectal cancer, a lot is down to lifestyle factors.

Eating healthily, reducing the amount of meat and fatty foods in your diet, and not smoking, are some good ways to decrease your colorectal cancer risk.

World.title: Germany news: Belgium blaze kept out of Germany for now
World.content:
Skip next section Growing number of young people not in work or training

08/17/2026 August 17, 2026 Growing number of young people not in work or training

The number of 20 to 24-year-olds in Germany who were neither employed nor doing training or studies rose to 10% in 2025 as part of a continuing trend, new figures have shown.

In 2022, the figure was 8.8%, the Federal Statistical Office said, using international comparative data from the European statistics authority Eurostat.

However, the figure from Germany is relatively low among all 27 EU nations and below the average of 12.9% for the bloc.

The Netherlands had the lowest percentage of people in the 20-24 age group who were unemployed or not doing some professional training, at 5.6%.

The figure was highest in Romania (22.8%), Bulgaria (17.3%) and France (16.2%).

Young people in rural areas of Germany were less likely than those in big cities to fall into the category (7.9% and 10.6% respectively).

World.title: US actress Hayden Panettiere dies at 36
World.content:
Hayden Panettiere's death was announced by her father in a statement to US network ABC news. The actress was known for her roles in TV shows such as "Nashville" and "Heroes."

Hayden Panettiere, best known for her roles in US TV shows "Heroes" and "Nashville," has died aged 36, US media reports said.

"It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden. She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her — and to the millions who watched her onscreen," Panettiere's father, Skip, was quoted by ABC news as saying.

The cause of Panettiere's death has not yet been announced. Her father has urged for privacy.

She would have turned 37 on Friday,

Who was Hayden Panettiere?

Panettiere began her career as a child actor, featuring in commercials and soap operas.

She gained ‌widespread recognition as the voice of Dot, the young princess ant in Pixar's 1998 animated success "A ​Bug's Life."

She earned a Grammy nomination for the film's children's spoken word album recorded a few years after its release.

Panettiere catapulted to fame with her role as Claire Bennett — a high school cheerleader ​with super powers — on NBC's television series "Heroes," which debuted in 2006 and went on to be a hit.

She also starred as up-and-coming country singer Juliette Barnes for six seasons on the musical drama "Nashville."

Panettiere also worked in two films of the satirical horror "Scream" franchise, "Bring It On: All Or Nothing," "I Love You Beth Cooper" and "Remember the Titans."

Her last appearance was in the ​psychological thriller "Sleepwalker," which released in ⁠the US in January this year.

Panettiere was vocal about her struggles

Panettiere was open about her struggles with alcohol addiction and depression.

She revealed that she had had dealt with addiction through her 20s.

Her younger brother — actor Jansen Panettiere — died in 2023 at 28 due to a heart condition.

Hayden's memoir was published earlier this year, where she spoke about her battle with mental health, the loss of her brother, and her decision to give full custody of her daughter to her former partner, Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko.

World.title: Hundreds flee as Belgium battles wildfire at German border
World.content:
A rapidly spreading wildfire has scorched about 2,700 hectares in the High Fens nature reserve near Belgium's border with Germany. Some homes in the German town of Monschau were evacuated overnight as a precaution.

Belgium is battling its largest wildfire on record which has burned around 2,700 hectares (6,700 acres) in the eastern High Fens nature reserve.

The fire approached to within 300 meters (984 feet) of the German border, causing authorities to carry out precautionary evacuations in the German town of Monschau.

Evacuations in Belgium

On Saturday, the European Union deployed three helicopters and two water bombers as Belgium deployed additional firefighters in a bid to bring the massive blaze under control.

The blaze is described as by officials as the largest in Belgium's modern history Image: Laurent Cavenati/Belga/AFP

Authorities ordered around 600 residents in parts of Waimes, Sourbrodt and Buetgenbach to evacuate as shifting winds and heavy smoke raised concerns that the fire could reach homes. Tourists were also advised to leave the area.

"You can't see a thing anymore, there's smoke everywhere," David Rodolfs, a restaurant owner in Waimes, told the AFP news agency.

A gymnasium in a neighboring municipality was opened up to offer shelter.

Reinforcements were pulled from across the country to fight the blaze Image: Dha/Photo News/IMAGO

How have firefighting efforts fared?

The blaze, which broke out on Friday, has spread rapidly across peatlands and pine forests. Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin told AFP he was "shocked" at the fire's speed and extent of the destruction.

"There is a risk that the fire could reach homes, but we are deploying all available resources to protect them," Nicolas Yernaux, a spokesperson for the regional authorities in Wallonia, said.

Difficult terrain has hampered firefighting efforts, with operations relying heavily on aerial resources and forcing firefighters to allow difficult-to-access areas to burn, according to Yernaux.

Meanwhile, Belgium activated the EU's civil protection mechanism, bringing in three helicopters and two water-bombing aircraft from the Czech Republic, Sweden and the Netherlands.

Firefighters from Germany and Luxembourg have also joined the response, while farmers have helped emergency crews by wetting down the area.

Residents in parts of the nearby villages were ordered to evacuate on Saturday afternoon as a precautionary measure Image: Dimitri Korczak/AFP

Evacuations in Germany's Monschau

Authorities in the German town of Monschau in the Eifel region, which is located just 2 kilometers from the border, told some 30 residents from 17 homes to evacuate as a precaution late on Sunday night.

However, the fire was said early on Monday to be no longer advancing toward the German border, with firefighters aided in their efforts by light rain, lower winds and high humidity.



Local farmers have headed to the fire zone to support emergency crews Image: Dha/Photo News/IMAGO

Monschau, a major tourist attraction in the Eifel region, has some 12,000 residents. It is particularly known for its picturesque Old Town with its half-timbered houses.

It is located just some 23 km from the site of another major blaze in Germany's Eifel region that forced some 2,000 people from their homes on Friday.

Climate change making wildfires spread faster

Belgium has experienced another spell of extreme heat, with temperatures reaching 37 degrees Celsius (98.6 Fahrenheit) in parts of the country.

Scientists say human-caused climate change is increasing the likelihood of hot and dry conditions that allow wildfires to spread faster and burn longer.

European Commissioner Hadja Lahbib called the blaze the latest sign of the "climate upheaval" affecting the continent.

"Never before has the wildfire season started so early in the year and reached such northern latitudes," she said.

Edited by: Karl Sexton, Saim Dušan Inayatullah

World.title: India temple stampede in Bihar kills 7
World.content:
At least seven people were killed after a stampede broke out at a Hindu shrine in eastern India. An investigation into the incident is underway.

A stampede at a temple in eastern India's Bihar state has left at least seven people dead and over a dozen injured, Indian media reported.

The incident took place at the Ashok Dham temple in the Lakhisarai district as a swell of devotees thronged the site to offer water to Lord Shiva on what Hindus consider an auspicious Monday of the ongoing holy month of Shravan.

Shivam Kumar, a senior police officer, told news agency ANI that an electric pole fell at the site, sparking panic that led to the stampede.

"We can tell you the exact reason only after verifying everything," he added.

Lakhisarai district magistrate Shailendra Kumar told ANI that a barricade broke because of the rush and people fell on each other.

He said at least 19 people with injuries were being treated in hospital.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi expressed his grief over the deaths in the incident.

"Pained by the loss of lives due to a stampede in Lakhisarai, Bihar. My thoughts are with the bereaved families in this hour of grief. May the injured recover at the earliest. The local administration is assisting those affected," the prime minister's office quoted him as saying.

Injured receiving treatment

A probe is underway to determine the cause of the crush.

Meanwhile, Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary said that his government had given orders for the injured to receive swift treatment.

"The news of the deaths of devotees in the accident has left my heart deeply distressed. My deepest condolences go out to the bereaved families," he wrote in a post in Hindi on X.

Crowd crushes are relatively common in India during religious festivals. In March, nine people, mostly women, were killed in a stampede at another temple in Bihar's Nalanda district.

World.title: Trump says US-South Korea military drills to be scaled back
World.content:
US President Donald Trump believes annual military drills with South Korea send an "inappropriate and hostile" signal to North Korea. Seoul says it is reviewing Trump's remarks.

US President Donald Trump announced on Sunday that he ordered the Pentagon to "substantially reduce" joint military exercises with South Korea.

Trump wrote on Truth Social that the annual exercises are not only costly but "send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile" to North Korea, which he said has been "unthreatening and respectful" to the United States.

His post comes as the US and South Korea are scheduled to begin one of their two main annual large-scale joint military exercises this week.

South Korea has been a major US ally, with their relations having endured through more than seven decades of political changes.

Trump noted that South Korea declined to help the US in actions against Iran and that he has a "very good relationship" with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

"I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, 'No thanks!'" Trump wrote.

"Therefore, and based on the fact that it is too late to cancel, I have instructed Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, to substantially reduce the Joint Military Exercises!" Trump said.

South Korea reviewing Trump comments

South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff told Reuters the drills started on Monday as scheduled, but the presidential Blue House said it was reviewing Trump's comments.

"The government is closely following President Trump's social media message today," read a statement given to the AFP news agency.

It added a hope that Trump's apparently "friendly relationship" with Kim Jong Un would lead to "meaningful dialogue between the two countries, opening discussions aimed at advancing peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula."

Annual drills meant to sharpen readiness against North Korean threats

The joint military exercises, called Ulchi Freedom Shield, are scheduled to run until August 27.

The drills involve 18,000 South Korean soldiers, the South Korean military told the Associated Press.

The exercises were expected to include operations to counter drones, disrupt GPS signals and defend against cyberattacks to adapt to North Korea’s evolving capabilities.

South Korea proposes talks to officially end war with North To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

North Korea has also been aiding Russia in its war against Ukraine by providing troops.

North Korea carries out weapons test in protest to drills

Trump's announcement comes days after North Korea reportedly fired ballistic missiles toward the sea.

Pyongyang last week threatened stern steps against the US and South Korea and called the summertime drills a "war rehearsal."

North Korea routinely denounces joint military exercises between the US and South Korea as dress rehearsals for an invasion.

World.title: Italy: Thieves steal key Renaissance paintings in Sicily
World.content:
Four Renaissance paintings by Antonello da Messina were stolen from his Sicilian hometown on Saturday after surviving earthquakes and centuries of history. Crooks took them while locals celebrated a religious holiday.

Criminals have once again targeted a small regional museum to steal priceless artworks on public display, this time in Messina, Sicily.

Local authorities say robbers bypassed alarm and security systems at the Regional Museum of Messina (MuMe), Italy, around 10:00 p.m. (2000 GMT) on Saturday evening as the city celebrated the high point of its "Ferragosto" summer holiday, the Catholic Feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

Thieves were able to make off with several panels painted by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina, the most important artist ever born on the island of Sicily.

Three of the five surviving panels from Antonello's 1473 "San Gregorio Polyptych" were taken in the robbery as well as a smaller, double-sided panel locked in an armored display case.

"We are devastated by what happened. They were some of Antonello da Messina's most important and best-known works. It is a tremendous loss for the museum, the city, the community and the art world," MuMe Director Marisa Mercurio told Italy's ANSA news agency.

Messina Mayor Federico Basile called the theft "deeply reprehensible," saying it was "even more painful" for having taken place as the city celebrated the Assumption of the Virgin.

The museum remained closed Sunday as investigators searched for evidence.

Saturday's theft followed a Friday announcement that three paintings stolen in northern Italy this March and worth some $10 million had been recovered by authorities Image: Italian Carabinieri Press Office/AFP

Works of 'enormous cultural, artistic and symbolic importance'

"It is an extremely serious and significant loss," said Mercurio, "They have stolen works of enormous cultural, artistic and symbolic importance, not only for Messina but for Sicily as a whole. All we can do now is hope they are recovered as soon as possible."

Though the sum financial loss has not been made public — initial estimates range from €70-€80 million ($81-$92 million) — Antonello's market value increased considerably in March of this year when the Italian state laid out $14.9 million (€13 million) for the purchase of another panel that he painted around 1460.

A moving two-sided panel in oil with an "Ecce Homo" portrayal of Christ (recto) and "Saint Jerome in the Desert" (verso), the purchase and news that the painting would soon return to Italy was greeted with enthusiasm.

Messina was among the cities hoping to display the newly returned work.

Antonello was born around 1430 and trained first in Naples before studying Provencal and Flemish painting and ultimately returning to Messina in 1457, where he would work until his death in 1474.

Seen as a key figure in what was an early example of technology transfer, Antonello is largely credited with bringing revolutionary new Flemish oil painting techniques to southern Europe while at the same time spreading knowledge of Italian perspective drawing among his colleagues north of the Alps.

The return of Antonello's painting to his hometown, went the argument, would have huge symbolic value for a city that lost most of its cultural heritage, including what remained of Antonello's life and work, on December 28, 1908 — when an earthquake flattened Messina and killed nearly 60% of its population in a matter of seconds.

Antonello's market value and reputation were given a boost when the Italian government laid out $14.9 million (€13 million) this March for the purchase of a panel he painted in 1460 Image: Mauro Scrobogna/LaPresse/picture alliance

What paintings were stolen in Sicily?

The paintings stolen on Saturday belonged to an altarpiece installed at Messina's Monastero San Gregorio until it was destroyed in the 1908 quake.

Referred to as the "San Gregorio Polyptych" in its post-quake state, it consisted of six tempera paintings on wooden panels.

The five pieces in the museum portrayed the "Annunciation of the Virgin" in two upper panels, and the larger "Madonna of the Rosary Enthroned" flanked by full-length portraits of Saints Gregory and Benedict below.

The works were the only by Antonello never to have left Messina.

Authorities say the thieves left two panels leaning against the exterior of the museum despite having removed them from the wall and gotten them outside.

Another work, the small, two-sided oil painting on wood taken from the armored case, bore the image of Christ on one side and a Franciscan monk with the Virgin and Child on the other.

Art detective lauds police after Louvre jewel heist arrests To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What will happen to the paintings now?

Saturday's robbery comes just days after Italian authorities announced the recovery of three stolen artworks by Auguste Renoir, Paul Cezanne and Henri Matisse worth about €10 million.

Those works were stolen from a regional museum, too, the Magnani Rocca Foundation in Parma, on March 22.

Five people — allegedly Moldavan gangsters — have been detained in connection with the theft.

Despite having (often outdated) alarm systems, museums present soft targets for criminals.

Brazen thefts at museums around the world have highlighted this problem — most dramatically in Paris, where gangsters stole priceless historic jewels from the famous Louvre in broad daylight on October 19, 2025.

Experts say the fact that stolen artworks are often instantly recognizable makes them impossible to sell via reputable channels. Instead, such objects are used as collateral among crime bosses.

In Germany, members of Berlin's infamous Remmo crime family were convicted and put in prison in connection with the 2019 theft of historic jewels from the Green Vault at Dresden's Royal Palace.

Most of the jewels from the heist were recovered, albeit damaged, but the cost to taxpayers was enormous. The jewels from the Louvre heist have yet to be recovered.

Sicily's most famous art theft happened more than half a century ago, when unknown perpetrators broke into the church of the Oratorio di San Lorenzo in Palermo to cut Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio's "Nativity with Saint Francis and Saint Lawrence" from its frame and spirit it away in the dead of night, never to be seen again, after having hung there for more than three centuries.
