World.title: Burgermeister to Open First Prague Restaurant on Wenceslas Square in 2027
World.content:
Berlin burger chain Burgermeister is preparing to enter the Czech market, with its first Prague restaurant expected to open in early 2027.

The company has chosen Wenceslas Square for its debut. The location will also serve as a base for Burgermeister’s planned expansion across the Czech Republic, with more restaurants already in the pipeline.

Burgermeister has built its reputation in Berlin over the past two decades, growing from a single restaurant in a former public toilet into an international chain with 32 locations across Germany and other European markets.



Burgermeister has not yet revealed the exact address or confirmed a specific opening date.

The Prague restaurant will follow the concept that made Burgermeister popular in Berlin. The chain focuses on freshly prepared burgers and fries, with part of its food production handled in-house. Its operations also include its own bakery.

From a former public toilet to an international burger chain

Burgermeister opened its first restaurant in the Kreuzberg district of Berlin in 2006. The location was far from a conventional restaurant site. It occupied a former public toilet beneath the railway tracks near Schlesisches Tor station.

The unusual setting quickly became part of the brand’s identity. Over the years, Burgermeister expanded beyond its original Berlin location and developed into a larger restaurant chain.

Today, the company has 32 branches and is pursuing its goal of building a pan-European network.

World.title: Russell Crowe to Perform in Prague for the First Time in May 2027
World.content:
Oscar-winning actor and musician Russell Crowe will bring his band, The Gentlemen Barbers, to Forum Karlín on May 23, 2027, for their first-ever Prague concert.

Russell Crowe is best known for his roles in Gladiator, A Beautiful Mind and A Good Year, but long before Hollywood, music was a major part of his life.

On May 23, 2027, the Oscar and Golden Globe winner will bring that side of his career to Prague for the first time, performing with his band The Gentlemen Barbers at Forum Karlín.



Tickets will go on sale soon via Ticketportal and Ticketmaster.

The concert will also mark the opening night of the band’s European tour.

The Gentlemen Barbers have been developing their sound over the past four years, although many of the musicians have worked with Crowe for decades. The lineup includes drummer Dave Kelly and trumpeter Stewart Kirwan, both former members of Thirty Odd Foot of Grunts, as well as musicians who have collaborated with Crowe on later projects.

The band also features pianist Stu Hunter, guitarist Chris Kamzelas and bassist James Hazelwood. Irish singer Lorraine O’Reilly, known for her powerful, raspy vocals, has performed with Crowe since they first met while recording a duet for the Bible Code Sundays album Walk Like Kings.

The result is a band that moves between R&B, gospel, country, dark waltzes and singalong anthems, with storytelling at the centre of its music.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by JV Classics (@jvclassics)

“There is an attitude about this band. It’s got a groove. We do a lot of story songs, but we also know we are here to blow out cobwebs and give the audience a good night,” Crowe says.

For Crowe, music has remained a constant alongside his film career. He began performing in bands, touring and releasing records before moving into musical theatre and eventually film. He has continued to perform throughout his decades in Hollywood, despite his demanding acting career.

“I love playing in pubs. It’s what I did growing up. Even though my day job has a huge claim on my time, I’ve never not played music,” he says.

Russell Crowe’s Indoor Garden Party & The Gentlemen Barbers takes place on May 23, 2027, at 8 p.m. at Forum Karlín in Prague.

World.title: How Much Can a Prague Taxi Driver Really Earn Each Month
World.content:
For passengers, a taxi ride can make the job look straightforward. Pick someone up, drive them across Prague, wait for the next booking and repeat.

But the income of a full-time taxi driver depends on far more than the fare shown on the meter or app.

Drivers working through platforms such as Uber and Bolt can generate more than CZK 60,000 in gross monthly revenue when working around 40 to 50 hours a week. What they actually keep, however, is considerably less.



Gross income can exceed CZK 60,000

Official figures for Prague’s taxi sector put the average gross monthly pay at roughly CZK 38,000. Drivers who work full time through ride-hailing platforms can earn more, particularly when they concentrate on periods of high demand.

According to Ondřej Krátký, founder of the Czech taxi platform Liftago, drivers can typically earn about CZK 250 to CZK 350 per hour. At the lower end of the market, however, some drivers make only around CZK 80 an hour, which is difficult to turn into a sustainable income in Prague.

Official statistics may also underestimate the money generated by some drivers because not every journey is paid through an app. Cash payments remain part of the business.

Fuel and commissions take a large share

Most Prague taxi drivers operate as self-employed contractors and use their own cars. That means they are responsible for almost all of the costs associated with the job.

Fuel is one of the largest expenses. Someone driving every day can spend more than CZK 10,000 a month on petrol or diesel alone.

Ride-hailing platforms also take a percentage of each fare. Depending on the service and other conditions, commissions can account for roughly 20 to 25 percent of the fare. Drivers must also cover vehicle maintenance, repairs, commercial insurance and the mandatory social and health insurance payments required of self-employed workers.

Once these expenses are taken into account, the amount left from gross earnings can fall by a third or more.

For a full-time driver, a realistic monthly amount after operating costs can therefore be somewhere between CZK 22,000 and CZK 35,000. The exact figure depends on the car, fuel consumption, working hours, platform commissions and the number and type of trips completed.

Tips make only a small difference

Tips are unlikely to transform a taxi driver’s income in the Czech Republic.

Unlike in countries where tipping is a major part of service workers’ earnings, Czech passengers generally round up the fare or leave a relatively small amount.

Uber allows passengers to tip through its app for up to 30 days after a journey, with the full tip going to the driver. Bolt offers a similar feature.

For most drivers, however, tips remain a minor addition to their monthly income rather than a significant source of earnings.

Timing can make a bigger difference

Drivers can increase their income by choosing when and where they work.

Friday and Saturday nights are among the busiest periods in Prague, particularly in the city centre. When demand rises sharply, ride-hailing platforms can increase fares, allowing drivers to generate more revenue from the same number of working hours.

Major concerts, festivals and other large events can have a similar effect. Airport journeys can also be attractive because they tend to cover longer distances than short trips within the city.

World.title: Czechia Now Ranks Among the World’s 10 Best Countries to Live In
World.content:
Czechia has placed ninth among 192 countries in the 2026 Rumavi Global Relocation Index, which assesses destinations based on factors including safety, healthcare, taxation, living costs and opportunities for people considering a move abroad.

The country scored 69.9 points in the overall ranking, putting it just outside the top five but ahead of Malta and several larger European economies. Estonia took first place with 72.8 points, followed by Singapore, Malaysia, Portugal and Taiwan.

Czechia performed particularly well in the ranking for families, where it placed third worldwide. The index also gave the country strong scores for safety, property rights and climate risk.



Within Europe, Czechia ranked fourth overall. Estonia, Portugal and Lithuania were the only European countries placed higher in the general ranking.

The results are based on the Rumavi Global Relocation Index 2026, a privately produced ranking designed for people considering relocation as well as investors. Rumavi evaluates 192 countries using 24 indicators grouped into four areas: finance and taxes, livability and health, safety and stability, and settling and opportunity.

Czechia scores particularly well for families

The index uses different weightings for different types of people considering a move. For families, safety, education, cost of living and healthcare carry greater weight than tax considerations.

Czechia’s overall result is less impressive for other groups. It ranked 20th among countries assessed for retirees and 25th for digital nomads.

The index also evaluates destinations for entrepreneurs and people primarily interested in tax efficiency, although the rankings can vary significantly depending on the category.

What the index measures

Rumavi says its ranking is intended to measure the practical conditions faced by someone moving to another country rather than simply assessing tourism or passport access.

The 24 indicators cover issues such as affordability, income tax, foreign-income taxation, banking, healthcare, housing, air quality, climate, digital infrastructure, education, business opportunities, language, visa access, property rights and startup ecosystems.

Each indicator is converted to a score between zero and 100, with higher scores representing more favorable conditions for someone relocating. The same data is then weighted differently for six groups: general applicants, retirees, digital nomads, families, entrepreneurs and people seeking tax advantages.

For the general ranking, the most heavily weighted indicators include street safety, foreign-income taxation, cost of living and climate comfort.

Rumavi’s methodology draws on sources including the World Bank, World Health Organization, OECD, World Justice Project, UNODC and other international datasets. Some indicators, including visa access, property rights for non-citizens and aspects of taxation, are classified as Rumavi assessments rather than direct institutional data.

World.title: Passenger Attacks Four Airport Staff After Being Denied Boarding in Prague
World.content:
A passenger attacked four employees of ground-handling company Menzies Aviation at Prague’s Airport on Thursday evening after being denied boarding on a flight to Rome.

The incident took place at Terminal 2, near Gate C9, shortly after 8 p.m., according to Zdopravy.cz.

The woman arrived late for boarding on a Ryanair flight. After being refused entry to the aircraft, she reportedly became aggressive and attacked members of the ground-handling staff.



One of the employees stepped between the woman and a colleague who was being confronted by her. The passenger then bit him.

Airport police were called to the scene and used restraint equipment to detain the woman. She was subsequently escorted from the boarding area and handed over to the Czech police.

“The woman was late for the boarding gate, and after being denied boarding, she physically attacked an airport employee,” Josef Urban, a spokesperson for the Foreign Police Directorate said.

“Responding officers detained her using restraint equipment, and the case is now being investigated as disorderly conduct,” he added.

The incident was also confirmed by Prague Airport spokesperson Jiří Hánich.

The injured employees required medical treatment following the attack. Four members of the Menzies team were reportedly involved in the incident.

Menzies Aviation has operated at Václav Havel Airport Prague since 1991. The company provides ground-handling services covering passengers, baggage, aircraft and cargo for a significant share of flights at the airport.

World.title: Around 300 Czech Citizens Evacuated Due to Fire in Croatia
World.content:
Some 300 Czech tourists are among the 1,000 evacuees with a Czech police officer sent to coordinate the emergency response.

Croatian prime minister Andrej Plenković is in the town holding a coordination meeting with all emergency services this morning. Croatian president Zoran Milanović is also expected later today.

“All those injured in last night’s fire are being provided with the necessary medical care,” Plenković said in an earlier update on X.

No fatalities have been reported. The spokesman said there were also no reports of serious injuries among Czech citizens.

Some tourists left the area on their own, while others are staying at evacuation centres in Omiš and Split. A Czech consul is on site and is in contact with local authorities and security forces.

Fire spreads across up to 1,000 hectares

Around 160 firefighters, supported by specialised firefighting aircraft, are battling the blaze.

The fire has caused significant material damage, according to eyewitnesses, with dozens of cars and homes reportedly destroyed. Strong winds have helped the flames spread across an area estimated at between 900 and 1,000 hectares.

Witnesses reported hearing gas cylinders exploding inside burning homes, while the streets were filled with the sirens of fire engines, ambulances and police vehicles. Large parts of Omiš have also been left without electricity.

Mass evacuation underway

Hundreds of people have fled the affected area, with some tourists escaping by boat, catamaran and other small vessels.

The organised evacuation is being coordinated through the Ribnjak sports hall in Omiš. From there, evacuees are being transported by bus to the Gripe sports centre in Split.

According to Omiš fire chief Slavko Tucaković, foreigners make up the majority of those evacuated.

World.title: Czech Villages Face Water Shortages as Drought Deepens
World.content:
Residents say they are cutting water use wherever possible, taking shorter showers, reducing garden watering and abandoning plans to fill swimming pool.

Communities across the Czech Republic are struggling with worsening water shortages as wells dry up and small streams disappear after years of increasingly severe drought, according to local media on Thursday.



In the village of Krsy in the Plzen Region, tankers are delivering drinking water daily to a reservoir above the village. Some private wells have already run dry, while others are close to empty.

Residents said they are cutting water use wherever possible, taking shorter showers, reducing garden watering and abandoning plans to fill swimming pools.

Authorities are urging households to connect to public water networks where available.

The shortages are also putting pressure on tourist destinations. In Horni Becva, in the Beskydy Mountains, the population doubles during the summer holidays.

The municipality’s two wells have been operating close to their limits, with firefighters called in to deliver water.

Hotels with wellness facilities are among the largest users, prompting local officials to ask businesses to reduce consumption.

Officials hope conditions will improve when the tourist season ends and autumn rains arrive.

World.title: This Website Tracks How Many Trams Are Still Running Without Air Conditioning
World.content:
A new website is giving Prague residents a live picture of how many trams are operating without air conditioning, highlighting an issue that has become particularly noticeable during the city’s summer heat.

The service, Smrdime.cz, was created by developer Christoph Korb. Its name is a play on the Czech word smrdíme, meaning “we stink,” and refers to the uncomfortable conditions passengers can face inside overheated trams.

The website uses live data to calculate the share of Prague’s trams that are currently running without air conditioning. The figures change throughout the day as new vehicles enter and leave service.

When the service was checked on Thursday, August 13, Prague was experiencing temperatures of around 37 degrees Celsius. At that point, 188 of the 256 trams in operation did not have air conditioning, representing about 71 percent of the fleet being tracked.



Of the 147 air-conditioned trams available, 77 were operating at the same time.

The figures provide a snapshot rather than a fixed daily total. As trams are taken out of service and replaced, the balance between air-conditioned and non-air-conditioned vehicles changes continuously.

The project draws attention to a long-standing issue facing Prague’s public transport system: a substantial part of the city’s tram fleet still lacks air conditioning.

The website is based on data from two publicly available sources. Transport information comes from Golemio, Prague’s open-data platform, while weather information is provided by Open-Meteo. The two data sources are used to calculate the current situation displayed on the site.

Korb built the service with Anthropic’s Claude Code development tool. He has also published the project’s source code on GitHub, allowing other developers to inspect the project and contribute to its development.

World.title: Minister sheds light on future of Paks II upgrade, motorway concession and “crazy mistake” of Orbán era
World.content:
Regarding the upgrade of the Paks nuclear plant, Dávid Vitézy, Hungary’s transport minister, said at a press conference that a comprehensive review of the entire project was under way. The current water level had been identified as an “event not expected to occur for many thousands of years”, and therefore the project documentation would need to be reconsidered, he said.

Government helps farmers

Government spokesperson Vanda Szondi said that so far, farmers have filed 31,000 claims for damages due to drought on 770,000 hectares. She noted that the deadline for filing claims had been extended until Aug 31. Szondi said the number of claims already exceeded that in 2022, another record year for drought. She added that the drought in 2022 had been described as the “drought of the century”. She also said that the yield per hectare of arable crops was 10-20 percent below the average for the past five years.

Paks II upgrade under review

In response to a question on the M6 motorway, Vitézy said the previous government had amended the motorway concession contract three times, including instances where “it is very difficult to identify the Hungarian public interest.” He added that the concessionaire, citing the war in Ukraine, had imposed war-related cost increases, meaning that the Hungarian state had assumed its financial risks.

Vitézy thanked everyone for their cooperation in the construction of the Paks underwater weir. “We do not discriminate on political grounds when it comes to whose stones we accept,” he added. He said authorities had also contacted Duna Aszfalt, and the company had made available the barges used in the construction of the Mohács bridge over the Danube. Regarding the upgrade of the Paks nuclear plant, he said that a comprehensive review of the entire project was under way. The current water level had been identified as an “event not expected to occur for many thousands of years”, and therefore the project documentation would need to be reconsidered, he said.

Photo: MTI

Government determined to develop Hungarian railways

In response to a question on railway development plans, Vitézy said that a lack of rolling stock would not be an obstacle to railway development. “At the same time, a great deal of work is needed to get the investor side in order, as during former minister Lázár’s time in office, the capacity, workforce and team capable of carrying out such projects in Hungary had been dismantled,” he said.

Regarding the review of the Otthon Start Programme, Vitézy said that there is no problem in itself with the government helping young people to buy their first home through subsidised loans, and that the programme’s core objective is worth maintaining. At the same time, he said aspects of the programme had encouraged abuse and property purchases made solely for investment purposes, which made a recently launched review by the finance ministry necessary.

Paks on the brink: Critical days ahead, ‘superhuman work’ underway to keep 2 turbines running

Minister talks about “crazy mistake”

Asked about the revamping of Budapest’s metro line 3, he said the funding secured was a signal of the government’s support for the capital. He said it had been a “crazy mistake” to order the carriages without air conditioning; at the same time, EU sanctions on the Russian manufacturer and lack of cooperation on part of the manufacturer to find a solution were causing “problems”. Vitézy said that members of the public have until early September to complete a questionnaire on transport reforms.

Russian-made metro carriages without AC system. Photo: BKK

Meanwhile, he said that the government was working to pinpoint projects opened under the previous administration to include in those financed with EU funding. “We can’t eye every one of them as suspicious.” The minister said it was a major dilemma as to which of the projects completed or put out to tender during the previous government’s term the cabinet should include in the list of those to be financed under the recovery plan. He said all necessary public procurement audits, “but it cannot be ruled out that some of the previous government’s actions might result in disputes,” the minister said.

World.title: Hungary’s housing in crisis: Government plans major push for affordable rentals – here’s how
World.content:
The government must intervene and incentivise rental housing construction, which the Wekerle Sandor Housing Construction Programme aims to address, Dávid Vitézy, the minister of transport and investment, said on Facebook on Sunday.

Vitézy insisted that opposition representatives were “fiercely trying to prevent the government from reforming housing policy”. He insisted they were “clearly representing the interests of companies that hoped for massive extra profits from incentives granted for priority investments.” He added that the government is reviewing these exemptions.

The previous government’s “ineffective” housing policy measures, Vitézy said, had left the current government with a housing deficit necessitating intervention. Last year, only 1,256 new homes were handed over per million people, which is “by far the lowest figure” in regional comparison, he said.

“This rate is about one-fifth of Austria’s or Poland’s housing construction, while Czechia and Romania build more than two to three times as many new homes as Hungary. This has contributed to a significant price increase in the housing market, far outpacing real wage growth,” he said.

Meanwhile, the average time people needed to work to afford a new home has grown to seven years from 5.9 years a decade ago, he added.

The Wekerle Programme, he vowed, would help create “more, easily accessible, and liveable homes” through tax and construction regulation changes, while the European Union’s Recovery and Resilience Facility can also be used to build new, affordable rental housing and dormitories.

Comprehensive programmes must be compiled by the end of the year, with the government involving local authorities, real estate, and construction industry stakeholders in the consultations, he said. The goal is to ensure that young people, career starters, and families have access to housing, he wrote.

World.title: Did the former Hungarian prime minister send a message to PM Magyar and the government? Here’s what he had to say
World.content:
Former Hungarian Prime Minister Ferenc Gyurcsány has issued an unexpected warning about the dangers of turning public anger and the desire for revenge into government policy, arguing that even legitimate grievances must be handled through the rule of law.

In a Facebook post published on Sunday, Gyurcsány said that wanting retribution after suffering a serious injustice was a natural human reaction. However, he stressed that what may be understandable for an individual cannot become the guiding principle of a state.

“What may legitimately drive an individual cannot serve as the basis of state policy.”

Gyurcsány, who served as prime minister between 2004 and 2009 and founded the Democratic Coalition (DK), withdrew from active politics in 2025.

‘Revenge is human – but the state must be different’

According to the former prime minister, people who have been deeply hurt or treated unjustly naturally want some form of redress, and there is no reason to be ashamed of that feeling. The problem arises, he argued, when personal anger becomes a principle of government.

Revenge is inherently personal: the injured person decides what they consider sufficient retribution. Such an approach, Gyurcsány said, cannot provide a sound basis for governing a country. A democratic state instead needs rules that apply equally to everyone and are proportionate, transparent and subject to scrutiny.

This means that punishment should reflect the seriousness of an offence rather than the intensity of the victim’s anger.

Warning comes amid Hungary’s accountability debate

Although Gyurcsány did not name any political figures, institutions or specific cases in Sunday’s post, his comments come at a time when accountability has become a major issue in Hungarian politics.

The Tisza-led government has made investigating alleged abuses of the previous political era a prominent issue. Parliament established several investigative committees earlier this year, while legislation has also been passed concerning the creation of the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office.

Against this backdrop, Gyurcsány argued that there are ultimately two possible paths for a government responding to widespread public anger.

One is to channel that anger into lawful accountability, proportionate punishment and compensation for those who suffered losses. The other is to turn revenge itself into a political strategy and continually search for new enemies.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

‘Revenge never becomes complete’

Gyurcsány argued that revenge is ultimately a dead end because it can never provide a definitive sense of closure. If those who have suffered injustice are denied lawful redress, he warned, private revenge may begin to take its place, as individuals lose faith in the state’s ability to deliver justice.

He also suggested that a political force which encourages demands for revenge while in opposition could lose credibility once it takes power if it fails to deliver what its supporters expect.

For Gyurcsány, the answer is therefore not to suppress or deny the desire for revenge, but to transform it into something compatible with democratic government: justice, accountability and restitution.

The former prime minister previously addressed similar themes, warning that a legitimate desire for justice can easily turn into a demand for retribution if it is not kept within appropriate legal and institutional boundaries.

World.title: Paks on the brink: Critical days ahead, ‘superhuman work’ underway to keep 2 turbines running
World.content:
“Superhuman work” is underway to raise the water levels of the River Danube near the Paks nuclear plant to keep two of its turbines operational, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said on Facebook on Sunday.

Tuesday and Wednesday will be critical, as an additional 14-15cm drop is expected in the water level, he said. The Danube currently stands 9 centimetres above the water level that would require the shutdown of the second-to-last turbine, a scenario that can only be avoided if the scuttling of the barges achieves the desired result, he said.

Rainfall is forecast in the Austrian catchment areas from Thursday, which could cause water levels to rise again, he said, adding that the construction of the underwater weir was progressing at “breakneck speed”. Water management experts have decided they will open the Ráckeve-Soroksár Danube branch lock on Monday, which will add 20 cubic metres of water per second to the main Danube branch, gaining an additional 2 centimetres, he said.

Have you read this? 5,000 tonnes of stone delivered to Paks: PM Magyar reveals what would have happened without intervention

Meanwhile, the slow scuttling of the two 80-metre barges is still under way, with the vessels expected to reach a 1-metre sinking level by Sunday evening. Pumping water into the hulls will resume on Monday morning, he said.

Magyar said the barges are already under immense water pressure. The cross-positioned barges are secured to 70-centimetre-diameter piles drilled 8 metres deep with unprecedentedly thick, 500-metre-long steel cables. Magyar concluded by expressing his gratitude to the hundreds of experts working in the heat at Paks.

World.title: ‘It happened in seconds’: Survivor reveals horror of deadly Polish bus crash on Hungary’s motorway
World.content:
A survivor of the devastating Polish coach crash on Hungary’s M3 motorway has described how the tragedy unfolded “within seconds”, as grief spreads across communities in southeastern Poland. Twelve people were killed when a bus carrying pilgrims returning from Bosnia and Herzegovina left the motorway and overturned early on Sunday.

The coach was carrying 57 passengers and two drivers when it crashed at around 1 AM near Mezőkeresztes, on the Nyíregyháza-bound side of the M3 motorway. The passengers were Polish citizens returning from a pilgrimage to Medjugorje.

Survivor: ‘It happened in seconds’

According to Polsat News, Wojciech Tatara, the elected representative of the village of Siedliska in southeastern Poland, spoke to one of the survivors by phone while the injured passenger was being treated in a Hungarian hospital. According to Tatara, most of the passengers had been asleep when the crash happened.

“He said it happened within seconds.”

The survivor is expected to remain in hospital for some time but is receiving good care, Tatara said. The tragedy has hit Siedliska particularly hard. Four of the people who died were residents of the village, according to Tatara. He said he personally knew all four.

“It is a huge shock, a black day in the history of Siedliska,” he told Polish media. The village had held its traditional harvest celebration just one day earlier. On Sunday, residents instead gathered in church to pray for those who died and for the recovery of the injured.

Polish bus overturns on M3 motorway in tragic accident. Photo: MTI

Children among those travelling on the coach

Children were also among the passengers, although Tatara said they did not suffer serious injuries. He spoke to the father of one of the children, who was travelling with his wife and children. The father himself suffered injuries serious enough to require continued hospital treatment, while his wife was expected to be discharged sooner.

The full list of those injured and their current conditions is still being established. According to Hungary’s National Ambulance Service, 12 people died, while one person suffered life-threatening injuries, nine were seriously injured and another 37 sustained lighter injuries.

The rescue operation was particularly difficult because several passengers became trapped underneath the approximately 24-tonne vehicle after it overturned onto its side. Firefighters initially entered through the coach’s windows and had freed 35 people by around 3 AM. Cranes and winches were subsequently used to lift the vehicle so rescuers could reach those trapped underneath. The injured were taken to hospitals in Miskolc, Debrecen, Nyíregyháza and Eger.

Read more about the accident:

12 killed in devastating bus crash on Hungary’s M3 motorway

Bus crash tragedy in Hungary: Company owner claims drivers were experienced, Polish PM to send special aircraft

Driver suspected of falling asleep

Hungarian police currently believe that the driver may have fallen asleep at the wheel. The coach reportedly left the motorway on a straight section after the Mezőkeresztes exit before overturning in a ditch. However, authorities have stressed that the exact circumstances of the crash remain under investigation.

Both drivers survived and were taken to hospital for examination. Police have said the driver suspected of being behind the wheel at the time of the crash will be taken into custody.

A Polish prosecutor’s office has also opened an investigation and is preparing to cooperate directly with Hungarian authorities. Polish prosecutors and police are expected to seek permission to participate in an examination of the crash site.

Families still trying to contact loved ones

The scale of the disaster has made it difficult for some families to establish contact with relatives. Some injured passengers were taken to hospital without their mobile phones, meaning relatives were still trying to determine whether their loved ones were among the survivors.

Poland’s embassy in Budapest has established a hotline for relatives of those killed or injured in the crash.

The Polish government has also responded to the tragedy, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk announcing that a special aircraft would be sent to Hungary carrying representatives of the foreign ministry and health services.

Polish President Karol Nawrocki expressed his condolences to the victims’ families, while Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said Polish diplomatic officials were maintaining contact with Hungarian authorities.

Polish bus overturns on M3 motorway in tragic accident. Photo: MTI

Pilgrimage group was returning from Medjugorje

The group had travelled from Poland’s Podkarpackie (Subcarpathian) Voivodeship and was returning from Medjugorje, the famous Catholic pilgrimage site in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Many of those on board came from the area around Strzyżów. The mayor of Strzyżów said 11 people from the municipality had taken part in the pilgrimage.

The disaster has also left those who cancelled their trip at the last minute confronting an unbearable sense of relief and shock.

One Polish man, identified as Wiesław, had planned to join the pilgrimage but cancelled for family reasons shortly before departure. Several of his acquaintances were on the coach.

After the crash, the husband of one of the victims called him and told him that his wife had died.

The tragedy is particularly painful given that this was not the first deadly crash involving Polish pilgrims travelling to Medjugorje in Hungary. In 2002, a Polish coach travelling towards the pilgrimage site crashed near Balatonszentgyörgy, killing 19 people and injuring 32, according to Index.

World.title: Budapest’s bike-sharing chaos could leave unsuspecting riders facing hefty fines
World.content:
Budapest’s newly relaunched MOL Bubi bike-sharing system is facing a growing problem: bicycles are increasingly being left outside designated docking points, potentially exposing unsuspecting users to surcharges of tens of thousands of forints.

The confusion is partly linked to missing or temporarily unavailable docking stations, particularly in the city centre. Several popular locations have stopped operating because of outstanding permits and disputes over public-space use.

Missing stations leave riders confused

One of the most notable examples is at Déli railway station, where a previously popular Bubi station is currently unavailable. During the service’s temporary suspension, other micromobility providers occupied the site under valid public-space agreements, reports Telex.

The Budapest Transport Centre (BKK) has also yet to receive all the approvals required to redesign and reopen the station. If everything goes according to plan, the location could receive a new public-space permit from 1 October at the earliest.

A similar situation has developed around Clark Ádám Square. The Bubi app shows that there are effectively no official Bubi stations between Széll Kálmán Square and the Elizabeth Bridge. In the 5th District, 11 planned stations are also awaiting approvals, with their construction expected in September, although their opening will depend on further permissions.

Riders may mistake other points for Bubi locations

The confusion is not limited to missing stations. Some users reportedly mistake collection points belonging to other services for valid Bubi drop-off locations. Manfréd collection points, for example, can contain older-generation Bubi bicycles, while Mobi points are currently used mainly by scooter services. This can make it difficult for users to distinguish where a new-generation Bubi bicycle can legitimately be left.

The BKK acknowledged that several factors are contributing to the problem, including the incomplete integration of Mobi points and the missing stations in the 1st and 5th districts. The transport authority said users are also still becoming familiar with the new network and its rules.

Stay up-to-date: Woman abused by man in Budapest in broad daylight, authorities do nothing

205 of 222 stations currently operating

Despite the disruption, the vast majority of the original network remains operational. Of the former 222 Bubi docking stations in Budapest, 205 – around 92 per cent – are currently operating. However, the biggest expansion is expected this autumn, when Mobi points are gradually integrated into the Bubi network.

Around 1,000 additional pick-up and drop-off points are expected to become available, shared by bicycle and scooter services. The expanded network is also planned to cover major transport hubs with at least 30,000 daily journeys, including all metro stations.

This will extend Bubi well beyond its current central coverage, reaching areas including József Attila-lakótelep, Angyalföld, Őrmező, Tisztviselőtelep, Századosnegyed, Örs vezér tere, Kőbánya-Kispest, Újpest-városkapu and Zugló. For now, however, riders are being left to navigate a confusing network where parking in the wrong place can potentially result in a substantial surcharge.

World.title: Cold front brings rain to Hungary on Monday to finally ease summer heat
World.content:
Hungary’s long spell of hot, settled weather is set to end on Monday as a cold front moves into the Carpathian Basin, bringing showers, thunderstorms, strong winds and cooler temperatures.

According to HungaroMet, atmospheric activity has already increased to the north and west of Hungary. The associated precipitation zone reached the Alps on Sunday, with showers and thunderstorms developing in several areas. Cooler air masses of oceanic origin are following the system and will soon reach Hungary.

Sunday remains hot

Sunday will remain mostly sunny and hot, with afternoon temperatures of 33–36°C. Clouds will gradually increase from the north-west later in the day, with showers and thunderstorms possible near the border.

The southerly wind will strengthen in many areas before easing during the evening. Overnight temperatures are expected to remain between 15 and 22°C.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Storms arrive in Hungary on Monday

The cold front will move across Hungary on Monday, bringing increasing cloud cover and showers and thunderstorms to more areas. The Great Plain may still enjoy several hours of sunshine.

The wind will turn north-westerly and become fresh to strong, while thunderstorms could bring gale-force gusts locally. Hail and torrential downpours are also possible. Temperatures will range from 27–36°C, with the hottest conditions expected in the south-east.

According to Időkép, some storms could organise into lines. However, the rainfall will be highly uneven, meaning the change is unlikely to end Hungary’s prolonged drought. Locally, more than 15–20 millimetres could fall, but most areas may receive only a few millimetres, while parts of central Hungary could remain dry.

There is better news for the Danube: 50–80 millimetres of rain could fall in parts of Lower and Upper Austria within the river’s catchment, potentially slowing or halting its current decline.

Stay up-to-date: Nearly 70 firefighters tackle forest fire in Hungary after power line failure

Cooler Tuesday ahead

By Tuesday, cloud cover should decrease across much of Hungary, although showers may linger in the south and east. Strong northerly and north-westerly winds are expected. Morning temperatures will fall to 11–17°C, with afternoon highs of 23–28°C.

The rest of the week should remain partly sunny and unsettled, with temperatures rising again to 28–33°C on Wednesday and 29–34°C on Thursday. Further showers and thunderstorms may develop from Thursday, while another stronger front could arrive around Friday.

World.title: India’s Independence Day in Budapest highlights the deep Hungarian ties behind the celebration
World.content:
India’s 80th Independence Day was marked in Budapest on 15 August with a ceremony that celebrated not only India’s freedom, but also the longstanding cultural links between India and Hungary.

The flag was hoisted at 9 AM at the Embassy of India, followed by a performance of Vande Mataram, India’s national song, by Hungarian friends of India alongside members of the Indian community. Certificates of Appreciation were also presented beside the flagpole.

The ceremony is featured in a new video produced by Magyar Minute, including an exclusive one-on-one interview with Indian Ambassador to Hungary Anshuman Gaur.

India’s Ambassador to Budapest Anshuman Gaur

‘Life is dear, but liberty is dearer’

One of the most striking elements of the celebration was the distinctly Hungarian thread running through the event. Ahead of the flag-hoisting ceremony, the embassy quoted Hungarian poet Sándor Petőfi, whose famous words – “life is dear, but liberty is dearer” – were presented as a message that resonates with both nations.

The connection between the two countries was also reflected in the cultural centre of the Indian Embassy in Budapest, which bears the name of Amrita Sher-Gil, one of India’s most celebrated modern artists.

Sher-Gil was born in Budapest on 30 January 1913 to a Hungarian mother and Sikh father. She later became a major figure in Indian art, and in 1976 the Archaeological Survey of India designated her works as National Art Treasures, meaning paintings held in India cannot be taken out of the country.

India’s 80th Independence Day Budapest India’s 80th Independence Day Budapest

Ambassador speaks about India, Hungary and freedom

In the interview, Ambassador Anshuman Gaur reflects on what India’s Independence Day means to him personally and what he hopes Hungarians will understand about his country.

Gaur has been a member of the Indian Foreign Service since 2001 and served as India’s Chief of Protocol between 2022 and 2025. He is also a published poet: his collection Isthmus of Time was launched in New Delhi in July 2017 by then Vice President M. Hamid Ansari.

The ambassador concludes the interview with a recitation of verses by renowned Indian poet Ramdhari Singh Dinkar, conveying the idea that Bharat is not simply the name of a territory, but the spirit of freedom and democracy within its people.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

80 years of Indian independence

India’s 80th Independence Day marks 79 completed years since the country gained independence from British rule on 15 August 1947.

The celebrations in Budapest also highlighted the importance of Vande Mataram, which first appeared in print in the Bengali journal Bangadarshan in November 1875. The song marked its 150th anniversary on 7 November 2025, with a year-long commemorative programme running until 7 November 2026.

The Indian community in Hungary has also grown significantly over recent years. According to the embassy, around 8,700 Indian nationals live in Hungary, including more than 2,000 in Budapest. Approximately 1,200 Indian students are studying in Budapest, Pécs, Szeged, Miskolc and Debrecen.

Certificates of Appreciation being handed out at India’s 80th Independence Day celebration in Budapest

The ceremony therefore offered more than a traditional Independence Day celebration: it provided a glimpse into the cultural connections that have brought Indian and Hungarian communities closer together.

World.title: Romania’s energy production falls 2.6% in first half of 2026
World.content:
Romania’s domestic energy production fell by 2.6% in the first six months of 2026 compared with the same period last year, according to provisional data published on Monday, August 17, by the National Institute of Statistics (INS) and quoted by Agerpres. Final electricity consumption also declined by 3.3% year-on-year.

Between January 1 and June 30, Romania’s primary energy resources decreased by 4.1%, while electricity resources rose by 1.1% compared with the first half of 2025.

The main primary energy resources totaled 15.502 million tonnes of oil equivalent, down by 656,400 tonnes of oil equivalent from the corresponding period last year.

Domestic production reached 7.929 million tonnes of oil equivalent, a decrease of 215,200 tonnes, or 2.6%. Imports declined by 441,200 tonnes, or 5.5%, to 7.572 million tonnes of oil equivalent.

Electricity resources totaled 34.691 billion kWh in the first half of the year, up by 369 million kWh from the same period of 2025.

Thermal power plants generated 7.680 billion kWh, down by 485.2 million kWh, or 5.9%. Nuclear power production declined by 598.6 million kWh, or 11.7%, to 4.530 billion kWh.

By contrast, hydropower production increased by 17.9% to 7.489 billion kWh, representing an additional 1.136 billion kWh compared with the first six months of last year.

Wind farms produced 3.273 billion kWh, up by 268.9 million kWh, or 9%. Solar power recorded the strongest increase, rising by 42.1% to 3.259 billion kWh, an increase of 965.3 million kWh year-on-year.

Final electricity consumption stood at 24.113 billion kWh, 3.3% lower than in the same period of 2025. Electricity consumption in the economy declined by 0.6%, while public lighting consumption dropped by 4.6% and household consumption fell by 11.8%.

According to the same report, electricity exports increased by 789.2 million kWh, or 11.4%, to 7.691 billion kWh. Technological consumption in grids and substations rose by 16.4% to 2.887 billion kWh.

World.title: Romanian director Florin Șerban’s ‘You Don’t Belong Here’ wins top prize at Locarno Film Festival
World.content:
Romanian director Florin Șerban’s You Don’t Belong Here (Nu e locul tău aici) won the Pardo d’Oro, or Golden Leopard, at the 79th Locarno Film Festival. The award marks Șerban’s return to feature filmmaking after an eight-year absence.

The father-son drama impressed the jury of the festival’s International Competition through “the strength of its screenplay, the uniqueness of its vision, and its exceptional command of cinematic language.”

The film follows Marius, the chief medical officer at a hospital in his small hometown, who is raising his teenage son, Ioan, alone after the death of his wife. Although confident in his professional life, Marius is unaware that his son spends his nights cycling through town and vandalizing cars with a gang of masked vigilantes. His world is shaken when he learns that police suspect Ioan of murder.

The cast includes Adrian Văncică, Teodor Butănescu, Alex Conovaru, Cristina Richter, Janir Izdrăilă, and Cosmin Dominte.

You Don’t Belong Here has also been selected for the main competition of the Sarajevo Film Festival.

“These exciting and timely awards are closely connected to the changes shaping both the film industry and our world,” Locarno Film Festival artistic director Giona A. Nazzaro said. “Whether it is the Romania of You Don’t Belong Here, the Brazil of The Riverbank, or the South Korea of Nowhere to Lay My Eyes, the jury highlighted the importance of cinematic form and language while also honoring works capable of reaching a broad audience.”

The Special Jury Prize at Locarno went to The Riverbank (A Margem do Rio) by Matheus Farias and Enock Carvalho. Meanwhile, Hong Sangsoo received the Pardo for Best Direction for Nowhere to Lay My Eyes. The complete list of winners can be found here.

The 80th Locarno Film Festival is scheduled to take place from August 4 to 14, 2027.

World.title: Four US officials argue leader of Romanian far-right party should not benefit from US visa
World.content:
Four US officials, two of whom are former ambassadors to Romania, signed a Jerusalem Post article arguing that George Simion, the leader of the far-right party Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR), should not have a visa to the United States.

The signatories, former US ambassadors to Bucharest Adrian Zuckerman and Mark Gitenstein, former United States ambassador to Belgium Ronald Gidwitz, and former governor of the state of Virginia, James S. Gilmore III, said that Simion was not compatible with American values. They noted that he frequently repeated narratives favorable to Russia.

“Simion has worked aggressively to portray himself as pro-American and aligned with the MAGA movement. Yet many of his positions suggest the opposite,” the four said in the article titled “What Is the memory of the Holocaust worth? Less than a US visa for George Simion?”

The opinion piece also highlighted Simion’s support for former presidential candidate Calin Georgescu, currently investigated for attempted coup.

“Despite Georgescu’s repeated antisemitic statements, praise for fascist figures, and attacks on Western institutions and leaders, Simion has continued to defend and promote him as a central figure in Romania’s nationalist movement,” the officials argued.

The article concludes by saying that the US should carefully analyze whether George Simion’s past is compatible with the values that America seeks to defend and whether he should benefit from the privilege of receiving a US visa.

“The United States has spent generations teaching that antisemitism must never be excused, normalized, or ignored. That principle should not bend for political convenience,” the same source mentioned.

World.title: Romania shoots down fourth Russian drone on national territory
World.content:
A drone entered the national airspace on the morning of August 16 from the Republic of Moldova, approximately 24 km north of Galati, the Ministry of Defence (MApN) announced, adding that the drone was shot down. Republic of Moldova confirmed that the drone was of type Shahed 138 (Geran 2) and it crossed its national territory coming from Ukraine’s territory.

An F-18 aircraft of the Spanish Air and Space Forces, which was carrying out NATO Enhanced Air Policing missions from Mihail Kogălniceanu Air Base, intercepted and shot down, in coordination with the Romanian military in the command centre, under safe conditions, the drone that had entered Romanian airspace.

It was the fourth Russian drone shot on Romanian territory, after a similar device hit an apartment building in Galati at the end of May. Two people - a mother and her son - were injured and taken to the hospital. Three drones were shot down by jet fighters within three days in July.

On the same day, on August 16, parts of drones were found in the water on the Black Sea beaches and close to the Neptun Alpha offshore platform. An entire drone, without an explosive charge, was found 1.5 km from a beach.

Romanian minister of defence Radu Miruţă on August 16 congratulated the Spanish pilots and the Romanian military at the command centre for a successful mission.

“Romania defends its airspace, and our allies are with us. Vigilance, rapid reaction and allied solidarity, these are the concrete guarantees of our security. Yes, Romania is in the first line of defence of the European Union," the minister added.

According to Moldova’s Ministry of Defence, quoted by NewsMaker.md and News.ro, the device, type Shahed 138 (Geran 2), came from the Ukrainian locality of Cotlovina, Reni region, and flew over the airspace of the Republic of Moldova through the village of Etulia in Gagauzia. The drone left the airspace at 04:49, through the town of Slobozia Mare, Cahul district, heading towards the town of Şivita, Galaţi, Romania.

World.title: Romanians buy more state bonds, particularly denominated in euros, in July
World.content:
The Ministry of Finance raised about RON 1.31 billion through the Fidelis bond issue carried out between August 7 and 14, double the RON 659 million raised in July, preliminary subscription data showed.

Some RON 423.5 million were subscribed for the lei tranches, compared to RON 202.6 million in July, Ziarul Financiar reported.

The most sought-after was the two-year issue, with an interest rate of 6.30%, where Romanians placed RON 183.1 million. This was followed by the four-year titles, with 6.90% (RON 90.6 million), the ten-year ones, with 7.50% (RON 85.4 million), and the tranche dedicated to blood donors, with 7.30% (RON 64.4 million).

The difference from last month, however, came from the foreign currency side. Subscriptions in euros rose to EUR 168.1 million (RON 880 million), from EUR 87.6 million in July, and almost 70% of the amount - EUR 115.8 million - went to the ten-year issue, with an interest rate of 6.30% per annum.

World.title: Romania's Romgaz posts 3.4% stronger net profit in H1 on tax, regulatory effects
World.content:
Romanian natural gas producer Romgaz (BVB: SNG) reported its net profit rose 4.7% y/y to RON 762.7 million (EUR 145 million) in Q2, while turnover fell 6.6% to RON 1.75 billion. Gross profit decreased by 8.3% to RON 796.6 million, while EBITDA fell 13.5% y/y to RON 864.6 million.

The decline in operating profit was partly offset by a 75.9% reduction in profit tax during the quarter.

Gas deliveries in Q2 were 10.2% lower than in Q1, while gas sales turnover fell 17.5% to RON 1.51 billion. Deliveries at regulated prices accounted for 66.8% of total volumes, down from 86.6% in Q2 2025.

Romgaz, Romania's largest natural gas producer, had a market capitalisation of RON 74.0 billion (EUR 14.1 billion) after its shares gained 127% y/y.

In the entire H1, Romgaz reported consolidated net profit of RON 1.74 billion (EUR 332 million), up 3.4% y/y, despite an 8.6% decline in turnover to RON 3.88 billion.

The increase in profit was driven mainly by lower taxation and a positive effect related to amounts owed by the Ministry of Energy under the emergency gas and electricity price-capping mechanism, rather than stronger operating performance.

For H1, income tax expense was 44.5% lower than a year earlier.

The H1 result also benefited from a net positive effect of EUR 123.8 million after Romgaz collected part of the amounts owed by the Ministry of Energy under OUG 27/2022, which introduced measures for capping electricity and gas prices. The company also reversed an impairment adjustment recognised in 2025.

World.title: Romania’s current account deficit up 1.5% y/y to EUR 30.5 mln in 12 months to June
World.content:
Romania’s current account (CA) deficit has more than doubled to EUR 2.96 billion in June on higher imports and dividend outflows, bringing the rolling 12-month deficit to EUR 30.5 billion – 1.5% more compared to the previous 12-month period, according to data published by the National Bank of Romania (BNR). The CA deficit to GDP ratio has, however, decreased to 7.9% in the 12 months, subject to revision upon Q2 GDP release, from 8.3% in the previous 12-month period.

The country’s rolling 12-month CA deficit has dropped in June-July 2025 after the local currency weakened versus the euro in May amid a stable exchange rate over the past years. The fiscal consolidation, inter alia via lower private consumption, maintained pressure on the country’s chronic CA deficit since then.

However, the expensive oil and petroleum products reversed the trend in the second quarter of 2026, and high dividends reported by FDI companies (reinvested or repatriated) pushed the CA deficit in June. Over the medium term, however, the CA deficit and particularly the CA gap to GDP ratio is expected to narrow along with fiscal consolidation.

Imports of goods increased by just over EUR 1 billion to EUR 11.2 billion in June, and the 12-month rolling imports of goods increased by nearly EUR 2 billion to EUR 124.6 billion.

The dividends generated by the FDI companies, in turn, increased by nearly EUR 0.7 billion to EUR 947 million in June, while they increased by EUR 1.3 billion to EUR 11.9 billion in the 12-month rolling period. The Romanian tourists’ spending abroad also increased significantly, by over EUR 1 billion to EUR 10.3 billion in 12 months to June 2026.

Overall, the outflows under the CA increased by 4.8% y/y or EUR 8.6 billion to EUR 186.8 billion in 12 months to June.

At the same time, the FX inflows generated by the exports of goods and services have advanced more uniformly – by 5.5% y/y or EUR 8.1 billion to EUR 156.3 billion in 12 months to June.

The FDI inflows to Romania deteriorated significantly, by 85% y/y to EUR 528 million in H1, or by 27.3% y/y to EUR 4.7 billion in 12 months to June. The new equity FDI investments were particularly low: EUR 432 million (-59% y/y) in H1 and EUR 877 million (-57% y/y) in 12 months to June.

The FDI to GDP ratio was only 1.3 % in 12 months to June, compared to a slightly larger yet still disappointing 1.9% in the previous 12-month period.

World.title: Romania’s GDP virtually flat for third consecutive quarter
World.content:
Romania’s seasonally adjusted GDP remained constant in the second quarter of 2026, compared to Q1, and was 2% y/y lower than in the same period of 2025, according to flash estimate data published by the statistics office INS. After the marginal 0.1% q/q contraction in Q1, Romania’s economic activity remained for the third consecutive quarter roughly at the same level – which is the same level as that of Q2 2024.

The country’s GDP in the whole first half of the year (H1) contracted by 1.6% y/y.

Under the national methodology (that uses the previous year period’s prices for GDP aggregation, as opposed to the whole year’s average prices used by Eurostat), Romania’s GDP decreased by only 0.4% y/y in Q2, after the 1.2% y/y decline in Q1 – resulting in a milder 0.8% y/y annual economic contraction for the whole H1 period.

Given the base effects generated by the higher GDP in the first three quarters of 2025, Romania will end 2026 with a significant negative performance (-1.3% assuming seasonally-adjusted GDP remains constant and there is no backward adjustment of data as of now).

Romania’s authorities imply the economic contraction was expected and needed as an intermediary stage before a more sustainable growth model.

Romania undergoes a deep fiscal consolidation process with the Resilience Facility money and cohesion funds from the European Union offsetting the scaling down of the fiscal stimulus. From a record 9.3% of GDP in 2024, Romania’s general government budget may end this year around 6% of GDP. Private consumption, mainly hit by the consolidation, lost its role as a key economic driver – which is good for overall sustainability – resulting in a negative correction of the country’s GDP.

On a moderately optimistic note, the Ministry of Finance believes that the Q2 flash data signals the beginning of a process of economic stabilisation, during which investments and net exports take on a more important role, while consumption moderates.

“The stakes of this period are the shift towards a growth model based more on investment, productivity and external competitiveness and less on consumption expansion supported by the accumulation of fiscal and external deficits,” the finance minister commented.

"Sustainable economic growth cannot be built on stimulating consumption through ever-increasing public deficits, but on investments, productivity, competitiveness and a stable fiscal framework, capable of supporting development without the accumulation of new imbalances," finance minister Alexandru Nazare emphasised.

Independent analysts expect economic recovery no sooner than 2027.

Analysts expect possibly another quarter of annual economic contraction in Q3, but potentially a positive impact from agriculture and eventually a mild economic contraction for the entire year. This would not be very bad news, given the circumstances, Raiffeisen Romania’s chief economist, Ionut Dumitru, noted, as cited by Ziarul Financiar.

Both Dumitru and ASF Romania’s president Adrian Codirlasu ruled out positive economic growth for the entire year. Codirlasu even floated the idea of another (q/q) economic contraction in Q3, driven by the problems on the electricity market.

Erste Group continues to expect a mild 0.3% recession in 2026, following the Q2 flash release, assuming Q2 quarterly growth will be revised slightly higher in future releases. However, should the flash estimate be confirmed in the detailed breakdown, Erste analysts said that they could revise their full-year forecast down by around 0.1-0.2pp.

Erste Group expects Romania’s economy to rebound towards its potential growth rate in 2027, with GDP growth reaching 2.5%.
