World.title: Refugees, Migrants Tell of ‘Merciless’ Mass Beatings at Bulgarian Detention Centre
World.content:
Before the alleged violence, activists say protests had been going on for weeks against conditions at Pastrogor and the act of detention.

According to Collettivo Rotte Balcaniche, “in reaction, at least one person was beaten up by a police officer, detained at the police station, and forced to sign a pledge not to take part in any future protests”.

The situation came to a head on July 26, when Collettivo Rotte Balcaniche organised a demonstration outside the centre. Refugees and migrants joined in from inside.

One of the videos seen by BIRN shows nine migrants in a small room screaming “open camp” and a number of activists standing on top of a car near the perimeter of the facility. The protest was peaceful, the activists say.

Speaking on condition of anonymity, a Moroccan detainee told BIRN that two men – from Turkey and Tunisia – escaped. Other sources confirmed this.

“Then a policeman came and spoke to me in English, telling me to tell my friends to go back to their rooms upstairs because the rapid response team was coming, and if they found us in the square, things would get worse,” the Moroccan man said. “Everyone understood the situation. It was dangerous, so we returned to our rooms quietly.”

It is unclear which police unit the man meant by ‘rapid response team’. However, descriptions offered by migrants and refugees suggest the officers may have been part of the Bulgarian Gendarmerie.

According to BIRN sources inside the detention centre, the officers were dressed in full anti-riot gear, with masks, batons and stun guns. They were accompanied by regular policemen. The sources say there were around 30 to 40 in total.

“My friend and I were in the first room,” the Moroccan man said. “One of the masked men, holding a weapon, opened the door and said, ‘Get down! Get down!’ When I laid down on the floor, about 15 policemen entered the room and started beating us with batons. I thought it was the end. They beat me until I lost consciousness. They injured my friend’s head. They beat us mercilessly. I’ve never been beaten like that in my life. They went through all the rooms like that.”

Two other detainees, from Morocco and Pakistan, confirmed the account.

All sources BIRN spoke to stressed that beatings were meted out indiscriminately, across the facility. Collettivo Rotte Balcaniche said that surveillance cameras were turned off before the violence began, but offered no evidence.

‘Drenched in blood’

The second Moroccan man said officers also destroyed any phone they found, “so that we don’t publish photos of the beating”.

But images and videos have emerged.

Those seen by BIRN show at least eight different people with serious injuries, including two with bleeding head wounds. One man was drenched in blood.

The Pakistani detainee said he knew of at least 18 injured.

“They treated us brutally, as if we were criminals and not asylum seekers,” he said, speaking, like the others, on condition of anonymity.

After the beatings, the first Moroccan man said he and 11 other people were taken outside. “They started hitting and cursing and pouring water on us,” he said. “I felt hysterical, I felt like I was suffocating.”

He said the physical and verbal abuse continued at a nearby police station until the following day.

“They said, ‘If you don’t like the food, don’t eat it. Don’t do this. Don’t speak.’ They forced us to sign pledges and told us, ‘If you don’t like this treatment, go back to your country.’”

‘European standards’

World.title: Turkey Welcomes PKK Disarmament Law Despite Fears About Its Misuse
World.content:
Turkey last week took its most concrete legal step yet towards ending more than four decades of conflict with the Kurdistan Workers’ Party, PKK.

But while this is generating a rare political consensus and cautious optimism, suspicions about the intentions of the government overseeing the process run deep.

For many Kurds and other critics of the government, the central question is not only whether the PKK will disarm.

It is whether this process will lead to greater democracy, freedom and equal citizenship – or whether President Recep Tayyip Erdogan will use an initiative clothed in the language of peace to consolidate his own power.

World.title: Proposed Legal Changes to ‘Limit Rights’ Send Chill Through Serbian Schools
World.content:
As president of the Forum of Belgrade Gymnasiums, which represents grammar school employees in the Serbian capital, Ana Dimitrijevic attended a ‘public debate’ on August 5 at which Serbia’s education ministry opened discussion on a string of amendments that it wants to make to the Law on the Foundation of the Education System.

The ministry officials portrayed the amendments as “cosmetic”, Dimitrijevic recalled. They were anything but.

“They mostly underestimated our intelligence by explaining basic things we all know very well and pretended they didn’t understand why the fuss, when the amendments are cosmetic and not so important,” Dimitrijevic told BIRN. “When we asked for precise definitions of some of the amendments, they said ‘It goes without saying’, even though we all know it doesn’t.”

After more than 18 months of open confrontation between Serbia’s government and its educational institutions, from secondary schools to universities, the education ministry chose the summer holiday period to unveil legal changes that education workers fear will limit the ability of staff, pupils and parents to take a stand against social injustice.

They will broaden the grounds for teaching licences to be revoked, limit children’s right to assembly in school and reduce parental participation in the education system.

World.title: Albania Ruling Party Documents Highlight Country’s Ageing Demographic
World.content:
Documents produced by governing Socialist Party experts for a reform of the country’s municipal set-up, seen by BIRN, reveal an ageing population that could have adverse economic consequences for Albania.

The “Administrative-Territorial Reform 2.0” documents, prepared by experts on a special parliamentary committee, also show how emigration and internal migration have emptied out small towns and rural areas while concentrating the population in a few urban centres.

At one end are several urban centres where both population and economic activity are increasingly concentrated. At the other end are peripheral areas, particularly in the northeast, southeast and mountainous regions, which are caught in a vicious cycle of population decline and subsistence economies, with few formal jobs.

In these areas, municipal budgets survive largely on central government transfers, with funds often used mainly to cover the salaries of local administration staff.

The Urban Mass Index, UMI, one of three analytical documents underpinning the proposed new map of 46 municipalities – which would merge 15 local government units with larger municipalities – documents the territorial transformation of Albania since the 1990s, with a few centres continuing to grow as an increasing number of municipalities lose residents.

The “dependency ratio” in the index, which measures the burden that children and elderly people place on the working-age population, shows that in 51 municipalities out of 61 in total, this burden is higher than the national average. In many of them, the number of elderly residents exceeds the number of children.

The data highlights an Albania divided into three distinct realities: a small group of municipalities that continue to attract population and economic activity; a group of municipalities with intermediate potential; and a majority of the country’s territory, which is losing the critical mass of population needed to sustain local economies and public services.

The analysis is based on data from the 2023 census and, as part of the technical report accompanying the reform proposal, suggests that Albania is experiencing a growing concentration of its population in an ever-smaller number of urban centres, while the rest of the country is losing residents, functions and development capacity.

The index results show that only 13 municipalities are classified as having a high level of urban mass and are home to 62.5 per cent of the population.

By contrast, 30 municipalities – covering almost half of the country’s administrative map – are classified as having a low level of urban mass and account for just 14.2 per cent of the population.

Another 18 municipalities fall into the intermediate or medium category.

According to the data, the country’s population is concentrated in the capital, which is home to more than half a million people, followed at a considerable

distance by the municipalities of Durres, Vlora, Elbasan, Shkoder, Fieri, Kamza and Berat.

At the other end of the scale, municipalities such as Pustec, Libohova, Himara, Kelcyra, Memaliaj, Selenica, Dropull, Finiq, Delvina and Kolonja have the smallest populations.

The ruling-party experts did not build the index solely on population size. It also combines other indicators, including population density, the spatial distribution of residents, the demographic dependency ratio and the level of urbanisation.

This means that a municipality may cover a large area, but if its population is concentrated in a small town while the rest of its territory is largely empty, it is considered structurally weak.

One of the most significant findings is that, on average, 57 per cent of Albania’s territory is uninhabited.

The analytical document notes that the country no longer has the same population distribution it had in 2014, when the current administrative-territorial division was introduced with the aim of creating larger and more efficient municipalities.

“Some areas have grown, while others have lost a significant share of their population,” the report says, arguing that some municipalities are struggling to secure sustainable finances, qualified staff and adequate administrative capacity.

The Socialists have submitted a bill to parliament proposing a new administrative-territorial map that would merge several smaller municipalities with larger neighbouring ones – without explaining how the proposed map would address these underlying problems.

The proposal has faced opposition from residents in the affected areas. Some fear mergers will leave them with even more limited access to public services.

World.title: Kosovo Detains Man Suspected of Spying for Serbian Intelligence
World.content:
Fehim Sali, second left, at a court hearing in Pristina on August 14, 2026. Photo: BIRN

Pristina Basic Court on Friday ordered 30 days of detention for a dual Kosovo and Serbia citizen, Fehim Sali, who is suspected of spying for Serbia’s intelligence agency, the BIA.

It is alleged that he passed the BIA information about Kosovo officials, politicians and Islamist radicals, including potential recruitment targets, and received money in return.

Sali, a resident of Kosovo’s southern Dragash/Dragas municipality, was arrested on Thursday at the Merdare border crossing point while entering from Serbia. He appeared before the Basic Court in Pristina on Friday.

“The court’s assessment took into account the circumstances relating to the risk of absconding, the risk of influencing witnesses and evidence, and the risk of repetition or continuation of the criminal offence,” the court said in a statement.

According to the prosecution file, Sali is suspected of “maintaining contact with BIA officers using four different mobile phones”, which were found during raids at his house on Thursday, alongside around 40,000 euros in cash.

The prosecution file alleges that Sali “worked as a recruited agent for Serbia’s Security Information Agency, BIA, in exchange for material benefits”. The file alleges that he acted on the instructions of a senior BIA officer identified as Zelimir Matovic, nicknamed Zeljko.

It alleges that Sali provided the BIA with information about Kosovo’s political situation and helped it identify officials of Kosovo’s own intelligence agency, the AKI. According to the case file, he photographed some of its officials to facilitate their identification.

Sali is also accused of providing information about members of the radical Islamist Wahhabi movement as well as other people whom he allegedly proposed to the BIA officer as potential targets for contact and recruitment.

According to prosecutors, Sali also “mediated matters and documents connected to Serbian state institutions and maintained contacts with people with political and social influence in Serbia and Kosovo, particularly members of non-majority communities”.

The prosecution stated that he provided some of these people with “guidance on political activity, with the aim of gathering and transmitting information of interest to the BIA”.

Prosecutors argue that these activities were carried out against the state interests of Kosovo and endangered its constitutional order and national security.

The prosecution also alleges that the 40,000 euros found and seized during a search of Sali’s home came from his alleged activities on behalf of the BIA.

According to the case file, the evidence against Sali includes his own statement.

Prosecutors claim he described in detail his alleged activities, including how and where he communicated with BIA officials, exchanged information and provided assistance to the Serbian intelligence service.

Prosecutor Bekim Kodraliu told media that Sali admitted having been recruited and maintained regular contact with BIA officials.

“The suspect himself stated that he had been recruited and had ongoing contacts with BIA officials,” Kodraliu said.

The case comes two months after another Kosovo espionage conviction involving Serbia’s intelligence service.

In June, the Pristina Basic Court sentenced a Kosovo Albanian man, Hysri Selimi, a former Islamic State member, to six years in prison for espionage.

Prosecutors said Selimi had provided the BIA with information about religious radicalisation in Kosovo, former members of the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, and people who had joined Islamic State.

World.title: Week in Review: Between the Absurd and the Unexpected
World.content:
Kosovo’s governance drama is beginning to border on the absurd. Weeks after the June election results were certified, two months after the elections were held, MPs have yet to elect a parliamentary speaker and deputies and, in doing so, constitute the new parliament.

The winning party, Vetevendosje, has the votes to elect a new speaker, and indeed a new government. But it has conditioned the election of a speaker on reaching a wider agreement with the opposition on the election of a new president. With deadlines imposed by the Constitutional Court passing, is Kosovo heading to a fourth parliamentary election in two years?

World.title: Thousands Flee, 14 Hospitalised as Wildfire Menaces Croatian Coastal Town
World.content:
Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic said on Friday that 14 people have been hospitalised, with ten in intensive care, after a wildfire that reportedly forced some 2,000 people to evacuate homes around the Dalmatian coastal town of Omis overnight.

“The government and all relevant services are coordinating to protect people and rectify the consequences of the large fire in Omis,” Plenkovic wrote on X.

The fire swept through forested areas to destroy property and vehicles. Chief national fire officer Slavko Tucakovic told media that he had “never experienced anything like this in my career”.

“Unfortunately, many houses were damaged or burned down. A large number of vehicles were also burned up,” he said.

The Croatian coast has seen record high temperatures this summer. The heatwave left dry vegetation as fuel for the fire, and the flames were spread by high winds, Tucakovic explained.

World.title: Kosovo’s LDK Drops Demand to Choose President in Bid to Resolve Crisis
World.content:
LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku addresses media on August 13, 2026. Photo: BIRN .

The opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, said on Thursday it had withdrawn its demands to name the country’s new president in an attempt to end the political deadlock that has paralysed Kosovo since parliamentary elections in June.

Lumir Abdixhiku, the LDK leader, said that while talks with the poll-winning Vetevendosje party’s leader Albin Kurti over a government partnership had not yet produced results, he was offering new talks about the election of a new president – which is crucial to avoid new parliamentary polls.

“From this moment, no one has any reason, alibi or the right to delay the inauguration of parliament, the formation of the government and starting negotiations on a new president. We are late and should not waste any more time,” Abdixhiku said in a video message after a meeting with the party’s parliamentary group.

“The constitutional uncertainty is a reality we cannot ignore … The crisis does not seem to have an end and it’s getting worse and worse,” he added.

“We are ready to discuss the election of a president who defends our republic’s interests and its constitution, represents people’s unity and exercises the constitutional responsibilities. We are not asking for any posts or any political compensation in return,” he continued.

In the June elections, Kurti’s Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the Assembly, well ahead of the Kosovo Democratic Party, PDK, which won 22. The LDK won 18 seats and has until now insisted on having the president’s post, which Vetevendosje has deemed a “disproportionate” demand.

Kurti will likely obtain a simple majority in the Assembly to form a new government, by again relying on the support of MPs from various ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk, Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

However, the wider crisis that led to the June 7 elections has not been solved; the parties still need to agree on the election of a new president within two months of the inauguration of the new parliament, or it will trigger another election.

Speaking on Friday, Kurti did not specifically say if he will accept the LDK offer, but welcomed Abdixhiku’s willingness to include other parties in negotiations over the presidency.

“We are open to further discussions in order to come to a name or names [for the presidency], someone who is out of the current political scene, out of daily party polemics, and who is a unifying figure,” Kurti said.

“We want to agree in advance in order to avoid new elections. The election of a parliament speaker and a cabinet is not a challenge, so we have to agree on the election of a president,” he added.

Meanwhile a group PDK MPs protested on Friday for the second day in a row in front of acting premier Kurti’s office, demanding the resumption of parliament’s inaugural session. This was interrupted last Saturday when Kurti asked for “more time” to discuss the issue of a new president with other parties.

So far, Abdixhiku and Kurti have met twice but have not found a common ground on new institutions. In his video address, Abdixhiku disclosed that the LDK was offered three ministries in Kurti’s next cabinet – “a disproportion we could not afford”.

World.title: Plenković: Main Tourist Season is Good, We Expect a Good Post-Season
World.content:
August the 17th, 2026 – PM Andrej Plenković has stated that despite challenges, the main summer tourist season is going well so far, with a good post-season also expected.

It’s mid-August and the temperatures are scorching. More tourists are arriving on the Adriatic coast than leaving it, despite the devastating fires that have ravaged central Dalmatia. Traffic remains heavy on most roads leading towards the coast, and a similar situation can be observed at airports located along the Croatian coastline.

Poslovni reports that during the morning hours, long queues of vehicles continue to form along the motorway, stretching from Lučko near Zagreb all the way to Bosiljevo near Karlovac. Occasional congestion has also been reported in the direction of the island of Krk and the wider Kvarner region, indicating continued strong tourist demand even after the traditional peak of the summer season.

Prime Minister Andrej Plenković assessed the current tourist season as better than expected, both in terms of the number of arrivals and overnight stays, and according to fiscalisation data and recorded revenues. Speaking about the positive indicators, Plenković emphasised the broader economic importance of tourism for Croatia.

“This is important for the economy, for GDP growth and for the Croatian economy as a whole,” the Prime Minister said. He added that the government hopes the positive trend will continue into the post-season period, which is traditionally a strong part of the tourist year in Croatia.

Tourism remains one of the key pillars of the Croatian economy, contributing significantly to employment, local business activity and overall economic growth. The sustained inflow of visitors in mid-August, combined with solid revenue figures, suggests that the 2026 season is performing well despite ongoing challenges such as rising costs in the hospitality sector and complex competitive conditions in the Mediterranean market.

With traffic still flowing towards the coast and airports remaining busy, industry observers and the government alike are counting on a solid post-season to further strengthen the overall results of this year’s tourist season.

World.title: Omiš Fire: Rescuers Describe the Fear of Those Rescued From the Sea
World.content:
August the 17th, 2026 – The catastrophic Omiš fire saw many running for their lives into the sea to escape the flames, with rescuers describing the fear in their eyes as they were pulled out of the water.

Hundreds of people managed to escape the rapidly advancing flames of the Omiš fire by fleeing directly into the sea. In their rescue, alongside the Harbour Master’s Office, the police and customs, the owners of more than 20 private boats also took part. Index writes that local residents are gradually returning to their homes in areas where the electricity supply has been restored. Some of them have lost all their property, with their houses, money and all their memories lost to the blaze, reports HRT.

“you could see the sheer fear for their lives in their eyes”

The situation was particularly dramatic at sea, where people were fleeing in desperation into the water from the fire. Among those who rushed to help them was Mario Popovac, who also took part in the rescue during last year’s fire near Marušići.

Popovac and his friends set off towards the location where people were cut off. While sailing through thick smoke and strong wind, they heard shouts from the water. “I stopped the boat and in the sea we saw dozens of people. It was difficult to approach them and pull them out, so we came closer with the stern and then used an oar to draw them towards the boat,” Popovac said.

Among those rescued was a heavily pregnant woman and parents with small children. On the first trip Popovac took 27 people onto his boat, including seven children aged four or five. “The parents were trying to hold their children up, but the waves and wind were washing over them and knocking them back down. The first two or three trips were very chaotic. Later, people called us from the beaches, so access was easier,” he said. He explained that because of the thick smoke they initially could not see the people in the water, but found them by following their shouts. They were floating fifty to a hundred metres from the shore.

solidarity in pure disaster

A large number of people joined the rescue with their own private boats. Popovac mentioned the example of a friend who loaded 20 people onto his four-metre-long boat. Popovac then took them onto his larger boat and transported them to safety.

“You could clearly see the sheer fear for their lives in their eyes. I’m glad that so many people came out with their boats. We all passed each other, helped one another and passed water around. People gave everything they had to pull others out,” Popovac said. Financial aid to Omiš has already been sent by numerous Croatian towns, including Pula, Sinj, Vukovar and Baška Voda. The final amount of damage from the fire has not yet been entirely determined, but it will be exceptionally large.

World.title: Omiš Wine Producer: Everything Was Destroyed Within an Hour
World.content:
August the 17th, 2026 – The tragedy of the horrendous Omiš fire knows no bounds as one local wine producer says his next harvest will be set back by about 7 years. He said that the fire engulfed everything he owned in just an hour.

Index reports that the massive Omiš fire destroyed the vineyard belonging to the Mimica family, and right before the harvest. For winemaker Marko Mimica, the fire destroyed in just one hour the plantings he had been investing in for 25 years. This year’s grape crop, which was already ready for picking, burned completely.

“It’s difficult at this moment in time to say anything coherent. Twenty-five years of work and struggle with this hillside disappeared literally in an hour,” said winemaker Marko Mimica in conversation with Nova TV. The harvest had been scheduled for Friday and the team had already been gathered, but the fire interrupted everything. “Everything was pointing to a more than good harvest despite the severe drought,” Mimica added.

a major setback and a long road ahead

Mimica emphasised that the chances of the existing vineyard recovering are very, very small. “Now, as a family we will gather ourselves and try to clean all of this up. We’ll try to get straight back into planting and revitalising new vineyards,” he stated, explaining that this work includes uprooting the destroyed vines, removing the fence and posts, and then clearing and preparing the whole terrain again.

This determined winemaker also thanked his colleagues who have constantly been offering him financial and moral support over the last two days. He is however more than aware that no money can compensate for such a loss. He assumes that a natural disaster will be declared, through which he hopes for state aid as well.

The process of planting a new vineyard, Mimica explains, takes two years. “On this karst, stone and meagre soil it will certainly take another five years until the first harvest. So that is a job of about seven years,” he specified. He took over the winery from his father five years ago and says he has enough strength to continue. He says that by giving up the winery he would also lose his own identity, which he has been building for almost 30 years.

World.title: Material Damage Caused by Omiš Fire is Astronomical
World.content:
August the 17th, 2026 – The material damage caused by the catastrophic Omiš fire is astronomical, with the full scale of the damage almost too difficult to cope with for some.

The horrendous fire that ripped through part of the central Dalmatian coastline has now finally been completely stopped, but it has left behind scenes of complete and utter destruction. Houses, business premises, boats and cars burned. Residents are returning to their properties and adding up the damage. One woman tragically lost her life in the fire, but her identity has not yet been officially confirmed, reports Net.hr.

Index reports that the residents of the hardest-hit areas are only now fully realising the true scale of the damage. In the places where firefighters fought the flames, today only the remains of life before the fire are left.

“It’s awful. At first I didn’t have that many emotions, but yesterday I cried the whole way as I looked at it all. I’m not so much sorry for myself as I am for other people. Look around, this is an apocalypse,” said Ivica Marijanović from Čelina. He estimates the damage to his property at between 700 and 800 thousand euros. “This is a catastrophe. It’s terrible,” Marijanović added.

Numerous business facilities were also destroyed in the fire. Boat service owner Ante Kovačić in Vrisovci lost almost all of his property. “Seven or eight boats burned at this location, and I have another location elsewhere where another four were damaged. The damage is huge. Here the work van was scorched, my scooter also burned. It’s a horror,” Kovačić said. Cafe owner Josip Čapeta said that he, his father and a worker stayed to defend the building while others were evacuating. “We stayed here to try and save it. We built this with our own hands and we stayed to fight to the end. We didn’t run,” he said. Despite their efforts, the cafe where eight people earned their living was not saved.

lingering fears will hang around for a long time to come

While some lost almost everything, others find reasons for gratitude in the remains. In the home of academic painter Miro Zovko in Stanići, the fire destroyed some artworks and instruments. “About 16 paintings burned there, there were instruments too. But thank God, my studio upstairs remained intact. And there could have been an explosion from all that resin,” Zovko said. Dominik Čapin from Stanići believes it is a real miracle that the fire did not engulf the entire house. “Today’s Our Lady was with us so that everything didn’t burn. Upstairs it was ten centimetres short of catching the wooden beams – everything would have burned,” he said.

The fear has not disappeared with the fire. Anica Tomić from Čelina described how she was saving a car while sparks were flying around her. “I took a hose from the neighbour and that’s how we were saving things. I can’t talk any more, I’m sorry. Now the panic is hitting me – now it’s worse and harder for me than it was these past two days,” she said through tears.

those injured remain in a critical condition in hospital

While the damage is being assessed on the ground, treatment of the most seriously injured continues in hospitals. At University Hospital Zagreb three patients are fighting for their lives and their condition is unchanged. At the Children’s Hospital in Zagreb, a minor is being treated who suffered burns on 25 percent of her body. She was operated on yesterday. “If everything goes according to plan, she’ll be taken off the assisted breathing device within the next 36 hours,” said Stjepan Višnjić, head of the Clinic for Paediatric Surgery.

At University Hospital Split seven more patients are being treated. “On Friday afternoon we had to operate on one patient whose condition had worsened and re-intubate her. Three patients are on the ward and there are no changes with them,” said Ivo Utrobčić from the Department of Plastic, Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgery and Burns at University Hospital Split.

The fire has left behind enormous material damage and the gravest consequence. The identity of the woman who died is still being established.

World.title: The Croatian River With the Remains of an Ancient City Below the Surface
World.content:
August the 16th, 2026 – There’s a Croatian river which is home to the remains of an ancient city and a 1,800 year old Roman barge. Over 9,000 fascinating artefacts have been discovered at this single location.

The Kupa River in Sisak is home to the remains of ancient Siscia, a Roman bridge and a cargo barge about 1,800 years old, while underwater research continues to uncover new traces of the past. The course of the Kupa River through Sisak today seems peaceful, a familiar part of the city’s everyday life. Putni kofer writes that along the banks there is a promenade and fishermen, kayaks can occasionally be seen on the river, and a few kilometres downstream it flows into the Sava. However, beneath that calm surface lies a completely different Sisak. Over the past hundred years or so, thousands of archaeological objects have been recovered from the riverbed, while underwater, parts of ancient buildings, traces of a Roman bridge and a large river barge that sailed the Kupa approximately 1,800 years ago have been preserved.

One of the most extensive archaeological collections found in European rivers

The scale of these finds is exceptional even far beyond Croatian borders. In a scholarly paper dedicated to the Roman river barge from Sisak, the collection of objects recovered from the Kupa is described as one of the most extensive collections of archaeological material found in European rivers. The objects span a long period of time, from the Copper Age to the Middle Ages, but the Roman layer is particularly rich, created in the centuries when Siscia was one of the important cities in this part of the Empire.

A large part of this collection was not found during classic archaeological excavations. It was brought to the surface by major dredging of the Kupa at the beginning of the 20th century, especially the works carried out in 1912. The monograph Urbanism of Roman Siscia states that the Archaeological Museum in Zagreb holds around nine thousand ancient artefacts dredged from the riverbed, while the Sisak City Museum mentions around ten thousand recovered objects and more than nine thousand archaeological finds in connection with these interventions. Items that at first glance have little in common were recovered from the Kupa at that time: military equipment and weapons, jewellery, coins, pottery, tools and everyday objects. Together, however, they give an unusually broad picture of the people who lived along this river for centuries and used it as a transport route, a source of food, a place of work and a connection with the rest of the world.

Segestica, then Siscia left behind enormous wealth…

The explanation for this wealth lies primarily in the location of the city. Segestica, and later Roman Siscia, developed right next to the river and an important navigable route that led via the Sava towards the Danube. Because of this, the Kupa was much more than the natural border of the city. People travelled and traded on it, a port and other facilities related to river traffic developed along it, and over the centuries objects ended up in the water in various ways. At the same time, the riverbed itself changed. Erosion of the left bank affected part of the area of the ancient city, so structures that once stood beside the Kupa are today partly located within it.

It is precisely this shifted edge of the ancient city that has become the focus of new research in recent years. Since 2021, systematic international underwater investigations have been carried out in the Kupa that no longer depend only on what the river happens to throw up or what dredging pulls out of it. Sonar, diving research and other methods have enabled archaeologists to document what still stands or lies on the bottom. The masonry remains of Siscia’s fortifications that collapsed into the water, large wooden piles connected with the Roman bridge, and parts of lead water pipes that crossed the river have been located. In 2025 the City of Sisak reported that remains of ramparts, bridges and other structures are being documented in the riverbed, so the relationship of ancient Siscia to the Kupa can now be reconstructed much more precisely.

a 1,800 year old roman barge lies in the depths…

Among all these traces, one vessel stands out whose story began long before the current research. At the Kovnica site a Roman river cargo barge was discovered as early as 1985, but the conditions at the time allowed only part of the structure to be investigated. The ship then remained underwater for decades until archaeologists returned to it in the 2025 campaign. A significantly larger part of the wreck, now known as Sisak 1, was then uncovered. The French Ministry of Culture states that the ship has so far been revealed to a length of at least twelve metres, with a preserved width of 3.34 metres, while one of its ends is probably still under bank sediment. It has been dated to the 3rd century, a time when river navigation was an important part of the transport system of Roman Siscia.

The construction of the ship itself is particularly interesting. Archaeologist Anton Divić explains that elements of local river shipbuilding can be recognised on it, as well as techniques known from the Roman maritime tradition. Sisak 1 is therefore important not only as a rarely preserved cargo ship, but also as evidence that different shipbuilding knowledge met and mixed in Siscia.

the home of discoveries from the 2nd century bc

Interestingly, the large cargo vessel is not the only old craft that the Kupa has preserved. More recent research has also revealed a series of logboats – simple boats hollowed out from a single tree trunk. Five of them have been investigated and dated so far, and the results obtained stretch from the 2nd century BC to the end of antiquity. Because of such a wide time span, not all the vessels can be linked to the same period or the same community.

Perhaps the most interesting thing today is that the story of Roman Siscia is not taking place only in museum display cases. Part of the city lies beneath modern Sisak, part of its former edges ended up in the Kupa, and part still remains to be investigated. Over the past century the Kupa has yielded thousands of objects, but its bed has clearly not yet told the whole story.

World.title: Rimac: Top Croatian Export Products are Luxury Cars and Battery Systems
World.content:
August the 16th, 2026 – Entrepreneur Mate Rimac has stated that some of the top Croatian export products are now luxury cars and battery systems.

Mate Rimac published on Facebook a table of the 50 largest Croatian goods exporters in 2025, compiled by the portal Lider. Index reports that among the top ten are two companies from Rimac’s business system. Bugatti Rimac took fourth place, and Rimac Technology seventh.

“Croatia’s top export products in 2025 are oil and derivatives, medicines, transformers, luxury cars and their components, dietary supplements, battery and propulsion systems for cars, aluminium foil, food, HVAC systems and pharmaceutical products,” Rimac wrote. This is Rimac’s summary compiled on the basis of the activities of the companies at the top of Lider’s ranking. The table itself ranks companies according to the value of their exports.

Who is actually on the table?

In first place is INA, which achieved 1.23 billion euros in exports in 2025. It is followed by Pliva Hrvatska with 474.4 million euros and Končar – Distribution and Special Transformers with 409.8 million euros.

Bugatti Rimac took fourth place with exports worth 369.1 million euros, which accounts for 94.33 percent of the company’s total revenues. In fifth place is Končar – Power Transformers with 313.5 million euros in exports, and sixth is dietary supplement manufacturer EMPWR with 227.4 million euros. Rimac Technology is in seventh place with exports worth 214 million euros, or an export share of 79.86 percent of total revenues. Also among the top ten are Aluflexpack Novi, Podravka and Klimaoprema.

According to Lider’s data, the 50 largest Croatian goods exporters in 2025 achieved a total of 7.4 billion euros in exports. At the same time, Croatian goods exports exceeded 25 billion euros, of which 21.7 billion was generated by the manufacturing industry.

World.title: The Night Omiš Will Never Forget – Everything Went Up in Flames in a Second
World.content:
August the 16th, 2026 – The night that Omiš will never forget was one marked by apocalyptic scenes and dramatic rescues from the sea.

An enormous fire that initially broke out in Lokva Rogoznica, driven by strong winds, spread rapidly towards Omiš. The fire threatened houses, reached the Adriatic Highway and forced residents and guests to flee into the sea to escape the flames. The testimonies of the people who found themselves facing the blaze show just how quickly the situation turned into a fight for survival.

“it all happened in a few seconds”

Dražen Ravlić was among the first to warn about the approaching fire. He said he noticed cars starting to turn back from the direction in which the fire was spreading. He immediately warned people at a nearby car park and called the firefighters.

“Everything happened very fast. I went ahead to the parking area and told people to move their cars,” he told Index. Together with a motorcyclist who happened to be there, he tried to help, but without equipment they could not do much. What remained in Ravlić’s memory were the sparks flying, carried by the wind. Afterwards he said he regretted that he could not do more.

Goran Lović, the owner of a cafe near the area where the fire first broke out, described how suddenly the blaze actually spread. “Everything went up in flames in a second,” he said. Lović believes the fire was started deliberately and handed surveillance camera footage over to the police. The cause of the fire has not yet been officially determined and this remains unconfirmed.

cars went up in flames and people fled into the sea for safety

When the fire reached the main road, the road was no longer a safe way out. Some people left their cars and headed towards the coast. Among them was Karla from Zagreb. At the moment of evacuation she was in a car, but the fire reached the road. “Cars started burning and then we went down towards the sea,” Karla said.

During the escape she fell and injured herself. With others she took shelter in a small cave by the sea, where they waited around two hours for rescuers. “Above us, the terrifying fire was blazing viciously,” she described. She managed to save only her documents, but says she is grateful to be alive. People fled into the sea or climbed onto boats they found along the shore. 194 people were rescued from the sea, mainly in the area from Nemira to Ruskamen. Intensive rescue operations lasted from after midnight until almost 03:00.

seasonal workers from mostar fled their apartment with barely anything

Two seasonal workers from Mostar said they fled their apartment with almost nothing. They spent the night in the car, waiting for the danger to pass and trying to find out what had happened to the place where they worked.

The café Mala Luka, where they worked, burned down completely. “We saw it approaching. I told her: “We’re not going to mess around.” We got into the car and left towards Omiš,” they said. Similar testimonies could be heard throughout the burned area. People described how in the dark they watered their yards, extinguished sparks carried by the wind and waited until the last moment before leaving their houses.

“when i saw there was no hope, i had to leave”

Marin Ozretić tried to defend his house as the fire came closer and closer. As the flames descended from the hill, he watered the pines and the area around the house, trying to stop the fire from spreading.

“I spent my entire life building this… When I saw there was no hope left for me, I just had to go,” he told Index. He described flames several metres high coming down from the hill. At the last moment he got into his car and left the area. He saved himself and the vehicle, but was unable to save his house.

Also at the fire site was Anđelko Kovačić, whose house in the old village, workshop and boats he was repairing all burned. Czech tourists who were staying in his apartment were left without a car and did not know how they would get home.

the morning light revealed the true scale of the unimaginable damage

Only when daylight came did the full extent of the fire become visible. Burned cars, destroyed buildings, blackened pines and large areas covered in ash remained. According to the latest information, 43 people sought medical help. Fourteen of them were kept in hospital, and eight were in life-threatening condition. During a search of the burned area, police also found the body of one person whose identity has not yet been released.

World.title: Omiš Resident Describes the Fire: It Was Like Being in Hell
World.content:
August the 16th, 2026 – An Omiš resident described the horrendous fire that swept through the area leaving a trail of unimaginable destruction behind it as like “being in hell”.

Index reports that a resident of Čelina near Omiš, Karlo, spent the night defending his house from the fire that devastated his village. One house burned down completely, and at one point the residents were left without water, so they tried to fight the flames with shovels. Children were evacuated to Omiš, while help is arriving in the affected area from all over Croatia.

“it was like we were in hell”

“It cannot be described in words. We were surrounded by smoke and fire. We used water for as long as we could, but our water supply depends on electricity. When the power went out, the water was gone too. Even the firefighters ran out of water, and we continued with shovels. By some miracle we managed to save some of the houses,” Karlo told N1. He said that it was primarily ruins which were entirely burned down in the village. “A house burned here too, that is the worst image of the fire I have in my mind. I don’t even want to mention the body that was found, it’s just beyond a horror.”

“the fire arrived in just 45 minutes”

Karlo said he didn’t expect the fire to spread so quickly. “We watched the light approaching. The fire reached our village in 45 minutes. We poured water all over the houses and that saved us. The night was endless, we couldn’t sleep or eat,” he described. They moved the children to safety in Omiš, while the men stayed to defend the property. “My mother stayed – she isn’t afraid of anything – and she was also watering the house. A neighbour’s car burned in a covered garage.” He admits he was not afraid, but he was fully aware of the danger.

help from across croatia

In the meantime, volunteers from all over Croatia are arriving at the fire site. Among them is Mario from Petrinja, who came with his father and son bringing a donation. “I was sleeping when my wife called and asked if I would drive a donation. I agreed, and I didn’t even know why. Within a few hours we gathered, people were calling, I didn’t even know where I was going. I came with my father and son,” he said.

World.title: Ülle Madise meets with MPs to discuss presidential candidacy
World.content:
Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise, who announced that she has agreed to run for president, will meet with the Riigikogu parliamentary groups on Monday to discuss her candidacy with MPs.

Estonia's president is elected by members of the Riigikogu and a candidate needs the support of 68 MPs out of a total 101.

Madise, who is midway through her second seven-year term as chancellor of justice, is the top choice of the coalition parties, Reform and Eesti 200, as well as the opposition Social Democratic Party.

Last week, the three parties collected 62 signatures in support of nominating Madise as a presidential candidate. However, several more votes will be needed to elect her president.

In the meetings with Riigikogu parliamentary groups on Monday, Madise will discuss her thoughts on the role of the president and answer MPs' questions.

She will meet with the Center Party at 10 a.m., the biggest opposition party Isamaa at noon, SDE at 2 p.m., and with unaligned Riigikogu members at 3 p.m.

Madise will also meet with Reform's Mart Võrklaev at 1.30 p.m., who, unlike his party colleagues, has not yet given his signature in the Riigikogu in support of nominating Madise as a presidential candidate.

Last week, Madise said she would not run unless she had broad support for her candidacy.

World.title: Linnahall shooting range in Tallinn could cost millions to make work
World.content:
Tallinn has offered Linnahall's former ice rink to the Estonian Defense League (EDL) for a temporary shooting range , but experts say repairs could cost millions.

Tallinn Deputy Mayor and EDL member Kristjan Järvan said the city had consulted two shooting range operators before pitching the proposal. He estimated the initial investment needed to convert the space at about €500,000.

"At least 55-meter shooting ranges could be built here, right inside the ice rink," Järvan said.

He argued the project could turn the largely unused concrete structure into a useful defense asset at a relatively modest cost. The Estonian Center for Defense Investments (ECDI) and EDL would ultimately decide whether to pursue it.

"Tallinn just sees this as an additional option we can offer," the deputy mayor added.

Järvan previously said the range would be temporary, operating until the city decides on a longer-term future for the long-neglected venue.

Fellow EDL member and Tondi shooting range owner Tõnis Orumaa said the former ice rink could work particularly well for tactical shooting because its open layout would allow firing in multiple directions.

"You've got a full-sized ice hockey arena, so you could fire across 180 degrees," he explained, adding that in traditional ranges, targets are all in one place at the far end.

But the rink would first have to be cleared out and its leaking roof made watertight, followed by ongoing maintenance costs. Orumaa estimated that renovating the roof alone could cost about €3 million.

Money would stretch further elsewhere

He noted that the EDL's Rapla District, meanwhile, is currently headquartered in a small space, while the Järva District is operating out of the Türi Subdistrict's facilities.

"For that money, we could build three district support centers," Orumaa said.

The same investment could also fund two or three comparable shooting ranges elsewhere in the country instead, he added.

The EDL already has a shooting complex near Tallinn, while the Estonian Defense Forces' (EDF) Central Training Area still offers the best training conditions.

The ice rink at Tallinn's Soviet-era Linnahall venue complex closed in 2009 and has remained unused since then. Whether the EDL wants to take on the building alongside its other priorities remains to be decided

World.title: Eneli Jefimova goes home from European swimming championships without a medal
World.content:
Swimmer Eneli Jefimova finished the European Aquatics Championships in Paris with another fourth-place finish, this time in the 50m breaststroke.

The Estonian, 21, had also finished fourth in the 100m breaststroke earlier in the week.

Jefimova had arrived in Paris as the defending champion in the 100m breaststroke, having won gold in Belgrade two years ago with a time of 1:06.41. She had also set a new Estonian record of 1:05.78 in the 100m semifinal this time around in Paris — improving on her own mark from May by three hundredths.

In the 50m final, Jefimova swam 30.00, having clocked 29.93 in the semifinal — a time that would have been good enough for gold in the final on the day. The ever-present Ruta Meilutyte of Lithuania took gold in 29.93, edging Italy's Benedetta Pilato (29.94) and Ireland's Mona McSharry (29.95) in an extremely tight race. Jefimova was next.

"This was a slightly worse swim than yesterday. But seven hundredths... I don't really know what was so different compared with yesterday. But right now I'm disappointed. Fourth place again, this time by five hundredths. It's a bit tough right now," Jefimova told ERR.

"In terms of times, definitely a very good European Championships, but in finals those times don't matter as much as medals. I would have liked to take a medal or two home from here as well," she went on.

In the 100m final earlier in the week, she finished fourth with 1:05.94, 0.16 seconds slower than her semifinal time, missing the podium by five hundredths. Britain's Angharad Evans won gold in a championship record 1:04.87.

"I actually felt pretty good during the swim," Jefimova said after the 100m final. "When the final 25 started, I felt like another gear kicked in, but then the finish just didn't work out at all."

She added she had been calmer than in previous years. "It's a process, and it's the fourth time I've gone 1:05 — that time is actually great. Today the other women were simply faster."

Other Estonians failed to advance from the morning heats earlier in the week. Kregor Zirk (52.87) and Alex Ahtiainen (52.42) finished 32nd and 29th in the men's 100m butterfly, missing the semifinal cut of 52.07. In the women's 50m backstroke, Maari Randväli (29.18) and Margaret Markvardt (29.76) placed 32nd and 39th, well off the 28.61 cutoff. Christopher Palvadre (2:16.54) and Ralf Roose (2:20.29) were 36th and 41st in the men's 200m breaststroke.

The 2026 European Aquatics Championships in Paris ran from July 31 to August 16.

World.title: Justice chancellor Ülle Madise to run for president
World.content:
Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise on Monday officially put herself forward as a candidate to be the next president of Estonia, ending weeks of speculation.

Estonia's president is elected by members of the Riigikogu and a candidate needs the support of 68 MPs of a total 101.

Discussions about potential candidates have been ongoing throughout the summer, and the election will take place at the start of September.

Madise, who is midway through her second seven-year term as chancellor of justice, is the top choice of the coalition parties, Reform and Eesti 200. Earlier this month, Madise said she would consider declaring herself a candidate if she had enough support from members of the Riigikogu.

On Monday, she said in a statement: "I am running for President of the Republic of Estonia. I feel great respect and humility as I write this. The role of the president carries the highest responsibility I could take on before the Estonian state and people."

Madise said she would meet with members of the Riigikogu on Monday to present her thoughts on the role of the president and answer MPs' questions.

"If I am elected President of the Republic of Estonia, I will accept with honor and humility the task of serving the Estonian people and the Estonian state as head of state," she wrote.

Presidential candidates are officially submitted August 21-24 and the election will take place on September 2. Further voting rounds will take place if no candidate wins enough votes during the first round.

Here is Ülle Madise's statement in full:

"I am running for President of the Republic of Estonia. I feel great respect and humility as I write this. The role of the president carries the highest responsibility I could take on before the Estonian state and people.

My views are no secret: Estonia's purpose is to be Estonia. Independence gives us the opportunity to do everything to make Estonia the best place to live, to raise children, to invent, to write poetry, to run a business. To preserve our language, culture and values; to be bold, to dream big and to make those dreams real.

The constitutional duty of the president is to safeguard what makes Estonia Estonia. Our people, language, culture, nature, freedom and peace. People are our greatest treasure. Everything possible must be done to ensure that children are born, that they can grow into good, educated individuals, do work they enjoy and receive fair pay, build a home and a family, and tie their lives to Estonia. For that, Estonia must be a good place to live. Clean nature, culture and atmosphere, freedom and responsibility, a caring and developing state.

Thirty‑five years ago, our freedom was reclaimed by people who dared more. Yes, today we have small generations. But let them become generations full of strength! If young Estonians have confidence, hope, initiative, education, well‑being and joy in life, we will build Estonia ever greater through cooperation between generations.

Estonia must carry more weight in the world. The president must be steadfast in opening doors and building bridges. This is not easy, but I am not afraid of those doors, thresholds, or rapid rivers. Estonia has much to offer the world, from the works and services to the products crafted by our people.

Who is suitable to be President of the Republic in the current circumstances will be decided by secret ballot in the Riigikogu or the electoral college. The Estonian state belongs to the Estonian people. The president belongs to their people.

As a presidential candidate, I am ready for open communication. Today and in the coming days, I will meet with members of the Riigikogu to present my views on the role of the president. I am also ready to answer questions from anyone else and explain my understanding of the president's role and responsibilities.

If I am elected President of the Republic of Estonia, I will accept with honor and humility the task of serving the Estonian people and the Estonian state as head of state.

Respectfully,

Ülle Madise"

World.title: 3 Estonian competitors got top-10 finishes at European athletics champs
World.content:
Three of Estonia's 20 athletes finished in the top 10 at the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham, England, which finished Sunday.

Team Estonia delegation chief Aivo Normak assessed the team's overall performance rating as "good," though no medals were won this time.

The strongest result came from decathlete Karel Tilga, with his 5th place and 8,286 points. Fellow decathlete Rasmus Roosleht was just two places behind with 8,199. Marleen Mülla tied for seventh in the women's pole vault.

Normak however singled out high jumper Karmen Bruus, who finished 13th with a jump of 1.88 in Saturday evening's final, as the biggest positive surprise – the athlete topped the mark she set in the final in the earlier heats. "She made the high jump final and cleared 1.90 meters or more again after a long time. Karmen's performance in qualifying was, in my opinion, one of the highlights for our team," Normak told ERR.

He also had praise for the sprinters on the team, who overcame difficult wind conditions in the 100m heats to reach the 200m semifinals. "They did what they needed to do and achieved their baseline goals," Normak noted.

Aivo Normak. Source: ERR

Many of the Estonian competitors also exceeded their ranking positions. "Someone who came in ranked 30th finished 24th, and so on. Seen in that light, there is quite a lot that is positive," Normak went on.

Another point Normak made was that around half the team were competing in the senior European Championships for the first time, which he said was a challenging adjustment. "The whole atmosphere of a senior championship, the procedures before the competition, the long waiting times in the field events — that is a challenge for the athletes," Normak said. "If they were not quite able to deliver this time, the positive thing is that they gained valuable experience so they can do better next time."

Conditions in Birmingham were far from ideal, in the recent heatwave to have hit England, as well as the changeable winds mentioned; Normak said in some cases, for instance the pole vault, it would have been preferable if things were set up so that the approach was made in the opposite direction to the one used.

Sprinter Henri Sai finished 23rd in the 200m semifinals despite a groin injury, while the decathlon saw defending champion Johannes Erm withdraw on day two due to heel pain. Risto Lillemets finished 12th.

Despite the overall mixed results, Normak said the experience gained by the younger athletes bodes well for the future. "There are always particular factors at a championship. The conditions here were perhaps not the most ideal, but the positive thing is that they gained valuable experience."

The European Athletics Championships in Birmingham ran from August 10-16 inclusive, with Estonia fielding 20 athletes across track and field events.

World.title: Outdoor swimming area to be built at Tallinn's Kalasadam
World.content:
A year-round outdoor swimming complex will be built at Kalasadam next to Tallinn's Linnahall and will be run by a Finnish company with a similar center in Helsinki.

The area between Kalarand and Linnahall has fallen into a rather bleak state over the years, and there are plans to renovate the area.

The new swimming complex project will be based on Helsinki's Allas outdoor pool and sauna complex, which is located in the capital's harbor, and created by Finnish real estate developer Nordic Urban.

The Tallinn project was designed by Estonian architectural firm Arhitekt Must.

"We drew inspiration from the history of Kalasadam and Kalarand and found fascinating old footage showing how there were low quays here where small fishing boats arrived, followed by higher ones for larger ships. Based on that, we created the concept of first having a lower seaside promenade, then a quay at the next height, then the pools and then terraces above. This created a similar play on the atmosphere of the quays," said architect Alvin Järving.

In addition to the complex with outdoor pools, the Kalasadam quay will be reconstructed, and a 200-meter-long promenade will be built and handed over for use by the city. Designs for the area were published in 2024 and can be seen below.

Both the area's developer, real estate company Kapitel, and the architectural firm have held extensive negotiations with the city.

"Exactly how to do it, where there is an opportunity to put café chairs, where there is simply a public edge, where fishermen can fish and so on — all of this has been discussed extremely thoroughly with the city," Järving said.

Construction of the outdoor swimming pool and leisure complex will likely begin at the end of this year, with completion expected in 2028.

In addition to Kalasadam, real estate company Kapitel also owns the adjoining area, totaling two hectares. A hotel project with more than 300 rooms is planned on the site of the adjacent parking lot and wasteland.

A new hotel is planned for Tallinn's Kalasadam area. Source: AS Kapitel

World.title: Estonia's bear population is rising as hunting becomes more difficult
World.content:
The bear population is increasing in Estonia's forests and may have even reached 1,500, as court rulings have placed additional restrictions on hunting, the Estonian Hunters' Society has said.

In recent weeks, several incidents of bears visiting people's yards have been reported, as well as filmed and shared online. The Environmental Board has issued a special permit to hunt two bears born last year because the bears have returned to people's yards after being scared away.

Peep Männil, chief wildlife specialist at the Environment Agency, said hunting depends on the number of animals in the wild, but this is currently no longer the case with bears.

However, a recent court ruling found conflicts with the Habitats Directive, as the bear is a strictly protected species in the European Union. No country has an exception.

In recent years, new rules have reduced the number of bears hunted in Estonia.

"In 2024, 101 bears were actually hunted, which was also, as far as is known, the largest number of bears ever hunted, but last year those court rulings already took effect quite early in the hunting season. Around 32 bears were hunted, and this year the number probably cannot be much higher either, and may even be lower," Männil said.

The court dispute has mainly focused on whether the Environmental Board has sufficiently justified the hunting of bears and whether other preventive measures have been used to prevent conflicts before bears are shot.

Männil said the growth of the bear population would be halted if at least 150 animals were hunted per season.

Last year, according to the Environment Agency's estimate, there were at least 1,100 bears in the wild in Estonia. There are no figures yet for this year, but the number of bears has likely increased.

"Since hunting was also very modest last year, the bear population has grown by about 5 percent a year over the past 10 years," Männil said.

In its estimates, the Environment Agency relies on data obtained from hunters across Estonia as well as data it collects itself.

"Every year, we identify different female bears with cubs born that same year. There may be a small margin of error there, meaning we may not be able to find all the female bears. In fact, what we provide is an estimate of the minimum population; it may be slightly larger," Männil said.

Marko Vinni, hunting adviser at the Estonian Hunters' Society, said the bear population is increasing every year because court rulings have created obstacles to carrying out traditional bear hunting.

Vinni said the hunters' estimate that there could be around 1,500 bears in the wild is not an exaggeration.

"If the Environment Agency has said that 300 bear cubs are born here every year, and if bear hunting has in fact not taken place here for the previous two years, then simple mathematics tells us that if, according to the Environment Agency's estimate, the bear population has been around 1,000 animals for the past couple of years, then adding the cubs born in the spring over three years should give us 900 animals. Natural mortality must always be taken into account as well, but even if we take a rough figure of 200 bear cubs that could be added to our population in the wild each year, we still get 600. The hunters' estimate of 1,500 animals in our wild – I don't think that is an exaggeration," he said.

World.title: Iraqi-British celebrity barber Ahmed Alsanawi takes A Star Barbers to Dubai
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Ahmed Alsanawi, an Iraqi-born British celebrity barber, is expanding his A Star Barbers brand to Dubai, marking the next step in a journey that started with a single UK barbershop in 2013.

Alsanawi was born in Baghdad and came to England with his family at the age of nine.

He subsequently trained himself in barbering before establishing A Star Barbers with his wife in southwest London.

After months of preparation, the brand has announced Dubai as its next destination, marking the well-known barber’s first big growth into the UAE.

Alsanawi has established a worldwide reputation via his work with some of football’s most famous people.

His clientele over the years has included Jude Bellingham, Declan Rice, Paul Pogba, Eden Hazard, Jack Grealish, and other top players, and his job has taken him all around the globe and to important football events.

His brother Abs is also a member of the A Star crew, having worked with Ahmed for years as the group expanded beyond its first barbershop.

A Star’s development has gone beyond haircuts.

The company has expanded into other enterprises, such as A Star Tattoos and the Fini by A-Star haircare line, which blends styling products with oud perfumes.

The Dubai shift is especially noteworthy considering Alsanawi’s Iraqi-British background.

He came to Britain as a boy unable to understand English, then went on to develop a well-known UK barbering business and become a trusted barber for international football players.

Dubai now offers A Star access to one of the Middle East’s most international premium grooming and lifestyle marketplaces, as well as a city that many of the brand’s players and celebrities frequent.

For Alsanawi, the inauguration signifies another step toward transforming an Iraqi-born entrepreneur’s firm in Britain into a worldwide brand, with Dubai serving as the next chapter in the A Star tale.

World.title: Iraq energy report warns oil and power vulnerabilities threaten economic stability
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq must undertake fundamental changes in its oil, power, and gas sectors after the 2026 regional crisis revealed severe weaknesses in the country’s energy-dependent economy, according to a new analysis from the American University of Iraq, Sulaimani (AUIS).

The August issue of the Iraq Energy Outlook, published by the university’s Dhia Jafar Center for Energy & Natural Resources, investigates how regional violence and interruption across the Strait of Hormuz affect Iraq’s oil exports, government finances, and electrical grid.

The analysis cautions that Iraq remains dangerously dependent on a single commodity and a single major maritime export route, with disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz fast translating into fewer oil revenues and financial pressure on the government.

That vulnerability was highlighted during the 2026 crisis, when constraints on shipping through Hormuz led Iraq to reduce southern oil output and declare force majeure at foreign-operated assets.

The report contends that Iraq should now prioritize diversifying its oil export channels as a national economic and security imperative. When Gulf shipments are hindered, other outlets such as Turkey, Jordan, Syria, and perhaps the Mediterranean may become available.

Among its recommendations to Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s government are to accelerate the Basra-Haditha pipeline, resolve energy disputes between Baghdad and Erbil, and develop potential land corridors through Jordan and Egypt that could eventually provide Iraqi crude access to the Mediterranean without passing via Hormuz.

The research also identifies severe issues with Iraq’s electrical system.

Peak power demand in 2026 is expected to surpass 55 gigawatts, while available supply remains below 20 GW, resulting in a probable shortage of at least 35 GW.

Despite years of investment in generating capacity, the research contends that Iraq’s electrical crisis is more about fuel security, efficiency, and governance, rather than just constructing more power plants.

Distribution losses are quite significant. Iraq generated around 166 terawatt-hours of power in 2024, but only about 67 TWh went to customers.

Around 82 TWh was lost at the distribution level alone, which means that roughly half of all energy produced was never paid to consumers.

Dependence on Iranian gas is another significant danger. Iranian supplies have traditionally contributed more than 40% of the fuel used in Iraq’s power production, but deliveries have grown more unpredictable due to sanctions, regional instability, and Iran’s own internal needs.

The report also highlights Iraq’s ongoing use of substantial amounts of associated gas while importing gas for power production, emphasizing the need to expand local gas processing capability.

Baghdad has so far avoided a full-fledged fiscal catastrophe by borrowing domestically, issuing treasury notes, making budget changes, and delaying payments.

However, the study sees these steps as transitory remedies that give the government time rather than addressing Iraq’s core reliance on oil income.

Energy subsidies are another significant expense.

Explicit fossil-fuel subsidies were predicted to be over $8 billion in 2025, almost three times their 2016 level, albeit dropping from a high of around $14.5 billion in 2022.

The report also discusses China’s growing role in Iraq’s energy industry, noting Beijing’s increasing involvement in oil production, infrastructure, electricity, and trade, but cautions that the relationship risks becoming increasingly unbalanced if Iraq becomes significantly more dependent on China than China is on Iraq.

Security is also recognized as a component of Iraq’s energy crisis.

The research advises putting armed formations, especially PMF-linked militias operating outside the official line of command, under effective state control and destroying oil-smuggling networks.

Taken together, the report portrays the 2026 problem as a warning to Baghdad.

Iraq has some of the world’s greatest energy reserves, but its economy remains fragile as long as the government’s finances are heavily reliant on oil, most crude exports are dependent on a single maritime corridor, and the electrical grid is sensitive to imported fuel and enormous network losses.

For the Al-Zaidi administration, the problem is no longer only generating more energy but also developing an energy infrastructure capable of defending Iraq’s economy when the next regional crisis strikes.

World.title: Iraq’s al-Nasr Coalition affirms state sovereignty, rejects Iran’s hegemony
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The al-Nasr Coalition, a political bloc led by former Iraqi Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi, has emphasized the importance of state sovereignty and rejected the notion of Iranian hegemony.

As a renowned Shiite leader who negotiated fierce regional conflicts throughout his tenure, al-Abadi has always rejected the idea that Iraq should serve as a less powerful ally for Iran.

Al-Abadi has publicly blamed Iranian political pressure for his failed attempt for a second term as prime minister. His coalition is fundamentally against classifying Iraq as a less powerful state or linking it to Iran’s regional conflicts.

The Al-Nasr Coalition’s fundamental principle is the absolute limitation of all weaponry to recognized state entities. This approach directly confronts the freedom of Iran-backed militias, which regularly operate outside of Iraq’s judicial and central government oversight.

Al-Abadi advocates for a balanced diplomatic approach. His coalition believes that Baghdad should maintain stable relations with both Washington and Tehran, while strongly insisting that neither country utilize Iraqi territory to resolve their disputes.

The coalition actively advocates for a strong, institutionalized, and national civil state. It believes that a structural and defensive mechanism capable of protecting Iraq from self-destruction and foreign intervention can be developed by strong domestic institutions and public confidence.

World.title: National Security Advisor urges Japanese firms to invest in Iraq’s economy
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — National Security Advisor Qasim Al-Aboudi met with Japanese Ambassador to Iraq Akira Endo on Sunday, August 16, 2026, affirming the federal government’s commitment to providing a secure and stable operating environment to attract foreign capital and revitalize the private sector.

According to an official statement from the National Security Advisory’s Media Office carried by the Iraqi News Agency (INA), the meeting focused on expanding bilateral cooperation, enhancing security frameworks for foreign commercial operations, and accelerating Japanese direct investments across Iraq’s industrial and developmental sectors.

Key Discussion Pillars & Diplomatic Priorities

Investor Protection & Security Guarantees: Al-Aboudi emphasized that Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi’s administration is prioritizing security measures to safeguard multinational corporate assets, streamline business licensing, and incentivize foreign direct investment (FDI).

Economic Revitalization & Job Creation: The strategic objective centers on transitioning from state-dependent employment to a dynamic private sector capable of absorbing Iraq’s young demographic workforce and eliminating unemployment.

Historic Ties & Tech Transfer: Al-Aboudi renewed Baghdad’s invitation for reputable Japanese industrial and engineering corporations to expand operations across Iraq’s energy, water management, and infrastructure initiatives.

Japanese Partnership Commitment: Ambassador Akira Endo reaffirmed Tokyo’s readiness to support Iraq across developmental spheres, underscoring Japan’s ambition to build comprehensive economic and commercial partnerships with Baghdad.

The diplomatic session highlights Baghdad’s strategy of linking national security policy directly with economic stability and foreign investor confidence.

By engaging Japanese institutional and technological capabilities, the Iraqi government aims to deploy advanced industrial solutions to upgrade infrastructure while offering long-term investment protections for international enterprises entering the Iraqi market.

World.title: Al Zaidi urges Italian firms to invest in Iraq’s energy and industry
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi urged Italian enterprises to take an active role in Iraq’s comprehensive development drive, affirming Baghdad’s commitment to deeper economic integration with Italy and the wider European Union, according to a statement released by the Prime Minister’s Media Office on Sunday, August 16, 2026.

The remarks came during a formal meeting at the Government Palace with the Ambassador of the Italian Republic to Iraq, Niccolò Fontana. The two officials reviewed bilateral ties and explored mechanisms to expand strategic partnerships across the energy, industrial, and agricultural sectors.

Key Discussion Pillars & Diplomatic Highlights

Economic Integration with Europe: Prime Minister Al-Zaidi emphasized Iraq’s strategy to broaden trade, technological transfer, and direct investment partnerships with Italy and European Union member states.

Target Investment Sectors: Baghdad is prioritizing Italian industrial and engineering expertise to modernize domestic energy infrastructure, agribusiness/irrigation technologies, and manufacturing sectors.

Italian Commitment to Bilateral Ties: Ambassador Niccolò Fontana reaffirmed Rome’s dedication to expanding cooperative frameworks and supporting private-sector participation in Iraq’s ongoing reconstruction and infrastructure programs.

The meeting aligns with the Iraqi government’s broader economic policy of diversifying international partnerships and attracting European industrial leaders to support non-oil industrialization, modernize water-efficient agricultural practices, and upgrade national infrastructure.

By engaging Italian firms, Baghdad aims to deploy advanced European technologies across capital investment projects while deepening institutional and commercial ties with Mediterranean and EU markets.
