World.title: Fuel price hike again on August 18 after last week’s rollback
World.content:
INCREASE. Another round of fuel price hikes takes effect in Manila, on April 7, 2026.

The increase undoes part of last week’s price cuts, with diesel again under pressure

MANILA, Philippines – Fuel prices are going up again starting Tuesday, August 18, after last week’s rollback as fuel markets remain volatile.

In a press conference on Monday, August 17, Energy Secretary Sharon Garin announced the following fuel price adjustments for the week of August 18 to 24:

Gasoline – increase of P2.49 per liter

Diesel – increase of P3.84 per liter

Kerosene – increase of P5.01 per liter

The adjustments will take effect on Tuesday, August 18.

The latest increase follows last week’s fuel price rollback, when oil firms cut pump prices by P4.70for gasoline, P4.30 per liter for diesel, and P4.88 per liter for kerosene.

That rollback had offered motorists some relief after the steep fuel price hikes in late July. On July 28, pump prices rose by P6.80 per liter for gasoline, P7.32 per liter for diesel, and P4.22 per liter for kerosene. A week earlier, on July 21, gasoline rose by P3.65 per liter, diesel by P10.68 per liter, and kerosene by P11.77 per liter.

The latest hike shows how quickly domestic pump prices can swing as global crude and refined fuel markets react to shifting supply conditions, foreign exchange movements, and geopolitical risks.

The DOE’s oil monitor as of August 11 showed that Dubai crude prices decreased by around $1.10 per barrel during the August 3 to 7 trading period. International prices of gasoline, kerosene, and diesel also declined by around $10.80 per barrel, $10.20 per barrel, and $10.20 per barrel, respectively.

Those declines were partly driven by expectations of a possible US-Iran agreement that could restore normal shipping flows through the Strait of Hormuz and ease supply concerns. But the DOE said risks remained, with shipping activity through the Strait still subdued and continued attacks on vessels in the Red Sea raising concerns over maritime security.

Diesel also remains vulnerable to tight regional supply. The DOE said middle distillate stocks in the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp region fell to their lowest level since July 2022, while strong distillate margins and low inventories were expected to continue supporting diesel prices.

Despite last week’s rollback, local pump prices remain well above levels seen before fighting involving Iran and US-Israeli forces broke out on February 28. In the last full week before the conflict, DOE data showed common retail prices in Metro Manila at P56 per liter for gasoline RON95, P54.70 per liter for gasoline RON91, P55 per liter for diesel, and P83.47 per liter for kerosene.

The Philippines is a net importer of petroleum products, making local pump prices vulnerable to global oil price swings, foreign exchange movements, regional refined fuel prices, and disruptions in international supply routes. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Exploration Drive Supports Shift Toward Higher-Value Mining
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is expanding geological and geophysical exploration to strengthen its mineral-resource base and support a strategic shift toward deeper processing and higher-value production.

By the end of this year, exploration is expected to cover 2.2 million square kilometers, with work completed at 25 sites. A key priority is the transition from regional 1:200,000-scale surveys to more detailed 1:50,000 geological mapping (GS-50).

This year, 20 GS-50 projects were launched to identify prospective areas for gold, copper, polymetals, rare earth elements, lithium, tungsten, molybdenum and other strategic minerals, reported the Ministry of Industry and Construction on Aug. 17.

The government has allocated 40.7 billion tenge (US$88 million) for geological surveys and seismic exploration in 2026-2028. Of this, 32.7 billion tenge (US$70.7 million) is allocated to GS-50 projects and 8 billion tenge (US$17.3 million) to seismic exploration. The program also plans six 2D seismic projects in the North Torgai and Shu-Sarysu sedimentary basins.

The program combines airborne geophysics, geochemical and laboratory studies, remote-sensing analysis, drilling and geophysical well logging. Its strategic value is to reduce geological uncertainty and improve the investment case for future mining projects.

From exploration to processing

The exploration program supports Kazakhstan’s strategic objective of moving beyond a predominantly raw-material economy.

At the Astana Mining & Metallurgy Congress 2026 on June 11, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov said the country aims to develop deeper processing and competitive value-added production. Over the past two years, more than US$1 billion worth of higher-value mining and metallurgical facilities have been launched.

The approach places greater importance on geological data. David Fogel, assistant secretary of Commerce and Director General of the U.S. and Foreign Commercial Service, said at the congress that mapping and surveying are fundamental to reducing uncertainty and attracting investment.

“If you don’t map the resources and the geography properly, then you’re not going to be very efficient and you’re not going to be able to attract large-scale investment,” Fogel said, adding that artificial intelligence is already transforming geological analysis and surveying.

His remarks underline a key point for Kazakhstan: exploration is not only about identifying deposits, but also about producing the reliable data needed to mobilize large-scale capital.

Tungsten as a test case

The Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty tungsten project illustrates this strategy.

The venture between U.S.-based Cove Capital and Kazakhstan’s Tau-Ken Samruk envisages a full production cycle covering mining, beneficiation and metallurgical processing in Kazakhstan. Cove Capital expects total investment requirements of at least US$1.1 billion, subject to completion of the definitive feasibility study and a final investment decision.

The planned output includes ammonium paratungstate (APT), a higher-value intermediate used to produce tungsten powders, tungsten carbide and other specialized materials.

Existing studies indicate potential combined production of around 12,000 tons of tungsten annually, although final capacity and project economics remain under assessment.

The project demonstrates the distinction between geological potential and commercial production. Kazakhstan’s ability to move projects from exploration and feasibility to financing and operations will determine whether its strategy generates sustained economic value.

International relevance

At AMM 2026, U.S. officials highlighted geological mapping as a way to reduce investment risks, while Saudi Arabia stressed the importance of integrated chains covering mining, processing, logistics and technology.

For Kazakhstan, exploration is therefore becoming the first stage of a wider industrial strategy.

The key indicators ahead will be commercially significant discoveries, progress toward feasibility studies and financing, and the development of processing capacity and supporting infrastructure.

The strategy’s success will ultimately depend not on the amount of territory surveyed, but on how effectively new discoveries are converted into mines, processing facilities and competitive products for global markets.

World.title: China’s Bid for an AI World Order: What’s Behind WAICO
World.content:
Trump locks Europe out of AI models; China presents the counter-proposal — a global AI platform, and everyone’s invited. What Beijing wants and why Europe remains skeptical.

By founding the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), China has created its own international framework for governing artificial intelligence — without the players that have traditionally shaped technology policy. For now.

The founding treaty was signed on July 16, in Shanghai by representatives from 29 countries, with UN Secretary-General António Guterres in attendance. The organization is headquartered in Shanghai. Founding members include Russia, Brazil, Indonesia, Pakistan, Malaysia, Kazakhstan, Kenya, South Africa, Serbia, Belarus, Cuba, Venezuela, and Zambia, among others. The United States, E.U. member states, and India are not participating.

In Chinese diplomatic circles, WAICO is described as a “major step” through which the People’s Republic is answering the Global South’s call for greater participation in AI development. The organization is meant to serve two purposes: spreading AI applications across the Global South and organizing training and seminar programs. The goal, Beijing says, is to use AI “for good.”

Four principles — and a jab at Washington

The conceptual framework rests on four principles that China’s leadership laid out at the first World AI Conference in Shanghai: openness and win-win cooperation, risk awareness, inclusivity, and solidarity in global governance.

Under win-win, Beijing groups scenario-based applications such as AI plus industry and AI plus health — in other words, integrating AI with existing economic sectors. AI must remain safe, reliable, and controllable, the argument goes. China says it is working on technical oversight, early-warning and emergency-response mechanisms, as well as laws, standards, and ethical guidelines. Misuse is to be prevented and AI kept under human control.

China rejects what it calls the overextension of national security — the principle of placing one country’s security above the interests of others. The target is clearly export controls and access restrictions.

Asked whether this language should be read as a response to the short-notice blocking of leading American models for European users, Beijing pointed out that Chinese models are open-source, rendering any accusation of bloc-building moot.

The fourth principle aims at multilateralism. Governance rules and technical standards should be coordinated internationally, and Global South countries should receive support in building their own capacities — to avoid, in China’s phrasing, new historical injustices.

What China is concretely offering

Over the next five years, China intends to provide 5,000 AI training slots for participants from Global South countries. Whether these are degree programs, scholarships, or short-term courses remains unclear. Plans also include AI cooperation centers with organizations such as ASEAN, the African Union, the Arab League, BRICS, and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization. A flagship project is an AI-powered early-warning system that, according to Chinese sources, forecasts typhoons and other extreme weather events in more than 30 countries.

How China translates technological cooperation into concrete projects — across blocs and without exclusive commitments — is currently on display in Kazakhstan. In June, the Central Asian country agreed with the American firm Firebird on investments of up to ten billion dollars in a computing cluster with up to 100,000 Nvidia GPUs in the coal-mining city of Ekibastuz. A month later, on the sidelines of the AI summit in Shanghai, more than 70 contracts with Chinese partners worth a combined total of over $15 billion were signed. The cross-sector package includes, among other things, a partnership with Huawei, the acquisition of Huawei technology, and further expansion of the data-center site in cooperation with the Hengtong Group.

Open to all — including Europe?

From Beijing’s perspective, an upgrade to an official UN body is not ruled out; the organization is still in its early stages, they say. Nor is EU membership excluded. The organization is in principle open to all and is not aimed exclusively at the Global South.

Beijing dismisses the accusation that the aim is to carve out new spheres of influence. It is not building blocs, the argument goes; the basis of cooperation is consultation and mutual benefit.

Still, the connection to the Digital Silk Road is hard to miss. When it comes to overlaps with the digital component of the Belt and Road Initiative — in areas like digital services, health, and education — the answers remain vague. WAICO programs are described more as a complement to existing relationships.

The European Reading

Sources in Brussels security circles say WAICO is read less as a development initiative than as a strategic instrument. What matters is not the announced training slots or cooperation centers but the question of who will shape infrastructure, technical standards, and digital ecosystems in the years ahead. Countries that adopt Chinese models, networks, and processes early on could find themselves increasingly tied to providers and decision-making centers in Beijing or Shanghai over the long term.

Kazakhstan, however, shows that such cooperation does not necessarily lead to exclusive dependency. Astana is working simultaneously with American and Chinese partners, deploying Nvidia processors while also integrating Huawei and other Chinese providers into the expansion of its digital infrastructure. The government is deliberately keeping multiple technological pathways open rather than fully aligning with either of the two major blocs.

That is precisely what makes the example strategically significant: for many Global South countries, the issue is less about making a geopolitical statement than about accessing capital, computing power, and rapid implementation. The contract goes to whoever most convincingly bundles financing, technology, and infrastructure. For Europe, this is nonetheless a warning: future dependencies will not be determined solely by where systems originate, but above all by who delivers them first and operates them over the long haul.

The EU has been working since 2025 on implementing its concept for AI gigafactories — facilities each housing more than 100,000 advanced AI processors. For now, however, the focus in government offices is mainly on sites, financing, and procurement.

What stands out is the speed at which contracts are being signed and capacities built up elsewhere. Kazakhstan is simultaneously engaging American and Chinese technology companies, while Europe is still translating its own sovereign model into practice. The question is whether the planned pace will be fast enough to keep up with international developments.

In Brussels, digital sovereignty is thus moving to center stage. Europe wants to build its own computing capacity while avoiding long-term dependence on individual foreign providers for critical infrastructure.

Arindrajit Basu of the Carnegie Endowment describes WAICO as a state-centric model that primarily serves Chinese interests. Other Western analyses characterize WAICO as a counterpart to the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative. Participants or countries that have expressed interest in the American format include EU member states, Japan, Australia, and India.

Beijing courts Washington

Notably, Beijing is said to be open to cooperation with the United States. The two countries should extend their hands to each other, diplomatic circles say. AI is a global field, and its development must ultimately work for everyone.

When confronted with the objection that the U.S. administration does not currently appear inclined to cooperate, the response is puzzlement at Washington’s course — along with a reference to jointly supported UN resolutions. In Chinese publications, the line is stated more plainly: it is in the greatest shared interest of both nations that AI serve all of humanity. Following government consultations, a bilateral AI dialogue has also been agreed upon.

Beijing’s multilateral foundation is a UN General Assembly resolution on international AI capacity-building, adopted unanimously on July 1, 2024, which China had introduced. It calls for human-centered, inclusive, and sustainable AI development and special support for developing countries.

Building on that, China points to its own programs: the Global AI Governance Initiative of 2023, a 13-point action plan for global AI governance from 2025, and an AI Capacity-Building Action Plan for Good and for All.

The five-year plan as engine

Domestically, the push coincides with the launch of the 15th Five-Year Plan for 2026–2030. According to Chinese sources, an intelligent economic system is to be built; the core AI industry, diplomatic circles say, has already reached a volume of more than 1.2 trillion yuan.

AI is no longer anything special in China, the narrative goes — it is already widespread, from smart manufacturing to consumer devices. At the same time, laws, regulations, application guidelines, and ethical principles are being continuously developed to keep AI safe and controllable.

China also sees itself as a provider of international public goods, including through the release of open-source models.

Export controls, energy, exchange rates

One sore point in Europe that stands in the way of closer cooperation is China’s export controls on critical minerals needed for semiconductors, batteries, and other key technologies. Beijing rejects the claim that these have caused lasting supply problems, pointing to expedited approval procedures and general licenses for companies. The additional controls, however, are suspended only until No. 10. Whether the relaxations will be extended or stricter licensing requirements will resume afterward remains an open question.

Beijing also pushes back against the recent accusation by Germany’s Chancellor Friedrich Merz that China is keeping the renminbi artificially low. Against the euro, the Chinese currency has in fact risen from around 8.27 to roughly 7.71 yuan per euro since late October — an appreciation of a good seven percent.

The latest currency report from the U.S. Treasury Department, dated July 23, also does not classify China as a currency manipulator. Due to a lack of transparency in its exchange-rate policy, however, the country remains on the U.S. monitoring list. Europe’s criticism of China’s trade surpluses, subsidies, and state-led industrial policy is far from settled.

Despite Merz’s sweeping announcements about resuming German-Chinese government consultations, no date has been set so far. The chancellor had indicated a meeting would take place this year, or early 2027 at the latest. There is, as they say, plenty to discuss.

The author is Alexander Dergay, the founder and managing partner of Orbis Nova, a research and analysis firm. Dergay is also cooperating with geopolitical foresight agency Nightingale Int. He worked for several years as an adviser and analyst specializing in geostrategic risk before serving as an foreign policy editor at the Berliner Zeitung and the Ostdeutsche Allgemeine Zeitung, Germany.

World.title: Scholars Call for Broader View of Golden Horde’s Legacy
World.content:
ASTANA – Three historians from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and the Republic of Tatarstan in Russia explored how the Golden Horde continues to shape the historical narratives and identities of their countries during a podcast organized by Kazakh historian and Golden Horde researcher Zhaksylyk Sabitov.

The discussion highlighted both the shared historical legacy of the medieval empire and the distinct national perspectives that have emerged across Central Asia and the Volga Region.

According to Damir Iskhakov, an ethnologist and researcher of Tatar ethnogenesis at the Marjani Institute of History in Kazan, perceptions of the Golden Horde have changed significantly in recent decades.

“There was a time when many Kazakhs believed their origins lay primarily with the Kipchaks or other earlier peoples rather than the Golden Horde. Today, historical evidence and the composition of Kazakh clans clearly demonstrate a direct connection with the Golden Horde,” he said.

He added that growing scholarly interest has strengthened understanding of the Golden Horde’s contribution to the formation of the Kazakh nation.

Gaibulla Babayarov, a specialist in ancient Turkic epigraphy and numismatics at the Institute of Oriental Studies in Tashkent, noted that bringing together experts from different countries enriches understanding of the Golden Horde.

“Each country has its own unique perspective, which makes discussions like this especially valuable,” Babayarov said.

Babayarov highlighted that the Golden Horde is often mistakenly viewed as unrelated to Uzbekistan’s history.

“In reality, the Golden Horde period played an important role in the ethnogenesis of the Uzbek people,” he said.

While most of present-day Uzbekistan belonged to the Chagatai Ulus, the country’s northwestern territories, particularly Northern Khorezm, were part of the Golden Horde. Many Uzbek clans originated in the Dasht-i Kipchak, with Babayarov estimating that nearly half of traditional Uzbek tribal groups trace their roots to that region.

“For this reason, the histories of the Golden Horde and the Chagatai Ulus should be studied together rather than separately. They share common roots and represent a shared historical heritage,” he said.

Clan system united Turkic peoples

The discussion also focused on the Golden Horde’s clan structure.

Iskhakov described the subject as one of the least studied areas of medieval history because of the limited number of surviving historical sources.

“One of our main tasks today is to trace how a relatively small number of original clans, perhaps 12 or 14, eventually evolved into the much larger clan system described in the Edige epic, which refers to the ‘Ninety-Clan Horde.’ What is remarkable is that many of these clans can still be traced among various Turkic peoples,” Iskhakov said.

He also noted that the Golden Horde was organized through a strict hierarchy of clans. The ruling dynasty was closely connected through marriage alliances with the leading emir families that helped govern the state.

Babayarov added that Soviet-era scholarship often overlooked clan history in Uzbekistan because Uzbeks were portrayed primarily as a settled people rather than a society with strong tribal traditions.

He noted that ethnonyms and clan names remain preserved in village names across much of Uzbekistan, particularly in the Samarkand, Kashkadarya and Surkhandarya regions.

Balancing genetics and history

Sabitov urged caution when interpreting genetic research in historical studies.

“Genetics is an important research tool, but it should not be used to determine who is or is not a ‘real’ representative of an ethnic group,” he said.

He noted that genetic studies often produce various conclusions depending on the questions researchers ask.

“If you search for similarities among Turkic peoples, you will find similarities. If you search for differences, you will find differences. Ethnicity cannot be reduced to DNA,” he said.

Iskhakov agreed, saying genetics is useful for tracing family relationships over several centuries but becomes much less reliable when applied to medieval populations.

“Ethnic identity is shaped primarily by shared historical memory, language and culture. Genetics represents only one small part of that much larger picture,” Iskhakov said.

Revisiting Tatar history

Iskhakov also recalled how Soviet historiography largely excluded the Golden Horde from the history of the Tatars.

He said that during the Stalin era, official scholarship promoted the theory that modern Tatars descended exclusively from the Volga Bulgars. While the Golden Horde was portrayed as unrelated to Tatar history.

Only after the collapse of the Soviet Union did historians begin integrating the Golden Horde into mainstream interpretations of Tatar ethnogenesis.

“Today, the Golden Horde occupies its rightful place in the multi-volume history of the Tatar people. We now recognize the contributions of the ancient Turks, the Bulgar period, the Kipchaks and the Golden Horde as equally important stages in our shared history,” Iskhakov said.

World.title: Archaeological Discoveries Across Kazakhstan Shed New Light on Medieval Life
World.content:
ASTANA – A series of recent archaeological discoveries across Kazakhstan is offering new insights into the history, culture and everyday life of communities that lived on the Great Steppe centuries ago.

Findings from archaeological sites in the Zhambyl, Turkistan and Pavlodar regions include medieval buildings, a mosque and paved streets, valuable artefacts and a remarkably preserved mobile dwelling associated with the Kimak-Kipchak period (9th-10th centuries). Together, the discoveries highlight the diversity of life in the medieval steppe and the region’s links with neighbouring civilisations.

Archaeologists working at the Akzhar settlement in Zhambyl Region have uncovered remains of structures dating to the 11th–12th centuries. The medieval settlement is located west of the Kurenbel village in the Zhualy district, between tributaries of the Akzhar River.

The excavations revealed structures made of mud brick, along with fragments of ceramics, iron and glass objects, stone tools and bones of domestic animals, reported the region’s Culture and Language Development Department. Researchers say the findings can help reconstruct the daily life of the people who inhabited the settlement during different periods.

The animal remains are of particular interest to researchers, as their study could provide information about the diet, economy and lifestyle of the settlement’s residents.

The excavations are being carried out as part of a scientific program studying the Syr Darya and Karatau regions in antiquity and the Middle Ages. Researchers expect the findings to help clarify Akzhar’s role in the development of medieval urban culture in the Karatau region.

Further south, archaeological work at the Otyrar settlement in the Turkistan Region has revealed several layers of historical development dating 13th-18th centuries.

Researchers identified five construction horizons containing residential and household areas, brick-paved streets and kilns used for firing bricks. One of the most notable discoveries was a collective burial site, known as a dakhma, identified for the first time at Otyrar.

At the lowest, fifth construction horizon, archaeologists uncovered the remains of a mosque dating to the Golden Horde period. A street paved with large stones led to the building and connected to a staircase made of fired bricks. According to the researchers, a paved street of this scale had not previously been documented at Otyrar.

The excavations also revealed painted window grilles, parts of inkpots, door or gate fittings, Chinese-style ceramic fragments, Chinese coins and coins minted in the names of rulers of the Golden Horde, a powerful state that dominated much of the Eurasian steppe from the 13th to 15th centuries.

One particularly notable discovery was a ring bearing an inscription, which researchers believe may have served as a seal in the medieval period.

The archaeological evidence points to Otyrar’s extensive connections with other parts of the region. Similar materials have been found at sites associated with Sogdiana, Tashkent, Fergana and Zhetysu, while imported objects and coins indicate the city’s participation in wider trade and cultural networks.

Researchers also believe the newly uncovered street could help reconstruct the layout of medieval Otyrar and identify commercial and public spaces that once stood along it. The excavations at the Otyrar settlement were conducted by a team led by Mukhtar Kozha, a professor and chief researcher at the Institute of Archaeology of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi International Kazakh-Turkish University.

In the Pavlodar Region, archaeologists have uncovered what researchers describe as an exceptionally rare example of a mobile dwelling from the Kimak-Kipchak period, reported the region’s press office.

The discovery was made at the Baidala burial ground in the Kenzhekol rural district of Pavlodar. The site is considered one of the significant archaeological monuments associated with the era of the Kimak Khaganate. According to researchers, the area may correspond to Imakia, described as a political center of the Kimak Khaganate, a medieval state or tribal confederation that existed roughly from the 9th to the early 11th century in what is now northeastern and central Kazakhstan and parts of western Siberia.

The most significant discovery is a fully preserved mobile dwelling consisting of a wooden wheeled structure with a tent-like covering. Archaeologists said its construction is similar to that of the traditional Kazakh yurt and that the discovery appears to be unprecedented in the archaeological record of the Eurasian steppe.

The dwelling was accompanied by a wooden saddle, stirrups, a bit, weapons, jewellery, silk textiles and other artefacts. These objects provide additional evidence about the material culture and everyday life of medieval nomadic communities. Before the discovery, knowledge about similar mobile dwellings largely came from written sources and schematic depictions.

Archaeological research at Baidala has been conducted for more than two decades led by archaeologist Timur Smagulov. Further excavations, conservation and restoration of the finds are planned, along with proposals to turn the complex into a museum site and develop it as an important historical and cultural heritage attraction.

The remains of buildings and streets reveal the organization of settled communities and their urban infrastructure, while the mobile dwelling offers a rare physical representation of nomadic life. Artefacts from Otyrar, meanwhile, point to the movement of goods, technologies and cultural influences across Central Asia and beyond.

For archaeologists, such discoveries are more than isolated objects or structures. They provide pieces of evidence that can be combined to reconstruct how people lived, travelled, traded and interacted across the Great Steppe.

While excavations and conservation work continue, researchers expect further discoveries to contribute to a more detailed understanding of Kazakhstan’s medieval heritage and its place in the broader history of Eurasia.

World.title: Preparing for Economy That Doesn’t Yet Exist: Why Kazakhstan’s Experiment Is Worth Watching
World.content:
One of the things that has surprised me most over the past year is how rarely my conversations with futurists actually stay focused on artificial intelligence. We usually begin there. We talk about generative models, autonomous agents, the next version of ChatGPT, the speed at which these systems are evolving. Yet after twenty or thirty minutes, AI almost disappears from the conversation. We find ourselves talking instead about labor markets, education, political institutions, governance and, eventually, something much larger than technology itself: the possibility that we are approaching the end of an economic model that has shaped modern societies for generations.

AI isn’t the story

That shift in perspective has been difficult to ignore. We often compare AI to the internet or smartphones because it makes the transformation easier to understand. Those technologies undoubtedly changed our lives. But they never challenged one of the central assumptions underpinning modern economies: that human labor is the primary engine through which value is created and wealth is distributed. Artificial intelligence might.

During one of our interviews, futurist Brett King made an observation that has stayed with me ever since. The more automation we introduce into the economy, he said, the less the traditional mechanics of capitalism function in the way they were originally designed. As he put it, it will be the end of capitalism as we know it. Whether or not one agrees with his conclusion is almost secondary.

The more interesting question is what governments should do if he is even partially right. Because history suggests that institutions rarely have the luxury of waiting until structural change is complete before deciding how to respond. By then, the transition is usually far more painful than it needed to be.

Perhaps this is why I have gradually become less interested in AI itself and more interested in leadership. Not political leadership in the conventional sense, but the ability of governments to think beyond immediate political cycles and prepare societies for an economy that does not yet fully exist.

Brett challenged another assumption that many of us have taken for granted over the last four decades: that markets, left largely to themselves, will eventually solve most problems.

“The free market hasn’t solved climate change. The free market hasn’t solved poverty. It hasn’t solved homelessness. This is not something that the free market is going to solve. This is a function of coordinated governance,” he told me.

It is a provocative argument, particularly at a time when governments around the world are still trying to determine how much they should regulate artificial intelligence and how much they should simply allow innovation to unfold. Yet there is something compelling about the distinction he makes.

Artificial intelligence is not disrupting a single industry. It is beginning to influence healthcare, transportation, logistics, finance, manufacturing, education and public administration simultaneously. Unlike previous technological revolutions, it does not fit neatly within the responsibility of one ministry or one regulator. It cuts across virtually every institution that modern states have spent decades building.

If that is true, then leadership acquires a different meaning. It becomes less about managing today’s economy efficiently and more about preparing citizens for tomorrow’s economy before it fully arrives. This is perhaps why Kazakhstan has become an unexpectedly interesting case study.

Preparing before the future arrives

For years, discussions about Kazakhstan’s future largely revolved around energy, critical minerals, connectivity and its geopolitical position between major powers. Increasingly, however, another narrative has begun to emerge, one that places artificial intelligence at the center of the country’s long-term development strategy rather than treating it as another digital policy initiative.

Over the past two years, the government has launched the International AI Center Alem.ai, expanded the AI-Sana education initiative, invested in computing infrastructure and accelerated efforts to integrate artificial intelligence into public administration.

That shift is also evident in Kazakhstan’s official discourse. Speaking at the second meeting of the Council for the Development of Artificial Intelligence, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said that “traditional growth models based on resources and labour are losing effectiveness” and warned that unless Kazakhstan rapidly transitions to a fully integrated, AI-powered, data-driven economy, it risks falling behind in the global technological race.

Whether every initiative succeeds is, in some ways, beside the point. History offers very few examples of governments navigating technological revolutions perfectly. But there is a meaningful difference between preparing too early and preparing too late. One risks investing in ideas that will inevitably evolve. The other risks discovering that the rules of the global economy have already changed. This is precisely what Brett was referring to when he spoke not about technology, but about time.

Modern societies, he told me, have become trapped inside quarterly earnings reports, annual budgets and electoral cycles. Yet transformative projects have never been built that way. Cathedrals took generations. The Panama Canal took decades. The Apollo program demanded sustained political commitment that extended far beyond a single administration. AI, he believes, belongs in that same category of civilizational change.

Listening to him, I found myself wondering whether our biggest challenge is not AI at all. Perhaps it is our shrinking political imagination. Can democratic governments still think thirty years ahead? Can they justify investments whose returns may only become obvious long after today’s leaders leave office? Those questions feel increasingly relevant when looking at Kazakhstan.

President Tokayev has repeatedly noted that digital transformation is no longer optional but essential for maintaining competitiveness in a rapidly changing world. Speaking at the AI conference this July in Shanghai, he stressed that no country should remain merely a consumer of AI technologies and that every nation must develop its own human capital so technological progress serves society rather than deepening inequality.

“No country should remain merely a consumer of artificial intelligence. Every nation must have the opportunity to develop its own human capital, digital infrastructure and institutional capacity. At its core, this is a matter of fairness and equity,” he said.

The human side of an AI economy

What I find interesting is not the ambition itself. Many governments now speak enthusiastically about AI. What stands out is the attempt to connect AI with education, state capacity and long-term economic planning rather than viewing it simply as another technology sector. That connection surfaced repeatedly during my conversations with both futurists Brett King and Ron Immink.

Ron approached the issue from an entirely different direction. He was less concerned with algorithms than with culture. Most leading AI systems, he pointed out, continue to think primarily in English. Yet languages carry different ways of understanding the world, different historical experiences and different cultural contexts. If artificial intelligence is to become genuinely intelligent, it cannot simply translate languages; it must learn to understand them.

That observation gave me a different perspective on a seemingly minor piece of news: Kazakh has become one of the fastest-growing languages on ChatGPT. It is easy to dismiss that as an interesting statistic. But perhaps it represents something larger. In the age of AI, language is no longer only a question of identity. It increasingly becomes a question of participation. Cultures that exist inside AI systems will inevitably have a stronger voice in shaping how those systems understand humanity itself.

Education raises a similar challenge. Ron believes our schools are still largely organized around the needs of an industrial economy, preparing students for stable careers inside systems that may not exist in their current form within a generation. Brett goes even further. He says that philosophy, psychology, ethics and lifelong learning may become just as important as engineering because the defining skill of the AI era will not simply be coding. It will be adaptation.

After months of interviewing futurists, I have come to think that AI is asking governments a surprisingly old question. Not whether they can innovate faster than everyone else, but whether they are capable of imagining a future that does not yet exist and preparing for it anyway. No one knows what the AI economy will ultimately look like. Predictions differ, technologies evolve faster than policies, and history has a habit of humbling even the most confident forecasts. There is no guarantee that every initiative launched today will produce the intended outcome. But perhaps that is not the point. The point is that waiting for certainty may no longer be an option.

Looking at Kazakhstan today, what I find noteworthy is less the technology itself than the shift in thinking behind it. AI is no longer being discussed simply as another digital industry or another innovation agenda. Increasingly, it has become part of a broader conversation about education, institutions, public administration and the country’s long-term economic direction. Whether through AI-Sana, investments in computing infrastructure, the development of Alem.ai, or recent efforts to integrate AI across government, the common thread is an attempt to prepare before the transition becomes unavoidable.

Perhaps that is what leadership will increasingly mean in the age of AI: not the ability to predict every technological breakthrough, but the willingness to create the conditions for a country to adapt to profound uncertainty. Kazakhstan appears to be making that bet today, investing in institutions, education and digital capacity before anyone can say with confidence what the AI economy will ultimately look like.

World.title: Data Center Valley Is More Than AI: It’s Kazakhstan’s Economic Diversification Bet
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan is advancing construction of the Data Center Valley in the Pavlodar Region, a large-scale computing infrastructure project intended to support artificial intelligence development, attract international technology companies and create a new export-oriented segment of the digital economy, as Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov reviewed progress on Aug. 13.

The first facility, with a planned capacity of 50 megawatts, is now under construction. Excavation work for the energy center and AI factory buildings is 90% complete, while foundation work and construction of administrative facilities are underway. Officials said the main buildings of the data center and power units are expected to be completed by the end of December 2026. Commissioning work is scheduled to finish in May 2027, with the facility expected to begin operations in June 2027.

Kazakhstan has also acquired a 215-megawatt substation to supply the site, and is developing water and telecommunications infrastructure. In the longer term, Data Center Valley is designed to expand in stages to a total capacity of up to 1 gigawatt. That would turn the project from a single data center into a large computing campus capable of hosting data centers, AI factories, GPU clusters and cloud platforms for international hyperscalers.

Why computing capacity is becoming strategic

As artificial intelligence requires large amounts of computing power, data centers are becoming an essential part of the infrastructure supporting the digital economy. For Kazakhstan, the potential opportunity is to move beyond being primarily a consumer of foreign digital services and develop the infrastructure needed to host computing capacity within the country.

“Data Center Valley is creating a new export potential for Kazakhstan. By locating computing capacity within the country, we are creating conditions for developing domestic AI solutions, attracting global companies and entering the international market for digital services,” Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev said.

According to Kazakhtelecom Board Chairman Bagdat Mussin, the project’s expansion will depend on confirmed client demand.

“Our first priority is to complete construction of the first facility in June 2027. At the same time, we are creating the engineering foundation that will allow us to gradually increase the campus capacity in line with confirmed customer demand,” he said.

The project will therefore need to solve two parallel challenges: building enough infrastructure to attract major technology companies while avoiding capacity that significantly exceeds demand.

From infrastructure to a digital ecosystem

The project is also being developed with international partners. Firebird AI and NVIDIA are involved in building an ecosystem around artificial intelligence, cloud technologies and next-generation digital services.

Another proposal discussed during the meeting, the Cloud First Policy, or Data Embassy project, illustrates this ambition. The initiative could allow foreign states to store data in Kazakhstan while retaining full legal sovereignty over it.

Data Center Valley is being developed as countries across the region seek to position themselves in the rapidly expanding market for artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure. The first 50-megawatt facility, expected to open in June 2027, will therefore be an early test of a much larger strategy.

World.title: Kazakh Voters Increasingly Seek Concrete Policy Solutions, Experts Say
World.content:
ASTANA — Healthcare, education and social protection are emerging as key areas of competition in Kazakhstan’s election campaign, with experts saying voters are increasingly looking beyond broad promises to how seven political parties intend to deliver measurable improvements in quality of life.

Those issues were at the center of an Aug. 14 meeting of the Sarap Expert Club in Astana, where researchers, healthcare and education specialists and human-capital experts examined how social concerns are shaping party platforms and voter expectations ahead of the election.

The election to the Kurultai, the country’s new unicameral Parliament, is scheduled for Aug. 23. Seven political parties are set to compete, with 545 candidates registered for the race. Campaigning will end at midnight on Aug. 21, followed by a campaign silence day on Aug. 22. More than 12.6 million people are eligible to vote on Aug. 23. As of Aug. 13, the Central Election Commission had accredited 656 observers representing foreign states and international organizations.

Experts said the parties largely agree on the problems across healthcare, education, employment and social protection but increasingly differ over who should provide the solutions, how they should be financed and how their effectiveness should be measured.

Zhuldyzai Iskakova, head of the Kazakhstan Institute of Public Development, which organized the Sarap meeting, said the televised debates helped make those differences more visible to voters. Three nationally televised debates have already aired live on Qazaqstan TV, Channel 7 and Jibek Joly, while the final debate is scheduled for Aug. 19 on 24KZ.

The first two debates drew a combined audience of around two million viewers, according to experts at the meeting.

“They examined their programs in detail and challenged one another,” Iskakova said. “There is a common perception that the parties are broadly similar and that it is difficult to understand what distinguishes them. In reality, there are fundamental differences between them.”

From social promises to competing solutions

Zhanar Sankhayeva, head of the Department of Political Research at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies, said political parties are placing greater emphasis on social protection, healthcare and education in their election programs.

“Healthcare is among the top three issues of greatest concern to citizens, while education ranks among the top six priorities affecting people’s everyday lives,” she said.

Sankhayeva said the substance of party platforms could play an important role in voters’ decisions. She cited a survey by the Institute of Public Policy in which 44.4% of respondents identified parties’ initiatives, policy proposals and campaign promises as one of the important factors influencing their choice.

The expert said public expectations in the social sphere are also evolving. While earlier demands focused largely on expanding access to education and healthcare, voters are increasingly concerned with the quality of the services they receive.

“I would describe the current competition between parties in the social sphere as a transition from a competition of social promises to a competition of concrete models for solving social problems,” she said.

Sankhayeva said the election campaign is now entering a “more mature phase.”

“Voters are also moving from a general interest in the election toward forming specific political preferences,” she said.

Long-term priorities

According to Nazarbayev University Vice President Gulmira Qanay, the quality of people’s lives is a clear indicator of how effective or ineffective state policies are. Health, education, safety, professional opportunities and confidence in the future are among the main factors shaping quality of life.

She highlighted the constitutional emphasis on developing human capital, science and education, which should be an important part of the agenda for the future members of the Kurultai.

“We can see major transformations taking place around the world. If we look at the achievements of leading countries over the past 50 years and examine how they reached their current level of development, much of what we see today is the result of investments made in science, education, medicine and the social sphere,” said Qanay.

However, she also stressed that improvements in quality of life require long-term investment rather than measures tied only to an election cycle.

“These are not achievements that appear in a day or two. (…) That is something future members of the Kurultai should also keep in mind,” she added.

After saying that government policy should ultimately be judged by whether it improves people’s quality of life, Qanay said the same principle should apply to higher education, with universities assessed less by formal credentials and more by what graduates are able to do afterward.

Qanay said Kazakhstan should place greater emphasis on developing intellectual capital and designing education policy around research, evidence and measurable outcomes, particularly as digitalization and artificial intelligence transform the skills and standards expected of universities and the wider education system.

Healthcare challenges

Healthcare illustrates the gap that can emerge between policy ambitions and the everyday delivery of public services. Bakytzhan Tazhibay, chair of the AQNIET Kazakhstan Sectoral Trade Union of Healthcare and Public Service Workers and a pediatric urologist, said his review of all seven party platforms showed broad agreement on the sector’s principal challenges.

These include unequal access to quality care between major cities and remote villages, a lack of transparency in the mandatory social health insurance system, shortages of medical personnel and the bureaucratic burden placed on healthcare workers.

“Any reform will remain on paper if we forget about the people responsible for putting it into practice,” Tazhibay said. “At the center of the healthcare system are doctors, nurses, paramedics and other medical workers.”

He identified staff shortages and professional burnout as direct threats to the quality and safety of patient care. Although healthcare salaries have increased, he said, many doctors and nurses still work more than one full-time position to provide an adequate income for their families. This problem is particularly acute outside major cities.

He described elections as a “moment of truth for society.”

“This is the time when the country’s course of development is set, determining what our social policies, labor laws, family support, and healthcare system will look like for years to come,” he added.

Tazhibay called for healthcare expenditure equivalent to at least 5%–6% of gross domestic product, more stable base salaries, workloads consistent with professional standards and greater public and trade-union oversight of the social health insurance system.

World.title: From Grain to Value Chains: Kazakhstan Seeks to Transform Its Agricultural Export Model
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has nearly doubled its agricultural exports over the past five years, reaching $7 billion in 2025 from $3.8 billion, according to an analysis published by the World Financial Review. The growth has strengthened Kazakhstan’s role as a food supplier to Central Asia and beyond. Still, it raises a broader question about the country’s agricultural future: can rising export volumes translate into a higher-value agri-food economy?

According to the World Financial Review, Kazakhstan’s growing agricultural capacity and location between major Eurasian markets are creating new opportunities for the country to play a larger role in regional food security. The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and the UN Food and Agriculture Organization project that international trade will become increasingly important to global food systems, with around 22% of calories consumed worldwide expected to cross international borders by 2034.

For Kazakhstan, which borders or has close transport links to rapidly growing markets in Central Asia, China, the Caucasus and beyond, this creates an economic advantage. The country can supply regions with growing food demand while using its agricultural surplus to expand exports.

Kazakhstan’s agricultural products are already exported to more than 72 countries. Grain and flour remain among its most important exports, particularly to neighboring markets. Over the first 11 months of the latest marketing season, exports of grain and flour reached 13.5 million tons, according to figures cited in the World Financial Review.

Shipments increased particularly sharply to regional markets. Exports to Afghanistan rose by 59% to 2.2 million tons, while supplies to Uzbekistan increased by 37% to 5.6 million tons. Exports to the Kyrgyz Republic reached 504,000 tons, up around 40%, while shipments to Turkmenistan rose 34% to 210,000 tons.

These figures underline Kazakhstan’s importance as a regional supplier. But they also reveal the limits of an export model based primarily on increasing volumes of agricultural commodities.

From exporting more to creating more value

The more significant shift may now be taking place in food processing. According to official data, agricultural exports reached $7 billion in 2025, up 37% year-on-year. More than half of this amount, around $3.6 billion, came from processed agricultural products, whose exports grew by 35% compared with the previous year. The figures suggest that Kazakhstan is beginning to capture a larger share of the value generated from its agricultural production.

Vice Minister of Agriculture Yerbol Taszhurekov said processing is becoming one of the main drivers of growth in Kazakhstan’s agro-industrial complex. Speaking at a March 5 briefing at the Central Communications Service, he said the country’s strategy is not simply to increase agricultural output but to retain more of the economic value generated by it within Kazakhstan.

“Our strategic task is not only to increase the production of agricultural raw materials but also to ensure their processing within the country, including deep processing that creates products with high added value. Processing forms new production chains, creates jobs in the regions and strengthens Kazakhstan’s export potential,” Taszhurekov said.

But not all processing represents the same level of economic transformation. Turning wheat into flour is already a step beyond exporting raw grain. Deep processing, however, can create products such as starch, gluten, amino acids, syrups, vitamins and bioethanol, connecting agriculture to more complex industrial supply chains.

This distinction may become increasingly important for Kazakhstan. The country’s long-term agricultural strategy is therefore not simply about producing more grain, but about moving further along the value chain. The government aims to increase the share of processed agricultural products to 70%. New deep-processing facilities planned by 2028 are expected to have a combined capacity of 5.8 million tons per year and attract around 1.9 trillion tenge (US$3.9 billion) in investment.

Changing the fields to change the export model

The transformation is also evident in what Kazakhstan produces. In recent years, the area under wheat cultivation has declined by nearly 900,000 hectares. In comparison, oilseed acreage has increased by more than one million hectares and land used for pulse crops has expanded by 275,000 hectares, according to the World Financial Review.

This is more than a change in crop statistics. A broader crop mix creates a wider raw-material base for domestic processing industries. Oilseeds, for example, can support vegetable oil production, while pulses and grain can feed into increasingly sophisticated food and industrial processing. Kazakhstan produced a record 4.8 million tons of oilseeds in 2025, while food production rose 8.1% to 3.9 trillion tenge (US$8 billion).

The shift suggests that Kazakhstan’s agricultural diversification is becoming increasingly connected to its industrial policy. Diversification in the fields is intended to support diversification in factories, which in turn could change the composition of exports.

World.title: The future of Abkhazia: from preserving the language to building a civic nation. A view from Abkhazia, video discussion
World.content:
Abkhaz language and civic nation

The editor of the newspaper Chegemskaya Pravda, Inal Khashig, and political scientist Astamur Tania discuss the challenges and state policy regarding the Abkhazian language, the shift in historical narratives surrounding the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, as well as the necessity of building an inclusive civic nation for the sustainable future of Abkhazia.

Main theses and arguments:

Preservation and Development of the Abkhaz Language — The language issue is viewed as the foundation of national identity, requiring not merely electoral campaigns, but a long-term state program encompassing education, ideology, and administrative measures. Overcoming Formalism in Language Policy — Existing legislative initiatives and laws (such as the 2007 law) face implementation problems; there is a risk that successive delays and amendments will boil down to a formalistic approach without real results. Balance Between the State Language and Interethnic Harmony — Grace periods for non-Abkhaz citizens to master the Abkhazian language are aimed at preventing discrimination and fostering a unified civic platform under conditions of inevitable bilingualism (Abkhaz and Russian). Countering Historical Revisionism — Attempts to rewrite the history of the conflict are observed in the Georgian information space (including the promotion of the pseudoscientific “Ingorokva theory” and the interpretation of the 1992 war exclusively as Russian aggression), which relieves Georgia of responsibility and hinders a peaceful settlement. Abkhazia’s Agency and the Reduction of Hate Speech — Abkhazia emphasizes its status as an established nation and an active subject of relations; both sides acknowledge the destructiveness of “hate speech” in the media, as a resumption of the conflict would be catastrophic for everyone. Formation of a Civic Nation and the Rule of Law — The key challenge is the transition from ethnic self-awareness to an inclusive civic nation that unites all ethnic groups in Abkhazia on the basis of shared values, legal order, security, and consensus.

Inal Khashig: Hello, Chegemskaya Pravda is on the air. Today, we are going to speak again about the very same topics that concern our Abkhaz society. This prolonged discussion regarding the Abkhaz language, the standards of proficiency in this language, the state language for members of parliament. At the parliamentary hearings, the parliamentary committee rejected – that is, did not recommend – the draft constitutional amendments proposed by the president. But, nevertheless, legally this does not mean, as I understood, that the issue has been removed from the agenda; one way or another, it can be included in the agenda of the parliamentary session, even without this recommendation from the profile committee. Our guest today is Astamur Tania.

Astamur Tania: Good day.

Inal Khashig: Good day. Generally, what do you think about this whole situation that has arisen with these amendments to the constitutional law?

Astamur Tania: Here, the topic of the Abkhaz language is periodically raised in the form of certain information campaigns, usually during some pre-election period or in connection with certain events. It is also impossible to manage without information campaigns. It is necessary to sharpen public attention on this problem.

I hope that this information campaign will not have an independent significance of its own, but will transform into some programmatic actions. Because, probably, everyone understands—both supporters of one approach and supporters of the second approach—that in itself this decision means little. Because here it should still be about a state program.

This program is both educational and ideological, because much rests even on questions of self-awareness. Because it is clear that with the help of the Abkhaz language it is impossible to obtain the volume of information necessary to participate in any competition. So, there must be some other incentives. Just like that, in a natural way, unfortunately, it will not work.

These must be administrative measures and measures of an ideological nature. The Abkhaz language is inextricably linked with issues of identity. This is a big task on all fronts.

Now, regarding the presidential initiative specifically: to be honest, I consider it rational. Some argue that it involves an unequal approach, but I believe it is not aimed at discrimination.

On the contrary, its purpose is to address potential concerns so that advancing the Abkhaz language development program is not perceived as discriminatory by non-Abkhaz residents. After all, preserving interethnic harmony, maintaining consensus, and building a unified civic platform are fundamental for our society.

From this perspective, the approach is entirely sound. However, we must ensure this does not lead to endless postponements. The state must actively work on this by defining clear criteria in legislation to specify what constitutes fluency in the Abkhaz language.

This requirement should apply not only to the parliament but also to the executive branch. Implementing it within the judiciary will be more complex, as it requires extensive work to adapt the full body of legal terminology, which demands highly specialized legal expertise.

Inal Khashig: There are terminologies. All of that exists.

Astamur Tania: I know that preliminary work has been carried out—mostly at the level of compiling dictionaries of legal terms, as far as I am aware. However, implementation within the judiciary is far more difficult purely due to professional constraints.

That is why I believe the presidential initiative reflects today’s realities. It creates a space for compromise among political participants and allows us to develop proper criteria for assessing Abkhaz language proficiency.

If we fail to reach an agreement and leave everything as it is—which could easily happen if the president’s proposed law fails to pass—we will remain at a standstill. The entire process could degenerate into a formalistic routine, similar to what we witnessed during the presidential elections, and only spread further.

Therefore, as an initial step, I view this approach as very reasonable. Since there is no discrimination involved, I see no basis to claim it is unconstitutional.

Inal Khashig: I have my own perspective on this, though doubts constantly trouble me. The initiative grants a deferment to non-ethnic Abkhazians, but I am convinced that in five years, by 2032, we will find ourselves with the exact same results.

Astamur Tania: That certainly cannot be ruled out.

Inal Khashig: Indeed. But my concern is the formalistic approach toward the Abkhaz language itself. For instance, the language law was adopted in 2007 and was meant to take full effect in 2015, requiring the entire Abkhaz bureaucracy to be fluent in the state language.

Yet, even if a good half of them are fluent today, we should consider ourselves lucky—especially since no actual testing or measurements were ever conducted.

Astamur Tania: If at least a “bad half” had command of it.

Inal Khashig: Yes, yes. I am afraid that, strictly speaking, we will simply do this—formalize the commission itself, which we will bring to formal absurdity. Like, here is a good guy, he knows 10 words.

Astamur Tania: If we do not change our attitude toward our state, then in the Abkhaz language, and in security, and in the economy, we will have roughly the same result. You are right. This is a broader question than the Abkhaz language. It is just that now it is at the peak of relevance due to the debates in parliament and in society. In fact, this is a question of our attitude.

Various arguments are brought up that the quality of parliamentarism may drop from this. It seems to me that despite the absence of this norm, the quality of our parliamentarism was declining anyway. So the problem, after all, is not only in the Abkhaz language. This is a hackneyed phrase that we always get the government we deserve, that it is a reflection of our society. Therefore, this is a giant societal problem. But it must be dealt with.

First of all, the authorities, you see—to change the quality of authority, those in power must work on changing the quality of society as well. This goal must be set. Not simply to sit out one’s tenure in parliament or executive power. It is necessary to influence society, its enlightenment, its self-awareness, its creative potential. Therein lies the main task. Otherwise, you are right, it will drift on its own, like everything else.

Inal Khashig: It seems to me that the situation around the Abkhaz language is indeed much broader. It shows, probably, our attitude toward the law in general. This applies not only to the Abkhaz language.

We have passed very many all sorts of legislative acts, proper laws, but then we tried in every way to bypass them. An active advertising campaign is taking place on the internet: acquire Abkhaz real estate, and so forth. So many lances were broken over this law on apartments, and still they sell Abkhaz real estate to foreigners. It is possible, it can be acquired.

Astamur Tania: Yes, that is also—you know what the matter is? It is impossible to contain the onslaught; it can only be directed into some profitable channel. Of course, it is possible for some time to contain the natural course of events with prohibitions. But we must nevertheless forecast how we can direct these investments, where our weak zones are.

Simply sitting like a dog in the manger will not work. Therefore, we must understand how in this harsh reality—what is our place. Today one hole was plugged, in another place it tore open. We must have some clear program of action, at least for the short term.

This concerns the economy, security, foreign policy, everything. What I am saying is very banal, but unfortunately, we always have a reactive response to something, to already accomplished facts. Although it was not difficult to predict that the course of events was leading to this. And we live for today. If an individual person can live for today like that, the state should not live like that.

Inal Khashig: The state somehow manages to.

Astamur Tania: It should still plan its future, the society.

Inal Khashig: I would like to switch to another topic now. Periodically, we are reminded of the unresolved Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, which continuously remains at a dead end. Last time, we discussed how Georgian perceptions of Abkhazia and the Abkhaz people have changed, particularly through the influence of Pavel Ingorokva’s theory, which took a strong hold in Georgian thought.

Shortly after our conversation, I watched an interview with the Georgian historian Tsurtsumia on a Georgian YouTube channel. He noted that Ingorokva’s theory is actually marginal and lacks official state support.

Nevertheless, just the day before yesterday, I came across a vividly animated video. It was set in Sukhumi on the embankment, depicting peaceful civilians in a setting reminiscent of 1992, when a Russian military aircraft suddenly swoops in and begins bombing. The people are shown fleeing the embankment, trying to escape by ship or heading into the mountains.

Astamur Tania: Those are slightly different scenes, probably. Maybe it is one pie, but different slices.

Inal Khashig: Yes, but you see, this is proceeding very actively – why I understood this is not only Ingorokva’s theory about who the Abkhaz are and what their origin is, but in Georgian society the understanding of what the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict was is changing very actively. And what happened 33 years ago, 34 years ago. How the war started.

According to this cartoon… A cartoon is a certain part of upbringing. It also has its own audience. Directed at a certain audience. At children. It is important for me to understand why the Georgians converted this conflict into a conflict not between Georgians and Abkhaz, but a certain conflict between Russia and Georgia.

Astamur Tania: That is completely understandable, as acknowledging it would require admitting responsibility for starting the armed conflict. By the way, Shevardnadze did admit this responsibility—and while he claimed Kitovani was to blame, Kitovani was not the Defense Minister of Russia, but of Georgia. Everyone remembers, and archival footage still shows, how this war began and how the local Georgian population reacted.

Acknowledging this would require erasing entire sections of history. Instead, there is an effort to reshape the narrative of 1992 and merge it with the events of 2008, framing everything around legislation and the narrative of post-2008 occupation. Yet, a detailed examination—including the report by the International Fact-Finding Commission led by Heidi Tagliavini—confirmed that responsibility for initiating military action in both instances lay with the Georgian side.

Naturally, there is a desire to obscure this in the media space to advance narratives about occupation, aiming to shape international opinion to justify a forceful resolution or delegitimize the Abkhazian state.

We must react to this. The fact that animated videos are being produced on this topic shows an intent to pass this worldview down to the next generation. If we carry such a perspective into the future, achieving a peaceful settlement or joint progress will be extremely difficult. This is why it is essential to present the fullest possible picture, starting with the factual timeline.

Regarding Zura Tsurtsumia’s comments: first, it is positive that Georgian-Abkhaz relations are being examined at a solid academic level, attempting to move beyond today’s propaganda clichés toward a historical assessment of the conflict’s roots.

However, claiming that Ingorokva’s theory is marginal ignores reality in the Georgian media landscape, where it remains the most widespread view on the origins of the Abkhazian people. While prominent Georgian scholars considered it pseudoscientific—such as Javakhishvili, who noted that ancient Adyghe tribes inhabited Western Georgia prior to the Kartvelians and recognized the Apsilals and Abasgs as direct ancestors of modern Abkhaz—these classical works are largely ignored by mainstream media.

Instead, hate speech dominates the discourse among commentators—and we must acknowledge that hate speech exists on the Abkhaz side as well. Neither side benefits from this.

Objectively, neither we nor Georgia have any interest in a renewed armed conflict, which would yield disastrous consequences for both. Some in Georgian society may assume their larger population makes it an easy victory, but that is far from reality. We cannot afford to trigger such a dangerous cycle.

Both sides are equally served by abandoning hate speech and language that demeans human dignity and belittles culture, especially given that all human cultures, including Abkhazian and Georgian, are products of historical interaction and symbiosis.

Finally, addressing Tsurtsumia’s assertion—which is not unique to him—that the Abkhaz nation was deliberately engineered by Soviet authorities to counter Georgia: while Soviet policies influenced the development of both the Georgian and Abkhazian nations in the late 19th and 20th centuries, it is vital to recognize that the Abkhaz national identity was not an artificial creation.

In fact, during the 1930s and 1940s, deliberate repressive measures were used in an effort to suppress the formation of the Abkhaz nation.

Inal Khashig: That was when schools were closed.

Astamur Tania: Schools were closed, and the destruction of the intelligentsia—the bearers of this very idea—took place at that time. This inflicted a serious trauma.

But one must understand that this process is accomplished. It is an accomplished fact. And in dialogue with the Abkhaz, everyone must proceed from the premise that this is not simply an ethnos, but a formed nation. With its own ideas about borders, policy, with its own national mythology. This is not always equal to history. Here there is a completely different approach.

As I once spoke with an Abkhaz, he said in his heart: why did Gurandukht, the daughter of the Abkhaz king, marry Gurgen, the ruler of Tao-Klarjeti? Since then, the unification of the Abkhaz state with the Georgian one began. That is the feudal era. It is an accomplished fact. We can only look at it like that. It sounds like a parody.

The same applies to this issue. It is closer to us. These are already accomplished facts. We must take them into account. Proceed from the fact that this is a given. Second, there were in fact certain inaccuracies there.

I do not want to delve into that now. In itself, this attempt to approach the understanding of the origins of the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict with a cool head, using academic material—if this happens more or less regularly, in the same calm atmosphere, then it seems to me that both societies can win from this.

Inal Khashig: On the other hand, it seems to me, given that this seems to be a recent event—the war is relatively a historical event, only 30 years ago—nevertheless, judging by what I read in social networks, certain articles, certain speeches of politicians or experts…

Astamur Tania: Very much so.

Inal Khashig: I still see a lot of statements specifically adjusting to the political opportunism of the moment. If you remember, in the 80s, in the 90s after the war, what were we called? Abkhaz separatists. Now you practically do not hear this term.

Astamur Tania: By the way, they started calling us Abkhaz separatists back during the war, and before that—Gudauta separatists. Although during that period Abkhazia had not yet declared that it was ceasing any relations with Georgia and was not going to live with it within common borders.

In its time, on the initiative of Georgian figures, the process of all kinds of division began in Abkhazia. They separated the Georgian sector from the Abkhaz State University. Then they withdrew the football team. Then they withdrew the Georgian faction from the Supreme Council. They began to sit separately. That is, they apparently assumed that gradually they would somehow paralyze things. And here the question arises: who was the separatist?

And the same with this term. And, by the way, “Gudauta separatists”—later this very term migrated into the documents of the United Nations. And for some time after the end of the war, when our authorities were already located in Sukhumi, they continued to call us Gudauta separatists. I think for the Abzhua Abkhaz this is a bit offensive. Gudauta-Abzzua separatists would have been sound better.

Inal Khashig: But, nevertheless, this term somehow went out of circulation. And we have already been switched to the idea that Abkhazia is a territory occupied by Russia. And at the same time, as for the Abkhaz—let us leave aside those social networks where we generally came down from the mountains, according to the Georgian version—in official rhetoric nothing is said about us anymore.

Astamur Tania: “Came down from the mountains” is also quite amusing, because on most of the coast, based on climatic conditions and the unhealthiness of this climate, it was practically impossible to live permanently. Even if you open the press of, say, the late 19th and early 20th centuries, it is evident that the affluent portion of the residents of the city of Sukhumi left Sukhumi for the summer period. Precisely when there was the peak of this disease, people left for the foothills, because living here was a bit dangerous.

Inal Khashig: And the most prosperous ones lived there.

Astamur Tania: Generally, we have a perception as if in the Middle Ages communications in Abkhazia—this applies to everything, we are talking about Abkhazia—ran along the coast like that; there was the Ancient Roman railway running, next to it the Byzantine highway, but in reality all communications passed through the foothills and across the ridges. It was later, with the arrival of the Russian Empire, that this network of communications familiar to us began to develop. And psychologically we begin to tie our perception of the past to what had already taken shape in the 19th and 20th centuries. There was no railway at the beginning of the 20th century yet.

Inal Khashig: This highway that exists now.

Astamur Tania: For example, construction of the Black Sea railway continued in 1918 still. The Russian Empire no longer existed, but it was unclear what would happen. But they continued to build it in the Gagra region in 1918. And now it seems that it was always there.

Inal Khashig: But nevertheless, I tried to understand. Why do they depict Abkhaz who did not participate in this conflict, or played some secondary role in this Georgian-Abkhaz conflict? In the war that took place in 1992-1993.

Astamur Tania: A moment is omitted. What quantity of weapons was transferred to Georgia under the Tashkent Agreement on the eve of the conflict? The Russian authorities of that time were far from being, to put it mildly, pro-Abkhaz.

This is evident from everything. This is visible if one reads at least the transcript of September 3 of the meeting of Shevardnadze, Yeltsin, Ardzinba, representatives of the North Caucasus, representatives of our various parliamentary deputations. Not only should documents be studied, one should read the transcript.

But why did Georgia start armed conflicts? It received at its disposal several motor rifle and tank divisions of the Transcaucasus Military District. Therefore, in their joy, they thought that it would be possible to quickly finish this business.

Inal Khashig: But nevertheless, why am I saying all this—I read an interesting Georgian perspective on why this is happening, that Abkhaz are being excluded from this conflict, that through such an exclusion—and, say, when a certain image of the enemy is removed from the Abkhaz in this conflict, in this war, if the Abkhaz played a non-primary role, it means they are not enemies. There is a hypothetical possibility they retain that later at some point we will make peace with them.

Astamur Tania: That is very hypothetical. In my opinion, it is impossible to do that. Because how can one take a segment of a section of thinking and take something out of there… It seems to me this is very much a laboratory theory.

Inal Khashig: But this is laboratory on the one hand, and on the other hand the Abkhaz themselves have their own perception of the war.

Astamur Tania: To reiterate: those in Georgia who deal with the Georgian-Abkhaz settlement or seek to study this issue must start from the accomplished fact of the Abkhazian nation’s existence. A nation cannot be treated as a third-party observer—it is an active subject. We are an active subject in our relations with Georgia. Recognized or unrecognized, by our internal structure, we are a nation—with our own statehood and our own distinct perception of both the past and the future.
