World.title: One Nation says staffer left hospitalised after assault
World.content:
A One Nation staffer was injured during an assault at the Royal Queensland Show in Brisbane on Friday, according to the party.

One Nation chief of staff James Ashby told 4BC a staffer in her 60s was on her way to the party's stall when she was verbally assaulted by three women and a man, before the situation escalated and the staffer was punched in the ribs.

"She now has one broken rib, she's got enormous bruising and she's had to go through the unedifying process of having to strip down in front of police so that they can take photographs of her injuries," Mr Ashby said.

He said the staffer had been released from the hospital over the weekend.

James Ashby says a One Nation staffer was assaulted at the Ekka in Brisbane on Friday. (ABC News: Jacob Kagi)

In a social media post, the party said a "much-valued female member of the One Nation team was physically assaulted by a group of three young women and one young man at the Ekka festival in Brisbane, leading to a broken rib".

"One Nation would like to condemn this violent attack in the strongest possible terms. The attackers should be ashamed of themselves," the statement read.

"The matter is with the Queensland Police and is currently being investigated."

Queensland Police Service said it was aware of the allegations, but had not received a formal complaint.

Mr Ashby said it was his opinion the staffer had been targeted due to her One Nation shirt.

"These are the same young women who demand respect for women, especially when it comes to domestic violence, and yet they stood by, spat on her and allowed their male counterpart to lay vicious blows on her to break a rib," he said.

He told the AAP the woman was "set upon with foul language" after walking through the gates.

"She ignored them, and as she continued walking they called her an ignorant (expletive) and that's when they set upon her."

Mr Ashby said it was his opinion the staffer had been targeted due to her wearing a One Nation shirt similar to this. (ABC News: Erin Somerville)

The staffer was recovering after being hospitalised but was badly bruised and shaken, Mr Ashby said.

"She's really shaken and extremely sore. Broken ribs aren't fun," Mr Ashby said.

"I don't want any of my staff feeling that way."

Queensland Ambulance Service said it had no record of ambulances dispatched to the Ekka for a woman in her 60s with injured ribs on either Thursday or Friday.

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce told reporters today the party had been in contact with the volunteer.

"This is not made up," he said. "This person was spat on, they were punched, they have a broken rib.

"We have got to really, within this space, call it for what it is. This is completely outrageous."

RNA chief executive Brendan Christou said the organisation had been made aware of an alleged incident by Queensland police.

"The safety and wellbeing of our visitors, exhibitors, staff and everyone involved in the Show is our highest priority, and this allegation is extremely concerning," he said.

"The Ekka is a family-friendly event and we do not condone any form of violence."

He said the RNA will assist police in any inquiries.

World.title: Former school worker admits to sexual abuse of children
World.content:
A former school worker from the NSW Far South Coast will be sentenced later this year after admitting to historical child sexual abuse offences, some of which were committed while he was underage.

The man, who is aged in his mid-30s and cannot be named for legal reasons, was originally charged with 59 offences.

Today he pleaded guilty in Batemans Bay Local Court to eight counts of sexual intercourse with a child.

Court documents reveal the man abused five boys and a girl at two locations on the Far South Coast over the span of a decade.

He appeared via video link from Nowra's South Coast Correctional Centre and was supported in court by two elderly family members, who sat in the front row of the public gallery.

The man abused six children at two locations on the NSW Far South Coast. (ABC News)

Outside court, the man's lawyer, Adam Sumbak, said he was pleased for all involved to see the case heading towards a resolution.

"For the victims, the community at large and the offender, it is a huge relief to have these matters move forward," he said.

The case was mentioned in court 21 times over more than two years, with the court hearing delays had been caused by the sensitivity and complexity of the case and police staff shortages.

The man was arrested in late 2023 and soon after NSW Police set up a task force to investigate further allegations and possible victims.

During a bail hearing in 2024, prosecutors told the court the man had previously worked at a local primary school and had two children in his care at the time of his arrest.

The man will be sentenced in Bega District Court in October. (ABC South East NSW: Adriane Reardon)

His offending began at the age of 14 when he sexually assaulted an eight-year-old boy in a small coastal town in late 2004.

Over the next three years, he assaulted a five-year-old and 10-year-old boy, and a 10-year-old girl multiple times.

As an adult in 2011, he assaulted a 10-year-old boy and assaulted him again when the boy became a teenager.

In 2017, he assaulted a seven-year-old boy.

He will be sentenced in Bega District Court via video link on October 6.

World.title: Duck the US canards that are flying in our gun debate
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Pauline Hanson’s predictable response to the gun buyback – that it’s not guns that kill but the people behind them – is straight out of the US National Rifle Association handbook (“Minns willing to face election gun fight”, August 17). This powerful and well-funded organisation repeats the canard even though the US has more mass shootings, gun suicides and gun homicides than any other country. Until something is done in the US to rein in the number of guns circulating, the public will have to suffice with “thoughts and prayers” after each shooting tragedy. At least we are striving to find a better way to deal with an increasing problem than vacuous platitudes. Bernard Moylan, Bronte NSW Premier Chris Minns and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese address the media on the gun buyback scheme. Matt Canavan has got himself confused. This is Australia, not the US (“Coalition slams PM over ‘failed’ arms buyback”, August 17). The Queensland senator is outraged that Labor’s gun buyback plans are “trampling our rights”. What rights, exactly? Australians do not have the right to gun ownership – it is a strictly regulated privilege governed by federal, state and territory laws. These laws require a “genuine reason” for gun ownership, such as farming or sport shooting. Self-defence is never a valid justification. Most Australians, aware of the terrible harm guns can inflict, would probably agree that gun ownership should be far more strictly regulated. Alison Stewart, Riverview Compare Australia’s gun fatality rate over the past year of less than one person per 100,000 with the US rate of 13 per 100,000. This points to weak gun laws combined with a proliferation of guns as the primary cause of gun deaths in America. It’s impossible to limit the number of potential murderers in a country, but you can easily control the number of guns available. Larry Woldenberg, Forest Lodge If we are asking law-abiding citizens to surrender legally acquired and legally stored guns, surely we must pay them the market value of each firearm surrendered. To do otherwise seems to me to be clearly unfair and, I suspect, politically stupid. Paul Meagher, Wahroonga AI, AI, premier It’s great to see that Premier Chris “Fast Track” Minns has allayed our concerns about AI’s impact on our energy and water, and to learn that data centre construction alone has saved NSW from recession, with 75-day approvals for new centres if they provide their own water and energy. Presumably, this means their artificial intelligence will manufacture extra rainfall to meet their cooling demands. We have ample sunlight for solar power, but even covering their whole roofs and walls in solar panels will not satisfy their energy appetite, so they will continue to gobble up more of the clean power that should be shared with the rest of us. I’m hanging on the premier’s detailed explanation on how they have buoyed the state’s economy. Is it through supply of all that computing equipment we don’t manufacture, or the myriad ongoing jobs they don’t provide, or just their large draw on construction industry labour and materials, that’s helping to drive up the cost of house construction? Dick Clarke, Elanora Heights



Addicted to immigration It’s not surprising that the majority of voters feel the government is handling immigration poorly (“Voters turn on Labor over migrant policy”, August 17). Immigration in this country has become an absolute mess and everyone with a vested interest simply wants more, with dire consequences. Apparently, farmers now can’t cope without migrant workers, aged care can’t cope without migrant workers and universities can’t make ends meet without foreign students. We don’t train enough doctors and nurses so to fill our need we take them from countries that can ill afford to lose them. In fact, the only remedy to all the “skills shortages” throughout our economy seems to be more immigration. On top of this, we can’t even seem to build enough houses for the people who already live here, and the vulnerable increasingly go homeless. It seems there are “growing pains” in every city and region, and the environment is coming a sad last everywhere we look. Australia is addicted to high immigration. It has been for a long time and desperately needs rehab. Andrew Cronin, Robertson Photo: Cathy Wilcox Stronger democracy Every Australian state and territory moved to four-year-terms long ago (“$93b push to hold federal election every four years”, August 17). The quickest way for the federal parliament to do the same is by legislation, rather than by referendum. For pity’s sake then, get on with it. There are many democracy-strengthening reforms that require mature debate, such as taxpayer-funded elections rather than through donations. Severe crackdowns also need to be imposed on lobbyists. It’s obvious that big business has far too much say on legislation in all jurisdictions. Money talks, even to “socialist” Labor. The latter has given us a lame NACC, skittish environmental reforms, irksome restrictions on independents and no progress on whistleblower reform. Compared to early federation, when world-leading electoral laws, state-arbitrated wage laws and pioneering welfare provisions were the norm, we now seem to be stuck in the mud. John MacKay, Asquith Advocacy group 4 Year Terms Australia is right to call for fixed four-year election cycles. To me, the biggest benefit would be better policymaking. Look at the current situation – just 18 months after the federal election, the government is already looking at policies to enhance its re-election prospects. No better example of this type of practice is the change made to GST payments to favour WA by the Morrison government in 2018, a decision now roundly criticised by the Productivity Commission. There are numerous other examples of half-baked policy initiatives taken with an eye to the next election. As noted, the question of a four-year term was last put to the Australian people in 1988 under the Hawke government. It was defeated. Australians are reluctant to change the Constitution, however, since 1988 public policies, especially in the federal sphere, have been poorly developed and administered. The public know this, and with bipartisan support, the proposal for a four-year term should be approved. The progress of this country demands it. Dennis Bluth, Cammeray As Rob Harris points out in his article, a three-year election cycle is a drag on our economy both in political decision-making and from the perspective of investors, who need to be more certain of government rules and regulations. A fixed four-year election cycle will help the federal government make bold decisions without the fear of an immediate backlash from the voters, as this will give time for those decisions to show results. Additionally, the electoral commission should be the only authority to decide election dates, not the prime minister of the day. Bipin Johri, Epping



Credibility problem Hyperbolised statements like “atheists have their own credibility problems” reflect the deep-seated fear that committed Christians and the hyper-religious harbour about anyone who rejects membership of their exclusive clubs (Letters, August 17). Further, Peter Juocys and other religious correspondents might be surprised to know that “God-deniers” often author the “textbooks, original papers and discoveries on human anatomy, biochemistry and ecology”. It is an outrageous assumption that engagement with high-order scientific knowledge, analysis and understanding is the exclusive domain of God-followers. Finally, it might be asked of those who make these myopic and conceited claims why their God also oversees the destruction of the “perfect design” of creation by his perfect creation – humanity. Robyn Dalziell, Kellyville Christians give God credit for unproven miracles, but why is he/she never assigned blame for atrocities? While it’s comforting to believe in a cosmic designer and claim the design is “perfect”, it ignores reality. If you think the designer has made a perfect creation, then ask why so much can go wrong with it. Take the “perfect” design of the human, for example, and consider the myriad ailments: cancer, multiple sclerosis, motor neurone disease, malformed organs, even bad eyesight … the list is almost endless. If that’s perfect design, then we want our money back. Worse, if the designer built all those ailments into the design, what kind of pernicious entity is it? Peter Thompson, Grenfell If Peter Juocys truly believes in the creativity of God over the scientific theory of evolution, could he kindly explain where God lived before he created the universe? And while Christians continue to give God credit for unproven miracles, why is he/she never assigned blame for well-recorded atrocities such as the Crusades, the Spanish Inquisition and the continuing armed conflict and torture around the world, much of which has its roots in religious rivalry of some kind. Jeremy Cornford, Kingscliff



Moral solution Dale Bailey is correct that children in non-government schools have a right to government funding, as their parents pay taxes (Letters, August 17). He stated that “private schools should receive taxpayer-funded support to the extent that Gonski determines”. An education system based on a fully funded Gonski model is a moral solution to the distorted funding system that disadvantages our important public education system. Those private schools building extensive property portfolios, constructing heated indoor swimming pools and wanting to buy public streets would then be working under a Gonski funding model. The money would be then filtered to the schools that most need it, instead of wealthy schools that operate as businesses. John Cotterill, Kingsford Roll with renewables Origin’s Frank Calabria is right to point to the challenges ahead if we are to successfully decarbonise the grid (“Energy giant warns big test still to come for power grid”, August 17). Australia has 18 coal-fired power stations. Eight are more than 40 years’ old and operating at just 60 per cent of capacity owing to breakdowns and maintenance. Three of these are slated for closure by 2030, the other five by 2035. Three more will also close around that time, bringing the number to 11. These represent 76 per cent of the nation’s coal-fired generating capacity. The three in NSW represent a massive 83 per cent of the state’s coal-fired capacity. Given this reality, we need to stop arguing about the benefits and supposed drawbacks of renewables and just get on with the rollout. The alternative is to risk regular blackouts. Ken Enderby, Concord Nodding with George As I was reading George Brandis’ article I found myself getting the nods – no, not falling asleep but agreeing with him (“While Liberals shoot their messenger, Labor squanders its chance for brave reform”, August 17). He is right about previous PMs being arrogant, the present PM thinking he is bulletproof and a government that needs to make more bold policy reforms. Brandis always writes well with his extensive knowledge of political history, though I rarely go along with his ideas. This time I agree with you, George. Rare, but true. Mark Nugent, Lugarno



Town square-off Instead of demolishing the Woolies opposite Town Hall to create an open space, why not keep the basement and ground-floor shopping areas (“Clover’s grand plan risks becoming an eyesore and more”, August 17)? They are always very busy with shoppers, especially those heading for a train. The upper floors could be converted to much-needed apartments to help alleviate the housing crisis for low- to middle-income city workers. We certainly don’t need a vast open area, considering Hyde Park is just up the road. If people are looking for trees and a place to sit in the shade, they can just go there. Pamela Cunningham, Camperdown I totally support Jim Stone, the lone defender of the square (Letters, August 17). Sydney Town Hall, St Andrews and the QVB will provide a ready-made historical backdrop and a far more pleasant perspective than the current view from outside Woolies. As for what to avoid, learn from the mistakes of the Leichhardt Italian forum, which lacked scale, shade and a decent range of al fresco cafes and dining options. Its Dante-inspired fountain, when it worked, resembled a bird bath, and its death blow came from residents’ objections to live music. Think: bold and open. Not: fussy and token. Peter Farmer, Northbridge Carriages missed Passenger growth on the M1 metro is already higher than forecast, and the addition of extra feeder bus services and more high-rise residential construction in the north-west means that even squashing into a crowded carriage at Crows Nest will no longer be an option. Extra carriages and/or more frequent services should be introduced sooner rather than later (“Surge in metro demand leaves passengers waiting”, August 17). Doug Walker, Baulkham Hills

World.title: James Packer’s bets on AI pay off after sell-down in gaming shares
World.content:
Exclusive BusinessCompaniesJames Packer James Packer’s bets on AI pay off after sell-down in gaming shares Kishor Napier-Raman August 17, 2026 — 6:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Billionaire James Packer has shifted his investment focus from gaming back to artificial intelligence, with his stake in computer chip manufacturer Nvidia now worth almost US$300 million ($422 million). Filings with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission made last week by a Cayman Islands-based holding company controlled by Packer show that the former Crown owner increased his holdings in Nvidia to 1.5 million shares in the March quarter of 2026. Billionaire businessman James Packer has shifted his investment strategy towards artificial intelligence. Seven News That stake rose in value to $US296 million ($417 million) in the quarter ending June 30, a 14 per cent increase in value. Nvidia, which manufactures specialised computer chips used by artificial intelligence companies, has soared thanks to the boom in that technology. With a market capitalisation of $US5.45 trillion ($7.67 trillion), it is the world’s most valuable public company, a crown it briefly lost to Apple last month. Packer has consistently shuffled his American portfolio through a tangled thicket of companies linked to his private investment vehicle, Consolidated Press Holdings, making it difficult to track its true value. However, recent filings show he has made a major bet on the technology.



Palidye Holdings (Caymans) Ltd, which holds the Nvidia shares, and also has a $US121 million stake in Facebook owner Meta Platforms and a $US115 million position in Microsoft. Palidye reports to the SEC on behalf of Consolidated Press International Ltd, another of Packer’s companies. Under the US regulator’s rules, a single investment manager can file quarterly reports on behalf of another where the two entities share investment discretion or have a parent-subsidiary relationship. Palidye’s total portfolio is currently valued at $US558 million. The company also has shares in Reddit, Afterpay owner Block, and e-commerce platform Shopify. Packer’s latest investments also reflect a shift in focus away from gaming and back towards artificial intelligence over the past year. A year ago, his company, Consolidated Press International Holdings, sold down its stake in Nvidia and bought 2.7 per cent of Las Vegas-based pokie machine manufacturer Light & Wonder, which is planning to move its listing from Wall Street’s Nasdaq to the ASX. He also bought a $US121 share in Flutter, the parent company of online bookmaker Sportsbet. Those purchases were Packer’s first foray back into gambling since he sold his shares in casino operator Crown Resorts to American private equity giant Blackstone for $3.3 billion in 2022. Packer’s exit from gaming came after a bruising series of state-based inquiries following allegations of money laundering at Crown casinos.



But recent filings indicate a pivot from gaming back to technology. The Light & Wonder stake, worth $US243 million as of last September, has been sold, as have his shares in Flutter. Palidye, the Caymans-based company, also sold a $US21 million stake in US sports betting company Penn Entertainment. It also bought shares in Las Vegas casino giant Wynn Resorts that was worth as much as $US147 million last year, which has since been sold. Related Article Weddings Billionaire James Packer weds former model in Italy In 2019, Wynn sought to engineer a takeover of Crown which would have given Packer a 10 per cent stake in the company. But Wynn pulled out of the deal after discussions were prematurely leaked to the media. Consolidated Press International made just two small purchases in the last quarter, buying circa $US1 million stakes in school bus manufacturer Blue Bird Corporation and nuclear energy start-up Deep Fission Inc. In several interviews, Packer has chalked down some of his recent investment strategy to the influence of Canadian-born Daniel Nadler, a billionaire artificial intelligence entrepreneur and poet.



“In truth, the only reason I’ve had some wins recently is because I’ve taken his [Nadler’s] advice,” he told The Daily Telegraph in 2024. Packer’s representatives were contacted for comment. In May, Consolidated Press Holdings settled a Federal Court lawsuit brought by former general counsel Catherine Davies, who departed last year after more than a decade. Packer was not a party to the lawsuit. Last week, the billionaire tied the knot for the third time, marrying Canadian model Kylie Lim on the Italian island of Sardinia. World.title: ‘We’ve got carried away’: The Australian Test team’s five biggest problems
World.content:
Analysis SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘We’ve got carried away’: The Australian Test team’s five biggest problems Daniel Brettig August 17, 2026 — 5:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Top order batting – Pat Cummins asked his batting order to get through a tricky first couple of hours on a fresh pitch in Darwin and they were completely unable to find a way to do so against a diligent but far from fearsome Bangladesh attack. Jake Weatherald’s perpetual motion at the crease speaks of technical tweaks but also nerves, and it is tough to see him keeping his place in Mackay. Marnus Labuschagne has already been dropped and recalled once in the past year, but is still struggling to find his best. Then there’s Travis Head and the question of his best position. Former opener Matthew Hayden was one seasoned voice to call for Matt Renshaw and Sam Konstas at the top, with Head moving to three. Ebadot Hossain of Bangladesh celebrates after taking the wicket of Marnus Labuschagne. Getty Images Tellingly, Cummins spoke not of a one-off problem but of a trend, meaning that the team’s batting difficulties will be the chief topic of internal conversation this week. He was also open about the selectors’ ability to make change: “Every Aussie Test we do you can kind of pick whatever, it’s not a World Cup squad. You’ve got a lot of available guys who are ready to go.” As Alyssa Healy put it on Fox Cricket: “It’s almost like they’ve underestimated themselves a little bit, the Bangladeshis. I mean, the whole of Australia probably did as well, but it’s almost like their humble approach has worked for them. We’ve got carried away with how big this summer is, but this is a wake-up call for Australia. Probably what they needed as well, after breezing through last summer.”



Nathan Lyon – In his first game back from hamstring surgery, 38-year-old Lyon was ineffective, certainly relative to the Bangladesh spinners, and also dropped a vital catch. There is no doubt Australia will need Lyon’s skills in India next year, but questions must be asked about whether he is an automatic selection, either ahead of Scott Boland or also the younger left-arm spinner Matt Kuhnemann. Meanwhile, Lyon needs to regain his ability to deceive batsmen in the air – Bangladesh had few problems reading his length here, despite a helpful breeze at times. Editor's pick Updated

Australian cricket Cummins flags batting changes after Australia’s bubble burst by Bangladesh Cummins said of Boland: “With Scotty, we all know how good he is, so we’ll turn up in Mackay, have a look at the pitch and work out your best bowling group. But with someone like Scotty in the squad you’re always trying to find a way to fit him in, he’s that good.” Domestic pitches – Something an excellent Darwin surface exposed was how Bangladesh’s batters were better equipped to keep out good balls and bat time, a theme that runs well down the ranks into the Sheffield Shield. Partly this is because of a preponderance of grassy result pitches that make life difficult for batters and a little too easy for seamers.



A topic of conversation at a recent Cricket Australia summit in Brisbane, it’s an issue that Head has highlighted the difficulty of: “You can sit outside and say we want a great balance between bat and ball, but if you ask the states and the boards and who runs the show, they’ll say we want to win Shields, so I don’t think they’d care less on what it looks like, they want performance and they want to win.” Talent pipeline – A major reason Australia are fielding their oldest ever Test team is a high level of selection scepticism about the younger talent coming through, something backed up by modest Shield aggregates in recent summers. Australian coach Andrew McDonald and Josh Hazlewood. Getty Images Based on those figures, there is no-one better available, but it will be up to the selectors to make some calculated gambles that go beyond pure statistics. Bangladesh provided a good reminder of that by how 25-year-old Tanzid Hasan (first-class batting average 39) and 26-year-old Hasan Mahmud (bowling average 28) seized their opportunities. Succession plan – Australia’s huge allotment of Tests over the next 12 months leaves open the question of whether the current regime will change out of exhaustion as much as anything else next year. But the conversations need to start now, and in some cases they already have. Head coach Andrew McDonald’s deal expires at the end of 2027, while Cummins’ captaincy tenure is also of uncertain duration. It may be easier to replace McDonald with one of Ryan Harris, Adam Voges or Tim Paine, but it is also a concern that Cummins’ stand-in remains the 37-year-old Steve Smith, whose career has operated on a series by series basis for several years.

World.title: Latrell ‘a chance’ to make long-awaited return; no Red V lifeline for Sloan
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Latrell ‘a chance’ to make long-awaited return; no Red V lifeline for Sloan Christian Nicolussi Updated August 17, 2026 — 5:48pm ,first published 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Latrell Mitchell could make a long-awaited return for South Sydney this weekend, with coach Wayne Bennett admitting: “He’s a chance. He’ll still have to get through a couple of training sessions, but he’s some chance.” Bennett said last week Mitchell was likely to be held back for the penultimate week of the season – a round-26 clash against the Gold Coast Titans – but welcomed the prospect of having Mitchell back a week earlier, especially if his body could cope with a few opposed sessions. Latrell Mitchell could make his long-awaited return from injury against the Warriors on Saturday. Steven Siewert Mitchell’s season looked over a few weeks ago, but he again trained away from the group on a soggy Monday morning as he overcomes a nerve issue in his lower back, which is causing problems down his leg and calf. The 29-year-old injured his back in an outstanding individual performance against Newcastle in round nine, then missed a week before aggravating it against the Dolphins during Magic Round. He hasn’t played since.



Should Mitchell’s name be included on the team sheet on Tuesday, Bennett hinted he was unlikely to start, and would be eased into the game off the bench. Tallis Duncan has been playing at left centre in Mitchell’s absence, but is even more effective in the back row, which he will do when Mitchell returns. Latrell Mitchell stretches out at a wet Heffron Park on Monday morning. Steven Siewert South Sydney need to win one of their remaining three games to cement a spot in the finals, and having a player such as Mitchell available would be a huge boost. The Rabbitohs host the high-flying New Zealand Warriors on Saturday at Accor Stadium, the Sydney Olympic Park venue where they have not lost a game this season.



“I don’t know how far off he [Mitchell] is – the physios have a better understanding of that – but he was out there today doing strides … he’s a step closer again,” outside back Campbell Graham said on Monday. South Sydney are looking to continue their unbeaten run at Accor Stadium against the Warriors this weekend. Steven Siewert “Whenever he’s ready to go, we’ll more than welcome him back. We need to keep building as a group; we want to be a well-oiled machine by the time he’s back so he can come in and do his thing. “He’s handled this situation well. And I’ve been there before where there’s no definite light at the end of the tunnel in terms of when you’ll be playing again. It’s a tough spot to be in. “But he’s full of energy, comes in every day smiling, and he’s great to have around the place.”



Graham played his “veteran’s card” to join the rehab group on Monday as part of “load management” to avoid any fresh calf injuries. “I was stoked to get through the game last Friday,” he said. “I’m not out of the woods just yet, and I still have to manage my training loads.” No Red V lifeline as Sloan seeks Super League answers Dragons flyer Tyrell Sloan says he has been “left in the dark” about the future of Castleford coach Ryan Carr, as St George Illawarra rule out extending an NRL lifeline to him and teammates Damien Cook and Mat Feagai if they look to back out of their Super League deals. Sloan conceded after the Dragons’ two-point win over Wests Tigers on Sunday that he has had second thoughts about his move to Castleford given the uncertainty around Carr’s position. Carr was a key reason Sloan signed a two-year deal with the club last month.



Carr, who coached Sloan as an assistant and interim head coach at the Dragons, has been absent from Castleford for the past two weeks after the club launched an investigation into the 38-year-old with little detail or public explanation as to why. Castleford head of football Chris Chester has spoken to the Dragons trio and told them they remain in the club’s plans for next season regardless of Carr’s situation. Loading St George Illawarra have moved on in their roster planning for 2027 and have privately conveyed that they do not have room for Sloan, Cook and Feagai in their salary cap after a significant recruitment and retention spree. “It definitely puts a big dent in things for me, I’ll be honest,” Sloan said. “Carry was a big reason why I signed over there.



“Obviously we had a relationship here at the Dragons and I don’t really know the situation with him. We’ve been left in the dark. “I’m really excited to go over there if Carry is there, but I just don’t know if that’s going to be the case there. Hopefully I’ll find out soon what’s going on and they make a decision. Dragons flyer Tyrell Sloan. Getty Images “I have thought about [trying to stay in the NRL], but I also have to keep playing good footy here to finish the season on a high.” Sloan, 24, has been playing with a new lease on life since Dean Young took charge of the Dragons, scoring eight tries in his past eight games.



His time under predecessor Shane Flanagan was far less consistent with several demotions to reserve grade, and 18 months ago he was given permission to explore an early exit from the joint-venture. Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 Twelve months ago, the Knights were heading for the wooden spoon. Holbrook must be coach of the year Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist Immortal Andrew Johns has argued Sloan is “too good a player to be leaving the NRL at this age”, but the Indigenous All Stars representative acknowledged his form in previous years hadn’t left him with many options. “I didn’t really have much [many options] in the NRL, and nothing really made sense, you know, to play in another jersey in the NRL,” Sloan said. “But Joey’s always been really good to me since I came into first grade and to be getting a fair rap from someone who has done everything in the game, I hold that in such respect. At the moment, I’ve got the Super League deal and at the end of it, I’ll only be 26. I’ve been in first grade since I was 18 so no matter what happens, I’d say I’ve got a lot of NRL left in me.”

World.title: ASX dips as banks and retail stocks drag
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX dips as banks and retail stocks drag Adrian Black Updated August 17, 2026 — 5:42pm ,first published August 17, 2026 — 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia’s sharemarket has started the week on the back foot as investor concerns about the economic outlook weigh on banks and consumer discretionary stocks. The S&P/ASX200 fell 42 points on Monday, down 0.46 per cent to 9073.2, as the broader All Ordinaries lost 34.2 points, or 0.37 per cent, to 9279. The ASX 200 fell 0.46 per cent on Monday, with JB Hi-Fi plunging. Getty Images Energy and raw materials were the only sectors to end the session convincingly higher as commodity prices advanced, while banks and consumer cyclical stocks dragged the exchange lower. In a worrying sign for the retail sector, consumer discretionary stocks fell 3 per cent after shares in segment bellwether JB Hi-Fi plunged more than 12 per cent.



The sell-off came despite a decent annual profit result and record group sales of $11.1 billion, as trading at its Australian flagship stores and The Good Guys dipped. Related Article Opinion

Big four Betting against the bank. ‘Widow-maker’ trades are making a comeback Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor With cost pressures, high interest rates and an uncertain outlook continuing to weigh on household spending, investors have set a high bar for local retailers. The macroeconomic gloom continued to weigh on the heavyweight financials sector, which has tumbled more than six per cent after spiking at an all-time high barely 10 days ago. NAB led the big four banks lower with a 4.6 per cent slump to $39.46 a share, after its third-quarter $1.8 billion cash profit was delivered alongside grim housing market forecasts.



Non-energy miners outperformed the market, up 1.8 per cent as BHP advanced ahead of its full-year results on Tuesday, helped by an upswing in the copper price. Gold miners were particularly strong as the precious metal edged higher to $US4395 ($A6177) an ounce, and battery minerals producers traded higher as lithium continued to rebound. Energy stocks gained 0.9 per cent, with strong leads from coal miners and uranium producers as refinery operators edged lower and Brent crude consolidated near $US82 a barrel. In other earnings news, Lendlease shares dived by more than 11 per cent after the real estate group swung to its fourth annual loss in five years as write-downs from its messy global retreat continued to hit its bottom line. Rail freight operator Aurizon fell a similar amount despite lifting its full-year profit by 24 per cent to $463 million.



Looking ahead, BHP, CSL and Cochlear will report on Tuesday, followed by Santos, Evolution, Temple & Webster, Whitehaven Coal and Mirvac on Wednesday, with July employment figures on Thursday. Related Article Energy Renewables are slashing power prices, but energy chiefs fear it may not last The Australian dollar was trading at its highest price in 11 weeks on Monday afternoon, buying US71.22¢, up from US70.68¢ on Friday at 5pm AEST. On Friday on Wall Street, the S&P 500 slipped 0.2 per cent from its record set the day before. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 107 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.3 per cent. Also raising uncertainty was a report showing that shoppers spent less at US retailers last month than the month before. That surprised economists, who were forecasting another month of growth.



On the bright side for financial markets, such a pullback in spending could take pressure off inflation. Inflation remains much higher than anyone would like, but reports earlier this week suggested the pace of price increases is decelerating. If inflation keeps trending that way, it could encourage the Federal Reserve to hold off on raising interest rates. Higher rates would help keep a lid on inflation, but they do so by intentionally slowing the economy and making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money. The downside of such data, including last week’s surprisingly weak report on the US jobs market, is that they raise the risk of a slowing economy. The Fed has no good tool to fix both a stagnating economy and high inflation at the same time, which is why what’s called “stagflation” is seen as a worst-case scenario. Some on Wall Street cautioned against overreacting to the weak data on US retail sales, even if it was broad-based. It could simply be a snap back after retail sales in earlier months were boosted by unusual factors such as big tax refunds, the World Cup and even an earlier Prime Day event at Amazon, said Jennifer Timmerman, senior investment strategy analyst at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. World.title: Blues make it official: Fraser to be announced as Carlton coach
World.content:
Josh Fraser will be confirmed as Carlton’s new senior coach on Tuesday. The Carlton board met on Monday to ratify the recommendation that Fraser be confirmed as coach and two sources with knowledge of the appointment confirmed to this masthead that he would be announced as the person to replace Michael Voss. Happy days: Josh Fraser will be Carlton’s new permanent senior coach. Getty Images Former VFL coach Fraser, who was appointed as caretaker when Voss departed in May, has overseen a stunning transformation of the team, winning 10 games and drawing another from 13 matches in charge. Final details of the length of his contract were being finalised, but a source with knowledge of the situation said it was likely to be a three-year deal.



Blues powerbroker Bruce Mathieson said Fraser had shown he can coach at the elite level. “It’s a great appointment for Carlton. He has them back on track and he will do a great job,” he said. The appointment comes less than 24 hours after the Blues capped their incredible in-season turnaround by locking in a wildcard spot with a draw against the Bulldogs. The Blues had one win from nine matches when Fraser, 44, took over in May. The deadlock at Marvel Stadium on Sunday means Carlton have 10 wins and a draw from 13 matches with the former Collingwood and Gold Coast ruckman in the coaches’ box.



Fraser was asked after Sunday’s dramatic draw how long he had wanted to put his hand up for the position. “It’s been crystallising in my mind that I wanted to go through the process, and the club approached me to see if I would be part of that,” he said. View post on X “That timeline got pushed out a little bit, and then things happened pretty quickly around committing to going through the process and then presenting. “But for me, it wasn’t like I was putting a presentation together in two days. This is a work in progress for anyone who wants to be a senior coach.”



Fraser was asked if the players were down on confidence when he took the reins. “I think when you’re not getting results, you need to scratch the surface around why,” he replied. Related Article Four Points

AFL 2026 The AFL’s quirky rule exposed amid frenzy of Saturday night’s draw “But the culture internally, I’ve felt, has been quite strong. Sometimes, when you’re not getting results, it’s hard to know a different way. “But again, they had an identity that was attached to contests and stoppage, which held us in good stead, and we just wanted to build that out. And we’ve done that to a point.



“But again, I can’t stress [enough], there’s so much work in front of this group, and that’s not to diminish the work that’s been done. That’s just the understanding that the competition moves quickly. “I think it’s pretty close, but we’ve still got to find the best version of ourselves that’s a consistent product on-field, and we’re working towards that.” Fraser had initially insisted that he did not want the job full-time. But that stance changed recently. Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 No Joshing: The AFL’s second draw in 24 hours confirms Carlton’s stunning run to finals spot He overcame a field that included Jaymie Graham, Corey Enright, James Kelly and Daniel Giansiracusa.



Fraser confirmed last week he had accepted an approach to be included in the process. “A fortnight ago, the club came to me and asked me to be a part of this coaching process,” Fraser said. “Then this week, I was in a position to go back to the club and accept that offer to go through the process.” In May, the former Collingwood ruckman and long-time development coach said he was unsure if he would apply for the role. “I’m ambitious, and I want to be a senior coach at some point. As we stand here right now, I probably don’t think I’m quite ready,” Fraser said after first taking over.



“But what this opportunity does give me is a chance to jump in the driver’s seat, learn a lot about myself, and hopefully at the end of it be better placed. I’m focused on how we collectively move this club forward. “This is not my job. I’m an interim coach, but I’ve got a job to do, and that is help the club.” The Blues will face Fremantle on Saturday in the final home-and-away game of the season before their wildcard clash the following weekend. Fraser will become the fourth senior coach at Carlton since AFL coaching games record holder Mick Malthouse finished in 2015. Brendon Bolton, David Teague and Voss have followed Malthouse.

World.title: James Packer’s bets on AI pay off after sell-down in gaming shares
World.content:
Exclusive BusinessCompaniesJames Packer James Packer’s bets on AI pay off after sell-down in gaming shares Kishor Napier-Raman August 17, 2026 — 6:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Billionaire James Packer has shifted his investment focus from gaming back to artificial intelligence, with his stake in computer chip manufacturer Nvidia now worth almost US$300 million ($422 million). Filings with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission made last week by a Cayman Islands-based holding company controlled by Packer show that the former Crown owner increased his holdings in Nvidia to 1.5 million shares in the March quarter of 2026. Billionaire businessman James Packer has shifted his investment strategy towards artificial intelligence. Seven News That stake rose in value to $US296 million ($417 million) in the quarter ending June 30, a 14 per cent increase in value. Nvidia, which manufactures specialised computer chips used by artificial intelligence companies, has soared thanks to the boom in that technology. With a market capitalisation of $US5.45 trillion ($7.67 trillion), it is the world’s most valuable public company, a crown it briefly lost to Apple last month. Packer has consistently shuffled his American portfolio through a tangled thicket of companies linked to his private investment vehicle, Consolidated Press Holdings, making it difficult to track its true value. However, recent filings show he has made a major bet on the technology.



Palidye Holdings (Caymans) Ltd, which holds the Nvidia shares, and also has a $US121 million stake in Facebook owner Meta Platforms and a $US115 million position in Microsoft. Palidye reports to the SEC on behalf of Consolidated Press International Ltd, another of Packer’s companies. Under the US regulator’s rules, a single investment manager can file quarterly reports on behalf of another where the two entities share investment discretion or have a parent-subsidiary relationship. Palidye’s total portfolio is currently valued at $US558 million. The company also has shares in Reddit, Afterpay owner Block, and e-commerce platform Shopify. Packer’s latest investments also reflect a shift in focus away from gaming and back towards artificial intelligence over the past year. A year ago, his company, Consolidated Press International Holdings, sold down its stake in Nvidia and bought 2.7 per cent of Las Vegas-based pokie machine manufacturer Light & Wonder, which is planning to move its listing from Wall Street’s Nasdaq to the ASX. He also bought a $US121 share in Flutter, the parent company of online bookmaker Sportsbet. Those purchases were Packer’s first foray back into gambling since he sold his shares in casino operator Crown Resorts to American private equity giant Blackstone for $3.3 billion in 2022. Packer’s exit from gaming came after a bruising series of state-based inquiries following allegations of money laundering at Crown casinos.



But recent filings indicate a pivot from gaming back to technology. The Light & Wonder stake, worth $US243 million as of last September, has been sold, as have his shares in Flutter. Palidye, the Caymans-based company, also sold a $US21 million stake in US sports betting company Penn Entertainment. It also bought shares in Las Vegas casino giant Wynn Resorts that was worth as much as $US147 million last year, which has since been sold. Related Article Weddings Billionaire James Packer weds former model in Italy In 2019, Wynn sought to engineer a takeover of Crown which would have given Packer a 10 per cent stake in the company. But Wynn pulled out of the deal after discussions were prematurely leaked to the media. Consolidated Press International made just two small purchases in the last quarter, buying circa $US1 million stakes in school bus manufacturer Blue Bird Corporation and nuclear energy start-up Deep Fission Inc. In several interviews, Packer has chalked down some of his recent investment strategy to the influence of Canadian-born Daniel Nadler, a billionaire artificial intelligence entrepreneur and poet.



“In truth, the only reason I’ve had some wins recently is because I’ve taken his [Nadler’s] advice,” he told The Daily Telegraph in 2024. Packer’s representatives were contacted for comment. In May, Consolidated Press Holdings settled a Federal Court lawsuit brought by former general counsel Catherine Davies, who departed last year after more than a decade. Packer was not a party to the lawsuit. Last week, the billionaire tied the knot for the third time, marrying Canadian model Kylie Lim on the Italian island of Sardinia. World.title: ‘We’ve got carried away’: The Australian Test team’s five biggest problems
World.content:
Analysis SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘We’ve got carried away’: The Australian Test team’s five biggest problems Daniel Brettig August 17, 2026 — 5:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Top order batting – Pat Cummins asked his batting order to get through a tricky first couple of hours on a fresh pitch in Darwin and they were completely unable to find a way to do so against a diligent but far from fearsome Bangladesh attack. Jake Weatherald’s perpetual motion at the crease speaks of technical tweaks but also nerves, and it is tough to see him keeping his place in Mackay. Marnus Labuschagne has already been dropped and recalled once in the past year, but is still struggling to find his best. Then there’s Travis Head and the question of his best position. Former opener Matthew Hayden was one seasoned voice to call for Matt Renshaw and Sam Konstas at the top, with Head moving to three. Ebadot Hossain of Bangladesh celebrates after taking the wicket of Marnus Labuschagne. Getty Images Tellingly, Cummins spoke not of a one-off problem but of a trend, meaning that the team’s batting difficulties will be the chief topic of internal conversation this week. He was also open about the selectors’ ability to make change: “Every Aussie Test we do you can kind of pick whatever, it’s not a World Cup squad. You’ve got a lot of available guys who are ready to go.” As Alyssa Healy put it on Fox Cricket: “It’s almost like they’ve underestimated themselves a little bit, the Bangladeshis. I mean, the whole of Australia probably did as well, but it’s almost like their humble approach has worked for them. We’ve got carried away with how big this summer is, but this is a wake-up call for Australia. Probably what they needed as well, after breezing through last summer.”



Nathan Lyon – In his first game back from hamstring surgery, 38-year-old Lyon was ineffective, certainly relative to the Bangladesh spinners, and also dropped a vital catch. There is no doubt Australia will need Lyon’s skills in India next year, but questions must be asked about whether he is an automatic selection, either ahead of Scott Boland or also the younger left-arm spinner Matt Kuhnemann. Meanwhile, Lyon needs to regain his ability to deceive batsmen in the air – Bangladesh had few problems reading his length here, despite a helpful breeze at times. Editor's pick Updated

Australian cricket Cummins flags batting changes after Australia’s bubble burst by Bangladesh Cummins said of Boland: “With Scotty, we all know how good he is, so we’ll turn up in Mackay, have a look at the pitch and work out your best bowling group. But with someone like Scotty in the squad you’re always trying to find a way to fit him in, he’s that good.” Domestic pitches – Something an excellent Darwin surface exposed was how Bangladesh’s batters were better equipped to keep out good balls and bat time, a theme that runs well down the ranks into the Sheffield Shield. Partly this is because of a preponderance of grassy result pitches that make life difficult for batters and a little too easy for seamers.



A topic of conversation at a recent Cricket Australia summit in Brisbane, it’s an issue that Head has highlighted the difficulty of: “You can sit outside and say we want a great balance between bat and ball, but if you ask the states and the boards and who runs the show, they’ll say we want to win Shields, so I don’t think they’d care less on what it looks like, they want performance and they want to win.” Talent pipeline – A major reason Australia are fielding their oldest ever Test team is a high level of selection scepticism about the younger talent coming through, something backed up by modest Shield aggregates in recent summers. Australian coach Andrew McDonald and Josh Hazlewood. Getty Images Based on those figures, there is no-one better available, but it will be up to the selectors to make some calculated gambles that go beyond pure statistics. Bangladesh provided a good reminder of that by how 25-year-old Tanzid Hasan (first-class batting average 39) and 26-year-old Hasan Mahmud (bowling average 28) seized their opportunities. Succession plan – Australia’s huge allotment of Tests over the next 12 months leaves open the question of whether the current regime will change out of exhaustion as much as anything else next year. But the conversations need to start now, and in some cases they already have. Head coach Andrew McDonald’s deal expires at the end of 2027, while Cummins’ captaincy tenure is also of uncertain duration. It may be easier to replace McDonald with one of Ryan Harris, Adam Voges or Tim Paine, but it is also a concern that Cummins’ stand-in remains the 37-year-old Steve Smith, whose career has operated on a series by series basis for several years.

World.title: Latrell ‘a chance’ to make long-awaited return; no Red V lifeline for Sloan
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Latrell ‘a chance’ to make long-awaited return; no Red V lifeline for Sloan Christian Nicolussi Updated August 17, 2026 — 5:48pm ,first published 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Latrell Mitchell could make a long-awaited return for South Sydney this weekend, with coach Wayne Bennett admitting: “He’s a chance. He’ll still have to get through a couple of training sessions, but he’s some chance.” Bennett said last week Mitchell was likely to be held back for the penultimate week of the season – a round-26 clash against the Gold Coast Titans – but welcomed the prospect of having Mitchell back a week earlier, especially if his body could cope with a few opposed sessions. Latrell Mitchell could make his long-awaited return from injury against the Warriors on Saturday. Steven Siewert Mitchell’s season looked over a few weeks ago, but he again trained away from the group on a soggy Monday morning as he overcomes a nerve issue in his lower back, which is causing problems down his leg and calf. The 29-year-old injured his back in an outstanding individual performance against Newcastle in round nine, then missed a week before aggravating it against the Dolphins during Magic Round. He hasn’t played since.



Should Mitchell’s name be included on the team sheet on Tuesday, Bennett hinted he was unlikely to start, and would be eased into the game off the bench. Tallis Duncan has been playing at left centre in Mitchell’s absence, but is even more effective in the back row, which he will do when Mitchell returns. Latrell Mitchell stretches out at a wet Heffron Park on Monday morning. Steven Siewert South Sydney need to win one of their remaining three games to cement a spot in the finals, and having a player such as Mitchell available would be a huge boost. The Rabbitohs host the high-flying New Zealand Warriors on Saturday at Accor Stadium, the Sydney Olympic Park venue where they have not lost a game this season.



“I don’t know how far off he [Mitchell] is – the physios have a better understanding of that – but he was out there today doing strides … he’s a step closer again,” outside back Campbell Graham said on Monday. South Sydney are looking to continue their unbeaten run at Accor Stadium against the Warriors this weekend. Steven Siewert “Whenever he’s ready to go, we’ll more than welcome him back. We need to keep building as a group; we want to be a well-oiled machine by the time he’s back so he can come in and do his thing. “He’s handled this situation well. And I’ve been there before where there’s no definite light at the end of the tunnel in terms of when you’ll be playing again. It’s a tough spot to be in. “But he’s full of energy, comes in every day smiling, and he’s great to have around the place.”



Graham played his “veteran’s card” to join the rehab group on Monday as part of “load management” to avoid any fresh calf injuries. “I was stoked to get through the game last Friday,” he said. “I’m not out of the woods just yet, and I still have to manage my training loads.” No Red V lifeline as Sloan seeks Super League answers Dragons flyer Tyrell Sloan says he has been “left in the dark” about the future of Castleford coach Ryan Carr, as St George Illawarra rule out extending an NRL lifeline to him and teammates Damien Cook and Mat Feagai if they look to back out of their Super League deals. Sloan conceded after the Dragons’ two-point win over Wests Tigers on Sunday that he has had second thoughts about his move to Castleford given the uncertainty around Carr’s position. Carr was a key reason Sloan signed a two-year deal with the club last month.



Carr, who coached Sloan as an assistant and interim head coach at the Dragons, has been absent from Castleford for the past two weeks after the club launched an investigation into the 38-year-old with little detail or public explanation as to why. Castleford head of football Chris Chester has spoken to the Dragons trio and told them they remain in the club’s plans for next season regardless of Carr’s situation. Loading St George Illawarra have moved on in their roster planning for 2027 and have privately conveyed that they do not have room for Sloan, Cook and Feagai in their salary cap after a significant recruitment and retention spree. “It definitely puts a big dent in things for me, I’ll be honest,” Sloan said. “Carry was a big reason why I signed over there.



“Obviously we had a relationship here at the Dragons and I don’t really know the situation with him. We’ve been left in the dark. “I’m really excited to go over there if Carry is there, but I just don’t know if that’s going to be the case there. Hopefully I’ll find out soon what’s going on and they make a decision. Dragons flyer Tyrell Sloan. Getty Images “I have thought about [trying to stay in the NRL], but I also have to keep playing good footy here to finish the season on a high.” Sloan, 24, has been playing with a new lease on life since Dean Young took charge of the Dragons, scoring eight tries in his past eight games.



His time under predecessor Shane Flanagan was far less consistent with several demotions to reserve grade, and 18 months ago he was given permission to explore an early exit from the joint-venture. Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 Twelve months ago, the Knights were heading for the wooden spoon. Holbrook must be coach of the year Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist Immortal Andrew Johns has argued Sloan is “too good a player to be leaving the NRL at this age”, but the Indigenous All Stars representative acknowledged his form in previous years hadn’t left him with many options. “I didn’t really have much [many options] in the NRL, and nothing really made sense, you know, to play in another jersey in the NRL,” Sloan said. “But Joey’s always been really good to me since I came into first grade and to be getting a fair rap from someone who has done everything in the game, I hold that in such respect. At the moment, I’ve got the Super League deal and at the end of it, I’ll only be 26. I’ve been in first grade since I was 18 so no matter what happens, I’d say I’ve got a lot of NRL left in me.”

World.title: ASX dips as banks and retail stocks drag
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX dips as banks and retail stocks drag Adrian Black Updated August 17, 2026 — 5:42pm ,first published August 17, 2026 — 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia’s sharemarket has started the week on the back foot as investor concerns about the economic outlook weigh on banks and consumer discretionary stocks. The S&P/ASX200 fell 42 points on Monday, down 0.46 per cent to 9073.2, as the broader All Ordinaries lost 34.2 points, or 0.37 per cent, to 9279. The ASX 200 fell 0.46 per cent on Monday, with JB Hi-Fi plunging. Getty Images Energy and raw materials were the only sectors to end the session convincingly higher as commodity prices advanced, while banks and consumer cyclical stocks dragged the exchange lower. In a worrying sign for the retail sector, consumer discretionary stocks fell 3 per cent after shares in segment bellwether JB Hi-Fi plunged more than 12 per cent.



The sell-off came despite a decent annual profit result and record group sales of $11.1 billion, as trading at its Australian flagship stores and The Good Guys dipped. Related Article Opinion

Big four Betting against the bank. ‘Widow-maker’ trades are making a comeback Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor With cost pressures, high interest rates and an uncertain outlook continuing to weigh on household spending, investors have set a high bar for local retailers. The macroeconomic gloom continued to weigh on the heavyweight financials sector, which has tumbled more than six per cent after spiking at an all-time high barely 10 days ago. NAB led the big four banks lower with a 4.6 per cent slump to $39.46 a share, after its third-quarter $1.8 billion cash profit was delivered alongside grim housing market forecasts.



Non-energy miners outperformed the market, up 1.8 per cent as BHP advanced ahead of its full-year results on Tuesday, helped by an upswing in the copper price. Gold miners were particularly strong as the precious metal edged higher to $US4395 ($A6177) an ounce, and battery minerals producers traded higher as lithium continued to rebound. Energy stocks gained 0.9 per cent, with strong leads from coal miners and uranium producers as refinery operators edged lower and Brent crude consolidated near $US82 a barrel. In other earnings news, Lendlease shares dived by more than 11 per cent after the real estate group swung to its fourth annual loss in five years as write-downs from its messy global retreat continued to hit its bottom line. Rail freight operator Aurizon fell a similar amount despite lifting its full-year profit by 24 per cent to $463 million.



Looking ahead, BHP, CSL and Cochlear will report on Tuesday, followed by Santos, Evolution, Temple & Webster, Whitehaven Coal and Mirvac on Wednesday, with July employment figures on Thursday. Related Article Energy Renewables are slashing power prices, but energy chiefs fear it may not last The Australian dollar was trading at its highest price in 11 weeks on Monday afternoon, buying US71.22¢, up from US70.68¢ on Friday at 5pm AEST. On Friday on Wall Street, the S&P 500 slipped 0.2 per cent from its record set the day before. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 107 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.3 per cent. Also raising uncertainty was a report showing that shoppers spent less at US retailers last month than the month before. That surprised economists, who were forecasting another month of growth.



On the bright side for financial markets, such a pullback in spending could take pressure off inflation. Inflation remains much higher than anyone would like, but reports earlier this week suggested the pace of price increases is decelerating. If inflation keeps trending that way, it could encourage the Federal Reserve to hold off on raising interest rates. Higher rates would help keep a lid on inflation, but they do so by intentionally slowing the economy and making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money. The downside of such data, including last week’s surprisingly weak report on the US jobs market, is that they raise the risk of a slowing economy. The Fed has no good tool to fix both a stagnating economy and high inflation at the same time, which is why what’s called “stagflation” is seen as a worst-case scenario. Some on Wall Street cautioned against overreacting to the weak data on US retail sales, even if it was broad-based. It could simply be a snap back after retail sales in earlier months were boosted by unusual factors such as big tax refunds, the World Cup and even an earlier Prime Day event at Amazon, said Jennifer Timmerman, senior investment strategy analyst at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. World.title: Blues make it official: Fraser to be announced as Carlton coach
World.content:
Josh Fraser will be confirmed as Carlton’s new senior coach on Tuesday. The Carlton board met on Monday to ratify the recommendation that Fraser be confirmed as coach and two sources with knowledge of the appointment confirmed to this masthead that he would be announced as the person to replace Michael Voss. Happy days: Josh Fraser will be Carlton’s new permanent senior coach. Getty Images Former VFL coach Fraser, who was appointed as caretaker when Voss departed in May, has overseen a stunning transformation of the team, winning 10 games and drawing another from 13 matches in charge. Final details of the length of his contract were being finalised, but a source with knowledge of the situation said it was likely to be a three-year deal.



Blues powerbroker Bruce Mathieson said Fraser had shown he can coach at the elite level. “It’s a great appointment for Carlton. He has them back on track and he will do a great job,” he said. The appointment comes less than 24 hours after the Blues capped their incredible in-season turnaround by locking in a wildcard spot with a draw against the Bulldogs. The Blues had one win from nine matches when Fraser, 44, took over in May. The deadlock at Marvel Stadium on Sunday means Carlton have 10 wins and a draw from 13 matches with the former Collingwood and Gold Coast ruckman in the coaches’ box.



Fraser was asked after Sunday’s dramatic draw how long he had wanted to put his hand up for the position. “It’s been crystallising in my mind that I wanted to go through the process, and the club approached me to see if I would be part of that,” he said. View post on X “That timeline got pushed out a little bit, and then things happened pretty quickly around committing to going through the process and then presenting. “But for me, it wasn’t like I was putting a presentation together in two days. This is a work in progress for anyone who wants to be a senior coach.”



Fraser was asked if the players were down on confidence when he took the reins. “I think when you’re not getting results, you need to scratch the surface around why,” he replied. Related Article Four Points

AFL 2026 The AFL’s quirky rule exposed amid frenzy of Saturday night’s draw “But the culture internally, I’ve felt, has been quite strong. Sometimes, when you’re not getting results, it’s hard to know a different way. “But again, they had an identity that was attached to contests and stoppage, which held us in good stead, and we just wanted to build that out. And we’ve done that to a point.



“But again, I can’t stress [enough], there’s so much work in front of this group, and that’s not to diminish the work that’s been done. That’s just the understanding that the competition moves quickly. “I think it’s pretty close, but we’ve still got to find the best version of ourselves that’s a consistent product on-field, and we’re working towards that.” Fraser had initially insisted that he did not want the job full-time. But that stance changed recently. Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 No Joshing: The AFL’s second draw in 24 hours confirms Carlton’s stunning run to finals spot He overcame a field that included Jaymie Graham, Corey Enright, James Kelly and Daniel Giansiracusa.



Fraser confirmed last week he had accepted an approach to be included in the process. “A fortnight ago, the club came to me and asked me to be a part of this coaching process,” Fraser said. “Then this week, I was in a position to go back to the club and accept that offer to go through the process.” In May, the former Collingwood ruckman and long-time development coach said he was unsure if he would apply for the role. “I’m ambitious, and I want to be a senior coach at some point. As we stand here right now, I probably don’t think I’m quite ready,” Fraser said after first taking over.



“But what this opportunity does give me is a chance to jump in the driver’s seat, learn a lot about myself, and hopefully at the end of it be better placed. I’m focused on how we collectively move this club forward. “This is not my job. I’m an interim coach, but I’ve got a job to do, and that is help the club.” The Blues will face Fremantle on Saturday in the final home-and-away game of the season before their wildcard clash the following weekend. Fraser will become the fourth senior coach at Carlton since AFL coaching games record holder Mick Malthouse finished in 2015. Brendon Bolton, David Teague and Voss have followed Malthouse.

World.title: Aurum extends gold resource potential with 80g/t hit in West Africa
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Aurum extends gold resource potential with 80g/t hit in West Africa Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Doug Bright August 17, 2026 — 5:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Aurum Resources has unearthed a swag of high-grade gold intercepts, including a stunning 3-metre hit grading an eye-watering 80.09 grams per tonne (g/t) gold, from drilling outside the existing combined resource envelope at its 3.22-million-ounce Boundiali project in West Africa. The results emerge from the company’s ongoing 100,000m diamond drilling program in Côte d’Ivoire, with assays from 46 holes also confirming a new zone of mineralisation at the until now thinly tested BST2 prospect in the southwest corner of Aurum’s extensive tenement suite, where it lies entirely outside the current combined mineral resource estimate. Extensive artisanal open pit gold workings attest to the prospectivity of Aurum Resources’ Boundiali gold project in Côte d’Ivoire, West Africa. The high-grade intercepts land at a moment when the global market remains buoyed by a strong gold price, after the precious metal touched record highs earlier in the year. Moreover, the results come as Côte d’Ivoire’s national gold output is projected to climb to 62 tonnes in 2026, highlighting the country’s favourable operating environment. Twenty kilometres southeast of BST2, drilling at the BST1 deposit, which already holds a 570,000-ounce resource, was designed to test for extensions and returned several impressive hits. The standout among these was a 3m intercept going 80.09g/t gold from just 66m downhole depth, which included an eye-watering 2m slice going 117.73g/t gold.



‘At the BST2 prospect...today’s results support further growth potential, although more drilling will be required.’ Aurum Resources managing director Dr Caigen Wang Other significant results from BST1 include a thick 38m section grading 4.20g/t gold from 65m around a 3m core at 30.52g/t gold. A separate hole returned 3.77m at 9.62g/t gold from 57.23m, including a rich 2.77m run assaying 12.75g/t gold. Perhaps more significantly for resource growth, drilling at the BST2 prospect, which currently has no defined resource, also delivered the goods. The best result was a 3m intercept grading a solid 27.65g/t gold from 144m, including a 1m section at a bonanza 78.13g/t gold. Another better hit at BST2 included 2m at 5.10g/t gold from 117m. Aurum says the results from BST2, formerly known as Gbemou, back up historical work that identified a 2km-long gold-in-soil anomaly at the prospect. Aurum Resources managing director Dr Caigen Wang said: “Our latest results from drilling at BST continue to de-risk and build our resource base for the Boundiali Gold Project. At BST1, new holes have intersected shallow high-grade mineralisation including 3m at 80.09g/t Au from 66m as well as confirming gold mineralisation in areas currently classified as Inferred. At the BST2 prospect, which sits entirely outside the current Mineral Resource, today’s results support further growth potential, although more drilling will be required before it can be classified.”



The company is in the middle of a massive 130,000m drilling program for the 2026 calendar year, with 100,000m allocated to Boundiali and 30,000m to its nearby 1.16-million-ounce Napié project. Combined, the two projects give Aurum a current group resource of 4.4 million ounces of gold. With 16 of its own diamond drill rigs busy on site and a healthy $54.7 million in cash as of June, the company appears well-funded to continue its aggressive exploration push. The latest assays will be fed into the next MRE update for Boundiali, targeted for the end of the third quarter this year. A definitive feasibility study for the project is expected to follow in late 2026. Aurum is clearly not resting on its laurels with its hefty 3.22-million-ounce Boundiali resource. The latest drilling proves there is still plenty of high-grade gold to be found around the margins of the known deposits. With bonanza hits extending the mineralisation at BST1 and a new high-grade zone emerging at the previously BST2 prospect, the upcoming resource update is shaping up to be significant.
