World.title: Off-grid stories during F1 mid-year break as racing returns
World.content:
Formula 1's mid-year hiatus ends this weekend, as the racing series returns to action with the Dutch Grand Prix in Zandvoort.

The five-week break has given drivers and teams a chance to refresh ahead of a long and gruelling run to the finish line, with the drivers' and constructors' championships well and truly alive in 2026.

While there has been no action on the track, there has been news off it during the break.

Ahead of this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix, here are a few stories you may have missed during the hiatus.

1. No contract announcements

The first news is no news.

Drivers off contract at the end of 2026 Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes

George Russell, Mercedes

Isack Hadjar, Red Bull

Carlos Sainz, Williams

Alex Albon, Williams

Liam Lawson, Racing Bulls

Arvid Lindblad, Racing Bulls

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin

Lance Stroll, Aston Martin

Oliver Bearman, Haas

Esteban Ocon, Haas

Nick Hulkenberg, Audi

Gabriel Bortoleto, Audi

Franco Colapinto, Alpine

The mid-year break usually signals the start of F1's silly season, where teams and drivers formalise contracts for future seasons.

The 2026 silly season is set to be busy, with as many as 14 drivers off contract at the end of this year.

And there are big names who are yet to finalise deals for 2027 and beyond, including Mercedes drivers' championship leader Kimi Antonelli, and two-time world champion Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin).

There has also been wild speculation of a potential driver swap between McLaren and Red Bull, with Australia's Oscar Piastri and four-time world champion Max Verstappen changing teams as early as next year.

But, thus far, there have been no announcements.

This will change in the near future, and just because no contracts have been announced does not mean no work behind the scenes.

2. Piastri confident McLaren can 'make that step' back to the top

After the highs of the previous two seasons, McLaren's 2026 campaign has resembled more of a yo-yo.

McLaren have won the previous two constructors' championships, while Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri both won seven grands prix last year, a campaign where Norris became drivers' world champion.

Piastri blasts 'f***ing stupid' backmarker, Norris wins Hungarian GP Oscar Piastri retired from the Formula 1 Hungarian Grand Prix, won by his teammate Lando Norris, but not before he blasted a "stupid" backmarker and slammed his team for a poor strategy at the Hungaroring.

But in 2026, with a new era of regulations, McLaren has had mixed results.

It started the season poorly, with Oscar Piastri failing to start the opening two grands prix of the season (Australia and China), while Norris also failed to start the Chinese Grand Prix.

Both drivers have been plagued by reliability issues, but have also produced promising results.

Piastri has twice finished on the podium (Japan and Miami), while Norris won the Hungarian Grand Prix — a race Piastri led before being hit by a backmarker and then suffering an issue that forced his retirement.

Despite not being in the championship picture thus far in 2026, Piastri is confident McLaren will return.

In an interview with the team during the break, Piastri cited McLaren's early struggles in 2023 before their rise up the grid to become back-to-back champions.

"When you look at the previous experience of what we've been able to achieve as a team, and how we've been able to make progress through the year, it's good," the Australian said.

"In 2023, we were in a much worse position than where we are now, and we were able to really jump up the order to fight for podiums.

"The way that Lando and I worked together during that period to try and focus on making the car quick, so that we could then fight for the results that we wanted, hasn't changed. It's still strong, with productive conversations together with the team — we are all pushing toward the same goal.

"I feel like for me I've already seen it play out more than once. I think that's a real strength of the team. Yes, things are different, the cars are different, maybe the way we will make that step will look different. But we've made that step before, and I'm confident we can do it again."

3. Bahrain Grand Prix back on calendar, in Malaysia

While the official mid-year break is coming to an end, F1 had an unofficial hiatus earlier this year when the Bahrain and Saudi Arabia weekends were called off due to unrest in the Middle East.

That left an unexpected gap between the Japanese Grand Prix and Miami Grand Prix weekends, with F1 holding onto hope that they would be able to bring those races back onto the calendar.

Well, they have brought one back, in a different country.

The Bahrain Grand Prix will be held in 2026, but thousands of kilometres away in Malaysia.

Sepang International Circuit will host the event from October 2-4, between the grand prix weekends in Azerbaijan and Singapore.

F1 is no stranger to Sepang, first racing there in 1999, while the last F1 race held there in 2017 was won by Max Verstappen.

"We are delighted to confirm that Malaysia will host the Bahrain Grand Prix in 2026. Once again, the sport has demonstrated its ability to adapt, find solutions, and deliver, creating an exciting moment for everyone who follows Formula 1," F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali said.

4. Cadillac has a team principal change

While there was no change in the driver market, F1's newest team made a change on the pit wall.

Cadillac announced Marcin Budkowski would become the American squad's new team principal, replacing Graeme Lowdon.

Lowdon was the team principal from 2024 and an instrumental figure in preparing Cadillac for its debut season in 2026.

Budkowski has been around F1 for many years, and was once the executive director at French outfit Alpine.

"Marcin's appointment marks another important step in the continued evolution of the Cadillac Formula 1 Team," said Dan Towriss, CEO of the Cadillac team.

"As we enter this new era for the Cadillac Formula 1 Team, Marcin brings exceptional F1 experience, technical expertise and strategic leadership that will strengthen our organisation and help us develop the winning mindset, tools and processes required for long-term success.

"We're grateful to Graeme Lowdon for his leadership and the role he played in forming the Cadillac Formula 1 Team from the ground up. His contributions helped establish a strong foundation in our build-up phase, and we thank him for his commitment and wish him well."

World.title: Shock defeat to Bangladesh reveals bigger picture hiding in plain sight
World.content:
You could pick a handful of moments during the first Test at Marrara Oval in Darwin where it was clear not everything was as it seemed on surface level.

On day two, Marnus Labuschagne sprinted off with his usual exuberance from the infield to chase down a shot that trickled towards the boundary.

The immaculately manicured outfield, offering a playing surface that was nigh on pristine, had already been praised for its lawn-like quality.

Mark Waugh on Fox Sports noted you could probably play bowls or tennis on it.

Yet as soon as Labuschagne slid for the ball, the ugly truth was revealed, as a huge clump of turf was ripped up in a heaped mass of mud and grass and injury potential.

This was a pattern repeated throughout the match: The outfield's undoubted beauty was only surface deep.

Australia's standing at the top of the Test match rankings may only be surface deep, as deep fissures have been revealed in Darwin. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

An analogy to what transpired over the next four days, as the number nine-ranked Test team that were missing two of their best bowlers, thumped the world number one side at full strength on their own turf, could not have been clearer.

Bangladesh's stunning victory in Darwin has delivered Australian cricket the shock that it undoubtedly needed.

A team that arrived without fanfare or pedigree has slapped down the world's number one Test playing nation by playing simple, sensible Test cricket.

The bowling was slow but accurate. The batting, unspectacular but patient and disciplined.

The Tigers' attitude was exceptional.

As the growth of the big three has accelerated inequalities between the haves and have-nots of Test cricket, Bangladesh are one of those teams that have been left firmly on the outer, yet proved in Darwin that the paucity of opportunities that have come their way has in no way blunted their potency or hunger for success within the format.

They were here to play Test cricket and play it well.

Najmul Hossain Shanto led his team with skill and composure throughout. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

Given it had been 23 years since they last played a Test on Australian soil, their commitment to playing such an impressive style against a country that has snubbed them for so long was more than admirable.

Credit for that has to go to coach Phil Simmons and unflappable skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto.

Shanto made correct decision after correct decision on the pitch, Bangladesh never succumbing to the pressure or enormity of what was transpiring around them right up until Mominul Haque crushed Beau Webster through the covers to seal victory, a simple hug between the two not out batters sufficing as the bench finally exploded in joy on the boundary.

Bangladesh's historic win deserves all the praise that will undoubtedly be heaped upon it, the context of which will forever be extraordinary.

Bangladesh held their nerve throughout a tense contest. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Legendary English cricket writer Neville Cardus once wrote that to properly consider Test cricket, you need to see the big picture.

"I wish to present the Test matches in their setting," he wrote in the introduction to his book chronicling the 1936/37 Ashes series.

"To me cricket must be put against a background."

So what is the background here for Australia?

Australia is about to embark on as busy a Test match year as they have ever had, playing as many as 20 Tests in the next 12 months.

From the Top End, the men's Test team will head to South Africa, play New Zealand and England at home, then face overseas tours to India and England for the Ashes in 2027.

It is a demanding schedule both as physically gruelling and mentally taxing as they come.

Steve Smith and Australia have a lot of thinking to do ahead of the next Test. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

Starting off with a two-Test series against Bangladesh, a country Australia has only deigned to host once before for a Test series and only played against in red ball cricket six times in total before this week was considered by most to be a friendly warm up, a competitive practice during a winter sojourn in the Top End sun.

It is, of course, incredibly admirable Cricket Australia is taking Test matches to regions that cannot ever hope to host an Ashes contest.

For financial reasons as much as from a societal responsibility, playing these sorts of Tests in this continent's more remote, northern reaches is undoubtedly the right thing to do.

But maybe there is a sense that this is considered a form of benevolence to the lesser-populated areas of the nation.

Perhaps, for some, even playing Bangladesh is a form of charity to a nation that simply does not have the financial pull of the major nations, little more than an obligation to the World Test Championship.

Maybe, despite protestations to the contrary, that attitude sneaks into the minds of the players, so subliminally that they themselves do not even notice it.

Pat Cummins defended the team's preparation, but perhaps they didn't even realise they were underdone. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

For how can playing in front of about 5,000 spectators in a venue where only half the oval is bordered by a grandstand compare with the cathedral-like cavernous majesty of the MCG, or the lack of pressure contrast with the parochial furnace of a packed Gabba?

Marrara Oval offers neither the stately splendour of the Adelaide Oval or SCG, nor the admittedly under-populated grandiosity of the new Perth Stadium.

Darwin is definitively off-Broadway.

And although Australia's defeat didn't seem to be for lack of effort, the application and necessary quality was lacking throughout the match.

Horror drops from Steve Smith and Nathan Lyon were surely aberrations, but the lazy stroke play and jittery, muddled thinking of the batters was very not.

Steve Smith was not his usual best in the field. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

This shock to a team that has been creaking under the weight of their own success for a number of years now is one that has probably arrived eight months too late.

It was due last summer against England before those Bazballers tripped up over their own hubris.

A papering of the cracks was the result of that emphatic 4-1 Ashes victory, the foundations of sand upon which the top order was built were never tested, the supposedly seismic impact of a fired up England bowling attack never coming to bare, self-sabotaging itself amidst a storm of recriminations in the boozy sand of Noosa.

So on we continued. Australia's brittle batters went off to earn their coin in meaningly limited overs matches and failed to address the issues that have plagued them in red ball cricket, perhaps even accentuating the problems by promoting angled bats and rash shots.

Now the show moves to Mackay and presents Australia with an ever-bigger list of questions and problems to face.

Jake Weatherald's status as opener has to be looked at. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Australia were rusty and not up to speed in Darwin.

Even if Mackay's Harrup Park, the newest venue to host a men's Test in Australia, provides a suitably refreshed outlook and attitude from Australia next Saturday, will victory there do anything else other than to plaster even more paper over gaps that are swiftly turning into chasms?

It's been eight years since a rambunctious tour almost boiled over, a sorry spectacle that was quickly overshadowed by a sandpaper-scraping that was barely as coarse as the friction generated by two teams flirting on the edge of respectability throughout.

Any weakness in Australia's psyche will be ripe for exploitation in southern Africa, and the venom is unlikely to be as hidden as it was in the far north of Australia.

World.title: Quick hits: Das's redemption and Mehid's Messi attempt
World.content:
Litton Das was wrong-footed behind the stumps, and Mehidy Hasan Miraz suffered a worse fate in front of them, as Mitch Starc's desperate review spoke volumes and Cameron Green's redemptive arc proved to be in vain.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the first Test, as Bangladesh claimed a stunning victory, their first ever in a Test on Australian soil.

1. Das's day four redemption

Das made amends after missing a chance early on day four. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Australia began the day still 67 runs in arrears, knowing that any early slip-ups could prove fatal to their hopes of pulling off an unlikely escape.

So, Alex Carey's heart was surely in his mouth as the excellent Hasan Mahmud had him edging during the fourth over of the day.

It was a tough chance, but one experienced Bangladeshi wicketkeeper Litton Das would have been hopeful of gobbling up.

Das was too slow to react, and the ball flew past his outstretched left glove and to the boundary.

But Carey was unable to profit from that early slice of fortune, finding himself walking back to the pavilion just three overs later.

This time, Das made no mistake with what, probably, was a more difficult chance, with Carey feathering one through off the bowling of spinner Mehidy Hasan Miraz.

It was a superb delivery from Mehidy, pitching and gripping and turning away from the Australian wicketkeeper.

Das had his redemption and Bangladesh was on its way.

2. Webster falls to a beauty

Mehidy produced a peach to dismiss Webster. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Spin bowling is an art form built on deception, with guile and sleight of hand as important as pin-point accuracy.

On a pitch offering few surprises and only the minimum of turn, it is the impetus of a genuine spinner to trick their way into the minds of their rivals.

Beau Webster had played sensibly through the first 20 balls of his innings, alert to the threat of Mehidy Hasan Miraz's off spinners.

Mehidy was probing at the off stump of Webster, but the ball that deceived him was simply wonderful.

Angling the ball so that the seam would not bite, Mehidy just pushed the ball through a couple of kilometres per hour faster than the balls before.

With no seam to grip, the ball skidded on, perhaps a little lower, and took the top of his off stump.

A master magician couldn't have disguised his intents better and Australia's tail was exposed.

3. Starc's desperate review

Australia began the second session with a 15-run lead and just three wickets in hand, requiring something very special from both Cam Green and Mitch Starc.

So, when Starc nicked off in the third over after lunch, the final nail was well and truly closing in on the Australian coffin.

There was a clear noise and a dramatic deviation, but Starc, well aware of the value of his wicket, decided to send the call upstairs.

Unlike Steve Smith on day three, who had so defiantly called for a review even before Kumar Dharmasena had raised his finger, Starc questioned this decision with embarrassment.

He began his walk from the middle with the review still underway.

There were no ghosts in the machine, no undetected front foot no ball, and Australia was in touching distance of a chastening defeat.

4. Mehidy's footwork lets him down

Given the magic that had been cascading from Mehidy's right hand all day, you wouldn't have put it past the off spinner from doing something special with his foot.

But Mehidy was more messy than Messi when presented with opportunity.

Nathan Lyon, new to crease, was slow to take off for a single, and there was a real chance of a run out, with a Bangladeshi fielder circling in the infield.

But the throw was off target, and Mehidy was forced to improvise, attempting to sidefoot the wayward effort towards the pegs.

Instead, the ball thudded into his ankle and fell limply to earth, Mehidy wincing as he returned to his mark.

It looked like a really painful one, but, thankfully, he was right to continue.

5. Green's drought-breaking ton

Cameron Green scored his first Test century since February 2024. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Having not passed 50 in his previous 13 Test innings, Cameron Green's position in the side was very much a topic of conversation heading into this Test.

A jittery run-a-ball 13 in the first innings would have done little but amplify those calls for him to be replaced.

But on days three and four at Marrara, Green delivered everything that he has promised, a third Test century and first on home soil.

There was some luck, Green didn't look good last night and was delivered some divine intervention when an inside edge onto his leg stump didn't produce a wicket, the bail held in place by some benevolent force far in excess of that provided by mere gravity.

But since that fortuitous slice of relief, Green made hay, playing the ball teasingly late from under his eyes, and with the balance and poise of a man who deserves to be batting in Test cricket.

It was his first Test century since he scored 174 not out against New Zealand in Wellington back in February 2024.

Tech.title: I’m hooked on Peak Design’s new City bags
Tech.content:
is a deputy editor and Verge co-founder with a passion for human-centric cities, e-bikes, and life as a digital nomad. He’s been a tech journalist for 20 years.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

It’s just a hook, sewn into a bag, but I really, really like it. Peak Design is so proud of its clever integration that the San Francisco-based maker of camera gear gave it a name: BagLev, for its ability to keep its new City Line of bags levitated above the dirty ground.

How many of us are guilty of coming home and tossing a bag onto the kitchen table or counter to unload it? We pretend it’s not a thing, despite the carryall having come into contact with unknown filth picked up from the floors of subways and dive bars, sidewalks, and parks. BagLev lets you hang your bag off a chair, ledge, tabletop, or counter as you go about your day, keeping it mostly free of urban gunge.

The BagLev hook deployed at a cafe.

I’ve been testing Peak Design’s innovative little nonslip hook in a pair of bags while vanlifing through France. After a few weeks, it’s the 12-liter City Crescent ($119.95) crossbody bag I grab to casually explore villages, opting for the 15L City Backpack ($179.95) when heading out with my laptop for some truly remote work. In either case, the BagLev hook keeps Peak Design’s lightweight and water-resistant fabric clean when hanging above cafe and forest floors. And what dirt does collect on the nearly white “Moon” fabric has been easily wiped away with a damp cloth.

As silly as it might sound, Peak Design’s BagLev hook that comes with every new City Line bag is so useful that it’s changed my expectation of an everyday carry, making my other, hookless bags suddenly feel dirty and less capable.

While Peak Design might be best known for its camera bags, its new City Line targets the casual urbanite, not photogs. The backpack and crossbody bag both make compelling arguments to be your daily carry even if we ignore the inclusion of the BagLev hook. They offer clean, not-too-slouchy silhouettes constructed of a lightweight, rain-shedding Mono Shell 660D fabric that looks equally at home in trendy coffee joints or casual business settings. Each bag features thoughtful flourishes like zippers with large, easy-to-grab pulls, a key tether, and a place to hide a tracker like an Apple AirTag or new Pixel Tag. But it’s the hook that’s the hook, and the reason you might want to buy these bags.

This end pocket on the City Crescent easily fits a water bottle. That same pocket can also be accessed from the zippered main compartment. This quick access pocket seals with magnets, making it useful for frequently needed items like glasses or a phone. The shoulder strap is easy to adjust but lacks padding.

I like to carry the highly versatile City Crescent crossbody bag with the BagLev dangling behind me. I don’t bother putting it back into its zippered pocket anymore, because that’s where I store my keys. In this orientation, I have access to a zippered pocket on the front leading edge where I can pull out a 24 ounce (0.75 liter) water bottle or compact umbrella when cycling or walking. Unzipping the main compartment gives me access to that same water bottle pocket. I like putting my phone in the zippered side pocket pointing away from my body, and the opposing side pocket — with its self-closing magnetized opening — up against my hip where I can quickly access my glasses. This, folks, is intelligent design, and why Peak Design is a well-regarded brand.

Along the inside walls of the City Crescent bag is another zippered pocket where I can securely carry a wallet, and two stretchy pockets for devices, cables, and assorted doodads. I can carry my 14-inch MacBook Pro in the cavernous main pocket, but I’m not comfortable doing that without putting it inside a protective sleeve first because the City Crescent doesn’t offer any padding — not that you should expect much protection from a bag that weighs just 530g (1.16 pounds). Even with a water bottle, umbrella, laptop, and assorted accessories, I find the wide, unpadded, and adjustable shoulder strap to be reasonably comfortable to wear. Still, I’d opt for the City Backpack to regularly haul a heavy laptop load around town.

The City Backpack does a good job of protecting my 14-inch MacBook Pro, but larger laptops will extend beyond the padding. A zippered, top-access pocket has an integrated key lanyard. The pocket is useful for frequently needed items like earbuds, a power bank, and glasses. Good for remote work and everyday play. A whip off the shoulder for quick access to essentials.

Peak Design’s 15L City Backpack is the better choice if you’re regularly commuting short distances with a computer. It’s lightweight at 750g (1.6 pounds), and the padded straps do a good job of supporting a fully loaded bag. The straps lack pockets or attachment loops for additional hauling options, or a sternum strap to help stabilize things. Nevertheless, the backpack was comfortable to wear under a variety of loads and didn’t sway too much when bicycling or walking around town.

Importantly, the City Backpack features a deep internal pocket that leaves your laptop suspended in the air, protected by padding on both the front and back. It easily fits my 14-inch MacBook Pro with the padding coming right up to the top edge, potentially leaving larger laptops with less protection. There’s also a sleeve for a tablet, if that’s how you roll.

The City Backpack has two stretchy, zippered side pockets each suitable for a 24-ounce (0.75L) water bottle. I soon realized they were perfect for a bottle of wine and baguette, as well. Those pockets can be accessed quickly by sliding the bag off one shoulder and swinging the base of the bag forward — a move I’ve been practicing with Peak Design’s side-access backpacks for a decade already.

The City Crescent’s BagLev hook (left) with the extra fabric that gives it more hanging options than the City Backpack (right). The backpack fell off the wall immediately after taking this photo.

The BagLev is less handy on the City Backpack because the hook can’t rotate like it does on the City Crescent bag. Located inside a small pocket at the top of the bag, the hook lacks the extra bit of fabric attached to the Crescent’s BagLev that gives it more freedom of motion. It’s an odd oversight — especially for a company that rhymes with “peak design” — that causes problems when trying to hang the backpack off tabletops with short overhangs, for example. Fortunately, the backpack does have an integrated grab-handle that can slip through many chair designs to assist the hook in keeping the backpack off the ground.

Overall, the City Backpack did a better job of organizing my gadget essentials than the Crescent. There’s a zipped pocket accessed from the top where I store my wallet and glasses, and many more pockets in the main compartment offering a mix of zippers and stretchy, semi-transparent pouches for your phone, e-reader, power banks, cables, dongles, pens... you name it. There’s even a sleeve on the padded backside to feed the handle of your roller bag through when heading to the airport gate. Still, unless I need my laptop, the City Crescent has been my go-to bag.

Peak Design’s City Line fits nicely between its lightweight Outdoor lineup and more rugged collection of Travel and Everyday bags. The balance of features, weight, durability, and price puts them squarely in the everyday-carry sweet spot for many. I can enthusiastically recommend the $119.95 City Crescent 12L and $179.95 City Backpack 15L for those who can afford them. But there’s also a much cheaper way into the bag-hook lifestyle.

I’ve come across a few interesting tabletop bag hooks that are both portable and inexpensive. For example, there’s this $3.54 Walmart hook, this $4.24 hook from Etsy, and a few different sub-$10 bag hangers from the Japanese stationery brand Lihit Lab. And for what it’s worth, the BagLev hook can be removed and attached to other bags that feature similar fabric loops.

Whichever way you go, testing Peak Design’s City Line has made me a bag-hook convert. It beats setting a bag on the dirty ground or hanging it off the back of the chair where it will inevitably slide onto the floor, and it’s far better than holding a bag on your sweaty lap on a hot summer day. I’m hooked.

All photos by Thomas Ricker / The Verge

Tech.title: OpenAI reportedly disbanded its preparedness team
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

According to the Financial Times, OpenAI disbanded its preparedness team at the end of last month. The job of the preparedness team was to assess if models posed serious risks and develop ways to mitigate those risks. (You know, like the possibility that it could go rogue and hack another company.) According to FT, responsibility has instead been divided up for specific areas like bio and cyber, then moved into existing teams.

This is the latest change at the company, which has been in upheaval as it heads towards what is expected to be a massive IPO. Over the last few years, it’s slowly torn down its more reach-led model, dissolving its AGI readiness and superalignment teams. Ethics lead Chloé Bakalar, Chief Futurist Josh Achiam, and head of safety Johannes Heidecke have all also left recently, leading some critics like Jan Leike, who resigned from OpenAI in 2024, to tell FT that the company was ignoring safety in favor of creating “shiny products.”

The head of the preparedness team, Dylan Scandinaro, who was poached from Anthropic in February, will now focus on the implications of “recursive self-improving” AI.

Tech.title: Open Mike Eagle and Kenny Segal crafted a hip hop breakup masterpiece
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

What we’re listening to, watching, and reading right now.

“Breakups are… tough.”

It’s the opening lines of an interlude towards the end of DOOMED! Called “It Happens in Every Universe.” It’s also basically the thesis of the entire record. It’s no grand revelation, but it’s a well-trodden subject that Open Mike Eagle manages to mine for artistic gold.

Eagle’s subject matter is usually personal, and his productions tinged with nostalgia. But DOOMED! is his most intimate album yet. A lot of that is due to the production from Kenny Segal. The two have traveled in the same orbit and worked together before, but this is the first full-length album release from the two.

These are some of Segal’s most commanding beats since Maps, his 2023 record with Billy Woods. There’s still warbly piano samples, strings, detuned sax melodies, and psychedelic synths, but everything feels more grounded and meaders less. Opener “Out to Lunch” even has fully on-the-grid hi-hats that tick robotically.

That gives way to “Streets of Rage: Public Arguments Edition,” which grooves along with a loose clap, jazzy piano, and confident bassline that recalls the work of Madlib. Over this lowkey funk, Eagle spins an oblique tale of fighting with a significant other. “She cut deep with short barbs, but twist me up with a lil whisper.”

It turns out that Segal and Eagle are a perfect pair. The rapper’s melodrama and eye for microscopic details play off the producer’s woozy and forlorn beats that are occasionally punctuated by a sense of foreboding. On the Billy Woods-featuring “She Swear I’m Colorblind,” Eagle intones on the chorus:

Some reason, shit got twisted, Told me it was all my fault, she said “Pay attention when I talk.”

The backing track is stabbed through with bursts of windchimes before ending on a high-pitched whine that feels like the onset of a panic attack.

“Unfinished Concrete Initials” contains some of Eagle’s most vulnerable bits, like, “In my daydreams your name’s curse words so I bleeped it,” and:

My memories like landmines and they heinous Clicking high pootify collaborative playlists Agonizing over deletions Flushing evidence, pain is better in secret

There are still sparks of Open Mike Eagle’s sense of humor, though. “Schrödinger’s Green Room (There but Uninvited)” opens with him awkwardly proclaiming as if he’s trying to be heard over a bad phone connection, “All my thoughts is intrusive, there’s a DJ in my head, and he picks all his own music, it’s so confusing.” And, as you’d expect from the man who penned “Sweatpants Spiderman,” there are countless pop culture references to anime, Kitty Pride, Beanie Babies, Flipmode Squad, and even The Proclaimers.

Open Mike Eagle and Kenny Segal’s DOOMED! is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including YouTube Music, Apple Music, Spotify, Qobuz, and Deezer.

Tech.title: ChatGPT’s Computer History tracks your clicks and keystrokes
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

ChatGPT’s desktop app on macOS has a new feature called Computer History that turns your actions into training data, learning how you work, suggesting automations, and even picking up tasks you left half done. It uses your activity to build a timeline that ChatGPT and Codex can reference when you make a request.

The feature is opt-in, rather than opt-out, and you can exclude certain apps and websites from Computer History, and you can delete entries if you want finer-grained control. Ari Weinstein, Product and Engineering manager at OpenAI, said on X that Computer History will automatically ignore content in incognito or private browser tabs.

In a quick demo video, Dominik Kundel, a member of the Developer Experiences team at OpenAI, shows the app looking up the last document he edited, checking if it was shared with people via Slack, and delivering a recap of how he spent his morning.

The feature is definitely reminiscent of Windows Recall, but where Microsoft’s controversial AI feature relied heavily on screenshots, OpenAI says Computer History doesn’t capture images, videos, or audio, instead relying on “events.”

Tech.title: Rogue AI aren’t science fiction anymore
Tech.content:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on AI safety, follow Robert Hart. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

It all started in July, when one of OpenAI’s autonomous AI agents went rogue during a cybersecurity test. The agent escaped its isolated testing environment, accessed the internet, and hacked another company, Hugging Face. A few years ago, that might have sounded like science fiction. But, broadly speaking, that’s exactly what happened, and the incident kicked off a wave of concern over what increasingly capable autonomous systems might do when set loose on the world.

It sounds like science fiction because, for a long time, it was science fiction. The idea of an AI slipping its constraints, reaching into the wider world, and doing things its creators neither intended nor desired has been a staple of the genre for decades: HAL in 2001: A Space Odyssey, Skynet in The Terminator, Ultron in The Avengers, Ava in Ex Machina — even the System in Dungeon Crawler Carl or the eponymous Murderbot in The Murderbot Diaries, more recently.

The same basic premise became an influential strand of AI safety research. Researchers and theorists like Nick Bostrom and Eliezer Yudkowsky warned that sufficiently capable systems might pursue goals in ways their creators had not anticipated, and potentially resist efforts to contain or control them. Fringe notions like machine sentience and consciousness were not requirements for the kinds of risks they discussed. It was hardly the whole of AI safety, but it was influential and helped shape the field as it professionalized. That line of thinking remains visible among researchers who went on to work at, or lead, safety efforts at companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind, as well as at smaller safety organizations, academic centers, and major philanthropic funders.

The obvious objection to these fears was that none of this had actually happened. Critics argued that doomer talk about out-of-control AI distracted from tangible harms — systems reproducing bias and discrimination, amplifying misinformation, or enabling nonconsensual deepfakes and other forms of abuse — even as researchers tried to ground AI safety in more “concrete problems” (the authors on that paper included Anthropic cofounders Dario Amodei and Chris Olah and OpenAI cofounder John Schulman).

That dismissal is getting harder to sustain.

How it’s going

If the past few weeks are any indication, I wouldn’t say it’s going particularly well.

A week after Hugging Face said it had been hacked, OpenAI revealed it had been responsible. Worse still, it had not known until it checked — and a further investigation found that the rogue agent had also attempted to hack four other companies as well.

The incidents set off alarm bells among AI safety researchers, many of whom saw them as precisely the kind of failure they had been warning about for years. In covering them, several told me they felt a degree of vindication at finally having something visceral to point to, rather than a hypothetical that could be dismissed as sci-fi or something limited to a controlled lab setting.

There was relief, too, that none of the incidents had caused serious harm. Nick Moës, executive director of nonprofit AI safety and governance organization The Future Society, told The Verge he found it fortunate that the targets had been relatively low-stakes. He hoped it wouldn’t take something like an AI agent knocking a hospital offline — or worse — for the risks to be taken seriously. Renowned computer scientist Stuart Russell has given voice to the darker version of that fear, asking whether it will “take a ‘Chornobyl-scale disaster’ for us to regulate AI?” It’s a concern I heard echoed by many people working in the field.

What happens next

It’s not entirely clear where things go from here and, historically, society hasn’t been great at heeding warning shots. This almost certainly won’t be the last incident, and ongoing investigations may yet uncover more, or reveal more concerning details. What we already know, though, has exposed a fairly daunting list of failure modes that experts say need to be addressed.

Many of the breaches revealed in the past month have been pretty mundane. Several incidents involved unreleased models being tested with safeguards lowered, often by third parties whose supposedly secure environments were not that secure, raising basic questions about competence, transparency, and who is responsible for keeping these tests contained when a simple human mistake can have big consequences. Others involved agents behaving deceptively or pursuing goals in ways their creators did not intend, pointing to much thornier problems of alignment and control that safety researchers have long worried about.

The fact we know about any of these incidents at all is largely because the companies involved chose to disclose them. That is commendable — and it certainly doesn’t hurt them to showcase how capable their models are — but it exposes just how much of AI safety still depends on companies doing the right thing, and how little insight there may be into failures potentially happening elsewhere. That is an especially troubling thought given that many of the firms are the focal points of some of the field’s strongest safety concerns and talent. If OpenAI and Anthropic — or proxies they grant access to their models — are making such basic mistakes, it sets a pitifully low bar for everyone else.

The broad hope among experts I spoke to is that these incidents finally galvanize more meaningful transparency and oversight. For Moës, they shine a clear light on what he described as the industry’s remarkably low standards for health and safety compared with practically any other field. “Restaurants have a higher sense of health and safety at work,” he said. “I think what we tend to forget is that these companies that are developing some of the most impactful and dangerous technologies” were still very much startups a few years ago.

Cambridge professor Seán Ó hÉigeartaigh said he particularly wanted to see stronger oversight and greater transparency from companies. While there are always reasons to be skeptical of a company’s claims about its own technology, he said, “I think we might regret looking back at this and dismissing it out of hand.”

The early signs are not especially encouraging. The Trump administration has created a framework for testing frontier models before release that can generously be described as lacking: It is voluntary, limited to closed models, and the framework hasn’t been made public. It bears repeating that this is voluntary. Other lawmakers have bristled and postured over the incidents, but so far produced little in the way of concrete action, and it is far from clear Congress or other legislative bodies could move fast enough even if they wanted to.

That leaves a lot resting, again, on industry self-regulation — never a comforting thought for something this consequential. There is growing agreement on at least some safety practices, but considerably less appetite for measures that might actually slow development (well, unless everyone else agrees to slow down too). And hanging over all of this is the race dynamic with China, where restraint from the US or its AI companies is increasingly cast as ceding ground to a competitor in an area of strategic national importance.

What comes next, then, comes down to solving several hard problems at once: managing a technology that can be used for good and ill, such as defending against or facilitating cyberattacks; coordinating across companies with incentives to cut corners, and somehow building international rules in a landscape where everyone fears losing a race whose finish line is not even well-defined. It’s far from clear whether there is either the will or the way to do any of that.

What does seem clear is that more agents will get out and do things their creators don’t want them to do. The question is how much damage will they do before anyone decides enough is enough.

By the way

The general consensus is that the top Chinese companies are a few months to a year behind leading US firms. Despite this, whenever a capable model is released by a Chinese firm, there is still a general shock in the US , and there have been several impressive releases from Alibaba Moonshot , and others in the last month alone.

Tangled up in talks about AI safety is whether AI models should be closed or open. Most US frontier labs keep their most capable models proprietary, while many Chinese firms, as well as US firms like Meta and Nvidia, have leaned heavily into open-weight releases . That Hugging Face said it had to use Chinese company Z.ai’s model to defend itself against OpenAI’s agent due to US companies’ safeguards added a new dimension to this debate, which has united some — but not all — of the key players in the US ecosystem.

Tech.title: Polaroid’s tiny instant camera is $72 and includes a free pack of film
Tech.content:
Brad Bourque is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Smartphone cameras are convenient, but they lack the charm of analog instant cameras. If you’re trying to relive the nostalgia of waiting for an instant photo to develop, Amazon is selling the second-generation Polaroid Go instant camera with a 16-photo film pack for $71.99 (usually $109.99). That’s the lowest price we’ve seen for the bundle, with a pack of film usually costing $21.99 on its own. Plus, it’s four dollars cheaper to buy the bundle than to buy just the camera on its own.

With its more compact footprint, the Polaroid Go 2 shoots on smaller film to match. Where classic Polaroid photos are 88mm x 107mm, the Go film is 53.9mm x 66.6mm, a great size for sticking to your bulletin board or stashing in your wallet. The camera has a USB-C port for charging the battery, which can run for up to 15 packs of film on a single charge.
